$$R^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}},\qquad \bar R^2=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1},\qquad F=\frac{(\mathrm{TSS}-\mathrm{RSS})/p}{\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p-1)}\sim F_{p,\,n-p-1}$$

with \(p=2\) inputs. \(R^2\) never goes down when you add an input, even a useless one; the adjusted version charges for each extra input. The F test asks whether all slopes could be zero at once. Note that with strongly correlated inputs the F test can be decisive while neither slope is individually significant.

Check yourself

With correlation 0.95 the fitted plane still predicts well. So why does multicollinearity matter?

It matters when you interpret the slopes or predict away from the data. The individual slopes are unreliable and can even flip sign between samples, and predictions for an x₁ and x₂ that do not follow the usual pattern can be badly wrong.

entries.title: Bending the line
entries.html:
Bending the Line

Raise the degree and the curve bends to follow the points. A little bending finds the pattern. A lot of bending memorises the noise: training error keeps falling while test error turns back up.

A straight line can only tilt. Give the model powers of \(x\) and it can bend, once for each extra degree. With enough bends it can pass through every training point exactly, and that is the trap: the points contain noise, and a curve that chases the noise is wrong everywhere between the points. The fit that looks best on the data it has seen is no longer the fit that predicts best.

Animation
The model
The data
Degree, and number of coefficients
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Test error (MSE)
–
Degree with the lowest test error
–

Try this. Watch the two error curves as the degree climbs. Where do they part ways? Then raise the number of points to 150: does degree 14 still overfit? Try the straight line as the truth with degree 10.

Still a linear model

$$\hat y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\dots+\beta_dx^d=\boldsymbol\beta^{\top}\boldsymbol\phi(x),\qquad \boldsymbol\phi(x)=(1,x,x^2,\dots,x^d)$$

The curve is not linear in \(x\), but it is linear in the coefficients. So nothing new is needed to fit it: build a matrix \(\Phi\) whose columns are the powers of \(x\) and solve the same normal equations as before, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\Phi^{\top}\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^{\top}\mathbf y\). Swapping raw inputs for features \(\boldsymbol\phi(x)\) is the idea behind kernels and, later, behind the hidden layers of a neural network.

Bias and variance

Average over many possible training sets, and the expected test error at a point splits into three parts:

$$\mathbb E\big[(y-\hat f(x))^2\big]=\underbrace{\big(\mathbb E[\hat f(x)]-f(x)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2}+\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\big(\hat f(x)\big)}_{\text{variance}}+\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{noise}}$$

Low degree: the model cannot take the right shape, so bias is high (underfitting). High degree: the model changes wildly from sample to sample, so variance is high (overfitting). Press “New random sample” at degree 2 and at degree 12 to see the two cases. Test error is lowest where the sum of the two is smallest.

Why training error cannot be trusted

Every polynomial of degree \(d\) is also a polynomial of degree \(d+1\) with the last coefficient zero. So the best degree-\((d+1)\) fit is never worse on the training data: training error can only go down. With \(d=n-1\) it reaches zero. Only held-out data can tell you when to stop, which is what validation sets and cross-validation are for.

The fit here uses Legendre polynomials in place of raw powers. They span the same curves but keep the arithmetic stable at high degree.

Check yourself

More data or a lower degree: which fixes overfitting?

Both. A lower degree removes the flexibility that chases noise. More data pins the flexible curve down so it has less freedom to wiggle. With 150 points a degree-14 curve behaves far better than with 20.

entries.title: Many small curves, joined smoothly
entries.html:
Many Small Curves, Joined Smoothly

One high-degree polynomial wiggles everywhere. A spline uses a low-degree piece between each pair of knots and joins the pieces so the seams do not show. Change the kind of join and watch what happens at the knots and beyond the ends of the data.

A draughtsman's spline is a thin flexible strip of wood, pinned at a few points and left to settle. It bends smoothly, as little as it can, and beyond the last pin it runs straight. A mathematical spline copies this: cut the \(x\)-axis at a few knots, use a simple polynomial on each stretch, and tie the pieces together so the joins are smooth. Flexibility is local: moving one point bends the curve nearby and leaves the far end alone, which is exactly what a single high-degree polynomial cannot do.

Animation
The model
The data
Coefficients fitted
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Test error (MSE)
–
Curvature at the two ends
–
Knots with the lowest test error
–

Try this. Step through the five kinds with 4 knots and watch the right-hand picture: where is the curvature broken, where is it continuous, and for which kind is it exactly zero at both ends? Then look at the shaded zones: which fit would you trust outside the data?

Piecewise polynomials and how smoothly they join

With knots \(\xi_1<\dots<\xi_K\), fit a polynomial of degree \(M\) on each interval and require the pieces to agree at each knot in value and in their first \(M-1\) derivatives. Steps (\(M=0\)) do not even agree in value. A linear spline (\(M=1\)) is continuous but has corners. A cubic spline (\(M=3\)) matches value, slope and curvature at every knot; only the third derivative jumps, and the eye cannot see that.

The cubic spline as a linear model

$$f(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_k\,(x-\xi_k)_+^3,\qquad (u)_+=\max(u,0)$$

Each term \((x-\xi_k)_+^3\) is zero to the left of its knot and switches on smoothly to the right, with value, slope and curvature all zero at the knot itself. So adding it changes the cubic from that knot onward without breaking smoothness. The model has \(K+4\) coefficients and is fitted by ordinary least squares, exactly like polynomial regression with different columns.

The natural cubic spline

A cubic spline is poorly controlled near the ends, where there are few points, and outside the data it shoots off like a cubic. The natural spline adds two conditions at each boundary knot \(a\) and \(b\):

$$f''(a)=0,\qquad f''(b)=0,\qquad\text{and }f\text{ is linear for }xb.$$

Zero curvature at the ends means the curve leaves the data as a straight line. These four constraints remove four coefficients, leaving \(K+2\) when the boundary knots are counted, so it is less flexible exactly where the data is thinnest. Its basis can be written

$$N_1=1,\quad N_2=x,\quad N_{k+2}(x)=d_k(x)-d_{K-1}(x),\qquad d_k(x)=\frac{(x-\xi_k)_+^3-(x-\xi_K)_+^3}{\xi_K-\xi_k}.$$

The smoothing spline

Choosing knots is awkward. The smoothing spline avoids it: use many knots and penalise curvature instead.

$$\min_f\ \sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-f(x_i)\big)^2+\lambda\int f''(x)^2\,dx$$

The first term wants to pass through the points; the second charges for bending. At \(\lambda=0\) the curve interpolates the data, and as \(\lambda\to\infty\) bending becomes unaffordable and the answer is the least-squares straight line. The remarkable fact is that the exact minimiser over all smooth functions is a natural cubic spline with a knot at every data point. The picture uses a close relative, a penalised spline: 14 fixed knots with a ridge penalty on the coefficients \(\theta_k\), since each \(\theta_k\) is the jump in the third derivative at its knot.

Counting flexibility

More knots, like a higher degree, lower the bias and raise the variance. The number of fitted coefficients (the degrees of freedom) is the dial, and test error picks its setting.

Check yourself

Why is a natural cubic spline usually preferred to a plain cubic spline with the same knots?

Near and beyond the ends of the data a cubic spline has freedom the data cannot pin down, so it swings wildly there. The natural spline gives up that freedom by forcing zero curvature at the ends. It has four fewer coefficients, lower variance at the boundaries, and it extrapolates as a straight line.

entries.title: One smooth curve per input
entries.html:
One Smooth Curve Per Input

With several inputs, give each its own smooth curve and add them up. The curves are found by taking turns: hold one fixed, smooth what is left over against the other, and repeat. Watch the two curves settle.

Splines and local regression bend a curve in one input. With many inputs, fitting a fully flexible surface needs an enormous amount of data, because the points thin out fast as dimensions are added. An additive model takes a middle road: each input gets its own free-form curve, but the curves only ever add. You lose interactions between inputs, and in exchange you get a model that needs far less data and can be read one picture at a time.

Animation

The model
The data
Turns taken
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Test error (MSE)
–
Test error of a flat plane, for comparison
–
Noise level σ² (best possible)
–

Try this. Press “Start over” and take one turn at a time. After the first turn f₁ is rough because f₂ is still flat. How many turns until nothing changes? Then choose the product x₁ × x₂ and see what an additive model cannot do.

The model

$$y=\alpha+f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)+\dots+f_p(x_p)+\varepsilon$$

Linear regression is the special case \(f_j(x_j)=\beta_jx_j\). Each \(f_j\) here is a natural cubic spline, though any smoother from the previous lessons would do. Since a constant can be moved between the curves freely, each \(f_j\) is centred to average zero and the level is carried by \(\alpha=\bar y\).

Backfitting

If \(f_2\) were known, finding \(f_1\) would be a one-dimensional smoothing problem: subtract what \(f_2\) explains and smooth the remainder against \(x_1\). Neither is known, so take turns:

$$r_{i}^{(1)}=y_i-\alpha-f_2(x_{i2}),\qquad f_1\leftarrow\operatorname{smooth}\big(r^{(1)}\ \text{against}\ x_1\big)$$$$r_{i}^{(2)}=y_i-\alpha-f_1(x_{i1}),\qquad f_2\leftarrow\operatorname{smooth}\big(r^{(2)}\ \text{against}\ x_2\big)$$

and repeat until the curves stop moving. The dots in each picture are these partial residuals: the part of \(y\) not yet explained by the other input. This is coordinate descent, the same idea used for the lasso, with whole functions in place of single coefficients.

Why it takes several turns

If the inputs are unrelated, one turn each is nearly enough. When they are correlated, part of the effect of \(x_2\) leaks into \(f_1\) on the first turn and has to be handed back on later turns. Raise the correlation and count the turns.

What it cannot do

A product such as \(y=x_1x_2\) has no additive part at all: averaged over \(x_2\), the effect of \(x_1\) is zero. The curves come out flat and the error stays high. Interactions must be added by hand as extra terms \(f_{12}(x_1,x_2)\), or left to models that find them on their own, such as trees and neural networks.

Check yourself

An additive model fits well and f₁ is a clear U shape. What can you say that you could not say from a neural network with the same accuracy?

You can state the effect of x₁ directly: holding the other inputs fixed, the prediction falls and then rises as x₁ increases, by the amounts shown on the curve. That reading is exact for an additive model. A neural network has no such single curve, because the effect of x₁ may differ for every value of the other inputs.

entries.title: Keeping the coefficients small
entries.html:
Keeping the Coefficients Small

Start with a degree-10 polynomial that overfits. Now charge a price for large coefficients. As the price λ rises the curve calms down: ridge shrinks every coefficient, lasso switches some off entirely.

An overfitted curve gets its wild swings from huge coefficients of opposite sign that almost cancel. So instead of forbidding high degrees, make large coefficients expensive. The model can still use them, but only where the data pays for it. One dial, \(\lambda\), sets the price: at zero you get the wild least-squares fit, at a very high price you get a flat line.

Animation
The penalty
The data
Price λ
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Test error (MSE)
–
Coefficients still in use, of 10
–
L1 norm ‖w‖₁ = Σ|wⱼ|
–
L2 norm ‖w‖₂ = √Σwⱼ²
–
λ with the lowest test error
–

Try this. Sweep λ under Ridge and watch the bars: they all shrink, but does any reach exactly zero? Switch to Lasso and sweep again. In the last picture, drag the cross and find where the lasso answer lands on an axis.

The penalised loss

$$\min_{\mathbf w}\ \frac{1}{2n}\lVert\mathbf y-X\mathbf w\rVert^2+\lambda\Big(\alpha\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1+\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_2^2\Big)$$

\(\alpha=0\) is ridge (squared penalty), \(\alpha=1\) is lasso (absolute-value penalty), anything between is elastic net. The features are standardised first so that the price is the same for every coefficient, and the intercept is not penalised.

What happens to a single coefficient

When the features are uncorrelated and standardised, each coefficient can be handled on its own, and both penalties have a one-line effect on the least-squares value \(\hat w\) (the first picture):

$$w_{\text{ridge}}=\frac{\hat w}{1+\lambda},\qquad w_{\text{lasso}}=\operatorname{sign}(\hat w)\,\max\big(|\hat w|-\lambda,\ 0\big).$$

Ridge multiplies every coefficient by the same factor below one: large ones lose the most, and none ever arrives at zero. Lasso subtracts the same amount \(\lambda\) from every coefficient's size: large ones barely notice, and any coefficient smaller than \(\lambda\) is wiped out. The second picture shows the consequence on a problem with 12 measurements of which 9 are pure noise. Least squares gives every one of them a non-zero weight. Ridge makes all the weights smaller. Lasso removes most of the noise features altogether and reports a shorter model.

The two norms

$$\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1=\sum_j|w_j|,\qquad \lVert\mathbf w\rVert_2=\sqrt{\sum_jw_j^2}$$

Both measure the size of the coefficient vector. Points at the same \(L_2\) norm form a circle; points at the same \(L_1\) norm form a diamond with corners on the axes. Paying a price \(\lambda\) per unit of norm is the same as fitting as well as you can while staying inside a ball of some fixed size, where a larger \(\lambda\) means a smaller ball:

$$\min_{\mathbf w}\ \lVert\mathbf y-X\mathbf w\rVert^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\lVert\mathbf w\rVert\le s.$$

The last picture shows this for two coefficients. The thin ellipses are the loss, lowest at the cross. The answer is where the smallest ellipse first touches the shaded ball. A circle has no corners, so the touching point is almost never on an axis: both coefficients shrink and neither is zero. A diamond sticks out furthest at its corners, so the ellipse very often touches a corner first, and at a corner one coefficient is exactly zero. Drag the cross around to see how large the set of positions is for which the diamond is hit at a corner.

Ridge shrinks

$$\hat{\mathbf w}_{\text{ridge}}=(X^{\top}X+n\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\top}\mathbf y$$

Adding \(\lambda I\) makes the matrix safely invertible and pulls every coefficient toward zero in proportion to its size. Large ones are pulled hard, small ones barely, so none arrives at exactly zero. It is the MAP estimate under a Gaussian prior on the weights, the same pull toward a prior you saw in the Gaussian module.

Lasso selects

For one coefficient with the others held fixed, the lasso solution is a soft threshold:

$$w_j\leftarrow\frac{S(\rho_j,\ \lambda\alpha)}{1+\lambda(1-\alpha)},\qquad S(\rho,\tau)=\operatorname{sign}(\rho)\,\max\big(|\rho|-\tau,\ 0\big),\qquad \rho_j=\tfrac1n\mathbf x_j^{\top}\big(\mathbf y-X_{-j}\mathbf w_{-j}\big)$$

The absolute-value penalty pulls with the same force however small the coefficient is, so once a feature's correlation with the residual \(|\rho_j|\) drops below \(\lambda\alpha\) the coefficient is set to exactly zero. Lasso does feature selection as a side effect. It is the MAP estimate under a Laplace prior. Cycling this update over the coefficients is coordinate descent, which is how the picture is computed.

Choosing λ

Training error always rises with \(\lambda\). Test error falls first, as variance is removed, then rises as the model becomes too stiff. The best \(\lambda\) sits at the bottom of that curve and is found on held-out data.

Check yourself

Two features are almost identical copies of each other. What do ridge and lasso each do with them?

Ridge splits the weight evenly between the two. Lasso tends to keep one and set the other to zero, and which one it keeps can change between samples. Elastic net was designed for this case: it selects like lasso but keeps correlated features together.

entries.title: Let the neighbours vote
entries.html:
Let the Neighbours Vote

No formula for the whole curve. To predict at one spot, look only at the points near it and weight them by closeness. Slide the spot along and the predictions trace out a curve. The bandwidth decides who counts as a neighbour.

Every method so far chose a shape in advance, a line or a polynomial, and then fitted it. Here the data chooses the shape. To predict at \(x_0\), ask the training points nearby what their \(y\) values were and average them, listening more to the closest ones. There are no coefficients to learn: the training data itself is the model.

Animation
The method
The data
Prediction at x₀
–
Effective number of neighbours
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Leave-one-out error (MSE)
–
Bandwidth with the lowest leave-one-out error
–

Try this. Shrink the bandwidth to 0.15: the curve chases every point. Stretch it to 3: the curve goes nearly flat. Then switch from a weighted average to a weighted line and watch what changes at the two ends of the data.

Kernel regression (Nadaraya–Watson)

$$\hat f(x_0)=\frac{\sum_{i}K\!\big(\tfrac{x_i-x_0}{h}\big)\,y_i}{\sum_{i}K\!\big(\tfrac{x_i-x_0}{h}\big)}$$

\(K\) is a bump centred at zero, drawn along the bottom of the picture; each point's weight is the height of the bump above it. Common choices are the Gaussian \(K(u)=e^{-u^2/2}\), the Epanechnikov dome \(K(u)=\max(1-u^2,0)\) and the box \(K(u)=\mathbb 1[|u|\le1]\). The kernel matters little. The bandwidth \(h\) matters a great deal.

Bandwidth is the bias–variance dial

A small \(h\) uses few neighbours: the estimate follows the data closely (low bias) but is noisy (high variance). A large \(h\) averages over many points: steady, but it flattens real bumps (high bias). In the limit \(h\to\infty\) every prediction is the overall mean. Roughly, variance scales like \(1/(nh)\) and squared bias like \(h^4\), so the best \(h\) shrinks slowly as data grows.

Local linear regression (LOESS)

$$\big(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\big)=\arg\min_{\beta_0,\beta_1}\sum_iK\!\big(\tfrac{x_i-x_0}{h}\big)\big(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1(x_i-x_0)\big)^2,\qquad \hat f(x_0)=\hat\beta_0$$

Fit a small weighted line near \(x_0\) and read off its height there. A weighted average is biased wherever the neighbours are lopsided, which always happens at the ends of the data, where all neighbours lie on one side. A local line corrects for the slope and removes that bias.

Choosing h without a test set

$$\mathrm{CV}(h)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\hat f_{-i}(x_i)\big)^2$$

Predict each point from all the other points and average the squared misses. Training error is useless for this choice, because it falls to zero as \(h\to0\) when each point simply predicts itself. Leave-one-out error has a real minimum, shown on the right.

Where this leads

The same weights \(K\) reappear as the kernel in kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes and support vector machines, and the weighted average is the ancestor of attention in transformers, where the weights are learned.

Check yourself

Why does training error go to zero as the bandwidth shrinks?

With a tiny bandwidth the only point with any weight near xᵢ is the point itself, so the prediction there is exactly yᵢ. That is memorising, and it says nothing about how the method does on new points. Leave-one-out error removes each point before predicting it, so it cannot cheat this way.

entries.title: Gaussian process regression: a belief about whole curves
entries.html:
Gaussian Process Regression: A Belief About Whole Curves

Most regression methods give you one curve. A Gaussian process gives you every curve that is consistent with the data, weighted by how plausible it is, and so it can tell you where it is sure and where it is guessing. Click to add measurements and watch the possible curves pinch together around each one and fan out in the gaps.

Imagine every smooth curve you could possibly draw across the picture, all at once, like a thick bundle of threads. That bundle is your belief before you have seen anything. Now someone tells you the curve passes close to a particular dot. Throw away every thread that misses the dot. What is left is still a bundle, but pinched at that place. Near the dot the remaining threads agree, so you are confident. Far from any dot they still spread out, so you are not. A Gaussian process does this with mathematics instead of scissors, and the average of the surviving threads is its prediction.

How it works, step by step

  1. Choose a kernel. It says how similar the curve’s height should be at two places, given their distance.
  2. Before any data, every curve the kernel allows is possible: the band is wide and flat.
  3. Add measurements. Curves that miss them become implausible and are dropped.
  4. The best guess at any place is a weighted average of the measurements, with weights set by the kernel.
  5. The band narrows near measurements and widens away from them.
  6. Fit the settings: adjust length scale, height and noise to make the data as probable as possible. The first step tries a coarse grid of settings and jumps to the best; later steps climb from there.

What just happened

Animation

The kernel
Data

Measurements
–
Score: log marginal likelihood
–
… of which data fit
–
… of which complexity penalty
–
Length scale / height / noise
–

Try this. Choose No Data Yet and watch the three curves wander freely. Click once in the picture. What happens to the band at that spot, and a little to each side? Add four or five more. Now drag the length scale down to 0.2 and up to 3. Which setting ignores the data and which one chases every dot? Press Fit the settings and watch the score climb. Choose A Gap in the Middle. How does the band behave inside the gap? Switch the kernel to Repeating and see the belief fill the gap with a pattern. Finally set your own x in the prediction box and read off the answer with its error bar.

The model

A Gaussian process is a distribution over functions such that the heights at any finite set of places are jointly Gaussian. It is fixed by a mean function, taken as zero here, and a kernel \(k(x,x')\) giving the covariance of the heights at \(x\) and \(x'\):

$$f\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,k),\qquad y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i,\quad\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_n^2).$$

Kernels on this page

$$k_{\text{smooth}}=\sigma_f^2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{r^2}{2\ell^2}\Big),\qquad k_{\text{rough}}=\sigma_f^2\Big(1+\frac{\sqrt3\,r}{\ell}\Big)\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\sqrt3\,r}{\ell}\Big),$$$$k_{\text{repeating}}=\sigma_f^2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{2\sin^2(\pi r/p)}{\ell^2}\Big),\qquad k_{\text{straight}}=\sigma_f^2\,(1+x\,x'),$$

with \(r=|x-x'|\) and period \(p=3\). The smooth one is the squared-exponential (RBF) kernel, the rough one is Matérn 3/2. The straight kernel turns the Gaussian process into Bayesian linear regression. The length scale \(\ell\) says how far you must move before the curve can change much.

The prediction

Let \(\mathbf K\) be the kernel between all pairs of measured places, \(\mathbf k_*\) the kernel between a new place \(x_*\) and the measured ones. Conditioning a joint Gaussian gives

$$\mu_*=\mathbf k_*^{\top}(\mathbf K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf I)^{-1}\mathbf y,\qquad\sigma_*^2=k(x_*,x_*)-\mathbf k_*^{\top}(\mathbf K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf I)^{-1}\mathbf k_*.$$

The mean is a weighted sum of the measurements. The variance starts at the prior value and has something subtracted for what the data told you. It does not depend on the measured heights at all, only on where you measured.

Choosing the settings

The probability of the data with the function integrated out is available in closed form:

$$\log p(\mathbf y)=\underbrace{-\tfrac12\mathbf y^{\top}(\mathbf K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf I)^{-1}\mathbf y}_{\text{data fit}}\ \underbrace{-\tfrac12\log\lvert\mathbf K+\sigma_n^2\mathbf I\rvert}_{\text{complexity penalty}}-\frac n2\log2\pi.$$

A tiny length scale fits anything and pays a heavy complexity penalty. A huge one is cheap and fits badly. Maximizing the sum balances the two without a validation set. The score can have several peaks: one explanation with a short length scale and little noise, another with a long length scale and more noise. So the Fit button first compares 36 settings on a coarse grid and moves to the best of them if it clearly beats the current one, then climbs by gradient ascent on \(\log\ell,\log\sigma_f,\log\sigma_n\), and stops when it gains less than 0.0005 in a step.

Cost

Everything needs the inverse of an \(n\times n\) matrix, which costs \(O(n^3)\). That is the practical limit of exact Gaussian processes: superb with a few thousand points, and in need of approximations beyond that.

Check yourself

In A Gap in the Middle the band is wide inside the gap. Would taking ten more measurements at the far left, where there are already several, narrow it?

Hardly at all. The predictive variance at a place depends only on how strongly the kernel ties that place to the measured ones. With a length scale of about 1, points at the far left are almost uncorrelated with the middle, so they subtract almost nothing from the variance there. To narrow the band in the gap you have to measure in the gap, or believe in a longer length scale or a repeating pattern that links the gap to the data you have.

entries.title: Generalized linear models: straight lines for data that cannot be straight
entries.html:
Generalized Linear Models: Straight Lines for Data That Cannot Be Straight

A straight line can predict minus three customers or a 130% chance of rain. Counts cannot go below zero and probabilities must stay between 0 and 1. A generalized linear model keeps the straight line and bends it through a link function so that predictions land where the data can actually be. Linear, logistic and Poisson regression turn out to be one method with three settings.

You want to predict how many ice creams a stall sells from the temperature. A straight line works in the middle and then predicts a negative number on a cold day. The fix is to stop predicting the count itself and predict its logarithm with a straight line instead. A logarithm can be any number, positive or negative, so the line is free to go wherever it likes, and when you undo the logarithm the prediction is always positive. For a yes-or-no outcome you do the same with the log-odds. The straight line lives on a scale where it cannot do harm, and a fixed bend carries it back to the scale of the data.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with a flat model: every prediction equals the average of the data.
  2. Move each data point to the link scale, where the model is a straight line. This gives a working value for each point.
  3. Give each point a weight: how much information it carries at the current fit.
  4. Fit a weighted straight line through the working values.
  5. Bend that line back through the link to get the new curve.
  6. Repeat until the fit stops changing. It usually takes five or six rounds.

What just happened

Animation

Data

Refits so far
–
Intercept and slope on the link scale
–
Deviance: misfit of the model
–
Deviance of a flat model
–
What one more unit of x does
–
Impossible predictions from the dashed line
–

Try this. On Ice Creams Sold, press One refit and follow the panel under the charts: the curve moves from flat to fitted in a handful of jumps. Look at the dashed straight line at the cold end. What does it predict there? Switch to Passed the Exam. The same procedure now draws an S-curve. Why is the right-hand chart still a straight line? Switch to Plant Height: how many refits does it need, and why? Then type your own x and read the prediction.

Three ingredients

A generalized linear model (Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972) has a linear predictor, a link function \(g\) connecting it to the mean, and a distribution for the scatter around the mean:

$$\eta_i=a+b\,x_i,\qquad g(\mu_i)=\eta_i,\qquad y_i\sim\text{a distribution with mean }\mu_i.$$
DataDistributionLink \(g(\mu)\)Mean \(\mu\)Variance
AmountsGaussian\(\mu\)\(\eta\)\(\sigma^2\)
Yes or noBernoulli\(\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}\)\(\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}\)\(\mu(1-\mu)\)
CountsPoisson\(\log\mu\)\(e^{\eta}\)\(\mu\)

The variance column matters as much as the link. Counts scatter more when the mean is large, and a yes-or-no outcome is most uncertain at a probability of one half. The model knows this and weights each point accordingly.

Fitting: iteratively reweighted least squares

The parameters maximize the likelihood. There is no formula for the answer, but Newton's method takes a pleasant form. At the current fit, compute for every point a working value and a weight,

$$z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{d\mu_i/d\eta_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(y_i)},$$

and then solve an ordinary weighted least-squares problem for the line through the \(z_i\):

$$(a,b)\leftarrow\arg\min_{a,b}\sum_i w_i\,(z_i-a-b\,x_i)^2.$$

For the three links above the weights simplify to \(1\), \(\mu_i(1-\mu_i)\) and \(\mu_i\). For the Gaussian case the working values are the data and the weights are all equal, so one refit gives the exact answer: that is ordinary least squares.

Deviance

The misfit is measured by the deviance, twice the gap in log-likelihood between the model and a perfect fit:

$$D_{\text{Poisson}}=2\sum_i\Big[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\mu_i}-(y_i-\mu_i)\Big],\qquad D_{\text{Bernoulli}}=-2\sum_i\big[y_i\log\mu_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\mu_i)\big].$$

For Gaussian data it is the familiar sum of squared residuals. The run stops when a refit lowers the deviance by less than \(10^{-8}\).

Reading the slope

On the link scale the slope has a simple meaning. With a log link, one more unit of \(x\) multiplies the expected count by \(e^{b}\). With a logit link it multiplies the odds by \(e^{b}\). With the identity link it adds \(b\).

Check yourself

On Ice Creams Sold, why does the fit give more weight to hot days than to cold days, when a least-squares line would treat them all the same?

For a Poisson count the variance equals the mean, and with a log link the weight of a point works out to be its fitted mean. On the link scale a hot day with 40 sales has a working value known to within about 1 part in √40, while a cold day with 2 sales could just as easily have been 0 or 5, which is a huge difference in logarithms. The hot days pin down the line more firmly on the log scale, so they are trusted more. Least squares on the raw counts makes the opposite mistake in another way: it assumes the scatter is the same everywhere.

entries.title: Robust regression: do not let one bad point steer the line
entries.html:
Robust Regression: Do Not Let One Bad Point Steer the Line

Least squares punishes a miss by its square, so a single wild measurement, ten times further off than the rest, pulls a hundred times harder. One typing error can tilt the whole line. Robust regression changes the punishment so that points far from the crowd count for less, or for nothing. Drag a point away from the others and watch which line follows it.

Ask twenty people to estimate the length of a table, and suppose one of them answers in inches while the rest answer in centimetres. The average of the twenty answers is ruined. The median is fine. Least squares is the average: it listens to everyone in proportion to how loudly they disagree. Robust regression behaves more like the median. It forms a first opinion, notices who is far from it, and turns their volume down before asking again.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start from a first line and measure every point’s miss (its residual).
  2. Estimate the typical size of a miss from the middle of the data, ignoring the extremes.
  3. Give each point a weight: 1 if its miss is ordinary, less if it is large.
  4. Refit the line by weighted least squares.
  5. The misses have changed, so recompute the weights and refit.
  6. Stop when the line no longer moves.

What just happened

Animation

The penalty
Data

Refits so far
–
True line: intercept, slope
–
Least squares
–
Robust
–
Typical miss (robust scale)
–
Points with weight below one half
–

Try this. On One Wild Point, press One refit a few times and watch the wild dot shrink as its weight falls. Then drag it further away, and then towards the far right end. Which line follows it? Choose A Third of the Data Is Wrong with Huber: does the robust line get anywhere near the grey one? Switch to Tukey. Still no. Now switch the first line to Start from a Search over Pairs of Points and run Tukey again. Then try Huber from that same start. Why does the starting line matter for Tukey and not for Huber? Finally choose Clean Data: how much do you lose by being robust when nothing is wrong?

From squared error to a gentler penalty

Least squares minimizes \(\sum_i r_i^2\) with \(r_i=y_i-a-b\,x_i\). An M-estimator replaces the square with a function \(\rho\) that grows more slowly for large misses:

$$\min_{a,b}\ \sum_i\rho\!\Big(\frac{r_i}{s}\Big),$$

where \(s\) is a robust estimate of the typical miss. This page uses the median absolute deviation, \(s=\operatorname{median}\lvert r_i-\operatorname{median}(r)\rvert/0.6745\), which half of the data can be wrong about without spoiling it.

Three penalties

$$\rho_{\text{Huber}}(u)=\begin{cases}\tfrac12u^2&\lvert u\rvert\le k\\k\lvert u\rvert-\tfrac12k^2&\lvert u\rvert>k\end{cases}\qquad\rho_{\text{Tukey}}(u)=\begin{cases}\tfrac{c^2}{6}\Big[1-\big(1-\tfrac{u^2}{c^2}\big)^3\Big]&\lvert u\rvert\le c\\\tfrac{c^2}{6}&\lvert u\rvert>c\end{cases}\qquad\rho_{\text{abs}}(u)=\lvert u\rvert.$$

Huber's penalty (1964) is a square near zero and a straight line beyond the cut-off, so large misses still pull, but with a constant force. Tukey's levels off completely: beyond the cut-off a point exerts no pull at all. The absolute value pulls every point with the same force however far away it is, which is what makes the median robust.

Iteratively reweighted least squares

Setting the derivative to zero gives a weighted least-squares problem with weights that depend on the residuals:

$$w_i=\frac{\rho'(u_i)}{u_i},\qquad w^{\text{Huber}}_i=\min\!\Big(1,\frac{k}{\lvert u_i\rvert}\Big),\qquad w^{\text{Tukey}}_i=\Big(1-\frac{u_i^2}{c^2}\Big)^2\ \text{for }\lvert u_i\rvertFix the weights, solve, recompute the weights, repeat. The run stops when intercept and slope both change by less than \(10^{-5}\).

What can go wrong

Huber's penalty is convex: there is one best line and the iteration finds it from any start. But its pull never drops to zero. When many points are bad, and above all when they sit together at one end of the data, the line is dragged almost as far as the least-squares line. Tukey's penalty ignores far points completely, which copes with much more contamination. The price is that it is not convex. There can be several lines that each look best to the points they have not discarded, and the answer depends on the first line. Started from least squares, which the outliers have already tilted, it may throw away the good points instead of the bad ones. Practical software starts from a very robust first fit. The one offered here tries the line through every pair of data points and keeps the one whose median miss is smallest (least median of squares): a line that half of the data can be wrong about.

Leverage

A point that is wrong in \(y\) near the middle of the data is easy to detect. A point far out along the \(x\)-axis has leverage: the line pivots towards it, so its own residual stays small and it keeps a high weight. Reweighting by residuals gives only limited protection against such points.

The cost of caution

On clean Gaussian data least squares is the best possible estimator. Huber with \(k=1.345\) and Tukey with \(c=4.685\) are chosen to keep 95% of that efficiency: a 5% insurance premium against bad data.

Check yourself

With a third of the data wrong, Tukey started from least squares settles on a poor line, while the same method started from the search over pairs finds the grey line. Nothing else changed. Why?

Tukey’s penalty gives zero weight to any point further than the cut-off from the current line. Least squares has been pulled towards the bad third, so measured from that tilted line the residuals are large everywhere and the robust scale is inflated; the reweighting then has no clear group to discard and can lock on to a compromise. The line found by the search over pairs passes through the good two-thirds, so measured from there the bad third is clearly far away, gets zero weight at once, and the fit is finished using only good points. A penalty that can ignore points entirely has more than one self-consistent answer, and the first line decides which one you reach.

entries.title: A line that gives probabilities
entries.html:
A Line That Gives Probabilities

Draw a line through the plane. Far on one side the model is sure of class B, far on the other sure of class A, and near the line it is unsure. Training tilts and slides the line until the probabilities match the data.

Linear regression draws a line through the points. For classification we want a line between the two groups, and more than a yes or no: we want to know how sure the model is. So compute a score that says how far a point is from the line and on which side, then squash that score into a number between 0 and 1. Points far on the B side get a probability near 1, points far on the A side near 0, and points on the line exactly one half.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Start with a random line.
  2. For every training point, compute its score z and probability p = σ(z).
  3. Compare p with the true label (0 for A, 1 for B). The gap p − y is the error.
  4. Move each weight a small step against the average of error × input.
  5. Repeat until the loss stops falling.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Log loss
–
Steps taken
–
Weights
–

Try this. Watch the line swing into place on the two clouds. Then choose the ring around a core: what accuracy can a straight line reach? Tick “Add squared features” and train again. Finally, on well-separated clouds with no penalty, watch the weights keep growing.

The model

$$z=w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2,\qquad p=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$$

\(z\) is the score, proportional to the signed distance from the line \(z=0\). The sigmoid \(\sigma\) is the S-shaped curve on the right. Rearranged, \(z=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\): the model is linear in the log-odds. Each unit of \(x_1\) multiplies the odds of class B by \(e^{w_1}\).

The loss

Choose the weights that make the observed labels most probable. The negative log of that probability, averaged, is the log loss (cross-entropy):

$$L(\mathbf w)=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Big[y_i\ln p_i+(1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\Big]$$

A confident correct answer costs almost nothing. A confident wrong answer costs a great deal, and the cost grows without limit as \(p\to0\) for a true B. This is maximum likelihood under a Bernoulli model, exactly as least squares was under a Gaussian one.

The gradient

$$\nabla L=\frac1n\sum_i(p_i-y_i)\,\mathbf x_i$$

The same form as linear regression: prediction minus target, times the input. There is no closed-form solution, so it is trained by gradient descent, but the loss is convex, so there is one minimum and descent finds it.

Three things to notice

The boundary is always straight in the features you give it. Adding squared features lets it draw circles and ellipses, the same trick as polynomial regression. On perfectly separable data the weights grow without bound: a steeper sigmoid always fits a little better, so there is no finite best. A penalty \(\lambda\lVert\mathbf w\rVert^2\) stops that. The output is a probability, so you can move the threshold away from 0.5 when the two kinds of mistake have different costs.

Check yourself

Why not fit a straight line to the 0/1 labels with least squares instead?

Its outputs are not probabilities: they run below 0 and above 1. And squared error punishes points that are very confidently correct, far from the boundary, which drags the line toward them. Log loss does not care how far beyond the boundary a correctly classified point is.

entries.title: More than two classes
entries.html:
More Than Two Classes

With three classes, give each class its own score and turn the three scores into three probabilities that add to one. Move the pointer over the picture to read the probabilities at any spot.

Logistic regression asked one question, "B or not?". With \(K\) classes, hold a small election at every point: each class gets a score from its own linear function, and the scores are turned into shares of the vote. The class with the highest score wins, and the margin of victory is the confidence.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Start with random weights, one set per class.
  2. For every training point, compute three scores and turn them into three probabilities.
  3. For each class, the error is its probability minus 1 if it is the true class, minus 0 otherwise.
  4. Move each class’s weights against the average of error × input.
  5. Repeat until the loss stops falling.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Cross-entropy loss
–
Steps taken
–

Try this. Move the pointer from the middle of one cloud to the spot where all three regions meet. What are the three probabilities there? Drag a point from one class deep into another class’s region and watch the loss.

The model

$$z_k=\mathbf w_k^{\top}\mathbf x+b_k,\qquad p_k=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{z_j}}$$

Exponentiating makes every score positive; dividing by the total makes them sum to one. This is the softmax function. Raising one score lowers every other probability. With \(K=2\) it reduces exactly to the sigmoid of the difference of the two scores.

The loss

$$L=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ln p_{i,\,y_i}$$

Cross-entropy: the negative log of the probability given to the correct class. Its gradient again has the familiar form, with one row per class:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf w_k}=\frac1n\sum_i\big(p_{ik}-\mathbb 1[y_i=k]\big)\,\mathbf x_i.$$

The boundaries

The boundary between classes \(j\) and \(k\) is where \(z_j=z_k\), a straight line. So the plane is cut into \(K\) regions by straight edges that meet at points.

Why it matters later

This is the last layer of nearly every neural network classifier, and of every language model, where the "classes" are the tens of thousands of possible next tokens. Dividing the scores by a temperature before the softmax sharpens or flattens the probabilities.

Check yourself

Adding the same constant to all three scores changes nothing. Why?

The constant multiplies the numerator and every term of the denominator by the same factor, which cancels. Only differences between scores matter. That is why one class’s weights can be fixed at zero without losing anything.

entries.title: Ask the neighbours
entries.html:
Ask the Neighbours

No training at all. To classify a new point, find the k training points closest to it and take a vote. Move the pointer over the picture to see who gets a vote. Small k follows every point; large k smooths everything out.

If you want to know whether a house is in a good school district, look at the houses next to it. k-nearest neighbours makes that the whole method: things that are close together tend to share a label, so let the closest known examples vote. Nothing is learned ahead of time. The training data is kept, and all the work happens at the moment of prediction.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Store every training point. That is all the training there is.
  2. For a new point, measure its distance to every stored point.
  3. Pick the k closest.
  4. Count their labels. The majority wins, and the share is the probability.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy

Vote at the pointer
–

Try this. Set k = 1 and read the train accuracy. Is it a good model? Raise k slowly and watch the islands around single points disappear. What happens to the boundary, and to both errors, when k gets close to the number of points?

The rule

$$\hat p(\text{B}\mid\mathbf x)=\frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf x)}\mathbb 1[y_i=\text{B}],\qquad \hat y=\text{the majority class in }N_k(\mathbf x)$$

where \(N_k(\mathbf x)\) is the set of the \(k\) training points nearest to \(\mathbf x\). It is kernel regression from the Regression module, applied to labels, with a box kernel whose width adapts to how dense the data is.

k is the bias–variance dial

With \(k=1\) every training point owns a small territory around itself. Training error is zero, the boundary is ragged, and a single mislabelled point creates an island of wrong answers: high variance. As \(k\) grows, votes are averaged over a wider area, islands dissolve and the boundary smooths: lower variance, more bias. At \(k=n\) every point gets the same answer, the overall majority. The effective number of parameters is about \(n/k\).

Distance is a choice

$$d_2(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\sqrt{\sum_j(a_j-b_j)^2},\qquad d_1(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\sum_j|a_j-b_j|$$

The answer depends entirely on what "near" means. A feature measured in large units dominates the distance, so features must be scaled first. And irrelevant features add noise to every distance.

Strengths and limits

It can draw any boundary and needs no assumptions. But it must store all the data and search it for every prediction, and it suffers the curse of dimensionality directly: in many dimensions the nearest neighbours are not near.

Check yourself

k = 1 gets 100% on the training data. Why is that not a reason to use it?

Each training point is its own nearest neighbour, so it always votes for its own label. That measures memory, not prediction. Test accuracy, or leave-one-out accuracy, is the honest measure, and it is usually best at a moderate k.

entries.title: One feature at a time
entries.html:
One Feature at a Time

Describe each class by a bell curve for each feature separately, and pretend the features have nothing to do with each other. It is a crude picture of the data and it often classifies well anyway. Make the features correlated and watch where the pretence starts to cost.

A doctor reasons backwards: given these symptoms, which illness is likely? But what is easy to learn from records runs forwards: given the illness, how common is each symptom? Bayes' rule turns one into the other. The "naive" part is a shortcut: treat each symptom as if it told you something independent of the others, so the evidence simply multiplies. That is rarely true, and the method works surprisingly often regardless.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Split the training points by class.
  2. For each class and each feature, compute the mean and the variance. That gives one bell curve per feature.
  3. Record what share of the points each class has (the prior).
  4. To predict: for each class, multiply the prior by the heights of its bell curves at the new point. The larger product wins.

What just happened

Animation

The model

Nothing to tune. The model is four means, four variances and the two class shares.

The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Test accuracy if the correlation were modelled
–
Share of class B (the prior)
–

Try this. With the correlation at 0 the dashed ellipses match the clouds. Slide it to 0.9: the clouds tilt but the ellipses cannot. Compare the test accuracy with the one from a model that does allow for correlation.

Bayes' rule for classes

$$P(c\mid\mathbf x)=\frac{P(c)\,p(\mathbf x\mid c)}{\sum_{c'}P(c')\,p(\mathbf x\mid c')}$$

\(P(c)\) is the prior, the share of each class. \(p(\mathbf x\mid c)\) says what the features of class \(c\) look like. A classifier built this way is called generative: it models how each class produces data. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models only the boundary.

The naive assumption

$$p(\mathbf x\mid c)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}p(x_j\mid c)$$

Within a class, the features are taken to be independent. With Gaussian features each factor is a one-dimensional bell curve, the four curves on the right:

$$p(x_j\mid c)=N\big(x_j;\ \mu_{jc},\ \sigma^2_{jc}\big).$$

In terms of the Gaussian module this is a diagonal covariance matrix per class: ellipses that can stretch along the axes but never tilt.

Why make such an assumption

A full description of \(d\) features needs on the order of \(d^2\) numbers per class; the naive one needs \(2d\), each estimated from a one-dimensional histogram. With thousands of features and little data (words in an email, say) the full model cannot be estimated at all and the naive one can. Training is a single pass of counting.

What goes wrong

Correlated features are counted as separate pieces of evidence when they are really the same evidence twice. The probabilities become overconfident, pushed toward 0 and 1. The decision often stays right even so, because only the ranking of the classes matters for the decision.

Check yourself

Naive Bayes says 99.9% for a spam email. Should you believe the number?

Believe the decision more than the number. When features are correlated the same evidence is multiplied in several times, so the probabilities are pushed to the extremes. The email is probably spam, but the true probability is likely well below 99.9%.

entries.title: One hill per class
entries.html:
One Hill Per Class

Fit a Gaussian hill to each class and assign every point to the taller hill. If the hills are forced to have the same shape, the line where they cross is straight (LDA). If each keeps its own shape, the crossing is a curve (QDA).

In the Gaussian module you fitted one hill to a cloud of points. Now fit one hill to each class. A new point belongs to whichever class's hill is higher above it, after weighting each hill by how common the class is. The boundary is the line on the ground directly below where the two hills cross. Whether that line is straight or curved depends on one decision: must the hills have the same shape?

How it learns, step by step

  1. Split the training points by class and compute each class’s mean.
  2. Compute the covariance of each class. For LDA, average them into one shared covariance.
  3. Record the share of each class (the prior).
  4. To predict: evaluate each class’s Gaussian at the new point, times its prior. The taller one wins.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy

Numbers the model had to estimate
–
Test accuracy of the other method
–

Try this. With equal spreads LDA and QDA give nearly the same boundary. Make class B much more spread out than A and switch between the two. Then try the ring around a core: which one can handle it, and why?

The model

$$p(\mathbf x\mid c)=N(\mathbf x;\ \boldsymbol\mu_c,\ \Sigma_c),\qquad \hat y=\arg\max_c\ \delta_c(\mathbf x),\qquad \delta_c(\mathbf x)=\ln\pi_c+\ln p(\mathbf x\mid c)$$

with \(\pi_c\) the class share. It is Naive Bayes without the naive assumption: the covariance is allowed to tilt.

QDA: each class has its own covariance

$$\delta_c(\mathbf x)=\ln\pi_c-\tfrac12\ln|\Sigma_c|-\tfrac12(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu_c)^{\top}\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu_c)$$

Setting \(\delta_A=\delta_B\) leaves terms in \(\mathbf x^{\top}(\Sigma_A^{-1}-\Sigma_B^{-1})\mathbf x\): a quadratic. The boundary is a conic: an ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. A tight class surrounded by a wide one gets a closed curve around it.

LDA: one covariance shared by all

If \(\Sigma_A=\Sigma_B=\Sigma\), the quadratic terms cancel and what remains is linear in \(\mathbf x\):

$$\delta_c(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_c-\tfrac12\boldsymbol\mu_c^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_c+\ln\pi_c$$

The boundary is a straight line, perpendicular to \(\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_B-\boldsymbol\mu_A)\). Equivalently: assign each point to the class whose mean is nearest in Mahalanobis distance. \(\Sigma\) is estimated by pooling both classes.

Which to use

In \(d\) dimensions with \(K\) classes, LDA estimates one covariance (\(d(d+1)/2\) numbers), QDA \(K\) of them. QDA is more flexible and needs more data; LDA is stiffer and steadier. It is the bias–variance trade again. LDA and logistic regression both give straight boundaries; LDA assumes Gaussian classes and is more efficient when that is true, logistic regression assumes less and is safer when it is not.

Check yourself

LDA and logistic regression both draw a straight line. When would they give different lines?

When the classes are not Gaussian with equal covariance, for example when there are outliers far from the boundary. LDA uses every point to estimate means and covariance, so distant points move the line. Logistic regression is driven mainly by points near the boundary and is less affected.

entries.title: Learning from mistakes
entries.html:
Learning from Mistakes

Start with any line. Visit the points one at a time. If a point is on the right side, do nothing. If it is on the wrong side, swing the line toward it. Repeat. When a straight line can separate the classes this always finishes. When none can, it never does.

This is the oldest learning algorithm, from 1958, and the simplest picture of what learning from examples means. The model makes a guess. If the guess is right, leave everything alone. If it is wrong, nudge the weights so that this example would have come out a little more right. That is all. A single artificial neuron with this rule is the ancestor of every neural network.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Start with a random line.
  2. Take the next training point and check which side of the line it is on.
  3. If it is on the correct side, change nothing.
  4. If it is on the wrong side, add η × (±1) × the point to the weights. The line swings toward it.
  5. After a full pass with no mistakes, stop.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Try this. On the two clouds, count the passes until a pass has no mistakes. Then choose the overlapping clouds or the checkerboard and let it run: does the mistake count ever reach zero? Drag one point across to the other side of the line and train again.

The model

$$\hat y=\operatorname{sign}\big(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x+b\big),\qquad y\in\{-1,+1\}$$

A hard yes or no: which side of the line \(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x+b=0\) the point falls on. The vector \(\mathbf w\) points across the line toward the positive side.

The update

For each point in turn, if it is misclassified, meaning \(y_i(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x_i+b)\le0\):

$$\mathbf w\leftarrow\mathbf w+\eta\,y_i\,\mathbf x_i,\qquad b\leftarrow b+\eta\,y_i$$

Adding \(y_i\mathbf x_i\) rotates \(\mathbf w\) toward a positive point or away from a negative one. After the update that point's score \(y_i\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x_i\) has gone up by \(\eta\lVert\mathbf x_i\rVert^2\): it is closer to being right, though not necessarily right yet.

The convergence theorem

If some line separates the classes with margin \(\gamma\), and all points lie within radius \(R\), the perceptron makes at most

$$\Big(\frac{R}{\gamma}\Big)^2\ \text{ corrections}$$

and then stops, whatever the order of the points. A wide gap between the classes means few mistakes.

Its limits

If no separating line exists, the updates never stop: the line keeps swinging as different points take turns being wrong. The checkerboard (XOR) is the famous example; the proof in 1969 that a single perceptron cannot solve it stalled neural network research for a decade, until hidden layers were shown to fix it. And when the data is separable, the perceptron stops at the first line that works, which may pass very close to some points. Choosing the best such line is the idea of the support vector machine.

Check yourself

Two runs on the same separable data end with different lines. Is one of them wrong?

Neither is wrong by the perceptron’s own standard: both separate the training data, and it stops as soon as that happens. Which line it reaches depends on the starting weights and the order of the points. They may differ in how well they generalise, which is the motivation for maximising the margin.

entries.title: The widest street between the classes
entries.html:
The Widest Street Between the Classes

Many lines separate two clouds. The support vector machine picks the one in the middle of the widest possible street between them. Only the points on the kerbs of the street matter: move any other point and nothing changes.

The perceptron stops at any line that separates the classes. But a line that scrapes past a training point leaves no room for error: a new point slightly different from that one lands on the wrong side. Better to leave as much room as possible on both sides. Picture the boundary as the centre line of a street and widen the street until its kerbs touch the nearest points of each class. Those touching points hold the street in place, like supports; every other point could be removed without changing anything.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Start with a flat score, so the street is infinitely wide.
  2. Find every point that is inside the street or on the wrong side (y·f(x) < 1).
  3. Pull the line toward classifying those points better, by C × each of them.
  4. At the same time shrink the weights slightly, which widens the street.
  5. Repeat with smaller and smaller steps until the pull and the shrink balance.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of

–
Test accuracy
–
Width of the street
–

–

–

Try this. Drag a point that is far from the street: does the line move? Now drag one of the ringed points. Then lower C to 0.01 and raise it to 100 on the overlapping clouds: what happens to the width of the street and to the number of ringed points?

The margin

With labels \(y_i=\pm1\) and \(f(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x+b\), scale the weights so the kerbs are at \(f=\pm1\). The distance from the centre line to a kerb is \(1/\lVert\mathbf w\rVert\), so

$$\text{street width}=\frac{2}{\lVert\mathbf w\rVert}.$$

Widening the street means shrinking \(\lVert\mathbf w\rVert\).

Hard margin

$$\min_{\mathbf w,b}\ \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf w\rVert^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i\,f(\mathbf x_i)\ge1\ \text{ for all }i$$

Every point must be on its own side, outside the street. Possible only when the classes are separable.

Soft margin

$$\min_{\mathbf w,b}\ \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf w\rVert^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\max\big(0,\ 1-y_i\,f(\mathbf x_i)\big)$$

Allow points inside the street or on the wrong side, at a price. The price is the hinge loss on the right: zero for a point at or beyond its kerb (\(y_if\ge1\)), then rising in a straight line. \(C\) sets the exchange rate. Large \(C\): violations are expensive, the street is narrow and follows the data closely. Small \(C\): a wide street with many points inside it, a smoother and steadier boundary. \(1/C\) plays the role of \(\lambda\) in ridge regression.

Support vectors

The solution has the form \(\mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i\) with \(\alpha_i>0\) only for points on or inside the street. Points safely beyond their kerb have zero hinge loss and zero gradient: the model does not know they exist. Compare logistic regression, where every point always pulls a little.

What comes next

The solution depends on the data only through inner products \(\mathbf x_i^{\top}\mathbf x_j\). Replacing those with a kernel gives curved boundaries at no extra cost. That is the next lesson.

Check yourself

You delete half the training points, none of them support vectors. What happens to the boundary?

Nothing. Points beyond the kerbs have zero hinge loss and contribute nothing to the solution, so removing them leaves the same optimum. Only the support vectors determine the line.

entries.title: Lift the data until a flat cut works
entries.html:
Lift the Data Until a Flat Cut Works

No straight line separates a ring from its core. But add a third coordinate, the distance from the centre, and the core sinks below the ring. Now a flat plane slices them apart. Seen from above, that flat cut is a circle.

Lay a red napkin flat on a table and scatter blue beads around it. No straight ruler laid on the table separates red from blue. Now pinch the napkin in the middle and lift: the red rises, the blue stays down, and a sheet of card slid in horizontally separates them perfectly. Nothing about the data changed. You gave it one more dimension to move in, and in the bigger space a simple flat cut was enough.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Compute the new coordinate z for every training point.
  2. Fit a linear classifier in the lifted space (x, y, z): a flat plane.
  3. To predict for a new point, compute its z the same way and see which side of the plane it is on.
  4. Seen from above, the plane’s edge is the curved boundary.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Test accuracy of a straight line, no lift
–
What separates the classes
–

Try this. Start with “None: stay flat” on the ring data and read the accuracy. Then choose z = x² + y² and watch the points rise. Rotate until you look along the plane. Switch to the checkerboard: which lift works there? Finally choose the RBF kernel and raise γ until the boundary wraps single points.

Lifting by hand

$$\phi(x_1,x_2)=\big(x_1,\ x_2,\ x_1^2+x_2^2\big)$$

In the lifted space fit an ordinary linear classifier, a plane \(w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2+w_3z=0\). Back on the table that plane is the set where \(w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2+w_3(x_1^2+x_2^2)=0\): a circle. A linear method plus a nonlinear lift gives a nonlinear boundary. For the checkerboard, the right lift is \(z=x_1x_2\), positive in two opposite quadrants and negative in the other two.

The problem with lifting by hand

You have to know which lift to use. You could add every product of features up to some degree, but the number of new coordinates explodes: degree 5 on 100 features is nearly a hundred million.

The trick

Many linear methods (SVMs, ridge regression, PCA) only ever use the data through inner products \(\mathbf x_i^{\top}\mathbf x_j\). After lifting they would need \(\phi(\mathbf x_i)^{\top}\phi(\mathbf x_j)\). A kernel is a function that returns that number directly from the original points, without ever computing \(\phi\):

$$k(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\phi(\mathbf a)^{\top}\phi(\mathbf b)$$$$\text{polynomial: }\ k(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=(1+\mathbf a^{\top}\mathbf b)^p\qquad\qquad \text{RBF: }\ k(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\exp\!\big(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf a-\mathbf b\rVert^2\big)$$

The polynomial kernel corresponds to all products of features up to degree \(p\), computed at the cost of one inner product. The RBF kernel corresponds to a lift into infinitely many dimensions.

What the model looks like

$$f(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,k(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x)+b$$

A weighted sum of bumps, one centred on each training point (for an SVM, only on the support vectors). The last option draws this \(f\) as a surface: hills over one class, hollows over the other, and the boundary where it crosses zero. \(\gamma\) sets the width of each bump: small \(\gamma\) gives broad bumps and a smooth boundary, large \(\gamma\) gives narrow spikes and a boundary that wraps each point, which is overfitting.

Check yourself

The RBF kernel lifts the data into infinitely many dimensions. Why does that not overfit hopelessly?

Because the fit is regularised. The margin of an SVM, or the penalty in kernel ridge, limits how much the function may wiggle regardless of how many dimensions it lives in. The flexibility that matters is set by γ and the penalty, not by the dimension of the lifted space.

entries.title: Twenty questions
entries.html:
Twenty Questions

Ask one yes-or-no question about one feature, the question that best sorts the classes. Then ask the best question inside each half, and again. Every question cuts a region in two with a straight, axis-parallel line.

In the game of twenty questions a good player does not ask "is it a giraffe?" first. They ask the question that splits the remaining possibilities most evenly into those it rules in and those it rules out. A decision tree plays this game with data: at each step it searches every feature and every cut point for the single question whose two answers are each as pure in one class as possible. The result reads like a flowchart, which is why trees are the easiest model to explain to someone else.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Put all training points in one region.
  2. For each region, try every feature and every cut point, and measure how much each cut lowers the impurity.
  3. Make the best cut. The region becomes two.
  4. Repeat inside each new region, until the depth limit or the minimum region size is reached.
  5. To predict, follow the questions down to a region and answer with its majority class.
  6. Then prune. Find the question whose removal adds the fewest training mistakes per region saved, and remove it with everything below it.
  7. Keep pruning one question at a time. Choose the size that does best on held-out data.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–

–
Regions (leaves) now
–
Depth with the lowest test error
–
