Try this. Step through the first three questions and find each one as a line on the left. Let the tree grow to depth 6 and look for tiny regions around single points. Then press “Prune One Step” repeatedly and watch the test accuracy: at how many regions is it best? Try the checkerboard: can a depth-1 tree do anything with it?

Measuring impurity

For a region where a fraction \(p\) of the points is class B:

$$\text{Gini}=2p(1-p),\qquad \text{entropy}=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$$

Both are zero when the region is pure (\(p=0\) or \(1\)) and largest when it is evenly mixed (\(p=\tfrac12\)). Gini is the chance that two points drawn from the region have different labels.

Choosing a split

A split "\(x_j\le s\)" sends \(n_L\) points left and \(n_R\) right. Its quality is the drop in weighted impurity:

$$\Delta=I(\text{parent})-\frac{n_L}{n}I(\text{left})-\frac{n_R}{n}I(\text{right})$$

Try every feature \(j\) and every threshold \(s\) between neighbouring data values, and take the largest \(\Delta\). Then repeat inside each child. This is a greedy search: each question is the best one right now, with no looking ahead. That is why a depth-1 tree fails on the checkerboard, where no single question helps and two together are perfect.

Predicting

Follow the questions down to a leaf and answer with the majority class there; the class share in the leaf is the predicted probability. The model is a piecewise-constant function on boxes.

Stopping

Left alone, the tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure: zero training error and a region for every noisy point. Limits on depth and on the number of points per leaf are the regularisation; alternatively grow fully and prune back using a penalty on the number of leaves.

Pruning

A better strategy than stopping early is to grow a large tree and then cut it back. Stopping early can miss a weak-looking question that opens the way to a very good one below it. For pruning, define the cost of a tree \(T\) as its training mistakes plus a charge for every leaf:

$$R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha\,|T|$$

where \(R(T)\) is the number of misclassified training points and \(|T|\) the number of leaves. For any internal node \(t\), collapsing the subtree \(T_t\) below it into a single leaf adds \(R(t)-R(T_t)\) mistakes and saves \(|T_t|-1\) leaves. The ratio

$$g(t)=\frac{R(t)-R(T_t)}{|T_t|-1}$$

is the number of extra mistakes per leaf saved: the price of keeping that branch. Weakest-link pruning repeatedly removes the node with the smallest \(g(t)\). This produces a nested sequence of smaller and smaller trees, one for each range of \(\alpha\), ending at the root alone. Training accuracy can only fall along the way. Test accuracy typically rises first, as branches that fitted noise are removed, and then falls as real structure goes. Choose the tree in the sequence that does best on held-out data or in cross-validation.

Strengths and weaknesses

No feature scaling needed, handles mixed feature types, finds interactions on its own, easy to read. But boundaries are staircases, so a diagonal edge takes many splits; and trees are unstable: a small change in the data can change the first question and with it everything below. Averaging many trees fixes the instability, which is the idea of random forests and boosting.

Check yourself

A tree splits first on x at 0.4. You add three new data points and now it splits first on y. What does this tell you?

Trees have high variance. Two different first questions were nearly equally good, and a small change in the data tipped the choice, which changes the whole tree below it. Predictions may be similar, but the structure is not stable. Averaging many trees grown on resampled data removes most of this.

entries.title: Semi-supervised learning: a few labels and a great many hints
entries.html:
Semi-Supervised Learning: A Few Labels and a Great Many Hints

Labels are expensive. A radiologist has to read the scan, a person has to listen to the recording. Unlabelled examples are nearly free. Semi-supervised learning uses a handful of labelled points together with a large pile of unlabelled ones, on the bet that the shape of the unlabelled data says where the classes are. When the bet is right, six labels can do the work of hundreds. This page also shows what happens when it is wrong.

You arrive at a party where you know two people, one from the chess club and one from the football team. Nobody else wears a badge. But people stand in groups, and you can see who is talking to whom. It is a fair guess that those standing with the chess player are chess people, and their neighbours too, and so on outwards until you meet the group spreading from the footballer. You have labelled the whole room from two labels and the pattern of who stands near whom. You will be wrong exactly when the pattern misleads: when the two clubs mingle, or when one sociable person links both groups.

How it works, step by step

    What just happened

    Animation

    Labels
    Labelled / unlabelled
    –
    Steps so far
    –
    Accuracy from the labels alone
    –
    Accuracy with the unlabelled data
    –
    Unlabelled points still undecided
    –

    Try this. On Two Crescents with three labels per class, compare the top-right picture with the left one once the run has finished. Where does the labelled-only answer go wrong, and why does the other not? Drop to one label per class and press New data and labels several times. How dependable is it now? Go back to three labels and choose Overlapping Clouds: compare the two accuracies over a few new data sets. What is different about this data? Switch to Self-Training on the crescents and watch the labels grow outwards from each seed. Finally click a grey or wrongly coloured dot to buy its label. Which single label helps most?

    The setting

    There are \(l\) labelled examples \((\mathbf x_i,y_i)\) and \(u\gg l\) unlabelled examples \(\mathbf x_j\). The unlabelled points tell us about the density of \(\mathbf x\). That is useful only under an assumption connecting density to labels:

    Cluster assumption. Points in the same cluster tend to share a label, so the boundary between classes should run through regions where data are sparse.

    Smoothness (manifold) assumption. Points connected by a path through dense data tend to share a label, even if they are far apart in a straight line.

    Label propagation

    Build a graph joining each point to its \(k\) nearest neighbours, with weights \(w_{ij}\) that decay with distance, and normalize each row: \(P_{ij}=w_{ij}/\sum_k w_{ik}\). Give every point a belief vector \(\mathbf f_i\) over the classes. Then repeat two steps (Zhu and Ghahramani, 2002):

    $$\mathbf f_i\leftarrow\sum_j P_{ij}\,\mathbf f_j\quad\text{for every point},\qquad\mathbf f_i\leftarrow\text{its true label}\quad\text{for the labelled points}.$$

    Each point replaces its belief by the average belief of its neighbours, and the labelled points are clamped back. Labels flow outwards along the graph like heat from fixed sources. The iteration converges to the harmonic solution, in which every unlabelled point's belief equals the weighted average of its neighbours':

    $$\mathbf F_u=(\mathbf I-\mathbf P_{uu})^{-1}\mathbf P_{ul}\mathbf Y_l.$$

    With very few labels the converged beliefs are nearly flat far from the labelled points, and cutting them at one half is unreliable. So the cut is placed where it gives each class the same share of the unlabelled points as it has among the labelled ones, a correction known as class mass normalization. It assumes the labelled points reflect the true class sizes. The run stops when no belief changes by more than 0.0001 in a step.

    Self-training

    Train any classifier on the labelled points. Use it to predict the unlabelled ones. Take the predictions it is most confident about, treat them as if they were true labels, and retrain. Repeat until everything is labelled (Yarowsky, 1995). Here the classifier is the simplest possible, the label of the nearest labelled point, with confidence measured by how close that point is, and five points are adopted per step. Self-training wraps around any model and is simple. Its weakness is that it believes itself: a confident early mistake is never revisited and is used to label its neighbours.

    When it helps and when it hurts

    On the crescents the classes are separated by a gap of empty space, and both assumptions hold. With a single label per class the same data give an excellent answer for one choice of labelled points and a poor one for another, because everything rests on where those two points happen to sit. On overlapping clouds the boundary runs through dense data, the cluster assumption fails, and the unlabelled points offer little: the two accuracies stay within a few points of each other. In general, anything that links two classes through dense data, such as a chain of intermediate examples, invites labels to flow across. Semi-supervised learning is not guaranteed to beat supervised learning. It can do worse, and the only real check is a labelled validation set, which is the very thing in short supply.

    Which label to buy

    Clicking a dot reveals its label. Choosing which labels to pay for is active learning. Labels are worth most where the method is undecided or where two colours meet, and least deep inside a region it already has right.

    Modern forms

    Deep semi-supervised methods use the same two ideas. Pseudo-labelling is self-training with a neural network. Consistency regularization asks the network to give the same answer for an unlabelled image and a distorted copy of it, which pushes the boundary away from dense regions. Pretraining a large model on unlabelled data and fine-tuning it on a few labels is the most successful version of the bet so far.

    Check yourself

    On Two Crescents, six labels plus the unlabelled points reach about 99%. On Overlapping Clouds the same method with the same number of labels gains almost nothing over using the labels alone. The algorithm did not change. What did?

    What changed is whether the shape of the data carries information about the labels. The crescents are separated by a band of empty space, so "connected through dense data" and "same class" mean nearly the same thing, and a label can safely travel along a whole crescent. In the overlapping clouds there is no gap: the densest region is exactly where the two classes mix. Following the density there tells you nothing about which class a point belongs to, so propagating labels through it is no better than asking the nearest labelled point. Unlabelled data help only when their structure lines up with the classes, and nothing in the unlabelled data can tell you whether it does.

entries.title: Many unstable trees, one steady vote
entries.html:
Many Unstable Trees, One Steady Vote

A single deep tree changes wildly when the data changes a little. So grow many trees, each on a slightly different version of the data, and let them vote. The errors that differ from tree to tree cancel out.

Ask one person to guess the weight of an ox and the guess may be far off. Ask eight hundred and average, and the result is startlingly close, because their errors point in different directions and cancel. A deep decision tree is an erratic guesser: accurate on average, but each one is thrown by the particular sample it saw. Bagging manufactures many such guessers from one data set and averages them.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Draw a new training set of the same size by picking points at random with replacement. About a third of the points are left out each time.
  2. Grow a deep tree on it, with no pruning.
  3. Repeat to get many different trees.
  4. To predict, let every tree vote and take the average.
  5. Score each training point using only the trees that never saw it. That is the out-of-bag estimate, a free test set.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Trees so far
–
One tree alone, average test accuracy
–
Out-of-bag accuracy
–
How often two trees agree
–

Try this. Look at the small pictures: each tree is ragged and no two are alike. Now look at the vote on the left. Step through from one tree to twenty and watch the test error of the vote fall below what any single tree achieves. Then set the depth to 1: does voting still help?

The bootstrap

We have only one training set, so we fake many: draw \(n\) points from the \(n\) training points with replacement. Some points appear twice or more, others not at all. The chance that a given point is left out of one resample is

$$\Big(1-\frac1n\Big)^{n}\ \approx\ e^{-1}\approx0.368,$$

so each resample contains about 63% of the distinct points. Each resample is a plausible alternative data set.

Bagging = bootstrap aggregating

$$\hat f_{\text{bag}}(\mathbf x)=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f^{*b}(\mathbf x)$$

Grow one tree \(\hat f^{*b}\) on each resample and average their predictions (or take the majority vote).

Why averaging helps

If each tree's prediction has variance \(\sigma^2\) and any two trees have correlation \(\rho\), the variance of the average of \(B\) trees is

$$\rho\,\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2.$$

The second term vanishes as \(B\) grows. The first does not: trees grown on overlapping data make some of the same mistakes, and no amount of averaging removes shared mistakes. Bias is unchanged by averaging. So bagging works best on models with low bias and high variance, which is why the trees are grown deep and left unpruned. Averaging stumps achieves almost nothing.

Out-of-bag error

Each point was left out of about a third of the resamples. Predict it using only the trees that never saw it, and compare with its label. This gives an honest error estimate with no separate validation set, close to what cross-validation would give.

More trees never overfit

Adding trees only makes the average steadier. The error curve flattens; it does not turn back up. The number of trees is limited by time, not by overfitting.

Check yourself

Bagging 100 linear regressions gives almost the same line as one linear regression. Why does it help trees and not lines?

A linear regression is stable: resampling the data barely changes the line, so there is little variance to average away, and the average of lines is just another line. A deep tree is unstable: resampling changes its splits completely, so the trees differ a lot and averaging them removes a large amount of variance.

entries.title: Make the trees disagree
entries.html:
Make the Trees Disagree

Bagged trees are too alike: they all reach for the same strong feature first, so they make the same mistakes. A random forest hides some of the features at every split. Each tree gets a little worse, the trees get much more different, and the vote gets better.

A committee of experts who all read the same newspaper is barely better than one expert: they share the same blind spots. A committee is strong when its members are individually competent and think differently. Bagging makes trees differ only through resampling, and if one feature is much more useful than the rest, every tree splits on it first and the trees end up alike. The random forest forces variety: at each split a tree may only choose among a random handful of features.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Draw a new training set of the same size by picking points at random with replacement. About a third of the points are left out each time.
  2. Grow a deep tree on it. At every split, look at only a random subset of the features.
  3. Repeat to get many different trees.
  4. To predict, let every tree vote and take the average.
  5. Score each training point using only the trees that never saw it. That is the out-of-bag estimate, a free test set.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy

–

–
Out-of-bag accuracy

Try this. With “features each split may look at” set to 1, read how often two trees agree. Set it to 2, which is plain bagging, and read it again. Compare the test error of the vote in both cases, on the overlapping clouds with depth 8.

The one change

Grow each tree on a bootstrap resample, as in bagging. But at every split, draw \(m\) of the \(p\) features at random and choose the best split among those \(m\) only. Typical choices are \(m\approx\sqrt p\) for classification and \(m\approx p/3\) for regression. With \(m=p\) it is bagging again. (Here \(p=2\), so the only choices are 1 and 2; with real data and dozens of features the effect is far stronger.)

Why it works

$$\operatorname{Var}\big(\text{average of }B\text{ trees}\big)=\rho\,\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2$$

For large \(B\) only \(\rho\sigma^2\) is left. Restricting the features makes each tree slightly worse, so \(\sigma^2\) and the bias rise a little, but it cuts the correlation \(\rho\) between trees sharply, and the product falls. The readout "how often two trees agree" tracks \(\rho\).

Feature importance

Each split lowers the impurity. Add up those reductions over every split in every tree, grouped by the feature that was used:

$$\text{importance}(j)=\sum_{\text{trees}}\ \sum_{\text{splits on }j}\frac{n_{\text{node}}}{n}\,\Delta I.$$

It ranks the features by how much sorting each one did. A second method shuffles one feature's values in the out-of-bag points and measures how much the accuracy drops.

In practice

Random forests need almost no tuning, do not need feature scaling, cope with many features, give out-of-bag error and importances for free, and rarely do badly. They are the standard first thing to try on tabular data. What they give up is the readability of a single tree.

Check yourself

Why does deliberately making each tree worse make the forest better?

The forest’s error depends on how good the trees are and on how correlated they are. Hiding features costs each tree a little accuracy but makes the trees far less alike. Once many trees are averaged, the shared, correlated part of the error is all that remains, so reducing the correlation matters more than the small loss in each tree.

entries.title: Each learner fixes the last one’s mistakes
entries.html:
Each Learner Fixes the Last One’s Mistakes

Start with a rule so simple it is barely better than a coin toss: one straight cut. See which points it gets wrong, make those points heavier, and fit the next cut to the reweighted data. Add the cuts together, each with a vote in proportion to its accuracy.

A student revising for an exam does not reread the whole book each evening. They work through practice questions, mark the ones they got wrong, and spend the next session on those. Boosting trains a sequence of simple models the same way: each new one concentrates on the examples its predecessors found hard. Individually each model is weak. Together, weighted by how reliable each proved to be, they are strong. Bagging built its trees independently and in parallel; boosting builds them one after another, each depending on the last.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Give every training point the same weight.
  2. Fit a weak learner (one cut) to the weighted points.
  3. Add up the weight of the points it gets wrong: its weighted error ε.
  4. Give it a vote α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε). Small error, big vote.
  5. Multiply the weight of each point it got wrong by e^α and each it got right by e^−α. Go back to step 2.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Learners so far
–
Weighted error of the latest
–
Its vote weight α
–
Heaviest point, relative to average
–

Try this. Step through the first five learners. The rings show each point’s weight: watch them swell on the points that keep being misclassified. On the ring-around-a-core data, how can a sum of straight cuts make a round boundary? Then add noise and run 100 learners: look at the heaviest point.

The algorithm

Labels \(y_i=\pm1\). Start with weights \(w_i=1/n\). For \(m=1,\dots,M\):

$$\varepsilon_m=\sum_{i}w_i\,\mathbb 1\big[h_m(\mathbf x_i)\ne y_i\big],\qquad \alpha_m=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon_m}{\varepsilon_m}$$$$w_i\leftarrow\frac{w_i\,\exp\!\big(-\alpha_m\,y_i\,h_m(\mathbf x_i)\big)}{Z_m}$$

where \(h_m\) is the weak learner fitted to the weighted data and \(Z_m\) rescales the weights to sum to 1. The final classifier is a weighted vote:

$$F(\mathbf x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m\,h_m(\mathbf x),\qquad \hat y=\operatorname{sign}F(\mathbf x).$$

Reading the formulas

\(\alpha_m\) is zero when \(\varepsilon_m=\tfrac12\) (a coin toss earns no vote) and grows as the error shrinks. The update multiplies the weight of a misclassified point by \(e^{\alpha_m}\) and of a correct one by \(e^{-\alpha_m}\). After the update, the learner just fitted has weighted error exactly \(\tfrac12\) on the new weights: the next learner is forced to find something different.

Why it works

AdaBoost is gradient descent, one learner at a time, on the exponential loss

$$L=\sum_i\exp\!\big(-y_i\,F(\mathbf x_i)\big).$$

If every weak learner has error at most \(\tfrac12-\gamma\), the training error falls at least as fast as \(e^{-2\gamma^2M}\): exponentially. Each stump has high bias; adding them removes bias. Boosting attacks bias, where bagging attacked variance.

Its weakness

The exponential loss punishes a badly misclassified point without limit. A mislabelled point gets heavier every round until the whole ensemble bends to accommodate it. AdaBoost is sensitive to label noise and outliers; gradient boosting with a gentler loss is the usual remedy.

Check yourself

A weak learner has weighted error 0.7, worse than chance. What does AdaBoost do with it?

Its vote weight α = ½ ln(0.3 / 0.7) is negative. AdaBoost uses it upside down: a rule that is wrong 70% of the time is right 70% of the time when reversed. Only an error of exactly one half is useless.

entries.title: Fit what is left over, again and again
entries.html:
Fit What Is Left Over, Again and Again

Start with the simplest prediction there is, the average. Look at the errors it leaves. Fit a small tree to those errors and add a fraction of it to the prediction. Look at the errors that remain, and repeat. Hundreds of small corrections add up to a flexible curve.

A golfer does not expect to sink the ball from the tee. The first shot gets it roughly toward the green. The second is aimed at what the first left: the remaining distance to the hole. Each later shot is smaller and corrects the leftover error of all the shots before. Gradient boosting plays the same way. No single tree is asked to model the data. Each is asked only to model what the ensemble so far has got wrong.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Predict the average of y for every point.
  2. Compute each point’s residual: its true value minus the current prediction.
  3. Fit a small tree to the residuals.
  4. Add a fraction ν of that tree to the prediction.
  5. Go back to step 2. Stop when the test error stops falling.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data
Rounds so far
–
Train error (MSE)
–
Test error (MSE)
–
Round with the lowest test error
–
Noise level σ² (best possible)
–

Try this. Take the first four rounds one at a time and watch the residuals on the right shrink toward zero. Then set the learning rate to 1 and run 300 rounds: when does the test error turn back up? Set it to 0.05: how many rounds does it need now, and how low does the test error go?

The algorithm for squared error

$$F_0(x)=\bar y,\qquad r_i^{(m)}=y_i-F_{m-1}(x_i),\qquad F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)+\nu\,h_m(x)$$

where \(h_m\) is a small regression tree fitted to the residuals \(r^{(m)}\), and \(\nu\in(0,1]\) is the learning rate. The final model is the sum of all the trees.

Why "gradient"

Think of the predictions \(F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n)\) as \(n\) adjustable numbers and the loss \(L=\tfrac12\sum_i(y_i-F(x_i))^2\) as a function of them. Its gradient with respect to \(F(x_i)\) is

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial F(x_i)}=-(y_i-F(x_i))=-r_i.$$

The residuals are the negative gradient. Adding a tree fitted to the residuals is one step of gradient descent, taken in the space of functions instead of the space of weights, with \(\nu\) as the step size. For any other differentiable loss, replace the residuals with that loss's negative gradient (the "pseudo-residuals") and everything else stays the same: log loss gives classification, absolute or Huber loss gives robustness to outliers. This generality is what separates gradient boosting from AdaBoost, which is the special case of exponential loss.

The three dials

Learning rate \(\nu\). Small steps mean each tree corrects only part of the error, leaving room for later trees to correct it differently. Smaller \(\nu\) needs more rounds and almost always generalises better. Number of rounds. Unlike bagging, boosting does overfit eventually: training error keeps falling toward zero while test error turns back up. Stop at the minimum of the validation error (early stopping). Tree depth. Depth 1 gives an additive model with no interactions; depth \(d\) allows interactions among up to \(d\) features. Depths of 3 to 6 are usual.

In practice

With subsampling of rows and columns and a penalty on leaf values, this is XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost: the strongest general-purpose methods for tabular data.

Check yourself

Halving the learning rate roughly doubles the number of rounds needed. Why bother?

With a large learning rate each tree commits fully to the residual pattern it happens to see, noise included. With a small one, each tree makes a cautious correction and hundreds of slightly different trees average out their individual quirks. The path to the answer is smoother and the test error at the best round is usually lower.

entries.title: Gradient boosting, engineered
entries.html:
Gradient Boosting, Engineered

The same idea as gradient boosting, with three additions that made it the standard tool for tables of data: it uses the curvature of the loss as well as the slope, it charges a price for every leaf and for large leaf values, and it prunes away splits that do not earn their keep. Run it on the built-in data or upload your own CSV.

Plain gradient boosting fits each tree to the residuals and adds it on. That works, but it leaves three questions open: how tall should each leaf's correction be, which splits are worth making, and when is a tree too complicated? XGBoost answers all three from one formula. It writes down the loss it wants to reduce, adds a charge for complexity, and then asks of every possible split: by how much would this lower the total? If the answer is less than the price of a new leaf, the split is cut off.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Start by predicting the same value for every row: the average.
  2. For every row compute the gradient g (how wrong, and which way) and the hessian h (how sharply the loss curves).
  3. Grow a tree to the depth limit. At each node pick the split with the largest gain, computed from the sums of g and h on each side.
  4. Prune: working up from the bottom, remove any split whose gain is below γ.
  5. Give each leaf the value −G / (H + λ) and add η times the tree to the prediction.
  6. Go back to step 2. Stop when the held-out loss stops falling.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data

Predict for your own row

Rounds so far
–
Training loss
–
Held-out loss
–
Round with the lowest held-out loss
–
Leaves in the latest tree
–
Splits pruned so far
–
Held-out accuracy
–

Try this. Take the first three rounds one at a time and read what each tree asked. Then set γ to 0 and to 3 and compare the latest tree: how many leaves survive? Set the learning rate to 1 and watch the held-out loss. Finally upload a CSV of your own: which column matters most?

The objective

$$\mathcal L=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\big(y_i,\hat y_i\big)+\sum_{m}\Omega(f_m),\qquad \Omega(f)=\gamma\,T+\tfrac12\,\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{T}w_j^2$$

The first sum is the fit to the data. The second penalises each tree \(f_m\) for its number of leaves \(T\) and the size of its leaf values \(w_j\). \(\gamma\) is the price of a leaf; \(\lambda\) shrinks leaf values toward zero, like ridge regression.

Second-order approximation

When adding tree \(f\) at round \(m\), expand the loss to second order around the current prediction:

$$\ell\big(y_i,\hat y_i+f(\mathbf x_i)\big)\approx \ell(y_i,\hat y_i)+g_i\,f(\mathbf x_i)+\tfrac12\,h_i\,f(\mathbf x_i)^2,\qquad g_i=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\hat y_i},\quad h_i=\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\hat y_i^{\,2}}.$$

For squared error \(g_i=\hat y_i-y_i\) (minus the residual) and \(h_i=1\). For log loss \(g_i=p_i-y_i\) and \(h_i=p_i(1-p_i)\). Using \(h\) as well as \(g\) is Newton's method in place of gradient descent: it knows how far to step, not only which way.

The best value for a leaf

For the rows that land in one leaf, let \(G=\sum g_i\) and \(H=\sum h_i\). The contribution of that leaf to the objective is \(Gw+\tfrac12(H+\lambda)w^2\), a parabola in \(w\) with minimum at

$$w^{*}=-\frac{G}{H+\lambda},\qquad\text{worth}\quad-\frac12\,\frac{G^2}{H+\lambda}.$$

With squared error and \(\lambda=0\) this is the average residual in the leaf, as in plain gradient boosting. \(\lambda\) pulls it toward zero, most strongly for leaves with few rows.

The gain of a split

$$\text{Gain}=\frac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda}+\frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda}-\frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right]-\gamma$$

The bracket is how much better two leaves do than one. Subtract \(\gamma\), the price of the extra leaf. Every candidate split is scored this way, which needs only the running sums of \(g\) and \(h\) as the rows are scanned in sorted order.

Pruning

The tree is first grown to the depth limit, taking the best split at each node even if its gain is small. Then it is pruned from the bottom up: a split whose gain is below \(\gamma\) is removed, and its parent is then checked in turn. Growing first and pruning afterwards matters. A split with little gain may open the way to a very good split beneath it, and a rule that stopped early would never find it. The ✂ marks in the tree picture are splits removed this way.

The other safeguards

Shrinkage: add only \(\eta\) times each tree. Row subsampling: each tree sees a random share of the rows, as in bagging. Column subsampling: as in random forests. Early stopping: watch the held-out loss and keep the round where it is lowest. Together with fast split-finding on sorted or histogrammed features, these make up XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost.

The numbers on this page use a standardised target for regression, so γ and λ are on the same scale whatever units your data is in; losses and predictions are reported in the original units. An uploaded CSV needs a header row; only numeric columns are used, and a target with exactly two values is treated as yes/no.

Check yourself

Why grow the tree fully and prune afterwards, when it would be cheaper to stop splitting as soon as the gain drops below γ?

Because gains are not always largest at the top. In a checkerboard pattern the first split gains almost nothing, and the splits beneath it gain a great deal. Stopping early would never reach them. Growing first lets the good deep splits be found, and pruning afterwards removes only the branches that turned out not to pay.

entries.title: A model that decides whom to trust
entries.html:
A Model That Decides Whom to Trust

Train several quite different models on the same data. Each is good in some places and poor in others. Then train one more model whose only job is to combine their answers: it learns how much to trust each one.

Before a big decision you might consult a lawyer, an accountant and an engineer. They will disagree. You would not simply take a show of hands: on a tax question you weigh the accountant's view most. Over time you learn whom to trust about what. Stacking gives a machine that role. Bagging and boosting combine many copies of the same kind of model by a fixed rule. Stacking combines models of different kinds, and it learns the rule.

How it learns, step by step

  1. Choose a few different kinds of model: here a straight line, 7 nearest neighbours and a small tree.
  2. Split the training data into 5 folds. For each fold, train the base models on the other four and record their predictions for the held-out fold.
  3. Now every training point has three predictions made by models that never saw it. Use those as three new features.
  4. Train the combiner (a logistic regression) to predict the true label from those three features.
  5. Retrain the base models on all the data. To predict: get the three base predictions, then pass them through the combiner.

What just happened

Animation

The model

Choose which model’s predictions fill the picture on the left.

The data
A click adds a point of
Train accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Test accuracy: straight line
–
Test accuracy: 7 neighbours
–
Test accuracy: small tree
–
Test accuracy: stacked
–
Combiner weights: line, neighbours, tree
–

Try this. Take the tour and compare the four pictures on the same data. On the two moons, which base model does the combiner trust least? Switch to the two clouds: do the weights change? Is the stacked model ever much worse than the best base model?

The model

$$\hat y=g\big(f_1(\mathbf x),\ f_2(\mathbf x),\ \dots,\ f_K(\mathbf x)\big)$$

The base models \(f_k\) each map the inputs to a prediction. The combiner \(g\), also called the meta-learner, sees only those \(K\) predictions and outputs the final answer. Here \(g\) is a logistic regression, so its weights say directly how much each base model counts.

The trap, and how to avoid it

If the combiner is trained on predictions the base models made for their own training data, it is fooled. A model that memorises, such as 1-nearest-neighbour, looks perfect there, and the combiner would hand it all the weight. The combiner must learn from predictions made on data the base models have not seen. So use cross-validation:

$$z_{ik}=f_k^{(-\text{fold}(i))}(\mathbf x_i)$$

the prediction for point \(i\) from base model \(k\) trained without \(i\)'s fold. Every training point gets an honest row \((z_{i1},\dots,z_{iK})\), and the combiner is fitted to those rows:

$$\min_{\mathbf w}\ \sum_i\ell\Big(y_i,\ \sigma\big(w_0+\textstyle\sum_kw_kz_{ik}\big)\Big).$$

When it helps

Stacking gains most when the base models are accurate and make different mistakes: a linear model, a neighbour-based model and a tree carve up the plane in unrelated ways. Combining five near-identical models gains nothing. It usually matches or slightly beats the best single model, which is why it wins competitions by small margins and why it is used less in practice, where one model is easier to maintain than several.

Relatives

A plain average of the base predictions is stacking with the weights fixed to be equal: simple and hard to beat. "Blending" is stacking with a single held-out set in place of cross-validation.

Check yourself

Why not train the combiner on the base models’ predictions for the training data itself?

Because those predictions are too good. Each base model has already seen those points, and flexible ones nearly reproduce the labels. The combiner would learn to trust whichever model overfits most. Using cross-validated predictions shows it how each model behaves on data it has not seen, which is what matters at prediction time.

entries.title: k-means: assign, move, repeat
entries.html:
k-Means: Assign, Move, Repeat

Give the computer a cloud of points and a number K, and it finds K groups with no labels to learn from. The whole algorithm is two steps repeated. Where it starts decides where it ends, which is why the starting rule called k-means++ matters so much.

Imagine a city that wants to open K post offices so that people walk as little as possible. If the offices were already built, each household would simply use its nearest one. If the households were already split into K districts, the best place for each office would be the centre of its district. k-means does not know either answer, so it guesses the offices and then alternates: send everyone to the nearest office, move each office to the middle of the people it serves, and again. Each of the two moves can only shorten the total walk, so the process must settle. What it settles on depends on the first guess.

How it works, step by step

  1. Choose K. Place K starting centres: all at random, or one at a time with k-means++.
  2. Assign: colour every point by its nearest centre.
  3. Move: shift each centre to the average of the points that carry its colour.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until no point changes colour.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Rounds so far
–
Sum of squared distances
–
Best known for this K
–
Random start: runs that reach the best
–
k-means++: runs that reach the best
–
Rounds needed, random / k-means++
–

Try this. Read the table under the pictures as you step: each row is one round, and the moves shrink toward zero. Choose Your Own Start and click all the centres into one group: can the algorithm recover? With Five Groups and Random Start, press Start over a few times and step through. How often do two centres begin in the same group, and can they ever leave it? Switch to k-means++ and step through the seeding: watch which dots grow before each pick. Then compare the two rows of bars in the middle picture. Finally choose Two Moons with K = 2: no starting rule can rescue that one. Why?

What it minimises

Let \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K\) be the centres and \(c(i)\) the cluster of point \(x_i\). k-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares (also called inertia or distortion):

$$J=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert x_i-\mu_{c(i)}\rVert^2 .$$

Assign holds the centres fixed and picks the best \(c(i)\) for each point: \(c(i)=\arg\min_k\lVert x_i-\mu_k\rVert^2\). Move holds the assignments fixed and picks the best centres. Setting \(\partial J/\partial\mu_k=0\) gives

$$\mu_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i:\,c(i)=k}x_i ,$$

the plain average, which is where the name comes from. Neither step can raise \(J\), and there are only finitely many ways to split \(n\) points into \(K\) groups, so the algorithm stops after a finite number of rounds. The top-right picture shows \(J\) falling at every step.

Why the start matters

\(J\) is not convex. It has many local minima, and the two steps only ever go downhill, so k-means lands in whichever valley the start belongs to. The classic failure: two starting centres fall inside one true group and none in another. The two centres split their group between them, a single centre elsewhere is left covering two groups, and no assign or move step can carry a centre across the gap, because every step is locally an improvement.

k-means++

k-means++ changes only how the K starting centres are chosen:

  1. Pick the first centre uniformly at random from the data points.
  2. For every point compute \(D(x)^2\), its squared distance to the nearest centre chosen so far.
  3. Pick the next centre from the data points with probability \(\dfrac{D(x)^2}{\sum_{x'}D(x')^2}\).
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until there are K centres, then run ordinary k-means.

A point sitting next to an existing centre has \(D^2\approx 0\) and is almost never picked. A whole group with no centre yet holds most of the total \(D^2\), so the next centre very probably lands there. The choice is random rather than "always the farthest point" on purpose: the farthest point is often an outlier, while sampling in proportion to \(D^2\) favours far regions that contain many points.

Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007) proved that this start alone, before any assign or move step, already gives \(\mathbb{E}[J]\le 8(\ln K+2)\,J_{\text{opt}}\). Random starts carry no such guarantee and can be arbitrarily bad. The cost is K passes over the data, repaid by fewer rounds afterwards. In practice both are also restarted several times and the run with the lowest \(J\) is kept.

Choosing K

\(J\) always falls when K grows, reaching zero at \(K=n\), so the lowest \(J\) cannot choose K. The usual tools are the elbow, the K after which the curve in the bottom picture flattens, and the silhouette, which compares each point's distance to its own cluster with its distance to the next nearest one. Neither is a proof. With the No Groups data set the elbow curve is smooth, which is the honest answer.

What it assumes

Because \(J\) uses plain squared distance, k-means prefers round groups of similar size and spread. It cuts long thin groups across the middle, splits a large group to tidy up two small ones, and cannot follow curved shapes at all. Rescaling one column changes the answer, so standardise features first. Gaussian mixtures relax the "round and equal" assumption, and DBSCAN drops the idea of a centre altogether.

Check yourself

k-means++ picks centres far from the existing ones. Why not simply always pick the single farthest point?

The farthest point from the current centres is very often an outlier: one stray point at the edge of the data. A centre placed on it is wasted. Sampling with probability proportional to squared distance means a far region with two hundred points is two hundred times more likely to receive the centre than one lonely point at the same distance. It is also what makes the proof of the 8(ln K + 2) guarantee work.

entries.title: A real job for k-means: fewer colours
entries.html:
A Real Job for k-Means: Fewer Colours

A photograph can contain tens of thousands of different colours. Treat every pixel as a point in red-green-blue space, run k-means, and repaint each pixel with the colour of its centre. The picture survives on K colours. Use the built-in picture or upload your own.

A box of crayons with only six crayons can still draw a recognisable landscape, as long as the six are well chosen: a sky blue, a leaf green, something for the roofs. Choosing those six is exactly a clustering problem. Pixels with similar colour should share one crayon, and each crayon should be the average of the pixels that use it, so that no pixel is repainted with a colour far from its own.

How it works, step by step

  1. Read every pixel as a point with three coordinates: red, green, blue.
  2. Pick K starting colours from the pixels (k-means++).
  3. Assign: give every pixel the nearest of the K colours.
  4. Move: change each of the K colours to the average of the pixels assigned to it.
  5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the picture stops changing.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The picture

Pixels
–
Different colours in the original
–
Colours after k-means
–
Bits per pixel, before → after
–
Average colour error (0 to 255 scale)
–
Rounds so far
–

Try this. Step through with K = 2, then 4, 8 and 16. At which K do you stop noticing the difference? Watch the colour cube while it runs: the rings slide into the dense strands of pixels. Then upload a photo of your own. Faces and skies need more colours than you expect, because smooth gradients break into bands.

The picture as data

A picture with \(n\) pixels becomes \(n\) points \(x_i=(r_i,g_i,b_i)\in[0,255]^3\). Where a pixel sits in the picture is ignored: only its colour matters. k-means with K centres \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K\) minimises

$$J=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert x_i-\mu_{c(i)}\rVert^2 ,$$

the total squared colour error of the repainted picture. Dividing by \(n\) and taking the square root gives the average colour error shown under the pictures. Nothing about the algorithm changes from the two-dimensional lesson: three coordinates instead of two.

Why this compresses

Storing a full-colour pixel takes 24 bits, eight for each of red, green and blue. After k-means each pixel only needs to say which of the K colours it uses, which takes \(\lceil\log_2 K\rceil\) bits, plus one small table of K colours for the whole picture. With \(K=16\) that is 4 bits per pixel, a sixth of the original. This is called vector quantisation, and the table of colours is the codebook or palette. The GIF image format works this way with up to 256 colours.

What to notice

The centres do not spread evenly through the colour cube. They go where the pixels are: a picture that is mostly sky spends several of its colours on slightly different blues, because that lowers \(J\) most. Small bright details, such as a red roof, get a colour of their own only when K is large enough that splitting a big region again would gain less than fixing the small one. Smooth gradients turn into visible bands, because nearby pixels with nearly equal colours fall on opposite sides of a boundary between two centres.

The same idea elsewhere

Replacing each item by the index of its nearest centre is used well beyond pictures: compressing audio, building visual "words" from image patches, speeding up nearest-neighbour search in large collections of embeddings (product quantisation), and the discrete codes of VQ-VAE models that you will meet in the generative part of this site.

Check yourself

Two pictures have the same number of pixels. One is a photo of a clear blue sky, the other a photo of a flower market. For the same K, which has the smaller colour error, and why?

The sky. Its pixels form one thin strand in colour space, so a few centres placed along that strand are close to every pixel. The flower market fills much more of the colour cube, so the same number of centres must each cover a wider range of colours and the average error is larger. How well k-means compresses depends on how concentrated the data is, not on how many points there are.

entries.title: Soft clusters: Gaussian mixtures and EM
entries.html:
Soft Clusters: Gaussian Mixtures and EM

k-means gives every point to exactly one cluster. A Gaussian mixture says each cluster is a bell shape, and lets a point belong 70% to one cluster and 30% to another. The EM algorithm fits it with two alternating steps. Start in one dimension, where every part of the idea can be seen, then move to two.

Suppose you measure the heights of a crowd without recording who is an adult and who is a child. The histogram has two humps. If you knew who belonged to which group, fitting a bell curve to each group would be easy. If you knew the two bell curves, you could say for any height how likely it is to be a child's. You know neither, so you guess the curves, compute everyone's probable group, refit the curves using those probabilities as weights, and repeat. That loop is the EM algorithm, and the pair of bell curves is a Gaussian mixture.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with K bell shapes: a centre, a spread and a weight for each.
  2. E-step: for every point, work out what share of it each bell is responsible for. Nothing moves; only the colours change.
  3. M-step: move each bell to the weighted average of its points, set its spread to their weighted spread, and set its weight to its share of all the points. Only the bells change.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the log-likelihood stops rising.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Rounds so far
–
Log-likelihood
–
Rise in the last round
–
Points shared between clusters (none above 90%)
–
Status
–

Try this. In One Dimension, press Start over and use One step. After each E-step look only at the colours of the dots and the band under them; after each M-step look only at how the curves moved. Put your point where two curves cross and read the top-right bar. Then choose Three Humps and set K to 3. In Two Dimensions, pick Three Stretched Groups with K = 3 and watch the ellipses turn; then restrict the shape to Circle and see what is lost. Seen as Hills shows the same fit as a landscape.

The model

The data are assumed to come from K Gaussians. Cluster \(k\) has a weight \(\pi_k\) (its share of the data, with \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\)), a mean \(\boldsymbol\mu_k\) and a covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_k\). The density of a point is

$$p(\mathbf x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k).$$

We want the parameters that maximise the log-likelihood of the data,

$$\ell=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k).$$

The sum inside the logarithm prevents a closed-form answer, which is why an iterative method is needed.

E-step: responsibilities

With the current parameters, Bayes' rule gives the probability that point \(i\) came from cluster \(k\):

$$r_{ik}=\frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j}\pi_j\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)} .$$

These are the colours in the picture: a point halfway between two clusters is drawn in a blend of their colours.

M-step: weighted fits

Treat each \(r_{ik}\) as a fraction of a point. With \(N_k=\sum_i r_{ik}\) the effective number of points in cluster \(k\),

$$\pi_k=\frac{N_k}{n},\qquad\boldsymbol\mu_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\,\mathbf x_i,\qquad\boldsymbol\Sigma_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\,(\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)(\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)^{\top}.$$

These are the ordinary maximum-likelihood formulas for a Gaussian from the first module, with every point counted according to its responsibility.

Why it works

Each E-step followed by an M-step can never lower \(\ell\). The E-step builds a lower bound on \(\ell\) that touches it at the current parameters, and the M-step moves to the top of that bound. So the curve in the lower right rises at every step and flattens at a local maximum. Like k-means, EM finds a local optimum that depends on the start, so it is usually started from a k-means++ seeding and restarted a few times.

How it relates to k-means

Force every covariance to be the same small circle, \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_k=\sigma^2\mathbf I\), and let \(\sigma\to0\). Each responsibility becomes 0 or 1, the E-step becomes "assign to the nearest centre" and the M-step becomes "move to the average". k-means is the hard, round limit of a Gaussian mixture. Choosing Circle in the controls shows the halfway case.

Cautions

A bell can shrink onto a single point, where its density, and with it the likelihood, grows without bound. Implementations add a small constant to the diagonal of each \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_k\), as this page does. More clusters always raise the likelihood, so K is chosen with a penalty for the number of parameters, such as BIC \(=-2\ell+p\log n\), or by likelihood on held-out data. And a mixture of Gaussians still cannot follow a curved shape such as the two moons with K = 2: it needs several bells per moon.

Check yourself

After EM converges, a point has responsibilities 0.5 and 0.5 for two clusters. k-means would have put it firmly in one. Which answer is more useful?

The 0.5 and 0.5 is information that k-means throws away: the model is telling you that this point is on the border and that its membership is uncertain. If a decision depends on the cluster, for example which offer to send a customer, knowing that the assignment is a coin flip matters. A hard label can always be recovered from the soft one by taking the larger share, but not the other way round.

entries.title: Build the family tree of the data
entries.html:
Build the Family Tree of the Data

There is no need to choose the number of clusters in advance. Start with every point alone, join the two closest clusters, and repeat until one remains. The record of who joined whom, and at what distance, is a tree called a dendrogram. Cutting it at any height gives a clustering.

Biologists do not sort animals into one fixed set of groups. They build a tree: house cats and lions join early, then cats with dogs, then all mammals, then mammals with birds. The tree holds every level of grouping at once, and you choose the level that suits your question. Hierarchical clustering builds the same kind of tree for any data, using nothing but the distances between points.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with every point as its own cluster.
  2. Measure the distance between every pair of clusters, using the linkage rule.
  3. Merge the closest pair, and draw the join on the tree at that distance.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until a single cluster is left.
  5. Cut the tree at any height: the branches below the cut are the clusters.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data

Clusters right now
–
Merges done
–
Distance of the latest merge
–
Largest jump in merge distance suggests
–

Try this. Step through the first ten merges on Three Round Groups: the early joins are tiny, and the last two are huge. That jump is how the tree tells you there are three groups. Then choose Two Moons with 40 or more points, finish the tree and cut it into 2, first with Single linkage and then with Complete. Only one of them follows the moons. Which, and why?

The agglomerative algorithm

Begin with \(n\) clusters, each holding one point. At every step find the two clusters \(A\) and \(B\) with the smallest distance \(d(A,B)\), merge them, and record the merge at height \(d(A,B)\). After \(n-1\) merges everything is in one cluster. Unlike k-means there is no random start: the same data and the same linkage always give the same tree.

Linkage: the distance between two clusters

Distance between two points is clear. Distance between two groups of points needs a rule, and the choice changes the result:

$$d_{\text{single}}(A,B)=\min_{a\in A,\,b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,\qquad d_{\text{complete}}(A,B)=\max_{a\in A,\,b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,$$$$d_{\text{average}}(A,B)=\frac{1}{|A|\,|B|}\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{b\in B}\lVert a-b\rVert,\qquad d_{\text{Ward}}(A,B)=\frac{|A|\,|B|}{|A|+|B|}\,\lVert\bar a-\bar b\rVert^2 .$$

Single linkage joins clusters that touch anywhere, so it can follow long curved chains, and for the same reason one stray point between two groups can bridge them. Complete linkage keeps every cluster compact and tends to break large groups. Average sits between the two. Ward merges the pair whose union adds least to the within-cluster sum of squares, the same quantity k-means minimises, and so gives round, even clusters.

Reading the dendrogram

Leaves along the bottom are the points. Each ∩-shaped join is one merge, and its height is the distance at which it happened. Short joins near the bottom connect near-identical points. A tall stretch of the tree with no joins means the clusters below it are far apart compared with their own size. Cutting there, with a horizontal line, gives a natural number of clusters: the number of vertical lines the cut crosses. The order of leaves left to right is partly arbitrary, since any join can be flipped, so only the heights carry meaning.

Cost

The method needs all \(\tfrac12 n(n-1)\) pairwise distances, so memory grows as \(n^2\) and a plain implementation takes about \(n^3\) time. It suits hundreds or a few thousand points, not millions. A merge can never be undone: an early mistake stays in the tree.

When to use it

When the number of clusters is unknown, when you want groups at several levels at once, or when you only have distances and no coordinates (for example edit distances between gene sequences). The dendrogram is itself a useful picture of the data.

Check yourself

On the two moons, single linkage recovers the two moons but average linkage does not. Explain in one sentence each.

Single linkage measures the gap between the nearest members of two clusters, and along each moon neighbouring points are closer to each other than to anything in the other moon, so each moon is chained together before the two ever join. Average linkage looks at all pairs of points, and the two halves of one moon are far apart on average, farther than half of one moon is from the nearby half of the other, so it merges pieces across moons.

entries.title: Clusters are crowded places
entries.html:
Clusters Are Crowded Places

DBSCAN has no centres and needs no K. It says a cluster is a region where points are packed densely, and it grows each cluster outward from point to point for as long as the crowd continues. Points in thin air are labelled noise. It can follow any shape.

Look at a satellite photo of a country at night. Cities are where the lights are packed together. You do not need to know how many cities there are, or what shape they have: you follow the lights, and a city ends where the lights thin out. A lone farmhouse is not a city. DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise) turns that into an algorithm with two numbers: how far to look, and how many lights count as "packed".

How it works, step by step

  1. Pick a point that has not been visited and count the points within distance ε of it, itself included.
  2. Fewer than minPts: mark it as noise for now and go back to step 1.
  3. At least minPts: it is a core point. Start a new cluster and put its neighbours in a queue.
  4. Take the next point from the queue and add it to the cluster. If it is a core point too, its neighbours join the queue. If not, it is a border point and the cluster does not spread through it.
  5. When the queue is empty the cluster is complete. Go back to step 1 until every point has been visited.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data

Points visited
–
Clusters found
–
Core points
–
Border points
–
Noise points
–

Try this. Step through the first cluster on Two Moons and watch the queue (gold rings) run along the moon without ever jumping the gap. Then drag ε slowly up: at what value do the two moons fuse into one cluster, and what does the right-hand plot show at that value? On Dense and Sparse Groups, try to find one ε that captures all three groups. You will not find one. That is the main weakness of DBSCAN.

The definitions

Fix a radius \(\varepsilon\) and a count \(\text{minPts}\). The \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood of a point is

$$N_\varepsilon(p)=\{q:\lVert p-q\rVert\le\varepsilon\},$$

which includes \(p\) itself. Every point is then one of three kinds:

  • Core point: \(|N_\varepsilon(p)|\ge\text{minPts}\). It sits inside a crowd.
  • Border point: not core, but inside the neighbourhood of some core point. It sits on the edge of a crowd.
  • Noise: neither. It belongs to no cluster.

A point \(q\) is density-reachable from a core point \(p\) if there is a chain \(p=p_1,p_2,\dots,p_m=q\) in which each point lies within \(\varepsilon\) of the one before and all of \(p_1,\dots,p_{m-1}\) are core points. A cluster is a core point together with everything density-reachable from it. The chain is what lets a cluster bend: each link is short, yet the two ends can be far apart.

The algorithm

The step list above is the whole algorithm. Each point's neighbourhood is computed once. With a spatial index that costs about \(n\log n\) in total; without one, \(n^2\). A border point within reach of two clusters goes to whichever reaches it first, which is the only way the result can depend on the order of the data.

Choosing the two numbers

minPts is usually set from the dimension \(d\) of the data: at least \(d+1\), and \(2d\) is a common default, larger for noisy data. Then for every point compute the distance to its minPts-th nearest neighbour and sort those distances, as in the right-hand picture. Points inside clusters have small values and stray points have large ones. A good ε sits at the bend between the long flat part and the steep rise. Points whose value lies above ε cannot be core points.

Strengths and limits

DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape, decides the number of clusters itself, and labels outliers instead of forcing them into a cluster, which also makes it a simple anomaly detector. Its limit is the single global ε: if one cluster is much denser than another, an ε small enough to separate the dense ones marks the sparse one as noise, and an ε large enough for the sparse one merges the dense ones. HDBSCAN and OPTICS address this by considering all values of ε at once. Distances also become less informative in very high dimensions, where every point is roughly as far from every other.

Check yourself

A point has only 3 neighbours within ε and minPts is 5, yet DBSCAN puts it in a cluster. How can that be?

It is a border point. It is not dense enough to be a core point itself, but it lies within ε of some core point, so it is density-reachable from that core point and joins its cluster. What it cannot do is extend the cluster: its own neighbours are not added to the queue. This is why a thin bridge of sparse points does not merge two clusters.

entries.title: PCA: find the direction that matters most
entries.html:
PCA: Find the Direction That Matters Most

Two measurements that rise and fall together are partly saying the same thing twice. Principal component analysis turns the axes to line up with the data, so that the first new axis carries as much of the spread as one number can, and the rest can be dropped with the least possible loss.

Hold a pencil under a lamp and look at its shadow on the table. Pointed at the lamp, the shadow is a dot and tells you nothing. Held sideways, the shadow shows the whole length. A shadow is a projection: it flattens the object and loses one dimension, and how much it loses depends on the direction. PCA asks for the direction of the lamp that keeps the longest shadow of the data. For a cloud of points, "longest" means the largest variance of the shadows.

How it works, step by step

  1. Centre: subtract the mean of each column, so the cloud sits on the origin.
  2. Compute the covariance matrix: the spread of each column and how they move together.
  3. Find the direction with the most spread. Here: start with any direction, multiply it by the covariance matrix, rescale, and repeat until it stops turning.
  4. The second component is the direction of most spread at right angles to the first.
  5. Project: keep each point’s position along the first component and drop the rest.

What just happened

Animation
Try a direction yourself

Move the slider and watch the gold curve: can you find its peak by hand?

The data

Angle of the line
–
Spread along the line (variance)
–
Share of the total spread kept
–
Spread lost (mean squared distance to the line)
–
Eigenvalues λ₁, λ₂
–
Angle of the first component
–

Try this. Before pressing anything, drag the angle slider and try to make the shadows as spread out as possible. Note your angle, then press Start over and step through: how close were you? Set the correlation to 0 and look at the two curves on the right. Why is there nothing for PCA to find? Finally choose A Curved Cloud: PCA still gives an answer. What does it miss?

Setting it up

Let \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\) be the points with their mean subtracted. The covariance matrix is

$$\mathbf S=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^{\top}.$$

Take a direction, a unit vector \(\mathbf w\). The shadow of \(\mathbf x_i\) on that direction is the number \(z_i=\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x_i\), and the variance of the shadows is

$$\operatorname{Var}(z)=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x_i)^2=\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf S\,\mathbf w .$$

This is the gold curve on the right, drawn for every angle.

The first component

We want to maximise \(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf S\mathbf w\) subject to \(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf w=1\). With a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\), setting the gradient of \(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf S\mathbf w-\lambda(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf w-1)\) to zero gives

$$\mathbf S\,\mathbf w=\lambda\,\mathbf w .$$

So the best direction is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix, and the variance it captures is \(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf S\mathbf w=\lambda\), its eigenvalue. The first principal component is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\). The second is the eigenvector with the next largest, and because \(\mathbf S\) is symmetric it is automatically at right angles to the first. In the Gaussian module these were the long and short axes of the covariance ellipse.

The same answer from the other side

By Pythagoras, for each centred point, (length)² = (shadow)² + (distance to the line)². The total of the left side is fixed by the data. So the direction that maximises the spread of the shadows is exactly the direction that minimises the total squared distance from the points to the line: the red curve is the gold curve turned upside down. PCA is at once "keep the most variance" and "the best-fitting line", where distance is measured at right angles to the line, not vertically as in regression.

How the direction is found

The animation uses power iteration. Start from any unit vector \(\mathbf w_0\) and repeat

$$\mathbf w_{t+1}=\frac{\mathbf S\,\mathbf w_t}{\lVert\mathbf S\,\mathbf w_t\rVert}.$$

Write \(\mathbf w_0\) as a mix of the eigenvectors. Each multiplication by \(\mathbf S\) stretches the part along the first eigenvector by \(\lambda_1\) and the rest by less, so after a few rounds the first eigenvector dominates. The error shrinks by a factor \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1\) every step: quickly for a long thin cloud, slowly for a nearly round one. Libraries use the singular value decomposition of the data matrix instead, which gives all components at once.

How much to keep

The total variance is \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\dots+\lambda_d\). Keeping the first \(m\) components keeps the share

$$\frac{\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_m}{\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_d},$$

and the mean squared reconstruction error is the sum of the eigenvalues that were dropped. The rebuilt point is \(\hat{\mathbf x}=\boldsymbol\mu+\sum_{k\le m}z_k\mathbf w_k\).

What PCA cannot see

PCA only looks at variances and covariances, so it only finds straight directions. On the curved cloud the data really has one degree of freedom, position along the curve, but no straight line captures it. PCA also knows nothing about labels: the direction of most spread need not be the direction that separates two classes. And it depends on units, since a column measured in millimetres has a thousand times the variance of the same column in metres. The next tab deals with that.

Check yourself

Regression of y on x and the first principal component both draw a line through the cloud. Are they the same line?

No. Regression minimises the vertical distances from the points to the line, because it treats x as given and y as the thing to predict. PCA minimises the perpendicular distances, treating both columns alike. The PCA line is steeper than the regression line of y on x whenever the points do not lie exactly on a line, and it lies between the regression of y on x and the regression of x on y.

entries.title: PCA on a real table: many columns into two
entries.html:
PCA on a Real Table: Many Columns Into Two

With two columns you can look at the cloud. With six or twelve you cannot, and that is where PCA earns its place: it finds the few combinations of columns that carry most of the variation, so a wide table can be drawn on one page. Use the built-in tables or upload your own.

A school report lists six marks for each student. If you had to describe a student with only two numbers, you would not pick two of the six subjects and discard the rest. You would say something like "overall, strong" and "better at sciences than at languages". Those are not columns of the table. They are combinations of columns, and they summarise the table well because the subjects are correlated. PCA finds such combinations automatically and tells you how much each one explains.

How it works, step by step

  1. Centre each column, and divide by its standard deviation so that units do not matter.
  2. Compute the correlation matrix: one number for every pair of columns.
  3. Find its eigenvectors, largest eigenvalue first. Each is a component: a recipe that mixes the columns.
  4. Read the scree plot and decide how many components to keep.
  5. Project: replace every row by its scores on the components you kept.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data

Rows
–
Columns
–
Spread carried by component 1
–
By components 1 and 2 together
–
Components needed for 90%
–

Try this. On the exam marks, step through and read the weights of component 1 and then component 2. One is "good at everything" and the other is "numbers against words": the table of six subjects is mostly two ideas. Now switch to Body Measurements and untick Standardise. Which column takes over component 1, and why? Then upload a table of your own with a header row.

From the table to the components

Let \(\mathbf X\) be the table with \(n\) rows and \(d\) columns. Standardise each column: \(z_{ij}=(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)/s_j\). The correlation matrix is

$$\mathbf R=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf Z^{\top}\mathbf Z,$$

a \(d\times d\) table whose entry \((j,k)\) is the correlation between columns \(j\) and \(k\). Its eigenvectors \(\mathbf w_1,\dots,\mathbf w_d\), ordered by eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d\), are the principal components. The entries of \(\mathbf w_k\) are called weights or loadings: how much of each column goes into component \(k\).

Scores

The score of row \(i\) on component \(k\) is \(t_{ik}=\mathbf w_k^{\top}\mathbf z_i\): multiply each standardised entry by its weight and add. The lower-left picture plots \((t_{i1},t_{i2})\) for every row. Two rows that are close in that picture are similar across all \(d\) columns, to the extent that two components capture the table.

The scree plot

With standardised columns each has variance 1, so the total is \(d\) and \(\sum_k\lambda_k=d\). Component \(k\) carries the share \(\lambda_k/d\). Plotting these shares in order gives the scree plot. Common rules for how many to keep: enough to reach 80 or 90% of the total; the components before the curve flattens; or those with \(\lambda_k>1\), meaning they carry more than one original column's worth. None is a law, and the right number depends on what the components are for.

Why standardise

Without it PCA uses the covariance matrix, and a column with large numbers dominates purely because of its units. Weight in kilograms with a standard deviation of 12 has a variance of 144; shoe size with a standard deviation of 2 has a variance of 4. Component 1 would be almost entirely weight. Standardise unless all columns share one unit and their differences in spread are meaningful.

Reading the arrows

In the lower-left picture each column is an arrow from the origin to its pair of weights on components 1 and 2. Arrows pointing the same way belong to columns that rise together. Arrows at right angles are unrelated, and opposite arrows are columns that trade off. A row lying far out along an arrow scores high on that column.

Cautions

Components are defined only up to sign: flipping all the weights of one component changes nothing. They are forced to be at right angles, which real underlying causes need not be, so the interpretation of a component is a suggestion and not a discovery. And a component with a small eigenvalue is not necessarily unimportant for a later prediction task: PCA never looked at any target.

Check yourself

A table has 10 columns and the first two components carry 95% of the spread. What does that tell you about the 10 columns?

That they are highly redundant. The rows lie very close to a flat two-dimensional sheet inside the ten-dimensional space, so the ten measurements are close to being ten different mixtures of only two underlying quantities plus a little noise. You could store two numbers per row and rebuild all ten columns with an error of 5% of the total variance.

entries.title: t-SNE: a map that keeps neighbours together
entries.html:
t-SNE: A Map That Keeps Neighbours Together

PCA can only cast a flat shadow. t-SNE gives up on preserving distances altogether and asks for less: points that are neighbours in the original space should be neighbours on the page. It starts from a random scatter and moves the points, a little at a time, until that is true.

Imagine seating guests at a wedding. You cannot reproduce on a floor plan every relationship among 150 people, but you can try to seat friends at the same table. You do not care how far table 3 is from table 9, only that each person sits near the people they are close to. t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) draws data this way. Here each "guest" is a 5 by 7 picture of a letter, a point with 35 coordinates, and the page has only two.

How it works, step by step

  1. In the original space, turn distances into probabilities: for each point, which others are its neighbours? Perplexity sets about how many.
  2. Drop all the points at random positions on the page.
  3. On the page, compute the same kind of neighbour probabilities, using a curve with heavier tails.
  4. Move every point: toward those it should be near but is not, away from those it sits near but should not.
  5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 a few hundred times.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Iterations
–
Mismatch (KL divergence)
–
Neighbours kept by t-SNE
–
Neighbours kept by PCA
–
Phase
–

Try this. Untick Show the True Letter, press Start over and run: the algorithm sees only grey dots, yet groups appear. Tick it again to check them. Then set perplexity to 2 and to 45 and compare the maps. Raise the pixel noise to 0.20: at what point do the groups dissolve? Run the same settings twice: the groups survive, but where they sit on the page does not. What does that say about reading distances between groups?

Step 1: neighbours in the original space

For each point \(i\), put a Gaussian on it and ask how much of its probability falls on each other point \(j\):

$$p_{j\mid i}=\frac{\exp\!\big(-\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j\rVert^2/2\sigma_i^2\big)}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp\!\big(-\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_k\rVert^2/2\sigma_i^2\big)},\qquad p_{ij}=\frac{p_{j\mid i}+p_{i\mid j}}{2n}.$$

Each point gets its own width \(\sigma_i\), chosen so that the distribution \(p_{\cdot\mid i}\) has a fixed perplexity \(2^{H(p_{\cdot\mid i})}\), where \(H\) is the entropy in bits. Perplexity is the effective number of neighbours: in a dense region \(\sigma_i\) comes out small, in a sparse one large, so every point ends up with about the same number of neighbours.

Step 3: neighbours on the page

For the positions \(\mathbf y_i\) on the page the same idea is used with a Student-t curve with one degree of freedom in place of the Gaussian:

$$q_{ij}=\frac{\big(1+\lVert\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j\rVert^2\big)^{-1}}{\sum_{k\ne l}\big(1+\lVert\mathbf y_k-\mathbf y_l\rVert^2\big)^{-1}} .$$

The heavy tails are the important design choice. In 35 dimensions a point can have many neighbours all at a moderate distance. On a flat page there is not enough room for that. With heavy tails, a moderate distance in the original space is matched by a much larger distance on the page, which gives the groups room to move apart instead of piling up in the middle (the "crowding problem").

Step 4: what is minimised

The positions are chosen to make \(Q\) resemble \(P\), measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence

$$C=\mathrm{KL}(P\,\Vert\,Q)=\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}},\qquad\frac{\partial C}{\partial\mathbf y_i}=4\sum_{j}(p_{ij}-q_{ij})\,\frac{\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j}{1+\lVert\mathbf y_i-\mathbf y_j\rVert^2}.$$

Read the gradient as forces. If \(p_{ij}>q_{ij}\) the two points are neighbours that sit too far apart, and they attract. If \(p_{ij}<q_{ij}\) they sit closer than they should, and they repel. Because the cost weights each term by \(p_{ij}\), putting true neighbours far apart is punished heavily, while putting strangers close costs little. t-SNE therefore protects local structure first.

Early exaggeration

For the first iterations every \(p_{ij}\) is multiplied by a constant (4 on this page). The attraction between neighbours is then far stronger than the repulsion, so tight clumps form while the map is still small and the clumps can slide past each other into a good arrangement. Then the factor is removed and the map relaxes.

How to read a t-SNE map

  • Trust: which points are grouped together.
  • Do not trust: the distance between groups, the size of a group, or its position. These change from run to run and with perplexity.
  • Perplexity between 5 and 50 is usual. Too small and the map shatters into fragments of a few points. Too large and distinct groups blur together. It must be smaller than the number of points.
  • The cost is not convex, so different random starts give different maps. Run it more than once.
  • There is no formula that places a new point on an existing map, unlike PCA.

UMAP

UMAP follows the same plan with different ingredients: a nearest-neighbour graph in place of the \(p_{ij}\), a different curve on the page, and a cost that is cheaper to optimise. It is much faster on large data and tends to keep somewhat more of the large-scale arrangement, but the same cautions about distances between groups apply.

Check yourself

On a t-SNE map, cluster A is twice as far from cluster B as from cluster C. Can you conclude that A is more similar to C than to B?

No. t-SNE is built to keep neighbours together and makes almost no attempt to preserve distances between points that are not neighbours. The heavy-tailed curve on the page deliberately stretches moderate distances by an amount that depends on local density, and the arrangement of groups changes between runs. To compare groups, go back to the original distances or use a method that preserves them, such as PCA.

entries.title: UMAP: draw the neighbour graph, then lay it out
entries.html:
UMAP: Draw the Neighbour Graph, Then Lay It Out

UMAP has the same aim as t-SNE: a flat map on which neighbours stay neighbours. It gets there by a different route. First it joins every point to its nearest neighbours to make a graph. Then it lays that graph out on the page with springs: joined points pull together, and random pairs push apart.

Think of a class of students and who is friends with whom. You can draw that as a network: a line between every pair of friends. To make the drawing readable you would put friends near each other and keep people who are not friends from landing on top of one another. UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) does this with data. The "friendships" are nearest neighbours in the original space, here the 35 pixels of each letter picture, and the drawing is the map.

How it works, step by step

  1. For each point, find its k nearest neighbours in the original space.
  2. Turn that into a weighted graph: the nearest neighbour gets weight 1, farther ones less, and each point uses its own scale.
  3. Drop all the points on the page.
  4. One epoch: pull together the two ends of each link, and for each pull push a few randomly chosen points away.
  5. Repeat step 4 with a step size that shrinks to zero. When it reaches zero the layout stops.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Epochs
–
Step size now
–
Links in the neighbour graph
–
Neighbours kept
–
Curve constants a, b
–
Status
–

Try this. Press Start over and use Ten epochs a few times: the graph is fixed from the start, and only the layout changes. Set the neighbours to 3 and run again: the map breaks into small pieces. Set it to 40: the groups hold together and start to merge. Then move the minimum distance from 0 to 0.9 and watch how tightly each group is packed. Notice how small the groups are next to the gaps between them: UMAP packs neighbours closely and leaves wide empty space, and the width of that space means nothing. Compare the finished map with the t-SNE tab for the same letters.

Step 1 and 2: the weighted neighbour graph
