For each point \(i\) take its \(k\) nearest neighbours. Let \(\rho_i\) be the distance to the very nearest one. The link from \(i\) to a neighbour \(j\) gets the weight

$$w_{j\mid i}=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\max(0,\;d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)-\rho_i)}{\sigma_i}\Big),$$

so the nearest neighbour always has weight 1, and \(\sigma_i\) is chosen for each point so that \(\sum_j w_{j\mid i}=\log_2 k\). A point in a sparse region gets a large \(\sigma_i\) and a point in a crowd a small one, so every point is connected about equally strongly whatever the local density. The two directions are then combined into one undirected weight,

$$w_{ij}=w_{j\mid i}+w_{i\mid j}-w_{j\mid i}\,w_{i\mid j},$$

the probability that at least one of the two directed links is present.

Step 4: similarity on the page

On the page, two points at distance \(d\) are given the similarity

$$q_{ij}=\frac{1}{1+a\,d^{\,2b}} .$$

The constants \(a\) and \(b\) are fitted so that this curve stays close to 1 up to the distance min_dist and then falls away, as in the top-right picture. With \(a=b=1\) it is exactly the heavy-tailed curve of t-SNE.

What is minimised

UMAP makes the page similarities match the graph weights by minimising a cross-entropy over all pairs:

$$C=\sum_{i\ne j}\Big[w_{ij}\log\frac{w_{ij}}{q_{ij}}+(1-w_{ij})\log\frac{1-w_{ij}}{1-q_{ij}}\Big].$$

The first term pulls linked points together. The second pushes unlinked points apart; t-SNE has no separate term of this kind. Computing the second term for all pairs would be slow, so UMAP uses negative sampling: each time it pulls a link, it also picks a few points at random and pushes them away. A random point is almost never a neighbour, so this approximates the second term at a small fraction of the cost.

Step 5: when does it stop?

The layout is found by stochastic gradient descent with a step size that falls in a straight line from its starting value to zero over a fixed number of epochs (300 here). UMAP does not test for convergence: it stops when the step size reaches zero. That is why the Status readout says "finished" and not "converged".

The two dials

n_neighbors sets the scale of structure that is kept. Small values look only at each point's closest few neighbours and give many small fragments. Large values tie distant points into the graph and show the broader arrangement, at the cost of fine detail. min_dist affects only the look of the map: near 0 the points of a group are packed into a tight clump, and larger values spread them out.

UMAP and t-SNE side by side

  • Both keep local neighbourhoods and both distort distances between far-apart groups. The cautions on the t-SNE tab apply here too.
  • UMAP works on a sparse graph of \(n\times k\) links instead of all \(n^2\) pairs, so it is much faster on large data.
  • UMAP usually starts from a spectral layout of the graph instead of a random scatter, which makes runs more alike. This page starts from a random scatter so that you can watch the map form.
  • A fitted UMAP can place new points on an existing map. Standard t-SNE cannot.
Check yourself

With n_neighbors = 3 the map of the letters breaks into more than six pieces. The data did not change. What did?

The graph. With only three neighbours per point, small groups of nearly identical pictures are linked among themselves and have no links to the rest of their own letter. Nothing pulls those fragments together, and the random pushes drive them apart. The map is a faithful drawing of a graph that is too sparse to show the six letters as six connected groups.

entries.title: Kernel PCA: straighten the data, then find its directions
entries.html:
Kernel PCA: Straighten the Data, Then Find its Directions

Ordinary PCA finds the straight direction along which the data vary most. That is no help when the structure is a ring inside a ring, or two interlocked crescents: no straight line tells the groups apart. Kernel PCA first measures how similar every point is to every other, and then runs PCA on the similarities. In effect it bends the space until the structure lies along straight axes.

Draw a small circle and a large circle around it on a sheet of rubber. No straight cut separates them. Now push the centre of the sheet up into a dome. The small circle rides up near the top and the large one stays low, and a horizontal slice separates them at once. Nothing about the points changed except the space they sit in. Kernel PCA never builds the dome explicitly. It only needs to know, for every pair of points, how similar they are, and that turns out to be enough to do PCA in the bent space.

How it works, step by step

  1. Choose a kernel: a rule that scores how similar two points are.
  2. Compute the similarity of every pair of points. With n points that is an n by n table.
  3. Centre the table, so that the cloud of points in the new space has its mean at the origin.
  4. Find the leading eigenvectors of the table. Each one assigns a number to every data point.
  5. Those numbers are the new coordinates: component 1, component 2, and so on.
  6. A new point is placed by comparing it with every data point.

What just happened

Animation
The kernel
Data

Variance in components 1 and 2 (of the bent space)
–
A cut on component 1 alone gets right
–
Best straight cut using components 1 and 2
–
Best straight cut in the original picture
–

Try this. On A Ring Inside a Ring, look at the shading for the nearness kernel: which component is high on one ring and low on the other? Press Run and watch the rings pull apart on the right. Switch the kernel to Plain. Can any cut along one axis separate the rings now? Go back to the nearness kernel and drag the reach down to 0.2 and up to 3. Where does the separation break down, and why at both ends? Try Polynomial on the rings. The squared terms a circle needs are inside that kernel, and still no straight cut on the first two components works. Why not? Then choose Two Crescents and hunt for a reach that separates them: there is a narrow window near 0.35, and it does not survive every new sample. Finally type your own point and see where it lands.

PCA written with inner products

Map each point to a new space, \(\mathbf x\mapsto\phi(\mathbf x)\), and do ordinary PCA there. Every principal direction is a combination of the mapped data points, \(\mathbf v=\sum_i\alpha_i\,\phi(\mathbf x_i)\), so everything can be written using only the inner products

$$K_{ij}=\phi(\mathbf x_i)^{\top}\phi(\mathbf x_j)=k(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j).$$

The function \(k\) is the kernel. If we can compute \(k\) directly, we never need \(\phi\). This is the kernel trick (Schölkopf, Smola and Müller, 1998).

Kernels on this page

$$k_{\text{RBF}}(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf z\rVert^2}{2s^2}\Big),\qquad k_{\text{poly}}(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)=(1+\mathbf x^{\top}\mathbf z)^2,\qquad k_{\text{plain}}(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)=\mathbf x^{\top}\mathbf z.$$

The slider is the reach \(s\). With the plain kernel the method is exactly ordinary PCA.

The algorithm

Centre the kernel matrix, which is the same as subtracting the mean in the new space:

$$\tilde{\mathbf K}=\mathbf K-\mathbf 1\mathbf K-\mathbf K\mathbf 1+\mathbf 1\mathbf K\mathbf 1,\qquad\mathbf 1_{ij}=\tfrac1n.$$

Solve the eigenproblem \(\tilde{\mathbf K}\boldsymbol\alpha_m=\lambda_m\boldsymbol\alpha_m\) and scale each \(\boldsymbol\alpha_m\) to length \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_m}\). The coordinate of any point \(\mathbf x\) on component \(m\) is then

$$z_m(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{m,i}\,\tilde k(\mathbf x,\mathbf x_i),$$

where \(\tilde k\) is the kernel centred in the same way. That formula works for points that were not in the data, which is how the shading and your own point are computed.

Choosing the reach

If the reach is very small, each point is similar only to itself. The kernel matrix is close to the identity, every direction is as good as any other, and the components pick out individual points. If the reach is very large, the kernel is nearly constant over the data and the method drifts back towards ordinary PCA. Useful structure appears when the reach is comparable to the distance between neighbouring points within a group and smaller than the distance between groups.

Cost and caveats

The eigenproblem is \(n\times n\), so the method costs \(O(n^3)\) and needs all the data kept in memory to place a new point. Unlike PCA, there is in general no way to map a point in the new space back to the original one. And the method is unsupervised: it does not know the groups. It keeps the directions of greatest variance in the bent space, which need not be the directions that separate anything. With the polynomial kernel on the rings, the squared radius is one of the available directions, but the first components are still dominated by plain \(x\) and \(y\), which vary more. On the crescents the nearness kernel separates the groups only for a narrow range of reach. The coloured dots and the "best single cut" readouts are there only so that you can judge the result.

Check yourself

With the nearness kernel and a reach of 3, the rings stop separating. The reach of 3 is larger than the whole data set. What has the kernel turned into?

When the reach is much larger than every distance in the data, the exponent is small everywhere and the kernel is approximately 1 minus the squared distance over 2s². After centring, the constant drops out and what remains behaves like the plain inner product of the points. So kernel PCA with a very long reach is close to ordinary PCA, and ordinary PCA cannot separate concentric rings because both rings have the same mean and vary equally in every straight direction.

entries.title: Factor analysis: the hidden causes behind things that move together
entries.html:
Factor Analysis: The Hidden Causes Behind Things That Move Together

Students who do well in algebra tend to do well in geometry. Students who read well tend to write well. Nobody can measure "mathematical ability" or "verbal ability" directly, but six test scores that rise and fall in two groups suggest that two hidden quantities are driving them. Factor analysis works backwards from the pattern of correlations to the hidden causes, and at the same time works out how much of each test is just its own noise.

A doctor cannot see "health" but can take a temperature, a pulse and a blood pressure, and knows these tend to go wrong together. Factor analysis treats every measurement as a sum of two things: a part driven by a few hidden quantities that many measurements share, and a private part that belongs to that measurement alone, such as a noisy thermometer. Things that move together are explained by the shared part. Everything else goes in the private part. The method is given only the measurements and has to deduce both.

How it works, step by step

  1. Guess the loadings (how each factor drives each test) and each test’s own noise.
  2. E-step: for every student, work out the most plausible values of the hidden factors given their scores and the current guess.
  3. M-step: with those factor values, refit the loadings as a regression of the scores on the factors.
  4. Set each test’s own noise to whatever variance the factors left unexplained.
  5. The model’s covariance is loadings × loadingsᵀ plus the noise on the diagonal. Compare it with the data.
  6. Repeat until the log-likelihood stops rising.

What just happened

Animation

The model
Data
Steps so far
–
Log-likelihood per student
–
Largest mismatch between the two grids
–
First principal component leans most on
–
First factor leans most on
–

Try this. Run it on Two Hidden Abilities and read the loadings: which tests share a factor? Set the number of factors to 1 and run again. Look at the right-hand grid: which block of the left grid can one factor not reproduce? Now choose One Unreliable Test, where the statistics exam was marked carelessly and its scores are very noisy. Compare the last two readouts. PCA chases the largest variance. Where does factor analysis put that noise instead? Untick the rotation box: the fit does not change at all. Why not?

The model

Each observation \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^p\) is generated from \(k$$\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_k),\qquad\mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf z+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Psi),\quad\boldsymbol\Psi\text{ diagonal}.$$

\(\boldsymbol\Lambda\) is the \(p\times k\) matrix of loadings and the diagonal entries of \(\boldsymbol\Psi\) are the uniquenesses. Integrating out \(\mathbf z\) gives the covariance the model implies:

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x)=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}+\boldsymbol\Psi.$$

All the correlation between different tests has to come from \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}\), because \(\boldsymbol\Psi\) only touches the diagonal.

Fitting by EM

The factors are hidden, so the model is fitted by expectation-maximization (Rubin and Thayer, 1982). With sample covariance \(\mathbf S\):

$$\textbf{E-step:}\quad\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}+\boldsymbol\Psi)^{-1},\qquad\mathbb E[\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x]=\boldsymbol\beta(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu),\qquad\mathbf C_{zz}=\mathbf I-\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\Lambda+\boldsymbol\beta\mathbf S\boldsymbol\beta^{\top}.$$$$\textbf{M-step:}\quad\boldsymbol\Lambda\leftarrow\mathbf S\boldsymbol\beta^{\top}\mathbf C_{zz}^{-1},\qquad\boldsymbol\Psi\leftarrow\operatorname{diag}\big(\mathbf S-\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\beta\mathbf S\big).$$

Each step cannot lower the log-likelihood

$$\ell=-\tfrac12\Big[p\log2\pi+\log\lvert\boldsymbol\Sigma\rvert+\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf S)\Big],\qquad\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}+\boldsymbol\Psi,$$

shown per student. The run stops when a step raises it by less than \(10^{-7}\). EM for factor analysis is slow near the end, so expect a few hundred steps.

How it differs from PCA

PCA looks for directions of largest total variance and makes no distinction between shared variation and private noise. If one test is very noisy, its variance is large and the first principal component points at it. Factor analysis gives every test its own noise term, so a noisy test gets a large uniqueness and is otherwise ignored. If all the uniquenesses are forced to be equal, factor analysis becomes probabilistic PCA.

Rotation

For any rotation \(\mathbf R\), the loadings \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf R\) give the same \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\top}\) and so exactly the same fit. The factors are identified only up to rotation. Analysts choose the rotation that is easiest to read. Varimax picks the one in which each test loads heavily on as few factors as possible, by maximizing the variance of the squared loadings within each factor. It changes the description, not the model.

How many factors

More factors always raise the likelihood. With \(p\) tests and \(k\) factors the model has \(pk+p-k(k-1)/2\) free parameters against \(p(p+1)/2\) covariances, so with six tests three factors already use up every degree of freedom, which is why the slider stops there. In practice the number is chosen by a likelihood-ratio test, an information criterion, or interpretability.

Check yourself

On One Unreliable Test, the first principal component leans most on the statistics exam, while the first factor does not. Both methods saw the same scores. Why do they disagree?

The statistics exam has by far the largest variance, because careless marking added a lot of random noise to it. PCA maximizes explained variance and has no way to tell shared variation from private noise, so its first direction points at the biggest variance it can find. Factor analysis has a separate noise term for every test. The statistics noise is uncorrelated with the other five tests, so no shared factor can explain it and it is absorbed into that test’s uniqueness. The factors are left to describe only what the tests have in common.

entries.title: Independent component analysis: unmixing two voices from two microphones
entries.html:
Independent Component Analysis: Unmixing Two Voices from Two Microphones

Two people talk at once in a room with two microphones. Each microphone records a different blend of the two voices. Nobody tells you what either voice sounds like or how they were blended. Independent component analysis recovers both voices anyway, from one assumption: the two sources have nothing to do with each other, and neither is plain Gaussian noise.

Mix two paints and you get a colour that looks more like mud than either original. Mixing independent signals does something similar: a blend of several independent things looks more like a bell curve than any one of them, which is the central limit theorem at work. So run the film backwards. Search for the two ways of combining the microphone recordings that look least like a bell curve. Those combinations must be the originals, because any leftover mixing would have made them more bell-shaped.

How it works, step by step

  1. Record the two mixtures. In the scatter plot they form a slanted parallelogram or blob.
  2. Centre the data and whiten it: rotate and rescale so that the cloud is round, with no correlation left.
  3. After whitening, the only freedom left is a rotation. Pick a starting angle.
  4. Measure how far from Gaussian each of the two outputs is, using kurtosis.
  5. Turn a little in the direction that makes the outputs less Gaussian.
  6. Stop when turning no longer helps. The two axes are now the sources.

What just happened

Animation

The room
Steps so far
–
Turning angle
–
Kurtosis of the two outputs
–
Match with the true sources
–
Match after whitening only (what PCA gives)
–
Match of the raw microphones
–

Try this. Press Run and watch three things: the cloud becoming round, then turning, and the bottom two traces on the right snapping into a clean hum and a clean sawtooth. Compare the last three readouts. Whitening alone is what PCA would give you. Is that enough? Slide the leak sliders to change the room and run again. Then choose Two Gaussian Noises. Look at the curve at the bottom right: where is its peak? What does the method do, and why can it not succeed here whatever the algorithm?

The model

Sources \(\mathbf s(t)\in\mathbb R^2\) with independent components are mixed by an unknown matrix:

$$\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf A\,\mathbf s(t).$$

We observe only \(\mathbf x\) and want an unmixing matrix \(\mathbf W\) with \(\mathbf y=\mathbf W\mathbf x\approx\mathbf s\). The order and scale of the sources can never be recovered, since any such change can be absorbed into \(\mathbf A\).

Step one: whitening

Subtract the mean and transform so that the covariance is the identity:

$$\mathbf z=\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf E^{\top}(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}),\qquad\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x)=\mathbf E\mathbf D\mathbf E^{\top}.$$

This is PCA followed by rescaling. It removes all correlation, and it does half the job: the sources themselves are uncorrelated with unit variance, so they must be a rotation of \(\mathbf z\). Uncorrelated is weaker than independent, though, and any rotation of \(\mathbf z\) is still uncorrelated. Second-order statistics cannot pick the right one.

Step two: the rotation

In two dimensions a rotation is one angle \(\theta\):

$$\mathbf y=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\mathbf z.$$

Choose the angle that makes the outputs as non-Gaussian as possible. This page measures that with the excess kurtosis, which is zero for a Gaussian:

$$\operatorname{kurt}(y)=\mathbb E[y^4]-3\quad(\text{for unit variance}),\qquad J(\theta)=\operatorname{kurt}(y_1)^2+\operatorname{kurt}(y_2)^2.$$

The curve at the bottom right is \(J(\theta)\). The run climbs it by gradient ascent and stops when the angle changes by less than \(10^{-4}\) radians. The curve repeats every 90°, because turning by a quarter-turn only swaps the outputs and flips a sign.

Why Gaussian sources cannot be separated

A whitened pair of independent Gaussians has a perfectly round distribution. Rotate it by any angle and it looks exactly the same. Every angle gives independent Gaussian outputs, the contrast \(J(\theta)\) is flat apart from sampling noise, and there is nothing to find. ICA can tolerate at most one Gaussian source.

Compared with PCA

PCA finds uncorrelated directions ordered by variance. ICA finds independent directions, which need not be at right angles in the original space and have no natural order. PCA uses the covariance only. ICA needs higher-order statistics, which is why it needs non-Gaussian data.

Beyond this page

The standard algorithm is FastICA (Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000), a fixed-point iteration that works in any number of dimensions and offers more robust measures of non-Gaussianity than kurtosis, which is sensitive to outliers. Real rooms add echoes and delays, so real audio needs convolutive versions of the model. ICA is routinely used to remove eye-blink artefacts from brain recordings and to find independent spatial patterns in brain imaging.

Check yourself

After whitening, the two signals are uncorrelated. Why is that not the same as having separated the sources?

Uncorrelated only means there is no straight-line relationship between the two signals. Independent means that knowing one tells you nothing at all about the other. Every rotation of a whitened cloud is still uncorrelated, so whitening leaves a whole circle of candidate answers, and only one orientation (up to swaps and signs) makes the outputs independent. You can see it in the scatter plot: after whitening the cloud is round overall but its sharp edges are tilted. Turning until the edges line up with the axes is the step that correlation cannot do and higher-order statistics can.

entries.title: Anomaly detection: finding the points that do not belong
entries.html:
Anomaly Detection: Finding the Points That Do Not Belong

A fraudulent card payment, a failing engine bearing, a typing error in a database. Nobody hands you labelled examples of what is wrong, and there are too few of them to learn from anyway. Anomaly detection works from the other end: learn what normal looks like, and flag whatever is far from it. Three ways of measuring "far" live on this page, and they do not always agree.

Play twenty questions to single out one person in a crowd. For someone ordinary you need many questions, because whatever you ask, plenty of others give the same answer. For the one person wearing a diving suit you need one. Being easy to describe apart from everyone else is what it means to be unusual. An isolation forest plays this game with random questions, many times over, and counts how quickly each point ends up alone.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a random handful of the data.
  2. Pick a feature at random and a cut point at random between its smallest and largest value. That splits the handful in two.
  3. Keep cutting each part the same way until every point is alone. This is one tree.
  4. Count how many cuts it took to isolate each point. A point far from the rest is cut off early.
  5. Build many trees and average the counts.
  6. Short average path = easy to isolate = anomaly. Flag the points with the shortest paths.

What just happened

Animation

Flagging
Data

Trees in the forest
–
Points flagged
–
Planted anomalies caught
–
Normal points flagged by mistake
–
Ranking quality (1 = every anomaly ranked above every normal point)
–

Try this. Press Add one tree a few times and watch the cuts that isolate your point. Click far from the data, then in the middle of a cloud, and compare the number of cuts. Now press Run and watch the shading settle as trees are added. On A Curved Band, switch between the three methods. One of them shades the hollow inside the curve as perfectly normal, one flags it firmly, and one is unsure. Which is which, and why? On Two Clouds, compare how the three treat the gap between the clouds. Then drag the flagging slider: the method ranks points, and you decide where to draw the line.

The setting

We have data \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\), mostly normal, with no labels. The goal is a score \(s(\mathbf x)\) that is high for points unlike the bulk. A threshold on the score, or a fixed share of points to flag, turns the ranking into decisions. Where to put the threshold is a judgement about costs: a missed fraud against a blocked customer.

Distance from the centre

Fit one Gaussian to all the data and measure how many standard deviations away each point is, allowing for the shape of the cloud. This is the Mahalanobis distance:

$$s(\mathbf x)=\sqrt{(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\top}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)}.$$

It is fast and easy to explain, and it assumes that normal data form a single elliptical cloud. When they do not, the centre may be an empty place that the method considers the most normal of all.

Distance to neighbours

Score each point by the distance to its \(k\)-th nearest neighbour:

$$s(\mathbf x)=\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf x_{(k)}\rVert.$$

Normal points have close neighbours and anomalies do not. This follows any shape, since it is purely local. It needs a meaningful distance, costs \(O(n)\) per query without an index, and depends on \(k\): with \(k=1\), two anomalies that happen to sit side by side hide each other.

Isolation forest

Each tree is built on a random subsample of \(\psi\) points by recursive random cuts (Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008). Let \(h(\mathbf x)\) be the number of cuts on the path that isolates \(\mathbf x\). The score compares its average over the trees with the average path length in a random tree of \(\psi\) points:

$$s(\mathbf x)=2^{-\mathbb E[h(\mathbf x)]/c(\psi)},\qquad c(\psi)=2H(\psi-1)-\frac{2(\psi-1)}{\psi},\qquad H(i)\approx\ln i+0.5772.$$

Scores near 1 are anomalies, scores well below 0.5 are ordinary, and if every score is near 0.5 there are no clear anomalies. No distances are computed, which keeps the method fast in many dimensions, and small subsamples work well because anomalies are isolated early in any case. Here \(\psi=64\). The cuts are parallel to the axes, and that is a real weakness. A point in the hollow of a curve, or in the gap between two clouds, has data on both sides of it along every single coordinate, so random cuts do not isolate it quickly, and the forest is less sure about it than the neighbour method is.

Judging a detector

The page planted a few anomalies so that the result can be checked. The ranking quality readout is the area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen planted anomaly scores higher than a randomly chosen normal point. It does not depend on the threshold. In real use there are no planted answers, and evaluation is the hardest part of the problem.

When the run stops

The forest keeps growing until the set of flagged points has not changed for 25 trees in a row, with at least 40 trees, or until it reaches 200.

Things that go wrong

Features on very different scales distort every distance, so standardize first. In many dimensions distances concentrate and everything looks equally far from everything else. If anomalies are common enough to form their own cluster, they stop being isolated and look normal. And a point can be unusual without being wrong: the detector raises a flag, and a person or a second system has to decide what it means.

Check yourself

On A Curved Band, the distance-from-the-centre method rates a point in the hollow of the curve as completely normal, the neighbour method flags it firmly, and the isolation forest is somewhere in between. No data point is anywhere near it. What explains the three answers?

The Mahalanobis distance assumes the normal data form one elliptical cloud around their mean. For a curved band the mean lies in the hollow, where there are no data at all, and the fitted ellipse covers the hollow and the band alike. So the emptiest region gets the best score. The neighbour method makes no assumption about overall shape. It asks only whether there are data points nearby, and in the hollow there are none, so it flags the point. The isolation forest asks how quickly random cuts parallel to the axes leave the point alone. The hollow has data to its left, to its right and above it, so a cut in either coordinate usually leaves some of the band on the same side, and the point takes longer to isolate than a true outsider would. Its score rises, but not as far.

entries.title: Watch a network learn a shape
entries.html:
Watch a Network Learn a Shape

A single neuron can only draw one straight edge. Put a few of them in a layer, feed that layer into another, and the edges combine into curves, rings and spirals. Here you can watch that happen: the picture inside each neuron shows what that neuron has learned to respond to.

Think of a sculptor who may only make straight cuts. One cut divides the block in two: that is one neuron. Three cuts can leave a triangle standing. With enough cuts, and a second sculptor who combines the pieces the first one made, any shape can be carved. A neural network works the same way. The first hidden layer makes straight cuts through the input space, and each later layer combines the pieces from the layer before into more elaborate regions.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with random weights. The answer is a meaningless smear.
  2. Forward pass: every point flows through the network, left to right, and comes out as a number between 0 and 1.
  3. Loss: compare those numbers with the true colours.
  4. Backward pass: work out how each weight should change to lower the loss, and nudge them all.
  5. Repeat. Stop when the loss stops falling.

What just happened

Animation

The network
The data
Epochs
–
Training loss
–
Test loss
–
Training accuracy
–
Test accuracy
–
Weights and biases in the network
–
Status
–

Try this. On the ring, set one hidden layer with 1 neuron, then 2, then 3, and train each time. How many neurons does it take to close a ring, and what do their little pictures look like? Then choose Two Spirals: one layer of 8 struggles, while three layers of 8 can do it. Watch the pictures inside the neurons get more complicated from left to right.

One neuron

A neuron takes its inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the total through an activation function \(\phi\):

$$a=\phi\big(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b\big).$$

The set of points where \(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b=0\) is a straight line, and the neuron is "on" on one side and "off" on the other. Look at any neuron in the first hidden layer: its picture is always a straight edge.

Layers

A layer is many neurons reading the same inputs. Stacking the weights into a matrix \(\mathbf W^{(l)}\) and the biases into a vector \(\mathbf b^{(l)}\),

$$\mathbf a^{(0)}=\mathbf x,\qquad\mathbf a^{(l)}=\phi\big(\mathbf W^{(l)}\mathbf a^{(l-1)}+\mathbf b^{(l)}\big),\qquad\hat y=\sigma\big(\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf a^{(L)}+b\big),$$

where the final \(\sigma\) is the logistic function, so that \(\hat y\) is the probability of the gold class. A neuron in layer 2 takes a weighted sum of the straight-edge pictures from layer 1 and bends the result, which is how corners and closed regions appear.

Why the activation must bend

If \(\phi\) were the identity, each layer would be a linear map, and a stack of linear maps is one linear map: \(\mathbf W^{(2)}\mathbf W^{(1)}\mathbf x\). The whole network would be a single straight cut, however deep. The non-linear activation is what lets layers build on one another.

What training does

The loss is the average log loss (cross-entropy) over the training points,

$$\mathcal L=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[y_i\log\hat y_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat y_i)\big].$$

Each epoch computes the gradient of \(\mathcal L\) with respect to every weight by backpropagation (its own tab) and moves the weights a small step against it. This page uses the Adam optimiser from the Foundations module. Training stops here when the loss has stopped falling.

Width and depth

More neurons in a layer give more cuts to work with. More layers let cuts be combined into pieces, and pieces into shapes, so a deep network can describe some shapes with far fewer neurons than a wide shallow one. The count of weights grows quickly: a layer of \(m\) neurons reading \(n\) inputs has \(m(n+1)\) parameters. When the network is much larger than the data needs, training loss keeps falling while test loss turns back up: the same overfitting you saw with polynomials.

Check yourself

A network with one hidden layer of 2 tanh neurons cannot separate the ring from its core. Why not?

Each first-layer neuron makes one straight cut, so two neurons give two lines. The output can only combine "which side of line 1" and "which side of line 2", and no region bounded by two lines is closed: it always runs off to infinity somewhere. Closing a region around the core takes at least three cuts, which is why three neurons are the minimum.

entries.title: Backpropagation: follow one example through, and back
entries.html:
Backpropagation: Follow One Example Through, and Back

Training a network means answering one question for every weight: if I nudge this weight up a little, does the error go up or down, and by how much? Backpropagation answers it for all weights in one backward sweep. Here a tiny network decides whether to take an umbrella, and every number is on the screen.

A restaurant serves a dish that is too salty. The head chef does not retrain the whole kitchen. She asks who added salt, and how much each contributed. The cook who made the sauce is mostly responsible; the one who salted the pasta water, a little. Each of them then asks the same of whoever supplied their ingredients. Blame is passed backward along the same routes the ingredients travelled forward, shared out in proportion to how much each route mattered. That is backpropagation. The dish is the output, the saltiness is the error, and the routes are the weights.

How it works, step by step

  1. Put the inputs in.
  2. Forward: hidden neuron 1 takes a weighted sum of the inputs and squashes it. Then hidden neuron 2 does the same.
  3. Forward: the output neuron does the same with the two hidden values. That is the network’s answer.
  4. Compare the answer with what really happened: the loss.
  5. Backward: how much is the output neuron to blame?
  6. Backward: so how should each weight into the output change?
  7. Backward: pass the blame to hidden neuron 1, then to hidden neuron 2, along the weights that connect them.
  8. Backward: so how should each weight into the hidden neurons change?
  9. Update: move every weight a small step against its gradient. Then start again.

What just happened

Animation

The example
The model
Network’s answer: chance of rain
–
What really happened
–
Loss ½(answer − truth)²
–
Updates so far
–
Status
–

Try this. Press Start over and use One step. Each press does one small calculation: watch the packets travel, then read the lines that appear under the picture, where the formula is filled in with the numbers from the picture. Twelve presses make one full update. Then press Run. After two full updates it speeds up, and you can watch the loss fall and the nine weights drift until it converges. Switch to It Stayed Dry: which weights reverse direction?

The forward pass

This network has inputs \(x_1,x_2\), two hidden neurons with \(\tanh\), and one sigmoid output:

$$z_j=w_{j1}x_1+w_{j2}x_2+b_j,\quad h_j=\tanh z_j,\qquad z_o=v_1h_1+v_2h_2+c,\quad\hat y=\sigma(z_o),\qquad L=\tfrac12(\hat y-y)^2 .$$

The backward pass is the chain rule

We want \(\partial L/\partial\) (every weight). Define the "blame" of a neuron as the derivative of the loss with respect to its total input, \(\delta=\partial L/\partial z\). For the output neuron,

$$\delta_o=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat y}\cdot\frac{\partial\hat y}{\partial z_o}=(\hat y-y)\;\hat y(1-\hat y).$$

A weight's gradient is the blame of the neuron it feeds, times the value that travelled along it:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_j}=\delta_o\,h_j,\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}=\delta_o .$$

The blame of a hidden neuron is the output's blame, carried back along the connecting weight and multiplied by the slope of the hidden neuron's own activation:

$$\delta_j=\delta_o\,v_j\,\big(1-h_j^2\big),\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{ji}}=\delta_j\,x_i,\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j}=\delta_j .$$

The general rule

For any layered network the same two lines repeat from the last layer to the first:

$$\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}=\big(\mathbf W^{(l+1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(l+1)}\big)\odot\phi'\big(\mathbf z^{(l)}\big),\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf W^{(l)}}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}\,\mathbf a^{(l-1)\top}.$$

One forward pass stores the values, one backward pass reuses them, and the cost of getting every gradient is about the same as computing the output once. Without this, each weight would need its own forward pass, which for a network with a million weights would be a million times slower.

The update

Every parameter then takes a step against its gradient, \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\partial L/\partial\theta\), with learning rate \(\eta\). The table lists all nine. On this page the loop stops when the loss is below 0.0005, where the answer is within about three percentage points of the truth.

What to notice

The gradient of a weight is a product of three kinds of factor: an error, some weights along the way, and slopes of activations. If the output is saturated, \(\hat y(1-\hat y)\) is near zero and everything behind it learns slowly even when the answer is badly wrong. If an input is 0, the weights leaving it get zero gradient and do not move. And a neuron connected to the output by a large weight receives a large share of the blame. The Activation Functions tab shows what these products do in a deep network.

Check yourself

Set cloud cover to 0 and step through. The two weights leaving that input have gradient exactly 0, whatever the error. Why, and is that a problem?

The gradient of a weight is the blame of the neuron it feeds times the value carried along it, and that value is 0. Changing the weight would change nothing about this prediction, so this example gives no information about it. It is not a problem in practice: other training examples have non-zero cloud cover and will move those weights. It is one reason inputs are usually centred so that they are not stuck at zero.

entries.title: The bend in every neuron
entries.html:
The Bend in Every Neuron

After a neuron adds up its inputs, it passes the total through a small curve called the activation function. That curve is what lets a network learn anything other than straight lines. Its slope also decides how well the learning signal survives the trip back through many layers. Send the signal back and watch what each curve does to it.

Photocopy a page, then photocopy the copy, and keep going. If each copy keeps only a quarter of the ink, the tenth copy is blank. If each keeps all of it, the tenth is as sharp as the first. Training a deep network sends a learning signal backward through every layer, and at each layer the signal is multiplied by the slope of the activation function. A curve whose slope is always small is a bad photocopier.

How it works, step by step

  1. Build a deep stack of layers with random weights and this activation, and send data forward through it.
  2. Start the learning signal (the gradient) at the last layer with strength 1.
  3. Step back one layer: the signal is multiplied by the weights and by the slope of the activation at every neuron.
  4. Keep stepping back. Slopes below 1 shrink it every time.
  5. Read the strength that reaches the first layer. That is how fast the first layer can learn.

What just happened

Animation
The network
Curve at the dot
–
Slope at the dot
–
Largest slope this curve ever has
–
Signal reaching the first layer
–
Average change per layer
–

Try this. Choose Sigmoid with 12 layers and send the signal back. How much of it reaches the first layer? Try tanh, then ReLU. Now make the network 24 layers deep and compare again. Finally, with Sigmoid, raise the size of the weights to 2.5: does that rescue it? Look at where the dot spends its time on the left picture to see why not.

The four curves

$$\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad\tanh(z)=\frac{e^{z}-e^{-z}}{e^{z}+e^{-z}},\qquad\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z),\qquad\mathrm{LeakyReLU}(z)=\max(0.1z,\;z).$$

Their slopes are

$$\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)\le\tfrac14,\qquad\tanh'(z)=1-\tanh^2(z)\le1,\qquad\mathrm{ReLU}'(z)=\begin{cases}1&z>0\\0&z\le0\end{cases},\qquad\mathrm{LeakyReLU}'(z)=\begin{cases}1&z>0\\0.1&z\le0.\end{cases}$$

Why the slope matters

Backpropagation gives the blame at layer \(l\) as

$$\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}=\big(\mathbf W^{(l+1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(l+1)}\big)\odot\phi'\big(\mathbf z^{(l)}\big).$$

Going back through \(k\) layers multiplies by \(k\) weight matrices and \(k\) sets of slopes. With the sigmoid every slope is at most \(\tfrac14\), so unless the weights are large the signal shrinks geometrically: this is the vanishing gradient. The first layers then learn thousands of times more slowly than the last, and a deep sigmoid network barely trains. Making the weights larger does not help, because large inputs push the sigmoid into its flat ends, where the slope is nearly zero (saturation).

Why ReLU changed things

For positive inputs ReLU has slope exactly 1, so the signal passes through unchanged, and nothing saturates on that side. About half the neurons are off for any given input, and those pass nothing, but the paths that remain open carry the signal at full strength. With suitably scaled weights the overall strength stays roughly constant however deep the network. ReLU is also cheap to compute. Its weakness is the dead neuron: one whose input is negative for every training example has slope 0 everywhere and never updates again. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope on the negative side so that such a neuron can recover.

Choosing one

  • Hidden layers: ReLU or a close relative (Leaky ReLU, GELU, SiLU) by default.
  • tanh: still used where outputs centred on zero matter, as in recurrent networks. It is better than the sigmoid for hidden layers because its slope reaches 1 and its output averages near zero.
  • Sigmoid: for an output that must be a probability, and for gates. Avoid it in deep hidden layers.
  • Output layer: chosen by the task, not by the trainability of the network: sigmoid for yes or no, softmax for one of many, none for a number.

What this page computes

The right-hand picture is a real calculation: a stack of layers 40 neurons wide with random weights of variance (size)²/40, fifty random inputs sent forward, and a random signal sent backward by the formula above. Each bar is the root-mean-square size of the signal at that layer. The Weight Initialization tab shows how the size of the weights should be chosen for each activation.

Check yourself

With the sigmoid, the gradient shrinks by roughly a factor of four or more per layer. A colleague suggests multiplying the learning rate of the early layers by a large number to compensate. What is wrong with that?

The factor differs from layer to layer, from weight to weight and from one moment in training to the next, so no fixed multiplier is right for long. A gradient that has shrunk by a factor of a million has also lost its information to rounding and noise. Fixing the cause works better: use an activation whose slope is 1 over much of its range, initialise the weights to preserve the signal, and add skip connections or normalisation in very deep networks.

entries.title: Where to start: the first weights decide whether it can learn
entries.html:
Where to Start: The First Weights Decide Whether It Can Learn

Before training, every weight is set to a small random number. How small matters a great deal. Too small, and the signal fades to nothing on its way through the layers. Too large, and it blows up or jams every neuron at its limit. Send a signal through ten layers and see which starting scale keeps it alive.

Line up ten people to pass a message by whispering. If each person speaks a little more quietly than they heard, the last one hears nothing. If each speaks a little louder, the last one is being shouted at and cannot make out a word. The message survives only if each person repeats it at the volume they heard it. The layers of a network are that line of people, the starting weights set each one's volume, and the goal of a good initialisation is to make every layer pass the signal on at the strength it arrived.

How it works, step by step

  1. Draw every weight at random with the chosen spread.
  2. Send 50 random inputs into the first layer.
  3. Forward, one layer at a time: each neuron adds up its weighted inputs and applies the activation. Watch the histogram.
  4. At the last layer, start a learning signal and send it backward, one layer at a time.
  5. Compare the first layer with the last: a healthy start keeps both the outputs and the learning signal about the same size everywhere.

What just happened

Animation
The network
Weight variance × inputs
–
Spread of outputs, first layer
–
Spread of outputs, last layer
–
Learning signal at the first layer, relative to the last
–
Verdict
–

Try this. With tanh, press Too Small and watch the histograms collapse to a spike at zero. Press Too Large: every neuron is jammed at −1 or +1. Xavier keeps a healthy spread. Now switch the activation to ReLU and press Xavier again: the signal fades, because ReLU throws away half of it at every layer. Press He. What number did He change, and why that number?

How the spread changes from layer to layer

Take a neuron with \(n\) inputs, each of variance \(\operatorname{Var}(a)\), and weights drawn independently with mean 0 and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(w)\). Its total input \(z=\sum_i w_ia_i\) has

$$\operatorname{Var}(z)=n\,\operatorname{Var}(w)\,\mathbb E[a^2].$$

So each layer multiplies the size of the signal by the factor \(n\operatorname{Var}(w)\), adjusted for what the activation does. Across \(L\) layers the factors multiply. A factor of 0.5 per layer leaves \(0.5^{10}\approx0.001\) after ten layers; a factor of 2 gives about 1000. Only a factor of 1 is stable.

Xavier (Glorot) initialisation

Near zero, \(\tanh(z)\approx z\), so the activation passes the signal through nearly unchanged and the factor is \(n\operatorname{Var}(w)\). Setting it to 1 gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(w)=\frac{1}{n_{\text{in}}}\qquad\text{or, balancing forward and backward,}\qquad\operatorname{Var}(w)=\frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}}} .$$

He (Kaiming) initialisation

ReLU sets every negative input to zero. For inputs symmetric around zero that removes half of \(\mathbb E[a^2]\), so the factor is \(\tfrac12 n\operatorname{Var}(w)\). Setting that to 1 gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(w)=\frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}} .$$

The slider on this page is \(n\operatorname{Var}(w)\): Xavier is 1 and He is 2.

The backward direction

The learning signal obeys the same arithmetic going the other way: at each layer it is multiplied by the weights and by the slope of the activation. If the forward signal vanishes, so does the gradient (vanishing gradients), and the early layers do not learn. If it explodes, the first update throws the weights far away (exploding gradients). With tanh and weights that are too large there is a third failure: the forward signal looks fine in size, because tanh is bounded, but every neuron sits at −1 or +1 where the slope is nearly zero, so the gradient still dies. The histograms piled up at the two ends are the sign of that.

Two things that are never done

Starting all weights at zero, or at the same value, makes every neuron in a layer compute the same thing and receive the same gradient, so they stay identical for ever: the layer behaves as one neuron. Randomness is needed to break the symmetry. Biases, on the other hand, are usually started at zero.

In practice

Libraries pick He for ReLU-type layers and Xavier for tanh by default. Batch normalisation and residual connections make deep networks far less sensitive to the starting scale, by rescaling the signal at every layer or by giving it a path around the layers.

Check yourself

A ten-layer ReLU network is initialised with Xavier variance 1/n instead of He variance 2/n. Roughly how much smaller is the signal at the last layer than it should be?

With ReLU each layer multiplies the variance of the signal by one half of n × Var(w). With He that is ½ × 2 = 1. With Xavier it is ½ × 1 = ½. After ten layers the variance is (½)¹⁰, about a thousandth, so the typical size of the signal (the standard deviation) is about 1/32 of what it should be. The gradient is reduced by a similar factor on the way back.

entries.title: Dropout: train with half the team missing
entries.html:
Dropout: Train with Half the Team Missing

A large network given a small, noisy set of examples will memorise them, mistakes included. Dropout is a simple cure: during every training step, switch off a random share of the neurons. No neuron can rely on any other being there, so the network has to learn the pattern in many overlapping ways. Two identical networks train here side by side, one with dropout and one without.

Imagine a team where one brilliant member knows everything and the rest have learned to pass every question to her. The team does well until the day she is away. Now imagine a manager who sends a random half of the team home each day. Nobody can depend on anyone in particular, so everyone has to become competent, and knowledge ends up spread across the team with plenty of overlap. On the day that matters, everyone comes in. That is dropout: the team is the layer, the members are neurons, and the days with absences are training steps.

How it works, step by step

  1. Give two identical networks the same small, noisy training set.
  2. Normal training: every neuron takes part in every step.
  3. Dropout training: before each example, switch off each hidden neuron with probability p, and scale up the ones that remain.
  4. Both networks update their weights. Repeat for many epochs.
  5. To predict, switch every neuron back on. Compare the two networks on data they have not seen.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Epochs
–
Normal: accuracy on training / new data
–
Dropout: accuracy on training / new data
–
Normal: loss on new data
–
Dropout: loss on new data
–

Try this. Run it and watch the left half: after a while it grows small islands around the wrongly labelled points, and the red curve on the right turns upward. The right half stays smooth. Set p to 0 and train again: the two halves now agree. Set p to 0.8: is more always better? Then raise the training points to 200. Does dropout still matter as much?

What it does during training

For each training example and each hidden neuron, draw a mask \(m_j\) that is 0 with probability \(p\) and 1 otherwise, and replace the neuron's output \(a_j\) by

$$\tilde a_j=\frac{m_j}{1-p}\,a_j .$$

The division by \(1-p\) (called inverted dropout) keeps the expected output the same, \(\mathbb E[\tilde a_j]=a_j\), so the next layer sees inputs of the usual size. Backpropagation uses the same mask: a neuron that was off receives no gradient on that step.

What it does at prediction time

Nothing. All neurons are on and no scaling is needed, because the scaling was already applied in training. The decision regions drawn on this page are the prediction-time network.

Why it works

Three ways to see it, all saying the same thing.

  • No co-adaptation. A neuron cannot rely on a specific partner, because that partner is absent a share \(p\) of the time. Fragile arrangements of neurons that fit a single odd training point do not survive.
  • An ensemble for the price of one. Each mask defines a different thinned network. With \(H\) hidden neurons there are \(2^H\) of them, all sharing weights. Training with dropout trains them all a little, and predicting with every neuron on approximates averaging their answers. Averaging many models reduces variance, as bagging did.
  • Noise as a penalty. Adding noise to the hidden layer makes solutions that depend on large, finely balanced weights perform badly, which pushes the network toward smaller, more evenly spread weights, much as an L2 penalty does.

The cost

Dropout makes the training loss noisier and higher, and training takes longer. If \(p\) is too large the network does not have enough capacity left on each step and underfits. Typical values are 0.5 for large fully connected layers and 0.1 to 0.3 elsewhere. With plenty of data there is little overfitting to cure and dropout helps less.

Batch normalisation, briefly

Batch normalisation is a different technique that is often mentioned alongside dropout. It rescales the inputs of each layer to mean 0 and variance 1 over the current mini-batch, then lets the layer learn its own scale and shift. Its main effect is to make deep networks train faster and more reliably, and the noise from using batch statistics also regularises a little. It does not have its own animation on this site yet.

Check yourself

With dropout the training loss is higher than without, yet the test loss is lower. How can a model that fits the training data worse be the better model?

The training set here contains wrongly labelled points. Fitting them perfectly means bending the boundary around each one, and those bends are wrong for new data. Dropout makes such narrow, single-point fits unstable, because the few neurons that would encode them are often switched off, so the network keeps only the broad pattern that many neurons agree on. Its higher training loss is mostly the mislabelled points it declined to memorise.

entries.title: Bayesian dropout: a network that knows when it is guessing
entries.html:
Bayesian Dropout: A Network That Knows When It Is Guessing

An ordinary network gives one answer and sounds equally sure everywhere, even far from anything it was trained on. A small change fixes that: leave dropout switched on when predicting, and ask the same question many times. Each time a different random part of the network answers. Where the answers agree, the network knows. Where they scatter, it is guessing.

Ask one expert a question and you get one answer, with no way to tell a fact from a guess. Ask a panel of fifty, each of whom studied slightly different notes. On a question from the middle of the syllabus they all say the same thing. On a question nobody covered, the answers are all over the place, and that disagreement is the useful information: it tells you not to rely on the answer. Dropout already contains such a panel. Every random choice of which neurons to switch off is a slightly different network that shares the same training. Leaving dropout on at prediction time lets you poll them.

How it works, step by step

  1. Train a network with dropout in the usual way.
  2. Ordinary prediction: switch every neuron on and get one answer for each x.
  3. Bayesian prediction: leave dropout on. Switch off a random share of neurons and predict the whole curve.
  4. Do it again with a different random share. The curve comes out slightly different.
  5. After many passes, the average is the prediction and the spread is the uncertainty.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Stage
–
Dropout passes so far
–
Uncertainty where there is data (±)
–
Uncertainty in the gap (±)
–
Uncertainty beyond the data (±)
–
Training points inside the 95% band
–

Try this. Watch the thin lines pile up: they bunch together over the dots and fan out in the gap and past both ends. Move your x into the gap and read the histogram on the right, then move it onto the data. Widen the gap to 3.2, then close it to 0. Finally raise p to 0.5: the band gets wider everywhere. Is the network really less sure, or did you just turn up a dial?

The recipe (Monte Carlo dropout)

Train with dropout as usual. To predict at \(x\), run \(T\) forward passes, each with a fresh random mask \(\mathbf m_t\), giving \(\hat y_t=f(x;\mathbf m_t)\). Then

$$\text{prediction}=\bar y=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat y_t,\qquad\text{model uncertainty}=s^2=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(\hat y_t-\bar y\big)^2 .$$

The green band on this page is \(\bar y\pm1.96\,s\). The passes stop when adding more no longer changes the band.

Why it is called Bayesian

A Bayesian treats the weights as uncertain: there is a whole distribution of weight settings consistent with the data, the posterior \(p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\), and a prediction should average over all of them,

$$p(y\mid x,\mathcal D)=\int p(y\mid x,\mathbf w)\,p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\,d\mathbf w .$$

That integral cannot be computed for a neural network. Gal and Ghahramani (2016) showed that training with dropout is mathematically equivalent to fitting an approximation \(q(\mathbf w)\) to the posterior, in which each neuron's outgoing weights are randomly either kept or set to zero. Each dropout pass is then one sample of weights from \(q\), and averaging passes is a Monte Carlo estimate of the integral. No change to the network or its training is required.

Two kinds of uncertainty

Model (epistemic) uncertainty comes from not having seen enough data. It is what the scatter of the passes measures, it is large in the gap and beyond the ends, and more data there would shrink it. Noise (aleatoric) uncertainty is the irreducible noise \(\sigma^2\) from the Bias and Variance lesson: the measurements themselves wobble, and no amount of data removes it. The total predictive variance is the sum,

$$\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)\approx s^2(x)+\sigma^2 ,$$

so the band drawn here, which shows only \(s\), is the uncertainty about the curve, not about a new measurement.

Why it matters

A model that can say "I do not know" can hand a case to a person, ask for more data where it is unsure (active learning), or decline to act. This is important in medicine, driving and anywhere a confident wrong answer is costly. An ordinary network extrapolates across the gap with a single smooth line and gives no warning.

Cautions

  • The size of the band depends on \(p\), which you chose. The method ranks regions by uncertainty much better than it gives the exact width. Check calibration on held-out data.
  • It tends to underestimate uncertainty, and far from the data it can still be overconfident.
  • It costs \(T\) forward passes per prediction.
  • Alternatives with the same aim: deep ensembles (train several networks from different starts and compare them), and Gaussian processes for small problems.
Check yourself

Two regions have the same wide band. In one, collecting more data would shrink it; in the other it would not. Which kind of uncertainty is each, and which one does this method measure?

The one that shrinks with more data is model (epistemic) uncertainty: the network has not seen enough examples there. The one that does not is noise (aleatoric) uncertainty: the outcomes themselves vary. The scatter of dropout passes measures only the first. To capture the second, the network must also predict a noise level, or one must be estimated from the residuals.

entries.title: Enough neurons can draw any curve
entries.html:
Enough Neurons Can Draw Any Curve

One hidden layer is enough, in principle, to copy any continuous curve as closely as you like. Each neuron contributes one simple piece, a bend or an S-shaped step, and the output adds the pieces up. Watch the pieces arrange themselves, add neurons one at a time, or draw your own curve and see how many neurons it takes.

A child with a box of identical wooden ramps can build the outline of any hill: a few ramps for a gentle one, many small ramps for a jagged one. The ramps are all the same simple shape. What changes is where each is placed, how steep it is, and whether it goes up or down. A neural network with one hidden layer builds curves this way. Each hidden neuron is one ramp or one step, and training is the work of sliding the pieces into place.

How it works, step by step

  1. Each hidden neuron makes one simple piece: it scales and shifts the input, then bends it.
  2. The output multiplies every piece by its own weight and adds them all up.
  3. Compare the sum with the target at 100 positions: the error.
  4. Adjust every scale, shift and weight a little to lower the error. Repeat until it stops falling.
  5. If the fit is still poor, add another neuron and train again.

What just happened

Animation

The network
The curve to copy

Hidden neurons
–
Numbers the network can adjust
–
Training steps
–
Error (mean squared)
–
Status
–

Try this. Press Add Neurons One at a Time on the wave and watch the bars on the right: how many neurons until the gold line sits on the dashed one? Then switch to the staircase with S-shaped pieces: count the steps in the staircase and the neurons needed. Change the pieces to Bends and try the skyline. Finally draw something of your own, the wilder the better, and find its number.

The network as a sum of pieces

With one input \(x\), \(H\) hidden neurons and one output,

$$\hat f(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{H}v_j\,\phi\big(w_jx+b_j\big).$$

Inside each term, \(w_j\) sets how sharp the piece is, \(-b_j/w_j\) sets where along the axis it sits, and \(v_j\) sets its height and whether it points up or down. The thin coloured lines in the picture are the individual terms \(v_j\phi(w_jx+b_j)\), and the gold line is their sum.

Why steps are enough

Take \(\phi=\tanh\) with a large \(w\): the piece is nearly a sharp step. Two steps at slightly different positions, one up and one down, make a narrow bump of any height. Any continuous curve can be approximated by a row of narrow bumps of the right heights, as a bar chart approximates a curve, and making the bars narrower makes the approximation as close as you like. With \(\phi=\mathrm{ReLU}\) each piece is a bend, sums of bends are piecewise-linear curves, and enough short straight segments follow any continuous curve.

The theorem

For any continuous function \(f\) on a closed, bounded interval and any tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a number of neurons \(H\) and a choice of weights such that

$$\big|\hat f(x)-f(x)\big|<\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }x\text{ in the interval.}$$

This holds for any activation that is not a polynomial (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991; Leshno and others 1993), and in any number of input dimensions.

What the theorem does not say

  • How many neurons. It may be very many. Rough or rapidly changing targets need more pieces, which you can check with the skyline or your own drawing. In high dimensions the number can grow exponentially.
  • That training will find the weights. The theorem says good weights exist. Gradient descent may stop at a worse arrangement, and running the same setting twice here can give different errors.
  • Anything about new data. Fitting 100 known points closely is not the same as predicting well away from them. That is the bias and variance story again.
  • That one layer is the best design. Deep networks can represent many useful functions with far fewer neurons than a single wide layer, because later layers reuse the pieces built by earlier ones.
Check yourself

The staircase target has four flat levels. About how many tanh neurons should be enough, and why does adding many more barely help?

Three, one for each jump between levels: a tanh neuron with a large input weight is one step, placed where it is needed and scaled to the height of that jump, and the output bias sets the first level. Once every jump has its own neuron the error is already close to zero, so extra neurons have nothing left to explain and receive almost no gradient.

entries.title: Batch normalization: keep every layer’s inputs in a sensible range
entries.html:
Batch Normalization: Keep Every Layer’s Inputs in a Sensible Range

In a deep network each layer feeds the next. If the numbers leaving one layer are a little too small, they shrink again at the next layer and fade to nothing. If they are a little too large, the units saturate. Either way learning stalls. Batch normalization puts a small correction after every layer: shift and rescale its outputs so that, over the current batch, they have mean 0 and spread 1. Two identical networks train side by side here, one with the correction and one without.

Picture a line of people passing a message by whispering. If each person speaks slightly too loudly, a few places down the line everyone is shouting and the words are lost. If each speaks slightly too softly, the message fades to nothing. A deep network has the same problem with numbers, and tanh units make it concrete: feed them values far from zero and they answer +1 or −1 whatever the input, with a slope of almost nothing, so no learning signal gets back through them. Batch normalization gives every person in the line a volume control that is reset at each step: whatever arrives, it is brought back to a standard level before being passed on.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a small batch of training examples and pass it through a layer.
  2. For each unit, compute the mean and the standard deviation of its values over the batch.
  3. Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. The unit’s values now have mean 0 and spread 1.
  4. Multiply by a learned scale γ and add a learned shift β, so the network can undo the step if that is better.
  5. Apply the activation function and move to the next layer. Gradients flow back through all of this.
  6. At test time there is no batch, so use running averages of the means and spreads collected during training.

What just happened

Animation

What makes training hard
Data
Passes through the data
–
Loss: plain network
–
Loss: with batch normalization
–
Training accuracy: plain
–
Training accuracy: with batch normalization
–
Typical size of what enters the last hidden layer: plain / normalized
–

Try this. Let it run with the default starting weights, which are a third of the careful size. Watch the bottom-right chart: what happens to the plain network’s bars from layer 1 to layer 6, and what does its loss do? Now set the weight size to 1 and start over. Which network ends with the lower training loss this time? Set the weight size to 4 with 8 hidden layers: the bars now overflow instead of vanishing. Across all three settings, which network did not care? Finally go back to weight size 1 and set the batch size to 2. Why would a tiny batch hurt the method that depends on batch statistics?

The transformation

For one unit with values \(z_1,\dots,z_m\) over a batch of size \(m\) (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015):

$$\mu_B=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_i,\qquad\sigma_B^2=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}(z_i-\mu_B)^2,\qquad\hat z_i=\frac{z_i-\mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\epsilon}},\qquad y_i=\gamma\,\hat z_i+\beta.$$

\(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learned, one pair per unit, starting at 1 and 0. They let the network choose any mean and spread it likes for each unit. What changes is that these are now set directly by two parameters instead of emerging from every weight in every earlier layer.

Backpropagation through it

The batch mean and variance depend on every example, so the gradient has three paths. With \(\partial L/\partial y_i\) arriving from above:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat z_i}=\gamma\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i},\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i}=\frac{1}{m\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\epsilon}}\Big(m\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat z_i}-\sum_j\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat z_j}-\hat z_i\sum_j\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat z_j}\hat z_j\Big),$$$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\gamma}=\sum_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\hat z_i,\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta}=\sum_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}.$$

The division by \(\sigma_B\) has a useful side effect. If all the weights into a unit are doubled, \(z\) doubles, \(\sigma_B\) doubles, and \(\hat z\) is unchanged: the layer's output no longer depends on the scale of its weights. That is why the normalized network shrugs off badly sized starting weights, too small or too large.

Training and testing differ

During training each example's output depends on which other examples share its batch. At test time predictions must not depend on that, so the batch statistics are replaced by running averages gathered during training:

$$\mu_{\text{run}}\leftarrow(1-\rho)\,\mu_{\text{run}}+\rho\,\mu_B,\qquad\sigma^2_{\text{run}}\leftarrow(1-\rho)\,\sigma^2_{\text{run}}+\rho\,\sigma^2_B.$$

The shading on the left-hand chart uses the running averages, as a deployed network would.

Why it helps

The original explanation was that it reduces "internal covariate shift", the drift in each layer's input distribution as earlier layers change. Later work suggests the main effect is that it makes the loss surface smoother and better conditioned, so larger learning rates are safe. Both views agree on the practice: networks with batch normalization train faster, tolerate careless initialization, and accept higher learning rates. The noise from batch statistics also acts as a mild regularizer.

What you will see on this page

The benefit here is robustness, not a better final answer. With starting weights of the careful size, the plain network trains just as fast on these small problems and usually ends with a lower training loss, because the batch-to-batch noise in the normalized network keeps its loss from settling all the way down. Move the weight size away from 1 in either direction and the plain network slows or stops, while the normalized one barely notices. In very deep networks a careful starting size is much harder to get right, which is where the method earns its place.

When it hurts

With a very small batch, the mean and variance are estimated from a handful of numbers and jump about from step to step. The normalization becomes a source of noise, and the running averages become poor stand-ins for it at test time. Layer normalization and group normalization avoid this by computing statistics within each example instead of across the batch, which is why transformers use layer normalization.

What this page runs

Two fully connected tanh networks with 10 units per hidden layer, the same starting weights (the Glorot value times the slider), the same batches and plain gradient descent. The run stops when the normalized network's loss has changed by less than 0.002 over 25 passes, or after 300 passes.

Check yourself

With starting weights a third of the careful size, the plain network’s loss sits at 0.693 while the normalized one learns at once. Both have exactly the same weights at the start. What is different inside them, and why 0.693?

In the plain network every layer multiplies the signal by weights that are too small, so its spread shrinks by roughly the same factor at each layer. After six layers what reaches the output is essentially zero whatever the input was, so the network gives every example a probability of one half, and the loss of that answer is ln 2 = 0.693. The gradients shrink by the same factor at every layer on the way back, so the early weights receive almost no signal and nothing moves. In the normalized network each layer’s values are divided by their own batch standard deviation before the activation, which restores a spread of about 1 whatever the size of the weights. Information gets through in both directions from the first step.

entries.title: Convolution: one small window, slid over the whole picture
entries.html:
Convolution: One Small Window, Slid Over the Whole Picture

A network that looks at pictures does not study every pixel separately. It slides a small window across the picture and, at each stop, asks one question: does this patch look like the pattern I am searching for? The answers form a new picture that lights up wherever the pattern was found. Draw on the picture, pick a pattern, and watch the window work.

Imagine looking for your keys in a dark room with a small torch. You do not light the whole room at once. You sweep the torch across it and, wherever the beam lands, ask the same question: "does this look like keys?" The torch is small, the question never changes, and it works wherever the keys happen to be. A convolutional layer does this with a picture. The window is the torch beam, the kernel is the question, and the output is a map of where the answer was yes.

How it works, step by step

  1. Place the 3 × 3 window on the top-left corner of the picture.
  2. Multiply each of the nine pixels under the window by the matching number in the kernel, and add the nine products.
  3. Write the sum into the matching cell of the output. If ReLU is on, write 0 for a negative sum.
  4. Slide the window one pixel and repeat, row by row, until the whole picture is covered.
  5. Pooling: cut the output into 2 × 2 blocks and keep only the largest number in each. The result is a quarter of the size.

What just happened

Animation
The picture
The layer
Window position
–
Sum at this position
–
Sizes: picture → output → pooled
–
Numbers this layer learns
–
Status
–

Try this. With the digit 7 and Vertical Edges, watch the output: it lights up on the upright stroke and stays dark on the flat top. Switch to Horizontal Edges and the opposite happens. Clear the picture and draw a single vertical line: where is the answer positive, where negative, and what does ReLU do to it? Then look at the pooled picture: move your line one pixel sideways and see how little the pooled picture changes.

The operation

Let \(X\) be the picture and \(K\) a \(3\times3\) kernel. The output at row \(i\), column \(j\) is

$$Y_{ij}=\sum_{a=0}^{2}\sum_{b=0}^{2}K_{ab}\,X_{i+a,\;j+b}\;+\;\text{bias}.$$

It is a dot product between the kernel and the patch of picture under it: large and positive when the patch resembles the kernel, near zero when it does not, negative when it is the reverse. An \(n\times n\) picture and a \(k\times k\) kernel give an output of size \((n-k+1)\times(n-k+1)\): here \(18\to16\). (This is strictly cross-correlation; deep learning libraries call it convolution.)

Why the kernels look as they do

The vertical-edge kernel has negative numbers on the left and positive on the right, so it adds up "right minus left". On a flat area the two cancel to zero. Where the picture changes from dark to bright going rightward the sum is large. The blur kernel is nine equal weights, an average. In a trained network nobody writes the kernels: they are the weights, and gradient descent learns them. First-layer kernels of real networks do turn out to be edge and colour-blob detectors much like these.

Two ideas that make it work

Local connections. Each output looks at only nine pixels, not all 324. Nearby pixels are what form edges and corners. Shared weights. The same nine numbers are used at every position, so the layer has 9 weights and 1 bias whatever the size of the picture, and a pattern learned in one place is recognised everywhere. A fully connected layer from 324 pixels to 256 outputs would have 83,200 weights.

ReLU and pooling

ReLU keeps positive answers and sets negative ones to zero: "the pattern is here" matters, "its opposite is here" is dropped. Max pooling then keeps the largest value in each \(2\times2\) block,

$$P_{ij}=\max\big(Y_{2i,2j},\,Y_{2i,2j+1},\,Y_{2i+1,2j},\,Y_{2i+1,2j+1}\big),$$

halving the width and height. It records that the pattern was found somewhere in the block without recording exactly where, which makes the result insensitive to small shifts and cuts the work for later layers by four.

Stacking layers

A real convolutional network has many kernels per layer, each producing its own output map, and several layers in a row. A second layer slides its windows over the maps of the first, so it combines edges into corners and curves. Each layer sees a larger area of the original picture (its receptive field): edges, then parts, then whole objects.

Check yourself

A convolutional layer with a 3 × 3 kernel is applied to a 1000 × 1000 picture instead of an 18 × 18 one. How many weights does the layer have now?

Still nine, plus one bias. The kernel is the layer, and the same nine numbers are reused at every position. Only the amount of computation and the size of the output grow with the picture. This is why convolutional networks can handle large images with few parameters.

entries.title: Residual connections: a shortcut around every layer
entries.html:
Residual Connections: A Shortcut Around Every Layer

Very deep networks used to be untrainable, because the learning signal faded before it reached the first layers. The cure was almost embarrassingly simple: let each block add its result to its own input, so that there is always a direct road past it. Send the learning signal back through a plain stack and a stack with shortcuts, and compare what arrives.

Think of a message passed along a line of sixty people, each of whom rewrites it in their own words. By the end it is unrecognisable. Now change one rule: each person passes on the original note untouched and staples their own comment to it. The original always arrives, and each person only has to add what they think is missing. A residual block works like that. Its layers do not have to reproduce their whole input, only to compute a correction to it, and the input itself travels along the shortcut.

How it works, step by step

  1. Build two stacks from the same random weights: one plain, one where every block adds its output to its input.
  2. Start a learning signal of strength 1 at the last layer of both.
  3. Plain stack: stepping back one layer multiplies the signal by the weights and the slope of the activation. It usually shrinks.
  4. Residual stack: the signal splits. One part goes back through the layer as before. The other takes the shortcut, unchanged. They add.
  5. Compare what reaches the first layer.

What just happened

Animation
The network
Plain stack: signal at the first layer
–
With shortcuts: signal at the first layer
–
Plain: average change per layer
–
With shortcuts: average change per layer
–

Try this. Run it at 20 layers, then at 60. In the plain stack the dot shrinks to nothing; with shortcuts it arrives intact. Switch the activation to Sigmoid: the plain stack is hopeless, yet the shortcuts still deliver. Now raise the size of the weights to 1.6. What happens to the signal with shortcuts, and why do real residual networks also use normalisation?

The block

A plain layer computes \(\mathbf a_{l+1}=F(\mathbf a_l)\), where \(F\) is "multiply by weights, apply the activation". A residual block computes

$$\mathbf a_{l+1}=\mathbf a_l+F(\mathbf a_l).$$

If the best thing a block can do is nothing, it only has to learn \(F=0\), which is easy. A plain layer would have to learn to copy its input exactly, which is hard.

Why the gradient survives

Differentiate the block:

$$\frac{\partial\mathbf a_{l+1}}{\partial\mathbf a_l}=\mathbf I+\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf a_l}.$$

Going back through \(L\) plain layers multiplies \(L\) factors \(\partial F/\partial\mathbf a\), and if each is a little smaller than 1 in size the product vanishes geometrically. With shortcuts each factor is \(\mathbf I+\partial F/\partial\mathbf a\). Multiplying these out gives the identity plus many other terms, so there is always a path from the loss to every layer along which the signal is multiplied by exactly 1. The gradient at layer \(l\) is
