$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf a_l}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf a_L}\Big(\mathbf I+\text{terms that pass through one or more blocks}\Big).$$

What it made possible

Before residual connections (He and others, 2015), adding layers beyond about twenty made networks worse, even on the training data: an optimisation failure, not overfitting. With them, networks of 50, 150 and more than 1000 layers trained successfully. Every Transformer block also has two shortcuts, one around attention and one around its feed-forward layers, and U-Nets use long shortcuts between matching layers.

The other side

The shortcut stops the signal from vanishing, but if the blocks' own contribution is large the sum can grow layer after layer, forward and backward. That is why residual networks pair shortcuts with batch or layer normalisation and with careful initialisation, often starting each block close to \(F=0\).

What this page computes

Both rows use the same random weight matrices, 30 neurons wide. The residual row scales each block's contribution by one half. The bars are the root-mean-square size of the gradient at each layer, computed with the formulas above for thirty random inputs.

Check yourself

In a residual network, what does a block compute if all of its weights are zero, and why is that a good place to start training?

It computes a(l+1) = a(l) + 0: the block passes its input through unchanged. A network made of such blocks is the identity from first block to last, so the signal and the gradient both travel through perfectly at the start. Training then only has to add useful corrections, block by block, instead of first repairing a scrambled signal.

entries.title: Train a U-Net: find the shape in the noise, pixel by pixel
entries.html:
Train a U-Net: Find the Shape in the Noise, Pixel by Pixel

Some tasks need an answer for every pixel: which pixels are tumour, which are road. Here two small convolutional networks learn, live, to pick out shapes from noisy pictures and mark every pixel as shape or background. They are identical except for one thing: one has skip connections and one does not. Watch their answers side by side, then draw your own shape and see what each makes of it.

To describe a photograph over the phone you would first step back and say what it shows: "a face, in the middle". That overview needs the picture shrunk in your mind, with the detail ignored. But if the listener must then redraw it exactly, the overview is not enough: they need the fine lines back. A U-Net does both. One half steps back, level by level, to grasp the content. The other half redraws at full size, and at each level it is handed the detail that was set aside at the same level on the way down.

How it works, step by step

  1. Make a random picture of one or two thin shapes, add noise, and keep the clean shape as the answer.
  2. Down: convolutions find edges, pooling halves the size, twice. At 4 × 4 the network knows roughly what is where and has lost the fine lines.
  3. Up: enlarge twice back to 16 × 16. With skips, each level is also handed the feature maps from the same size on the way down.
  4. Compare the output with the true shape, pixel by pixel, and backpropagate through every convolution.
  5. Repeat with fresh pictures. Check both networks on pictures they have not seen.

What just happened

Animation

The data
Training steps
–
Without skips: overlap with the truth
–
With skips: overlap with the truth
–
Weights: without / with skips
–
Status
–

Try this. Press Start over and watch the two right-hand columns. Both begin as grey fog. The one with skips sharpens into thin clean lines; the one without stays blobby, because everything it knows had to pass through a 4 × 4 bottleneck. Draw a small circle in the bottom row, then a single thin line. Which network can draw a one-pixel line, and why can the other not?

The shape

The encoder (down path) alternates convolutions with pooling, halving the width and height each time and increasing the number of feature maps, so that later layers see large areas. The decoder (up path) alternates upsampling with convolutions back to full size. A skip connection copies the encoder's feature maps at each size and joins them to the decoder's maps of the same size:

$$\mathbf d_l=\operatorname{conv}\big(\big[\operatorname{up}(\mathbf d_{l+1}),\;\mathbf e_l\big]\big).$$

Drawn with the sizes shrinking then growing, the network forms a U, and the skips are the horizontal rungs (Ronneberger and others, 2015).

Why the skips are needed

Halving a picture three times leaves one number for every 64 pixels. Exact positions of edges are gone and no amount of upsampling can bring them back: the decoder would have to invent them. The skip supplies them directly. The deep path answers "what is here?", the skip answers "exactly where?", and the decoder combines the two.

What this page trains

Two real convolutional networks, trained live by backpropagation. Each has three \(3\times3\) convolution layers on the way down (4, 6 and 8 feature maps at sizes 16, 8 and 4), two on the way up and a final one that outputs one number per pixel, turned into a probability by a sigmoid. Pooling is \(2\times2\) max pooling and enlargement repeats each pixel. The loss is the cross-entropy between the output and the true shape at every pixel. The two networks start from the same random kernels and see the same pictures; the only difference is whether the encoder's maps are joined to the decoder's at sizes 8 and 16. The score shown is intersection over union: pixels both mark as shape, divided by pixels either marks.

Where U-Nets are used

Segmenting medical scans (the original purpose), satellite images and road scenes; removing noise and sharpening images; and as the denoising network inside image diffusion models, which you will meet in the Generative AI module. There the input is a noisy picture and the output is an estimate of the noise, pixel for pixel.

Check yourself

A U-Net has its skip connections removed and is trained to outline cells in microscope images. What kind of mistakes would you expect in its output?

The right objects in roughly the right places, but with blurred, blobby outlines: neighbouring cells merged, thin gaps closed, small cells missed. The bottleneck keeps what is in the image and approximately where, and loses the exact positions of edges. Without the skips the decoder has to guess the boundaries from the coarse map.

entries.title: Autoencoders: squeeze a picture into two numbers, and get it back
entries.html:
Autoencoders: Squeeze a Picture Into Two Numbers, and Get It Back

Give a network a picture, force it through a bottleneck of just two numbers, and ask for the same picture back on the other side. To succeed it has to discover on its own what matters about the pictures. Nobody tells it which letter is which, yet the letters sort themselves into groups on the map of those two numbers. Drag across the map to see what each spot turns into.

Suppose you must describe a friend's face over a bad phone line using only two numbers. You could not send the picture. You would have to agree on a scheme first: perhaps the first number says how round the face is and the second how long the hair. A good scheme lets the listener redraw something close to the original. An autoencoder invents such a scheme by itself. The encoder is you, the two numbers are the phone line, the decoder is the listener, and the scheme is whatever makes the redrawn pictures match best.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a 5 × 7 picture of a letter: 35 numbers.
  2. Encoder: squeeze the 35 numbers through a hidden layer down to 2. That pair is the code, a point on the map.
  3. Decoder: expand the 2 numbers back through a hidden layer to 35.
  4. Compare the output with the original picture, pixel by pixel. That is the error.
  5. Adjust all the weights to lower the error, and repeat over all the pictures until it stops falling.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Epochs
–
Error per pixel
–
Pixels reproduced correctly
–
Numbers per picture: before → after
–
Status
–

Try this. Press Start over and train. At first every picture lands on the same spot and comes back as the same grey blur. Watch the points pull apart into groups, and the second row sharpen. When it has converged, drag the diamond slowly from the A group to the H group: the decoded picture morphs from one letter into the other. Untick Show the True Letter and train again to see that the grouping does not depend on the labels.

The model

An encoder \(f\) maps the input \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{35}\) to a short code \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^{2}\), and a decoder \(g\) maps the code back:

$$\mathbf z=f(\mathbf x),\qquad\hat{\mathbf x}=g(\mathbf z),\qquad\mathcal L=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\big(\mathbf x_i,\;g(f(\mathbf x_i))\big).$$

Here both are small networks, \(35\to H\to2\) and \(2\to H\to35\), and \(\ell\) is the cross-entropy between each original pixel and the predicted one. The target is the input itself, so no labels are needed: this is unsupervised (more precisely, self-supervised) learning.

Why the bottleneck matters

If the code were as large as the input, the network could copy its input straight through and learn nothing. Two numbers cannot hold 35 pixels, so the network must keep what distinguishes one picture from another and drop the rest. Pictures that share most of their pixels need nearly the same code, so they land close together on the map. That is why the letters form groups without ever being told they are letters.

Relation to PCA

With no hidden layers and no activation, the best possible autoencoder with a two-number code finds the same plane as the first two principal components. The non-linear layers let it bend that plane into a curved surface that fits the data better. An autoencoder is a non-linear generalisation of PCA.

The decoder is a generator

The decoder turns any point of the map into a picture, including points that no training picture landed on. Dragging the diamond between two groups gives pictures in between. In a plain autoencoder the regions between groups can decode to rubbish, because nothing trained them. The variational autoencoder fixes this by making the codes fill the map smoothly, which turns the decoder into a proper generative model. That is the start of the Generative AI module.

What autoencoders are used for

  • Compression and visualisation: a short code in place of a long input.
  • Denoising: train with a corrupted input and the clean picture as the target.
  • Anomaly detection: an input unlike the training data is reconstructed badly, and the size of the error flags it.
  • Pre-training: the encoder's code is a compact set of features for another task.
Check yourself

After training, a picture of the letter K, which was never in the training set, is fed in. What do you expect to come out, and how could that be put to use?

Something that looks like a blend of the letters it does know, probably closest to H or X, because the decoder can only produce pictures of the kind it was trained on. The reconstruction will differ from the input in many pixels, so the error will be much larger than for a familiar letter. That is the basis of anomaly detection with autoencoders: a large reconstruction error signals an input unlike the training data.

entries.title: Word embeddings: words that keep the same company end up as neighbours
entries.html:
Word Embeddings: Words That Keep the Same Company End Up as Neighbours

A network cannot read letters; it needs numbers. The trick is to give every word a position on a map and let the positions be learned from text alone, by one rule: words that appear in the same company should sit close together. Here 28 words start scattered at random and sort themselves into royalty, animals, food and cities without ever being told those groups exist.

You can guess a lot about a stranger from the company they keep. If someone is always seen with a crown, a throne and a palace, you do not need a dictionary to guess their role. Words work the same way: "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" (J. R. Firth, 1957). Word embeddings turn that saying into arithmetic. No one defines any word. The positions come entirely from which words appear near which.

How it works, step by step

  1. Give every word a random position.
  2. Take a pair of words that appear together in the text, such as “king” and “crown”.
  3. Pull the two a little closer together.
  4. Take a random word that did not appear with the first, and push the two a little apart.
  5. Repeat over all the pairs, many times, until the map stops changing.

What just happened

Animation

The model
Passes over the text
–
Error
–
Word you clicked
–
Its nearest neighbours
–
Words whose nearest neighbour is in their own group
–

Try this. Press Start over and train with the colours off, so you see what the model sees: grey words drifting. Turn the colours on at the end. Click “queen” and read its neighbours. Then set the random pairs to 0 and train again: with only pulling and no pushing, what happens to the whole map?

The model (skip-gram with negative sampling)

Every word \(w\) gets a vector \(\mathbf u_w\), and a second vector \(\mathbf v_w\) for when it plays the role of context. For a pair \((w,c)\) seen together in the text and \(k\) randomly drawn words \(n_1,\dots,n_k\), the loss is

$$\mathcal L=-\log\sigma\big(\mathbf u_w\cdot\mathbf v_c\big)-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\log\sigma\big(-\mathbf u_w\cdot\mathbf v_{n_j}\big).$$

The first term is small when the dot product of a true pair is large, so true pairs are pulled into alignment. The second is small when the dot product with a random word is very negative, so random pairs are pushed apart. Gradient descent on this loss is the pulling and pushing in the animation. This is word2vec (Mikolov and others, 2013).

Why similar words end up together

"King" and "queen" need never appear side by side. Both appear with "crown", "throne" and "palace", so both are pulled toward the same context vectors and arrive in the same region. Similarity of meaning is measured by the cosine of the angle between two vectors,

$$\cos(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\lVert\mathbf a\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf b\rVert},$$

which is what the bars on the right show.

Why the pushing is needed

Pulling alone has a trivial solution: put every word at the same point. The random "negative" pairs give the model something to lose by doing that.

Real embeddings

Real ones have 100 to several thousand dimensions and are learned from billions of words. In that much space, directions acquire meaning: the step from "man" to "woman" is close to the step from "king" to "queen". Two dimensions, as here, have room for groups but not for such directions. Embeddings also absorb the biases of the text they are trained on. In a Transformer the embedding table is the first layer, and each word's vector is then reshaped by its sentence, which a fixed table like this one cannot do: "bank" gets one position whether it is a river bank or a savings bank.

The text used here

The "text" is a small list of word pairs built for this page: each of 16 words is paired with three context words of its group (for example king with crown, throne, palace). It is a toy corpus, not real text.

Check yourself

“King” and “queen” end up close together although the text never contains the pair (king, queen). How?

Both words appear with the same context words: crown, throne, palace. Training pulls king toward the context vectors of those words and pulls queen toward the same three vectors. Two words pulled toward the same targets end up near each other. The embedding encodes shared company, not direct co-occurrence.

entries.title: Recurrent networks: reading one letter at a time, with a memory
entries.html:
Recurrent Networks: Reading One Letter at a Time, with a Memory

Your phone suggests the next word as you type. To do that it has to remember what came before. A recurrent network reads a sequence one item at a time and keeps a small memory that it updates at every step. Here one learns to spell a phrase you choose, letter by letter, and then writes it back on its own.

When you read a sentence you do not start afresh at every word. You carry a running sense of what the sentence has said so far, and each new word updates it. A recurrent network (RNN) has exactly one such running summary: a vector called the hidden state. At every step it takes the new item and the old summary, mixes them, and produces a new summary. Nothing else is remembered, so whatever the network needs to know about the past has to be squeezed into that vector.

How it works, step by step

  1. Learn: read the phrase many times. At each letter, guess the next one, measure the error, and adjust the weights (backpropagation through time).
  2. Write: start with the first letter and an empty memory.
  3. Mix the letter just read with the memory so far. That mixture is the new memory.
  4. From the new memory, work out how likely each letter is to come next, and take the most likely.
  5. Feed that letter back in as the next input, and repeat.

What just happened

Animation

The phrase

The model
Stage
–
Times it has read the phrase
–
Error per letter
–
Letters it now predicts correctly
–
Weights
–

Try this. Let it learn “hello world” and watch the line of text above the pictures improve from nonsense. In the phrase, the letter “l” is followed once by “l”, once by “o” and once by “d”. Step through the writing and look at the memory column each time it reads an “l”: the cells differ, and that is how it knows which one it is on. Now set the memory to 1 cell and run again. Then type your own phrase.

One step

Let \(\mathbf x_t\) be the letter at step \(t\), written as a vector with a 1 in that letter's position and 0 elsewhere. The memory \(\mathbf h_t\) and the prediction \(\hat{\mathbf y}_t\) are

$$\mathbf h_t=\tanh\big(\mathbf W_{xh}\mathbf x_t+\mathbf W_{hh}\mathbf h_{t-1}+\mathbf b_h\big),\qquad\hat{\mathbf y}_t=\operatorname{softmax}\big(\mathbf W_{hy}\mathbf h_t+\mathbf b_y\big).$$

The same three weight matrices are used at every step. That is what "recurrent" means, and it is why the network can read a sequence of any length with a fixed number of weights.

Learning: backpropagation through time

The loss is the cross-entropy between the predicted next letter and the true one, added up over the phrase: \(\mathcal L=-\sum_t\log\hat y_t[\text{true next letter}]\). To get gradients, unroll the network in time, as in the left picture, and treat it as a deep network with one layer per step and shared weights. Blame flows from each prediction back through the memory to all earlier steps:

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf h_t}=\mathbf W_{hy}^{\top}\big(\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t\big)+\mathbf W_{hh}^{\top}\Big[\big(1-\mathbf h_{t+1}^2\big)\odot\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf h_{t+1}}\Big].$$

The gradient of each shared matrix is the sum of its gradients at all steps.

Why memory is needed

In "hello world" the letter l is followed by l, by o and by d. A model that sees only the current letter cannot do better than guess among them. The RNN can, because by the time it reads each l its memory holds a trace of the letters before it. The number of memory cells limits how much can be kept: with too few, different histories collapse onto the same memory and the predictions blur.

The weakness, and LSTM and GRU

Going back \(k\) steps multiplies the gradient by \(\mathbf W_{hh}^{\top}\) and by tanh slopes \(k\) times, the same repeated product as in the Activation Functions lesson. Over long gaps it vanishes, so a plain RNN learns short-range patterns well and long-range ones poorly. The LSTM and the GRU add gates, small sigmoid layers that decide at each step how much of the old memory to keep, how much new information to write and how much to reveal. The LSTM's memory update is \(\mathbf c_t=\mathbf f_t\odot\mathbf c_{t-1}+\mathbf i_t\odot\tilde{\mathbf c}_t\): when the forget gate \(\mathbf f_t\) is near 1 the memory, and the gradient with it, passes through unchanged, much like a residual shortcut through time. Those gated versions are not animated on this page.

Where RNNs stand now

For language, Transformers have largely replaced RNNs because attention lets every position look directly at every other. RNNs are still used for streaming signals and small devices, and the idea of a state carried through time appears throughout machine learning.

Check yourself

The network has learned “hello world” and is writing it back. It has just read the second “l”. The input is the same as for the first “l”, yet it now predicts “o” instead of “l”. Where is the difference stored?

In the memory (the hidden state). The prediction depends on the new memory, and the new memory is computed from the current letter and the previous memory. Before the first l the previous memory encoded “he”; before the second it encoded “hel”. Same input, different previous memory, so a different new memory and a different prediction.

entries.title: LSTM and GRU: a memory with a gate on it
entries.html:
LSTM and GRU: A Memory with a Gate on It

“The keys, which I left on the table next to the lamp, ___ missing.” To choose “are” you must still remember “keys” ten words later, and not be thrown by “table” and “lamp”. A plain recurrent network rewrites its whole memory at every word, so the trace fades. An LSTM puts the memory on a conveyor belt with gates that decide what gets on and what is wiped. Follow one fact down both.

A plain recurrent network keeps its memory on a whiteboard that it wipes and rewrites, in slightly smudged form, at every single word. After fifteen rewrites the first note is illegible. An LSTM (long short-term memory) keeps a notebook instead. At each word it makes three small decisions: which old lines to cross out, whether to write anything new, and which lines to read aloud. If it decides "cross out nothing, write nothing", the note is exactly as it was. Remembering becomes the default, and forgetting is a choice.

How it works, step by step

  1. Read “keys”. Both networks store the fact “the subject is plural” as +1.
  2. Plain network, next word: the whole memory is multiplied by a weight and squashed. A little is lost every time.
  3. LSTM, next word: the forget gate decides how much of the old memory to keep (near 1 = keep), and the input gate decides whether the new word may write (near 0 = no).
  4. A distracting word arrives (“table”, singular). The plain network must mix it in. The LSTM keeps its input gate shut.
  5. At the blank, read the memory: clearly positive means “are”.

What just happened

Animation
The gates
Plain network at the blank
–
LSTM at the blank
–
Plain network: learning signal reaching “keys”
–
LSTM: learning signal reaching “keys”
–

Try this. Read the sentence through and compare the two dots at the blank. Now drag the forget gate down to 0.7: the LSTM forgets too. Put it back and open the input gate at the distracting words to 1: “table” and “lamp” overwrite the fact. So the LSTM is only as good as its gates, and the gates are what training learns. Last, raise the plain network’s weight above 1.2: does that rescue it?

The plain network

$$h_t=\tanh\big(w\,h_{t-1}+u\,x_t\big),\qquad\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_1}=\prod_{t=2}^{T}w\,\big(1-h_t^2\big).$$

The memory passes through a multiplication and a squashing at every step, and the learning signal back to the first word is a product of \(T-1\) factors. If they are below 1 it vanishes. If \(w\) is made large to compensate, \(\tanh\) saturates and \(1-h^2\) goes to zero instead.

The LSTM

The LSTM has a separate cell state \(c_t\), the conveyor belt, and three gates, each a sigmoid layer with outputs between 0 and 1:

$$f_t=\sigma(\cdot)\ \text{forget},\quad i_t=\sigma(\cdot)\ \text{input},\quad o_t=\sigma(\cdot)\ \text{output},\qquad c_t=f_t\,c_{t-1}+i_t\,\tilde c_t,\qquad h_t=o_t\tanh(c_t),$$

where \(\tilde c_t=\tanh(\cdot)\) is the candidate to be written and every \((\cdot)\) is a weighted sum of \(x_t\) and \(h_{t-1}\). The key line is the update of \(c_t\): the old memory is multiplied by \(f_t\) and added to, with no squashing. So

$$\frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_1}=\prod_{t=2}^{T}f_t ,$$

and when the forget gates are near 1 the memory and its gradient pass through almost unchanged for as long as needed. It is the same idea as a residual shortcut, applied through time.

The GRU

The gated recurrent unit merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates. An update gate \(z_t\) blends old and new, \(h_t=(1-z_t)\,h_{t-1}+z_t\,\tilde h_t\), and a reset gate controls how much of the past feeds the candidate. It has fewer weights than an LSTM and usually performs about as well.

What this page simplifies

In a real LSTM the gates are computed from the current word and the previous state by learned weights. Here the gates are set by you with sliders, and each network holds a single number, so that the effect of the gates can be seen in isolation: the forget gate is the same at every word, and the input gate is open at "keys" and set by the slider at the distracting words. The curves are exact for those settings.

Check yourself

With the forget gate at 0.98 the LSTM keeps about 75% of the fact after 14 words. Why does 0.98 matter so much more than, say, 0.90?

The fact is multiplied by the forget gate at every word, so what remains is the gate value raised to the number of words. 0.98 to the power 14 is about 0.75, while 0.90 to the power 14 is about 0.23. Small differences per step compound over long gaps, which is why LSTMs are often initialised with the forget gate biased toward 1.

entries.title: Attention: learning which word to listen to
entries.html:
Attention: Learning Which Word to Listen to

In “the cat sat on the mat because it was tired”, what does “it” mean? Change one word, “because it was soft”, and the answer flips to the mat. Here a small attention layer learns that skill from examples. Nobody tells it which words are animals or which adjectives suit them. Watch it work that out, then build your own sentences, including ones it never saw in training.

You are in a library with a question. Every book has a title on its spine. You compare your question with each title, pull out the few that match, and read mostly from those. Your question is the query, a title is a key, and what is inside the book is its value. Attention does this softly: instead of choosing a few books it reads a little from every book, in proportion to how well its title matched. In a sentence every word is at once a reader with a question and a book with a title.

How it works, step by step

  1. Give every word a random key and every adjective a random question (query): two numbers each.
  2. Take a training sentence. The question comes from its last word; compare it with every word’s key by a dot product.
  3. Softmax turns the scores into shares. The share on the correct word should be high.
  4. It is not, at first. Nudge the question toward the key of the right word, and that key toward the question; push the others away.
  5. Repeat over all training sentences until the error stops falling. Then try sentences it has never seen.

What just happened

Animation

The model
Passes over the training sentences
–
Training error
–
Unseen sentences answered correctly
–
In your sentence, “it” is
–
Was your sentence in the training set?
–

Try this. Press Start over and watch the map: at first the dots are a jumble and “it” spreads its attention evenly. As training runs, animals drift one way and places the other, and each adjective’s line swings toward its kind. When it stops, switch “tired” to “soft” and watch the arcs jump. Change the word order: the answer follows the meaning, not the position. Find a sentence marked as never seen in training: is it still right? Then press Explain This Sentence.

The calculation

Let word \(i\) have query \(\mathbf q_i\), and word \(j\) have key \(\mathbf k_j\) and value \(\mathbf v_j\), all vectors of dimension \(d\). The match score, the share and the output are

$$s_{ij}=\frac{\mathbf q_i\cdot\mathbf k_j}{\sqrt d},\qquad\alpha_{ij}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}}}{\sum_{m}e^{s_{im}}},\qquad\mathbf o_i=\sum_j\alpha_{ij}\,\mathbf v_j .$$

In matrix form, with the queries, keys and values stacked as rows of \(\mathbf Q,\mathbf K,\mathbf V\),

$$\operatorname{Attention}(\mathbf Q,\mathbf K,\mathbf V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{\mathbf Q\mathbf K^{\top}}{\sqrt d}\Big)\mathbf V .$$

On this page you see one row of it: the row for the word “it”.

Where queries, keys and values come from

In a real network each word starts as one embedding vector \(\mathbf x_j\), and three learned matrices produce the three roles: \(\mathbf q_j=\mathbf W_Q\mathbf x_j\), \(\mathbf k_j=\mathbf W_K\mathbf x_j\), \(\mathbf v_j=\mathbf W_V\mathbf x_j\). Training adjusts those matrices so that useful words end up attending to each other. On this page they are learned. Every word has a key of two numbers and every adjective a query of two numbers, all starting at random, and gradient descent on the loss \(-\log\alpha_{\text{correct word}}\) moves them. Two numbers are used so that the result can be drawn as a map. One simplification remains: the query is read directly from the adjective at the end of the sentence. In a full Transformer the word “it” would first gather that adjective through an earlier attention layer and then ask its question.

Why divide by \(\sqrt d\), and what sharpness does

Dot products of long vectors are large, and large scores push the softmax to put everything on one word, where its gradient is nearly zero. Dividing by \(\sqrt d\) keeps the scores at a sensible size. The sharpness slider multiplies the scores before the softmax: small values flatten the shares toward equal, large values approach picking the single best match.

Why attention replaced recurrence

  • Direct access. Any word can read from any other in one step, however far apart. An RNN has to carry the information through every step in between.
  • Parallel. All words are processed at once, not one after another.
  • Readable. The shares \(\alpha_{ij}\) can be inspected, as here, although in deep models they are only a partial explanation of what the model does.

What is still missing

Attention on its own ignores word order: shuffle the sentence and the shares are the same. Transformers add position information to the embeddings. They also run several attentions side by side (multi-head attention), each free to look for a different relationship, and stack many layers with residual shortcuts between them.

Check yourself

If all the queries and keys were identical vectors, what would the attention shares be, and what would each word’s output become?

Every score would be the same number, so the softmax would give every word the same share, 1/n. Each output would be the plain average of all the values: every word would receive the same blurred summary of the sentence. Attention is useful only because different words ask different questions and offer different keys.

entries.title: Train a Transformer and watch it work out what to look at
entries.html:
Train a Transformer and Watch It Work Out What to Look at

This is a real Transformer, small enough to train in your browser in seconds. Its job: read five letters, then write them out backwards. Nobody tells it how. Watch the attention square as it learns: a diagonal line appears, which is the network discovering that to write the first output it must look at the last input. Then give it your own letters.

Picture a meeting where everyone holds a page of notes about themselves. In each round two things happen. First, everyone looks around the room and copies onto their own page whatever is relevant from the others' pages: that is attention. Then everyone goes quiet and thinks over their own page alone, rewriting it: that is the feed-forward layer. Nobody throws their old page away; they add to it, which is the shortcut. After many rounds each page describes its owner in the light of everyone else in the room. A Transformer runs that meeting with words.

How it works, step by step

  1. Make up a random sequence of five letters, and the right answer for it.
  2. Forward: letters become vectors, positions are added, attention lets each position gather from earlier ones, and a small network turns the result into a guess for the next letter.
  3. Compare the guesses with the right answer: the loss.
  4. Backward: backpropagation finds how every weight should change, including the ones that decide where attention looks.
  5. Repeat with fresh sequences until it gets them all right. Then it answers sequences it has never seen.

What just happened

Animation

Try it yourself

Training steps
–
Error
–
Fresh sequences fully correct
–
Its answer for your letters
–
The inspected output looks mostly at
–
Weights in the model
–

Try this. Press Start over and watch the lower-left square while it trains: first a blur, then a line. For Write It Backwards the line runs from top right to bottom left; switch the task to Copy It and it runs the other way. Type your own five letters and move the Output to Inspect slider: the arcs show which input letter each output is reading. Before training, where does it look?

The stages

With \(n\) tokens and vectors of size \(d\), stack the token vectors as the rows of an \(n\times d\) matrix.

$$\mathbf X=\mathbf E+\mathbf P\qquad\text{(embeddings plus positions)}$$$$\mathbf A=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{(\mathbf X\mathbf W_Q)(\mathbf X\mathbf W_K)^{\top}}{\sqrt d}+\mathbf M\Big),\qquad\mathbf Z=\mathbf A\,(\mathbf X\mathbf W_V)\qquad\text{(self-attention)}$$$$\mathbf R_1=\operatorname{norm}(\mathbf X+\mathbf Z)\qquad\text{(shortcut and normalise)}$$$$\mathbf F=\max(0,\;\mathbf R_1\mathbf W_1)\,\mathbf W_2,\qquad\mathbf R_2=\operatorname{norm}(\mathbf R_1+\mathbf F)\qquad\text{(feed-forward, shortcut, normalise)}$$

The mask \(\mathbf M\) is \(-\infty\) wherever a word would look at a later word and 0 elsewhere, which makes those attention shares exactly zero.

Positions

Attention treats its inputs as a set: shuffle the words and each gets the same result. Order is restored by adding to each word a vector that depends only on its position. The original design uses waves of different lengths,

$$P_{pos,2i}=\sin\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big),\qquad P_{pos,2i+1}=\cos\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big),$$

so that each position has a distinct pattern. This page learns its position vectors instead, which works as well for short sequences.

Predicting the next word

The final vector of the last token is compared with the embedding of every word in the vocabulary, \(\text{logits}=\mathbf r\,\mathbf E_{\text{vocab}}^{\top}\), and a softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Training adjusts every matrix so that the true next word gets a high probability, using backpropagation as in any network. With the mask, one pass through a sentence trains the prediction at every position at once.

A real model

GPT-style models stack dozens of such blocks, use vectors of thousands of numbers, and run many attention "heads" side by side in each block, each with its own \(\mathbf W_Q,\mathbf W_K,\mathbf W_V\). The parts are the ones shown here.

What this page trains

One block with one attention head, vectors of 16 numbers, and about 2,000 weights. For simplicity it leaves out normalisation and learns its position vectors. It is trained by backpropagation with the Adam optimiser on random five-letter sequences, 12 at a time, and stops when it writes every fresh sequence correctly.

What it has to discover is a rule about positions: to write output number \(i\) of the reversed sequence it must read input number \(6-i\). So the query and key matrices learn to use the position vectors, which is the line you see in the attention square. The value matrix learns to carry the letter itself across, and the final layer reads it out. Nothing in the code states this rule. It emerges because it lowers the loss.

Check yourself

Without the position signal, would “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give the word “bites” different vectors at the end of the block?

No. Attention computes each word’s output from the set of all word vectors, weighted by how well they match. Without positions the same three vectors are present in both sentences, so every score, every share and every output is identical; the two sentences are indistinguishable to the block. Adding a different position vector to each slot is what lets it tell who did the biting.

entries.title: Graph neural networks: tell me who your friends are
entries.html:
Graph Neural Networks: Tell Me Who Your Friends Are

Some data is not a table or a picture but a web of connections: friendships, molecules, roads, web pages. A graph neural network learns from such data by letting every node repeatedly ask its neighbours what they think and update its own view. Here two people in a small social network have told us which club they joined. Watch that knowledge spread along the friendships until everyone has an answer.

Suppose you move to a new town and want to know which football team a stranger supports. You do not know, but you know two of their friends, and each of those has friends whose team you do know. Ask around: each person forms a guess from their friends' guesses, and passes their own guess on. After a few rounds of gossip, a reasonable answer has reached everyone, because friends tend to agree. A graph neural network is this gossip, with learned rules for how to combine what is heard.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start: the labelled nodes know their club. Everyone else is undecided, at one half.
  2. Message: every node sends its current belief along each of its friendships.
  3. Aggregate: every node averages the messages it received together with its own belief.
  4. Update: that average becomes its new belief. Labelled nodes keep their known answer.
  5. Repeat. Each round carries information one friendship further. Stop when the beliefs no longer change.

What just happened

Animation

The model
Rounds
–
Largest change in the last round
–
Nodes placed in their true club
–
Labelled nodes
–
Status
–

Try this. Step through three rounds and watch the colour spread outward from the two ringed nodes, one friendship per round. Notice the nodes on the bridge between the two groups: they stay pale. Now untick “Labelled nodes keep their known answer” and run: every node drifts to the same colour. That is over-smoothing, and it is why very deep graph networks are hard to build. Then click nodes to label different people and see how few labels are enough.

Message passing

Let \(\mathbf h_i^{(t)}\) be the vector held by node \(i\) after round \(t\) and \(\mathcal N(i)\) its neighbours. One round, or one layer, is

$$\mathbf h_i^{(t+1)}=\phi\Big(\mathbf W\cdot\frac{1}{1+|\mathcal N(i)|}\Big[\mathbf h_i^{(t)}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal N(i)}\mathbf h_j^{(t)}\Big]\Big).$$

Each node averages its own vector with its neighbours', multiplies by a learned matrix \(\mathbf W\) and applies an activation. This is essentially the graph convolutional network of Kipf and Welling (2017). The same \(\mathbf W\) is used at every node, as a convolution reuses one kernel at every pixel, so the layer works on a graph of any size or shape.

What this page shows

Each node holds one number, its belief that it is in the gold club, and the round is the plain average with no learned weights (\(\mathbf W=1\), no activation). Labelled nodes are reset to their known value after each round. That is the untrained core of a graph network, known on its own as label propagation. A trained network would also use each node's own features and learn \(\mathbf W\) so that the averaging emphasises what matters.

Depth is reach

After one round a node knows about its friends; after two, about friends of friends. A network with \(k\) layers sees exactly \(k\) steps away. That is the graph version of the receptive field.

Over-smoothing

Averaging with neighbours makes connected nodes more alike every round. With nothing to hold them apart, all nodes of a connected graph converge to the same value, and the network can no longer tell them apart. That is why practical graph networks are shallow, usually two to four layers, or use residual shortcuts back to each node's original features.

Where they are used

Predicting properties of molecules (atoms are nodes, bonds are edges), recommending products (people and items), estimating travel times on road maps, detecting fraud in payment networks, and weather forecasting on a mesh of the globe. A Transformer is a graph network on a graph in which every token is connected to every other, with attention deciding the weight of each edge.

Check yourself

A node is five friendships away from the nearest labelled node. What is the smallest number of rounds after which its belief can differ from one half, and what does that say about choosing the number of layers?

Five. Information moves one friendship per round, so after four rounds nothing from a labelled node has reached it. In a graph network the number of layers sets how far each node can see, so it must be at least the distance over which the relevant information has to travel, but not much more, because each extra round also blurs neighbouring nodes together.

entries.title: Transfer learning: do not start from zero
entries.html:
Transfer Learning: Do Not Start from Zero

A child who can already read does not learn a new alphabet game from nothing. Networks can reuse knowledge too. First a network studies hundreds of labelled letter pictures. Then a new question arrives, “is this letter a vowel?”, with only a handful of examples. One learner starts from scratch. The other keeps what the first network learned to see and only learns the new answer. Watch which one copes.

A chef who has cooked Italian food for ten years is asked to make a Thai dish from three recipes. A beginner given the same three recipes will struggle, because three recipes cannot teach knife skills, timing or how to taste. The chef already has all of that and only needs to learn what is new. Most of what a network learns on one task with a lot of data, how to see edges and strokes, how to read grammar, is useful for other tasks with little data.

How it works, step by step

  1. Stage 1, pretraining: a network learns to name six letters from 300 noisy pictures. Its first layer learns to see strokes.
  2. A new task arrives: say whether a letter is a vowel. There are only a few examples.
  3. Learner A, from scratch: a fresh network with random weights is trained on those few examples.
  4. Learner B, transfer: copy the pretrained first layer, freeze it, and train only a new last layer on the same few examples.
  5. Test both on pictures neither has seen.

What just happened

Animation

The new task
Stage
–
Pretrained network: letters named correctly
–
From scratch: accuracy on new pictures
–
Transfer: accuracy on new pictures
–
Examples the new task provides
–
Weights trained: scratch / transfer
–

Try this. Run it with 1 example per letter: six pictures in all. Compare the two rows of small pictures on the left: one set is clean strokes, the other is noise that happened to fit six examples. Then raise the examples to 12 per letter. The gap closes. When is starting from someone else’s network worth it, and when does it stop mattering?

The recipe

Split a network into a feature extractor \(\phi\) (the early layers) and a head \(g\) (the last layer).

  1. Pretrain \(g_A(\phi(\mathbf x))\) on task A, which has plenty of data.
  2. For task B, keep \(\phi\), throw away \(g_A\) and attach a fresh head \(g_B\).
  3. Train on task B. Either freeze \(\phi\) and train only \(g_B\) (as on this page), or fine-tune: train everything, with a small learning rate so that \(\phi\) changes only a little.

Why it helps

It is the bias and variance trade-off again. Training from scratch on six examples means fitting every weight, here 889 of them, to six pictures: enormous variance, and the first-layer pictures on the lower left show the result. Freezing \(\phi\) leaves only the head's 25 weights to fit, and they are fitted on features that already separate the letters cleanly. Far fewer free numbers and better inputs mean much lower variance. The price is bias: if task B needs features that task A never taught, a frozen \(\phi\) cannot supply them.

When it works, and when not

  • Works when the two tasks share low-level structure: the same kind of pictures, the same language, the same sensor.
  • Helps most when task B has little data. With plenty, training from scratch catches up, as the slider shows.
  • Can hurt (negative transfer) when the tasks are unrelated, because the frozen features discard what the new task needs.
  • Freeze or fine-tune? Freeze with very little data, fine-tune with more, and unfreeze from the last layer backward.

Why this matters now

Almost nobody trains a large model from zero. Vision models are pretrained on millions of images and language models on a large share of the public internet, then adapted with a few thousand examples, a few dozen, or just a written instruction. Those pretrained networks are called foundation models, and fine-tuning methods such as LoRA appear in the Language Models module.

About this demonstration

Both tasks use the same six letters, so the new task is a new question about familiar pictures. That is the easiest kind of transfer. The accuracy curves are averaged over four independent draws of the few examples, because with so few examples a single try is mostly luck.

Check yourself

With 12 examples per letter the two learners end up level. Does that mean transfer learning was pointless there?

Not quite. It reached that accuracy while training only 25 weights instead of 889, so it was cheaper and faster, and it got there with far fewer epochs. But the accuracy advantage is gone: once the new task has enough data of its own, a network trained from scratch can learn good features for itself. Transfer pays most when data for the new task is scarce.

entries.title: One-shot and few-shot learning: recognize a new thing from a single example
entries.html:
One-Shot and Few-Shot Learning: Recognize a New Thing from a Single Example

Show a child one picture of a giraffe and they will know giraffes for life. A classifier trained the usual way needs thousands. Few-shot learning closes the gap by changing what is learned. The network is not taught the classes it will be asked about. It is taught, on other classes, how to compare, so that when five symbols it has never seen arrive with one example each, it can sort new drawings among them. With one example per class this is one-shot learning.

Someone who has learned to read one alphabet finds a second one easy. They have not seen its letters before, but they know what matters about a letter: which strokes there are and how they join, not the exact position on the page or the thickness of the pen. Shown one new character, they can pick it out from others at once. What they carried over is a way of looking, not a list of answers. Few-shot learning trains a network on many small "tell these apart" exercises with ever-changing symbols, so that the only thing worth learning is that way of looking.

How it works, step by step

  1. Invent a small task from the training alphabets: pick a few symbols, a few examples of each, and some extra drawings to classify.
  2. Pass every drawing through the network. Each becomes a point in an 8-dimensional space.
  3. Average the example points of each symbol. That average is the symbol’s prototype.
  4. Classify each extra drawing by its nearest prototype, and measure the error.
  5. Adjust the network so that drawings land nearer their own prototype and further from the others.
  6. Repeat with a new task. At test time do steps 2 to 4 on symbols never seen before: no retraining.

What just happened

Animation

The task
Draw your own

Training tasks so far
–
Unseen symbols, one example each
–
Unseen symbols, at the number of examples chosen
–
Comparing raw pixels, same tasks
–
This task
–

Try this. Before training, look at the top-right map: the drawings of different symbols are jumbled together, and the accuracy is close to what raw pixels give or worse. Press Run. Watch the groups pull apart, on symbols the network has never trained on. When it stops, compare the three accuracy readouts. Slide the examples per symbol from 1 to 5: how much does each extra example buy? Raise the number of symbols to tell apart to 6, then lower it to 2. Push the sloppiness up and see which method suffers more. Then draw your own symbol in the grid, or copy one from the task and change a few squares until the answer flips.

The task

An \(N\)-way \(K\)-shot task gives a support set with \(K\) labelled examples of each of \(N\) classes and asks for the classes of some query examples. \(K=1\) is one-shot learning and small \(K\) is few-shot. The classes at test time are disjoint from the classes used in training, so memorizing classes is useless.

Prototypical networks

An embedding network \(f_\theta\) maps each input to a point (Snell, Swersky and Zemel, 2017). Each class is represented by the mean of its support points, its prototype:

$$\mathbf c_n=\frac1K\sum_{i\in S_n}f_\theta(\mathbf x_i).$$

A query is assigned to classes by a softmax over negative squared distances to the prototypes:

$$p(y=n\mid\mathbf x)=\frac{\exp\!\big(-\lVert f_\theta(\mathbf x)-\mathbf c_n\rVert^2\big)}{\sum_{m}\exp\!\big(-\lVert f_\theta(\mathbf x)-\mathbf c_m\rVert^2\big)}.$$

Nothing in this rule is specific to particular classes. Give it any support set and it classifies.

Training in episodes

Training imitates the test. Each step samples a fresh task from the training classes, computes prototypes from its support set, and minimizes the cross-entropy of its queries:

$$\mathcal L(\theta)=-\sum_{(\mathbf x,y)\in Q}\log p(y\mid\mathbf x).$$

The gradient flows through the queries and through the prototypes into the embedding. Because the classes change every episode, the network cannot succeed by recognizing classes. It has to learn an embedding in which drawings of the same symbol land close together whatever the symbol is. This is the sense in which the method is called meta-learning, or learning to learn.

Why not compare pixels?

Nearest-prototype classification works in any space, including raw pixels, and that is the dashed baseline. Pixels fail because two drawings of one symbol shifted by a square can share fewer pixels than drawings of two different symbols. The trained embedding has learned, from other alphabets, which differences matter.

Relatives

Siamese networks (Koch and others, 2015) train a network to say whether two inputs are the same class, and classify a query by its most similar support example. Matching networks (Vinyals and others, 2016) classify by attention over the support set and introduced episodic training. With one example per class a prototype is just that example, so the three methods nearly coincide in the one-shot case. Optimization-based methods such as MAML take another route and learn starting weights that adapt in a few gradient steps.

The same words elsewhere

"Few-shot" is also used for large language models, when a handful of worked examples are placed in the prompt. The mechanism differs, since no prototypes are computed and no weights change, but the idea is the same: the model was trained broadly enough to pick up a new task from a few demonstrations. Strong pretrained features with a simple classifier on top are now a very competitive few-shot method.

What this page runs

Symbols are three random pen strokes on a 7 by 7 grid. Each drawing is redrawn with jittered stroke ends, a random shift of up to one square and a few flipped pixels. There are 200 training symbols and a separate, unlimited supply of test symbols. The embedding is a network with one hidden layer of 48 tanh units and 8 outputs, trained with Adam on 5-way tasks with 3 examples and 5 queries per class. Accuracy is measured every 100 tasks on 100 fixed test tasks of unseen symbols. Training stops when the one-shot accuracy has not improved by more than 0.7 points over 800 tasks, or after 6,000 tasks.

Check yourself

After training, the network classifies drawings of symbols it has never seen, from one example each, far better than comparing pixels. Its weights were never updated on those symbols. What did training on other symbols give it?

An embedding: a way of turning a drawing into a point so that drawings of the same symbol land close together and different symbols land apart, whatever the symbols are. Because every training task used a different set of symbols, the network could not lower its loss by memorizing them. The only thing that helped across all tasks was to become insensitive to what varies between two drawings of one symbol (a small shift, a wobbly stroke, a stray pixel) and sensitive to what distinguishes symbols (which strokes are present and where they join). That knowledge is about drawings in general, so it transfers. At test time the single example of each new symbol only has to mark a location in that space.

entries.title: Autoregressive models: write one letter, then ask what comes next
entries.html:
Autoregressive Models: Write One Letter, Then Ask What Comes Next

Every chatbot writes the same way: it looks at what has been written so far, works out how likely each possible next piece is, picks one, and repeats. That is all “autoregressive” means. Here the model is as simple as it can be: it has read a short text and counted which letter tends to follow which. Watch it write, then give it your own text to learn from.

Play a game: I say "once upon a", and you say the next word. You did not need to think. You have heard that phrase finished the same way many times. An autoregressive model plays this game with itself. It writes a piece, reads back what it has written, guesses the next piece, and continues. The only thing that changes from the toy on this page to the largest language model is how it makes the guess: by counting here, with a Transformer there.

How it works, step by step

  1. Learn: read the text once. For every run of k letters, count which letter came next.
  2. Write: look at the last k letters written so far.
  3. Look up the counts for that context and turn them into probabilities.
  4. Pick the next letter at random according to those probabilities. Temperature makes the choice bolder or safer.
  5. Add the letter to the text and go back to step 2.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The text it learns from

Context right now
–
Different letters seen after it
–
Letter picked
–
Letters in the training text
–
Perplexity on the training text at this memory
–

Try this. Set the memory to 0 and write: a soup of letters in roughly English proportions. Raise it to 1, 2, 3, 4: syllables appear, then words, then phrases. At 6 it mostly copies the text back. Why? Then put the memory at 3 and move the temperature to 0.2 and to 2. Finally paste a paragraph in another language, or a song you know, and see what it writes.

The idea in one line

The probability of a whole sequence can always be split into a product of next-item probabilities, by the chain rule:

$$p(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\big(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}\big).$$

So a model that can answer "what comes next, given everything so far?" is a complete model of sequences. To generate, sample \(x_1\), then \(x_2\) given \(x_1\), and so on.

The model on this page

It assumes the next letter depends only on the previous \(k\) letters, and estimates the probability by counting in the training text:

$$p\big(x_t\mid x_{t-k},\dots,x_{t-1}\big)\approx\frac{\text{count}(x_{t-k}\dots x_{t-1}\,x_t)}{\text{count}(x_{t-k}\dots x_{t-1})}.$$

This is an n-gram model with \(n=k+1\). Training is one pass of counting. A neural language model replaces the table of counts with a network, which lets it use thousands of items of context and share what it learns between similar contexts.

Temperature

Before sampling, each probability is raised to the power \(1/\tau\) and the results are rescaled to add up to 1:

$$p_\tau(x)\propto p(x)^{1/\tau}.$$

With \(\tau<1\) likely letters become more likely still, and the text is safe and repetitive. With \(\tau>1\) the choices even out, and the text is varied and error-prone. \(\tau\to0\) always takes the single most likely letter.

Memory against data

Longer context gives better guesses but splits the text into more and more distinct contexts, each seen fewer times. With a short text and \(k=6\), most contexts were seen once, so the model has exactly one continuation to offer and reproduces the text. That is overfitting. Perplexity, \(\exp\big(-\tfrac1T\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid\text{context})\big)\), is the model's average number of equally likely choices per letter. On the training text it always falls as \(k\) grows, which is why it must be measured on text the model has not seen.

Why it matters

GPT-style models, WaveNet for audio and PixelCNN for images are all autoregressive. Their strengths: an exact likelihood and simple training (predict the next item). Their weakness: generation is one item at a time, and an early mistake cannot be taken back.

Check yourself

With a memory of 6 letters the output is nearly a copy of the training text. Is that a better model than memory 3?

It is a better memoriser, not a better model. With a short training text almost every 6-letter context occurred once, so only one continuation has a non-zero count and the model can do nothing but replay the text. It has the lowest perplexity on the training text and would do badly on new text, where most 6-letter contexts never appeared at all. Memory 3 has seen each context many times and has learned patterns it can recombine.

entries.title: Variational autoencoders: a map with no empty regions
entries.html:
Variational Autoencoders: A Map with No Empty Regions

An ordinary autoencoder gives each picture a spot on a map, but the space between the spots is no-man’s-land: decode a random point and you get rubbish. A variational autoencoder makes two changes. Each picture becomes a small cloud instead of a point, and all the clouds are pulled toward the centre. The map fills in, and now any point you pick decodes to something sensible. That makes it a generator.

Imagine a library where every book has a shelf position. In a badly run library each book sits at an exact spot and the gaps between them are empty: reach in at random and you grab air. In a well-run library each book has a small zone, the zones are packed side by side around the entrance, and similar books are neighbours. Now any spot you reach for holds a book, and walking along a shelf takes you smoothly from one subject to the next. A variational autoencoder (VAE) trains the librarian to shelve like that.

How it works, step by step

  1. Encoder: turn a picture into a cloud on the map: a centre and a width for each of the two code numbers.
  2. Draw one random point from that cloud.
  3. Decoder: turn that point back into a picture.
  4. Loss, part 1: how different is the output from the original? Part 2: how far is the cloud from a standard bell at the centre of the map?
  5. Adjust all weights to lower the sum, and repeat. To generate, skip the encoder: pick a random point from the standard bell and decode it.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Epochs
–
Reconstruction error per picture
–
Distance of the clouds from the centre (KL)
–
Codes that fall inside the outer ring
–
Status
–

Try this. Train with β = 1 and look at the row of generated pictures: most are recognisable letters. Set β to 0 and train again. That is a plain autoencoder: the codes fly far outside the rings, and random draws decode to smudges. Now set β to 6: the clouds collapse onto the centre, everything decodes to the same blur. Somewhere between, the map is both organised and full. That tension is the whole idea.

The model

The encoder maps a picture \(\mathbf x\) to the parameters of a Gaussian over codes, and one code is sampled from it:

$$q(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x),\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol\sigma^2(\mathbf x)\big),\qquad\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\quad\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I).$$

Writing the sample as \(\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) is the reparameterisation trick: the randomness sits in \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), outside the network, so gradients can pass through \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\sigma\). The decoder maps \(\mathbf z\) to a picture.

The loss

$$\mathcal L=\underbrace{-\mathbb E_{q}\big[\log p(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z)\big]}_{\text{reconstruction}}+\beta\,\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x)\,\Vert\,\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\big)}_{\text{keep the clouds near the centre}},\qquad\mathrm{KL}=\tfrac12\sum_j\big(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-\log\sigma_j^2-1\big).$$

The first term wants each picture's cloud to be small and far from the others, so that pictures can be told apart. The second wants every cloud to be the same standard bell at the centre. Neither wins. The compromise is clouds that overlap a little and together fill the bell, which is what makes random draws from \(\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) decode well. With \(\beta=1\) the negative of \(\mathcal L\) is the evidence lower bound (ELBO) on \(\log p(\mathbf x)\).

Generating

Draw \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) and run the decoder. No picture is needed as input. Because neighbouring codes decode to similar pictures, moving along a line in code space morphs one picture into another.

The trade-off, and what came next

VAE samples tend to be blurry: the decoder hedges across everything a code might mean. Raising \(\beta\) organises the map but loses detail; lowering it does the reverse. VAEs are still everywhere, mostly as compressors: latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion run their diffusion inside the code space of a VAE, and decode at the end.

What this page trains

A real VAE on 150 letter pictures of 35 pixels, with a two-number code, encoder \(35\to24\to(\boldsymbol\mu,\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2)\) and decoder \(2\to24\to35\), trained by backpropagation with Adam until the loss stops falling.

Check yourself

With β = 0 the reconstruction error is lower than with β = 1. Why would anyone accept the higher error?

Because the purpose is to generate, not to copy. With β = 0 nothing ties the codes to the centre, so they spread wherever is convenient and leave gaps. A random draw from the standard bell then lands where the decoder was never trained, and decodes to rubbish. The KL term costs some reconstruction accuracy and buys a code space in which every region means something.

entries.title: GANs: a forger and a detective train each other
entries.html:
GANs: A Forger and a Detective Train Each Other

Two networks play against each other. The generator turns random numbers into fake data and has never seen the real thing. The discriminator sees both and tries to tell them apart. Each time the detective gets better, the forger has to improve, and the other way round. Watch the gold fakes chase the dark real points across the plane, and watch what can go wrong.

A forger paints fake banknotes and a detective inspects them. The forger never sees a real note. All they learn is what the detective says: "fake, the ink is wrong". They fix the ink. The detective, now seeing better fakes, learns to check the paper. The forger fixes the paper. Round after round both improve, and in the end the fakes are indistinguishable from the real thing. Neither could have got there alone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) sets up that contest between two networks.

How it works, step by step

  1. The generator turns a batch of random numbers into points. At first they land anywhere.
  2. Discriminator’s turn: it is shown real points and fakes, told which is which, and adjusts to tell them apart better.
  3. Generator’s turn: it makes new fakes and is told only how real the discriminator found them. It adjusts to fool it more.
  4. Repeat. The background changes as the detective learns; the gold dots move as the forger responds.
  5. There is no finish line: the aim is a balance where the fakes sit on the real data and the detective can only guess.

What just happened

Animation

The data
The model
Steps
–
Discriminator loss
–
Generator loss
–
Real points the discriminator calls real
–
Fakes the discriminator calls real
–
Clusters the generator covers
–

Try this. Run it on the six clusters and count how many the gold dots cover as training goes on. They often lock onto two or three first, then jump: that is mode collapse, the best-known GAN failure. Watch the two loss curves: neither goes to zero, and that is correct. Raise the learning rate to 6 and train again. Then try One Blob, where there is nothing to collapse onto.

The two players

The generator \(G\) maps random noise \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) to a data point \(G(\mathbf z)\). The discriminator \(D\) maps a point to the probability that it is real. They play

$$\min_G\max_D\;\;\mathbb E_{\mathbf x\sim\text{data}}\big[\log D(\mathbf x)\big]+\mathbb E_{\mathbf z}\big[\log\big(1-D(G(\mathbf z))\big)\big].$$

\(D\) wants both terms large: real points scored near 1, fakes near 0. \(G\) wants the second term small.

Training

Alternate two steps. Discriminator step: ordinary classification, real against fake, with \(G\) held fixed. Generator step: hold \(D\) fixed and backpropagate through it into \(G\). In practice \(G\) maximises \(\log D(G(\mathbf z))\), which gives stronger gradients early on than minimising \(\log(1-D(G(\mathbf z)))\). The generator's only teaching signal is the gradient of the discriminator's opinion: which way should each fake move to look more real?

The ideal end point

For a fixed generator the best discriminator is \(D^*(\mathbf x)=\dfrac{p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf x)}{p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf x)+p_G(\mathbf x)}\). If the generator matches the data exactly, \(D^*=\tfrac12\) everywhere: the detective is reduced to tossing a coin, and both losses settle near \(\log2\approx0.69\) and \(2\log2\approx1.39\). So unlike every other lesson on this site, a falling loss is not the goal, and there is no test for convergence. This page stops after a fixed number of steps.

What goes wrong

  • Mode collapse. The generator finds a few outputs that fool the detective and produces only those. The detective catches up, the generator jumps elsewhere, and they chase each other. Nothing in the objective rewards covering all of the data.
  • Instability. Two networks optimising against each other can oscillate or diverge, and the balance is sensitive to learning rates.
  • Vanishing signal. If the detective becomes too good, its opinion is flat near the fakes and the generator learns nothing.

Where GANs stand

From 2014 to about 2020 GANs produced the sharpest generated images, and they are still used where speed matters, since generation is one forward pass. Diffusion models have largely replaced them for images because they train stably and cover the data better.

What this page trains

Two real networks, each with two hidden layers of 32 neurons, trained with Adam. The generator maps two random numbers to a point in the plane.

Check yourself

After long training the discriminator’s accuracy is about 50% on both real and fake points. Has training failed?

No, that is the best possible outcome. If the generator’s points are distributed exactly like the real data, no rule can tell them apart, and the best the discriminator can do is guess. A discriminator that stays near 100% accuracy means the generator is still producing detectable fakes; one near 50% means either success or, less happily, that the discriminator is too weak to notice differences that are there.

entries.tab: DDPM and IDDPM on a picture
entries.title: DDPM and improved DDPM: bury a picture in noise, then bring it back
entries.html:
DDPM and Improved DDPM: Bury a Picture in Noise, Then Bring It Back

Stir a drop of ink into water and it spreads until nothing of the drop is left. That direction is easy. A diffusion model learns the other direction: it removes a little noise at a time until a picture appears. Choose a picture, watch it dissolve, then watch the denoiser bring it back. Whether the same picture returns depends on how much of it survived, and that is decided by the noise schedule, which you can redesign here: the original DDPM schedule, the improved one from IDDPM, or your own.

A sculptor starts with a rough block and removes a little at a time until the statue appears. Nobody could carve a statue in a single blow, but each small cut is easy: look at what is there, decide what does not belong, take it off. A diffusion model generates the same way. It starts from a block of static and removes a little noise at each step. It learns what "does not belong" by first watching real pictures being buried in noise, where it knows exactly what noise was added. If you bury a picture only part of the way, enough of it shows through for the sculptor to recover that same picture. Bury it completely and the sculptor is free to carve any statue it knows.

How it works, step by step

  1. Forward, one step: shrink the picture slightly toward grey and add a little fresh random noise. The noise schedule says how much at each step.
  2. Repeat up to the turning point you chose. The further you go, the less of the original is left in the mix.
  3. Reverse: ask the denoiser, “given this noisy picture, what was the clean one?” Its answer blends the pictures it knows, weighted by how well each one fits.
  4. Step toward that guess and add back a little fresh noise. The reverse-noise setting says how much.
  5. Repeat down to step 0. If enough of the original survived at the turning point, the same picture comes back.
  6. Generate: start from pure static instead. There is no original to recover, so any picture the model knows can appear.

What just happened

Animation
The noise schedule
The reverse process
The pictures the model knows

Step
–
Share of the original left (√ᾱ)
–
Share of noise (√(1−ᾱ))
–
The denoiser thinks this is
–
Steps on which the denoiser can still recognise the original: your schedule / the alternative
–
Result
–

Try this. Choose the sunflower and press Run. The picture is noised for 60% of the steps of the linear DDPM schedule and then denoised: the sunflower comes back. Now move “Turn back” to 100% and run a few times. Sometimes a different picture comes back. Read the two share readouts at the turning point to see why. Next compare the two strips in the middle of the right-hand picture: under the linear schedule the picture is already static halfway through, and under the cosine schedule it fades evenly. That waste is what IDDPM fixed. Design your own schedule with the β sliders and watch the curves and the “still recognisable” readout. Then lower the reverse steps to 10%: does the denoiser still get home? Finally choose Generate a Picture from Pure Static and run it several times.

The forward process: adding noise

Let \(\mathbf x_0\) be a picture with pixel values scaled to \([-1,1]\). Each step mixes in a little Gaussian noise:

$$\mathbf x_t=\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\;\mathbf x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\;\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t,\qquad\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I).$$

The numbers \(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_T\) are the noise schedule. Because Gaussians combine neatly, any step can be reached from the original in one jump. With \(\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}(1-\beta_s)\),

$$\mathbf x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\;\mathbf x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\;\boldsymbol\varepsilon .$$

\(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\) is how much picture is left and \(\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\) how much noise: the two solid curves at the lower right. The step slider uses this formula to jump anywhere.

The reverse process: removing noise

A network \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t)\) is trained to predict the noise that was added, by minimising

$$\mathcal L_{\text{simple}}=\mathbb E_{\mathbf x_0,\,t,\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon}\Big[\big\lVert\boldsymbol\varepsilon-\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\;t\big)\big\rVert^2\Big].$$

Predicting the noise is the same as predicting the clean picture, since \(\hat{\mathbf x}_0=(\mathbf x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\). One reverse step then draws \(\mathbf x_{t-1}\) from a Gaussian whose centre lies between the current noisy picture and the guess:

$$\mathbf x_{t-1}=\underbrace{\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat{\mathbf x}_0+\frac{\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x_t}_{\text{mean}}+\sigma_t\,\mathbf z,\qquad\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I).$$

This is DDPM, denoising diffusion probabilistic models (Ho, Jain and Abbeel, 2020). They used a schedule in which \(\beta_t\) rises in a straight line, and \(\sigma_t^2=\beta_t\).

Why the picture you chose comes back, or does not

The reverse process only sees the noisy picture. When you turn back early, \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\) is still well above zero, the original shows through, and the denoiser's guess is that picture. At the very end of a schedule \(\bar\alpha_T\) is practically zero: the noisy picture is static that would look the same whichever picture you began with. Nothing is left to say it was the sunflower, so the reverse process is free to end on any picture it knows. That is not a fault. It is exactly what makes diffusion a generator: begin from fresh static and a new sample appears. Starting the reverse process from a partly noised picture, as the first button does, is how diffusion models are used to edit or restore an existing image.

IDDPM, part 1: the cosine schedule

Nichol and Dhariwal (2021) noticed that the linear schedule destroys small pictures far too quickly. Look at the middle strips: with the linear schedule the picture is gone about halfway through, so the remaining steps are spent turning static into static and teach the network very little. They proposed choosing \(\bar\alpha_t\) directly, as a smooth curve that falls gently at both ends:

$$\bar\alpha_t=\frac{f(t)}{f(0)},\qquad f(t)=\cos^2\!\Big(\frac{t/T+s}{1+s}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\Big),\qquad \beta_t=1-\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_{t-1}},$$

with a small offset \(s=0.008\) and \(\beta_t\) capped at 0.999. Information is removed at a nearly even pace from the first step to the last. The readout "steps on which the denoiser can still recognise the original" measures the difference. The ideal denoiser on this page sees through far more noise than your eye does, so judge the strips by eye and the readout by number.

IDDPM, part 2: how much noise to put back

For the size \(\sigma_t\) of the fresh noise in the reverse step there are two natural choices. The largest sensible value is \(\sigma_t^2=\beta_t\). The smallest is the variance the step would have if the clean picture were known exactly,

$$\tilde\beta_t=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t .$$

DDPM fixed one of them. IDDPM lets the network output a number \(v\) between 0 and 1 for every step and pixel, and uses a blend of the two on a logarithmic scale:

$$\sigma_t^2=\exp\!\big(v\,\log\beta_t+(1-v)\,\log\tilde\beta_t\big).$$

On this page you set \(v\) by hand with the reverse-noise slider. The two ends differ most in the last few steps, where \(\tilde\beta_t\) goes to zero and \(\beta_t\) does not. To train \(v\), IDDPM adds a small multiple of the full likelihood bound to the simple loss, \(\mathcal L_{\text{hybrid}}=\mathcal L_{\text{simple}}+\lambda\,\mathcal L_{\text{vlb}}\).

IDDPM, part 3: fewer reverse steps

With a well-chosen variance, sampling does not have to visit every step. Pick a shorter list of steps \(t_1>t_2>\dots\), treat each jump from \(t\) to \(s\) as one step with \(\beta'=1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_s\), and apply the same formulas. A model trained with 4,000 steps could then be sampled in about 100. The "reverse steps used" slider does this. The DDIM and Samplers tab takes the idea further.

Why the first guesses are blurry

The best possible answer to "what clean picture is behind this static?" is the average of all the pictures it could have been, weighted by how likely each is. At high noise many pictures are plausible, so the average is a blur. As noise is removed the candidates narrow and the guess sharpens. The fresh noise added at each step helps decide which candidate wins.

What this page computes

The forward process, the schedules, the reverse mean and the reverse variance are exactly the formulas above. For the denoiser this page does not train a network. It uses the mathematically ideal denoiser for a tiny data set: when the model "knows" only the \(K\) pictures in the list, the best guess is

$$\hat{\mathbf x}_0=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\,\mathbf x^{(k)},\qquad w_k\propto\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x^{(k)}\rVert^2}{2(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\Big),$$

the bars at the top right. Because it knows so few pictures, it can pick out the original from astonishingly little: a picture has thousands of pixels, and a faint trace spread over all of them adds up. A real diffusion model replaces this sum with a U-Net trained on millions of pictures. When such a model denoises a heavily noised photo it returns a picture like the original, not the original itself, and it can produce pictures that are in none of its training data. The next tab trains a denoising network on simple data. The built-in pictures are drawn by code, and an uploaded photo is shrunk to 32 × 32 pixels.

Check yourself

You noise the sunflower all the way to the last step of the linear schedule and denoise it, and a cat comes back. A classmate says the denoiser made a mistake. Did it?

No. At the last step of that schedule the share of the original left in the mix is practically zero, so the noisy picture is static that could have come from any picture with almost equal probability. The information that it was a sunflower has been destroyed, not hidden, and no denoiser, however good, can read what is no longer there. From that point the reverse process is generating a new sample, and which picture it lands on is decided by the random noise. Turn back earlier, or use a schedule that still keeps a trace at the turning point, and the sunflower returns.

entries.title: Train a diffusion model: teach a network to undo noise
entries.html:
Train a Diffusion Model: Teach a Network to Undo Noise

The previous tab used an ideal denoiser. Here a real network learns the job from scratch. The “pictures” are single points in a plane, arranged in a shape, so that you can see everything at once. The network is shown noisy points and asked what noise was added. Once it can answer, hand it a cloud of pure noise and watch 400 points walk back into the shape.

Hide a friend's sketch under a thin sheet of tracing paper covered in random speckles and ask someone to remove the speckles. With one sheet it is easy.
