Stack forty sheets and the sketch is invisible, but the job can still be done one sheet at a time, as long as the person has learned what sketches look like and so can tell speckle from line. Training a diffusion model is practising that single-sheet job at every thickness of the stack. Generating is starting with forty sheets of speckle and nothing underneath, and peeling.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a batch of real points. Give each a random noise level t and add that much noise.
  2. Ask the network: “this noisy point, at level t: what noise was added?” Compare with the truth and backpropagate.
  3. Repeat for three thousand batches.
  4. Generate: start 400 points as pure noise at the highest level.
  5. At each level, the network estimates the noise in every point, a little of it is removed, and a little fresh noise is added. After 40 levels the points form the shape.

What just happened

Animation

The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Error at guessing the noise
–
Noise level while generating
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–

Try this. Let it train and generate, then press Generate Again a few times: new points each time, always forming the shape. Now switch to the spiral and press Start over, and during training press One step to move 50 steps at a time, generating at 100, 500 and 3000 steps by pressing Generate Again. How does the quality of the generated shape track the error curve? Watch the arrows during generation: far from the data they all point inward; near the end they point at the nearest part of the shape.

Training

Pick a real point \(\mathbf x_0\), a level \(t\) uniformly from \(1,\dots,T\), and noise \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\). Form the noisy point in one jump, \(\mathbf x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), and train the network to recover the noise:

$$\mathcal L=\big\lVert\boldsymbol\varepsilon-\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t)\big\rVert^2 .$$

That is the entire training loop. No adversary, no encoder: plain regression with a target that is known exactly, because we added the noise ourselves. This is why diffusion models train so stably.

Why the error never reaches zero

Many different clean points and noises give the same noisy point, so the noise cannot be known exactly. The best possible answer is the average over all the ways \(\mathbf x_t\) could have arisen, and the remaining error is irreducible, as in the Bias and Variance lesson. A loss that flattens at a value well above zero is what success looks like here. This page trains for a fixed 3,000 steps, by which time it has flattened.

What the network has really learned

The predicted noise points away from the data. Its negative, scaled, is the score, the direction in which the probability of the noisy data rises fastest:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf x}\log p_t(\mathbf x)\approx-\frac{\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x,t)}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}} .$$

The arrows in the picture are this field. At high noise it is simple and points toward the middle of the data. At low noise it is detailed and points at the nearest part of the shape. Learning one field per noise level, from coarse to fine, is what lets generation start from anywhere.

Generating

Start from \(\mathbf x_T\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) and apply, for \(t=T,\dots,1\),

$$\mathbf x_{t-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_t}}\Big(\mathbf x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t)\Big)+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\mathbf z .$$

Each point follows the arrows a short way and is jostled by fresh noise \(\mathbf z\). The jostling matters: without it the points would bunch up along the centre of the shape.

What this page trains

A real network with two hidden layers of 64 neurons. Its input is the two coordinates of the noisy point and eight numbers that encode the noise level as sine and cosine waves. It is trained with Adam on batches of 128, with \(T=40\) levels. Image models do the same with a U-Net in place of this small network and a picture in place of the point.

Check yourself

After training, the error at guessing the noise is about 0.3, not 0. Yet the generated points land on the shape. How can a network that is “30% wrong” generate well?

The error is an average over all noise levels, and at high noise the question has no exact answer: the same noisy point could have come from many clean points, so even a perfect network must be wrong by a fixed amount. What matters for generation is that the network’s answer is the correct average, which gives the right direction to move in at every level. Following correct average directions for forty small steps leads onto the data.

entries.title: DDIM and samplers: the same network, far fewer steps
entries.html:
DDIM and Samplers: The Same Network, Far Fewer Steps

The diffusion model in the earlier tabs walks through every noise level, one small step at a time. Real image models have a thousand levels, so that walk is slow. A sampler is the rule for getting from noise to data, and you can change it after training without touching the network. Here one network is trained once, with 100 noise levels, and then asked to finish the job in 100 steps, in 10, or in 3.

Think of walking down a foggy mountain to a village. The DDPM rule is a cautious walker who takes a thousand tiny steps and is nudged sideways by a random gust after each one. DDIM is a walker who, at every stop, asks a guide "where do you think the village is?", then strides a long way in that direction and asks again. The guide is the same in both cases: it is the trained network. The first few answers are vague ("somewhere down there"), and later answers are sharp, so a handful of well-spaced questions is enough. Because there are no gusts, starting from the same spot always leads to the same door.

How it works, step by step

  1. Train as in the previous tab: add a random amount of noise to real points and teach the network to guess that noise. There are 100 noise levels.
  2. Measure: generate with 1, 2, 3 and up to 100 steps, with and without added randomness, and count the points that land on the shape.
  3. Generate: start from pure noise and choose a short list of levels to visit, for example 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0.
  4. At each stop the network guesses the noise. Removing all of that noise gives a guess of the finished point.
  5. Jump: put the guess back at the next level on the list by adding the right amount of noise. DDIM reuses the noise the network just guessed. The DDPM rule mixes in fresh random noise.
  6. After the last jump the points are finished.

What just happened

Animation

The sampler
The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Times the network was called
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–
Average shift from the last run with the same starting noise
–

Try this. Let it train and measure. With η at 0, set the steps to 100 and note how many points land on the shape, then try 20, 10, 5 and 2. How few steps can you get away with? Now press Same Noise Again several times: the shift readout stays at 0.00, because nothing random is left in the walk. Move η to 1 and repeat: the same starting noise now ends somewhere new each time, and the routes turn jittery. Now look at the two lines in the chart. Where do both fall, and how far apart are they at 5 steps and at 50? Last, watch the top-right picture on a 10-step run: how early does the network already know roughly where the points belong?

Two things the network's answer gives you

At level \(t\) the noisy point is \(\mathbf x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\). The network returns \(\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}=\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t)\). Solving the same equation for \(\mathbf x_0\) turns that into a guess of the finished point:

$$\hat{\mathbf x}_0=\frac{\mathbf x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}} .$$

The top-right picture plots \(\hat{\mathbf x}_0\) for every point. Early on it is a blurry average of the data. It sharpens as the level falls.

The jump

To move from level \(t\) to any lower level \(s\), not only \(t-1\), rebuild a noisy point at level \(s\) from the guess:

$$\mathbf x_s=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_s}\,\hat{\mathbf x}_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_s-\sigma^2}\;\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}+\sigma\,\mathbf z,\qquad \mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I),$$$$\sigma=\eta\,\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar\alpha_s}{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\sqrt{1-\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_s}} .$$

The total noise in \(\mathbf x_s\) is always \(1-\bar\alpha_s\), which is what level \(s\) should contain. The slider \(\eta\) decides how much of it is new. With \(\eta=1\) and every level visited this is exactly the DDPM step from the previous tab. With \(\eta=0\) no new noise enters: this is DDIM (Song, Meng and Ermon, 2021).

Why skipping levels is allowed

Training only ever used the one-jump formula for \(\mathbf x_t\) given \(\mathbf x_0\). It never used the chain of small steps. DDIM's observation is that many different step-by-step processes share those same one-jump distributions, so a network trained for one of them is already trained for all of them. Choosing a sampler is choosing among those processes after the fact. That is why the page trains once and then moves the two sliders freely.

What you give up and what you gain

Each jump treats the network's current guess as if it stayed correct across the whole jump. Over a short jump that is nearly true. Over a long jump the direction should have bent, so the error grows as the number of steps falls: the bottom-right chart shows quality dropping at the left. With \(\eta=0\) the routes are smooth curves. With \(\eta=1\) every step also adds a random kick, and the routes are jagged. In large image models the \(\eta=0\) rule usually keeps its quality better when the steps are few, which is why DDIM made fast sampling practical. On this small two-dimensional problem the two lines in the chart stay close to each other. The clear effect here is the one both lines share: below about five steps, quality collapses.

The same noise gives the same picture

With \(\eta=0\) the only randomness is the starting point \(\mathbf x_T\). Generation becomes a fixed map from noise to data. Three useful things follow. A result can be reproduced from its seed. Sliding smoothly between two starting noises gives a smooth blend between two outputs. And the map can be run backwards, from a real picture to the noise that would produce it, which is how many image-editing methods begin.

Other samplers

As the steps shrink, the \(\eta=0\) rule traces the solution of an ordinary differential equation, called the probability-flow ODE. Once generation is seen as solving an ODE, any numerical solver can be used. Euler's method is the plain version. Heun's method and the DPM-Solver family look at the slope more than once per step and reach the same quality with fewer network calls. The sampler names in image tools, such as "Euler", "Heun", "DPM++" and "DDIM", are these choices. The network is the same in every case.

What this page trains

The same small network as the previous tab, two hidden layers of 64 neurons, trained for 2,500 batches of 128 with \(T=100\) noise levels. The quality number is the share of generated points that fall within 0.1 of a real data point. For the chart it is measured on 200 fresh points for each setting, so it wobbles by a few percent from one training run to the next.

Check yourself

A classmate says: "DDIM with 10 steps must need a network trained with 10 noise levels." What is wrong with that?

The network is trained with all 100 levels and is never retrained. Training only teaches it to guess the noise in a point at any single level. How those guesses are strung together into a walk is decided afterwards by the sampler. DDIM visits 10 of the 100 levels and uses the network’s guess at each one to jump straight to the next, so the same weights serve 100 steps, 10 steps or 3.

entries.title: Stable Diffusion in miniature: from a prompt to a picture
entries.html:
Stable Diffusion in Miniature: From a Prompt to a Picture

Stable Diffusion is three ideas bolted together. Compress pictures into a small code, so the hard work happens on a few numbers instead of a million pixels. Run diffusion on that code. And steer the diffusion with a prompt. This page builds all three for real, small enough to train in your browser: choose a prompt, set how strongly to follow it, and watch eight pictures form.

An architect does not design a building by placing bricks. She works on a small floor plan, where moving a wall is one pencil stroke, and only at the end is the plan turned into a building. And she works to a brief: "three bedrooms, lots of light". Stable Diffusion generates pictures the same way. It does its diffusion on a small plan of the picture, called a latent, steered by a brief, the prompt. Only at the very end does a decoder turn the finished latent into pixels.

How it works, step by step

  1. Train the compressor (a VAE): squeeze each 35-pixel picture to a code of 2 numbers and back.
  2. Encode every training picture. From here on the pictures are put away: only their codes and their captions are used.
  3. Train the denoiser on the codes: add noise to a code, show it the noisy code and the caption, and ask what noise was added. One time in seven the caption is hidden.
  4. Generate: start eight codes as pure noise. At each step ask the denoiser twice, with the prompt and without, and push the answer further in the direction the prompt suggests (guidance).
  5. After 40 steps, run the finished codes through the decoder. Only now do pixels appear.

What just happened

Animation

Generation
Stage
–
Prompt
–
Noise level while generating
–
Generated pictures that match the prompt
–
Numbers the denoiser works on, per picture
–
Training error now
–

Try this. Let it train both parts and generate. Then press each prompt in turn: the gold dots walk to a different region of the map each time, and a different letter comes out. Set guidance to 0 and generate: the prompt is ignored and you get a random mix of letters. Raise it to 3, then 8: more of the eight match, and they bunch tightly together. What is lost at very high guidance?

Part 1: compress (the VAE)

An autoencoder is trained first and then frozen. Its encoder \(\mathcal E\) maps a picture \(\mathbf x\) to a latent \(\mathbf z=\mathcal E(\mathbf x)\), and its decoder \(\mathcal D\) maps a latent back to a picture. In the real model a \(512\times512\times3\) picture (786,432 numbers) becomes a \(64\times64\times4\) latent (16,384 numbers), 48 times smaller. Diffusion in that space is far cheaper than in pixels, which is what made the model usable on an ordinary graphics card. Here 35 pixels become 2 numbers.

Part 2: diffuse in latent space

Everything from the DDPM tabs applies unchanged, with \(\mathbf z\) in place of the picture. Noise is added to latents, \(\mathbf z_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf z_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), and a denoiser is trained to predict it, now with the caption \(c\) as an extra input:

$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E\Big[\big\lVert\boldsymbol\varepsilon-\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf z_t,\,t,\,c)\big\rVert^2\Big].$$

In the real model the denoiser is a U-Net and the caption enters through attention layers: every position in the latent attends to the words of the prompt (cross-attention).

Part 3: follow the prompt (classifier-free guidance)

During training the caption is replaced by an empty one a fraction of the time, so the same network learns both "denoise toward this caption" and "denoise toward any picture". When generating, both are computed, and the difference between them is exaggerated by a guidance scale \(w\):

$$\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}=\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf z_t,t,\varnothing)+w\,\Big[\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf z_t,t,c)-\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf z_t,t,\varnothing)\Big].$$

\(w=0\) ignores the prompt. \(w=1\) is the plain conditional model. \(w>1\) pushes harder toward what the prompt adds, which makes results match the prompt more reliably and makes them less varied. Very large \(w\) gives over-saturated, distorted pictures; values around 7 are typical for images.

The whole pipeline

  1. The prompt is turned into vectors by a text encoder.
  2. A latent is filled with random noise.
  3. For each step, the denoiser predicts the noise twice (with and without the prompt), guidance combines them, and the sampler removes a little noise.
  4. The decoder turns the final latent into a picture.

This page beside the real thing

HereStable Diffusion 1.5
Picture5 × 7 pixels, black and white512 × 512 pixels, colour
Latent2 numbers64 × 64 × 4 = 16,384 numbers
Promptone of six fixed captionsany text, up to 77 tokens
Text encodera lookup: one switch per captionCLIP, a Transformer (123 million weights)
Denoisera small network, about 5,400 weightsa U-Net with attention (860 million weights)
Sampling steps4020 to 50, with faster samplers
Training data150 picturesabout two billion captioned images

The three parts and the way they connect are the same. What a model of this size cannot do is combine ideas it has never seen together, which is where the scale of the real model matters.

Check yourself

Why is the caption hidden from the denoiser in a fraction of the training examples? It seems to throw information away.

So that one network learns two things: how to denoise given a caption, and how to denoise with no caption at all. Guidance needs both at generation time, because it works by comparing the two answers and exaggerating their difference. Without the caption-free examples the network would have no sensible answer for an empty prompt, and there would be nothing to compare against.

entries.title: Score matching: learn which way is “more likely”
entries.html:
Score Matching: Learn Which Way Is “More Likely”

Suppose you could stand anywhere in the plane and ask one question: in which direction does the data get denser? That arrow is called the score. With arrows everywhere you can generate data by dropping points at random and letting them climb, with a little jitter. The surprise is that the arrows can be learned without ever knowing the density itself, by practising one simple job: removing noise.

Imagine a dark hillside with a few campfires. You cannot see the fires, but everywhere you stand you can feel which way is warmer. Follow the warmth and you reach a fire. The score is that "warmer this way" arrow, with data density in place of heat. There is one difficulty: far from every fire you feel almost nothing, and what you do feel is unreliable. The fix is to begin with huge bonfires whose warmth reaches the whole hillside, walk toward them, and then shrink the fires in stages. Each stage only has to guide you from "roughly right" to "a bit more exactly right".

How it works, step by step

  1. Take real points. Choose one of ten noise levels for each and add that much noise.
  2. Ask the network which way leads back toward the clean point. The right answer is known, because we added the noise ourselves. Backpropagate.
  3. Repeat for 2,500 batches. The network now gives an arrow at every place, for every noise level.
  4. Generate: scatter points at random over the whole picture.
  5. Langevin step: move each point a little way along its arrow and add a little random jitter. Repeat.
  6. Annealing: start with the arrows for the largest noise level, which reach everywhere, and work down to the smallest, which are precise.

What just happened

Animation

Generating
The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Error at guessing the noise
–
Noise level shown, and its size σ
–
Learned arrows within 25° of the exact ones, at that level
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–

Try this. After training, drag the noise-level slider from 1 to 10 and compare the two arrow pictures. At level 1 the arrows are simple: everything points at the middle of the data. At level 10 they are detailed near the data. What do the learned arrows do far from the data at level 10, and how does the bar chart show it? Now choose Only the Level Shown with level 10 and press Generate Again. Do all the points find the shape? Try level 1, then a middle level such as 5 or 6. On these small shapes a well-chosen middle level can do about as well as the full ladder. What would you have to know in advance to choose it? Then switch back to All Ten Levels: which problem of the smallest level does starting large solve, and which problem of the largest level does finishing small solve?

The score

For a density \(p(\mathbf x)\) the score is the gradient of its logarithm:

$$\mathbf s(\mathbf x)=\nabla_{\mathbf x}\log p(\mathbf x).$$

It points toward higher density, and it is longer where the density changes faster. Writing a model as \(p(\mathbf x)=e^{-E(\mathbf x)}/Z\) shows why the score is convenient: the awkward constant \(Z\), which makes probabilities sum to one, disappears when you take the gradient of the logarithm. A network can output a score without anyone ever computing \(Z\).

Learning it by denoising

We do not know \(p\), so we cannot compute its score to train against. Vincent (2011) showed a way around this. Blur the data with Gaussian noise of size \(\sigma\): \(\tilde{\mathbf x}=\mathbf x+\sigma\boldsymbol\varepsilon\). The score of the blurred density \(p_\sigma\) is the minimiser of

$$\mathcal L(\sigma)=\mathbb E_{\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\varepsilon}\Big\lVert\,\mathbf s_\theta(\tilde{\mathbf x},\sigma)+\frac{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big\rVert^2 .$$

In words: the arrow at a noisy point should point back along the noise that was added, \(-\boldsymbol\varepsilon/\sigma=(\mathbf x-\tilde{\mathbf x})/\sigma^2\). Many clean points could have produced the same noisy point, and the average of all their "way back" arrows is exactly \(\nabla\log p_\sigma\). This page trains the network to output \(\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}\) and uses \(\mathbf s_\theta=-\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}/\sigma\), which is the same loss multiplied by \(\sigma^2\) so that every level counts equally.

Checking against the exact answer

For the 500 data points on this page, the blurred density is a mixture of 500 small Gaussians, one on each point, and its score has a closed form:

$$\nabla\log p_\sigma(\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_i w_i(\mathbf x)\,(\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x),\qquad w_i(\mathbf x)\propto\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf x-\mathbf x_i\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big).$$

That is the top-right picture. The network never sees this formula. The bar chart counts how many of its arrows fall within 25° of it.

Generating: Langevin dynamics

Given a score, repeat

$$\mathbf x\leftarrow\mathbf x+\frac{\alpha}{2}\,\mathbf s_\theta(\mathbf x,\sigma)+\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mathbf z,\qquad\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I).$$

Climb the arrow a little, then jitter. Without the jitter every point would end on a peak of the density. With it, and with a small step \(\alpha\), the points settle into samples spread according to \(p_\sigma\) itself.

Why one noise level is a poor bet

With a small \(\sigma\) the blurred density is almost the real one, but training only ever showed the network points close to the data. Far away, where random starting points land, the arrows were never practised and cannot be trusted. Even the exact score has a second problem there: between two separate groups it is nearly blind to how many points each group holds, so the groups receive the wrong shares. With a large \(\sigma\) the arrows are reliable everywhere, but they lead to a blurred version of the data. On the two-dimensional shapes of this page a middle level happens to work about as well as the whole ladder, as you can check. For images, the distance from a random start to the data is vastly larger than the detail that has to be resolved, and no single level covers both.

Annealing

Song and Ermon (2019) train one network on a ladder of levels \(\sigma_1>\sigma_2>\dots>\sigma_L\) and sample by running Langevin dynamics at each level in turn, with step \(\alpha_i\propto\sigma_i^2\), using the result of one level as the start of the next. The large levels move the points across empty space. The small levels sharpen them. This page uses ten levels from 1.2 down to 0.05, each 0.7 times the one before, with twelve Langevin steps per level.

The link to diffusion

A diffusion model's noise prediction is this same quantity under another name: \(\nabla\log p_t(\mathbf x)=-\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x,t)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\). Its many noise levels are the ladder, and its sampling loop is annealed Langevin dynamics with a particular choice of step sizes. Song and others (2021) joined the two views into one framework in which the noise level changes continuously.

Check yourself

The loss compares the network’s arrow with the direction back to one particular clean point. But many clean points could have produced the same noisy point. Why does training on these conflicting targets give the right answer?

Because the loss is a squared error, and the single arrow that minimises a squared error against many targets is their average. At a given noisy point the targets are the “way back” arrows to every clean point that could have produced it, weighted by how likely each one is. That weighted average is exactly the gradient of the log of the blurred density, which is the score. The individual targets conflict, but their mean is what we wanted all along. It is the same reason the error never falls to zero.

entries.title: Flow matching: draw a straight line from noise to data
entries.html:
Flow Matching: Draw a Straight Line from Noise to Data

Diffusion reaches data by a winding, noisy road. Flow matching asks for the simplest road there is: pair each noise point with a data point, join them with a straight line, and teach a network the direction of travel along those lines. Generating is then following the arrows from noise for a few steps. Many recent image and video models are trained this way.

Picture a crowd spread randomly over a field, and a set of chairs arranged in a ring. Give each person one chair at random and tell them to walk straight to it at steady speed, arriving after one minute. Now film the crowd from above. At every spot and every moment there is a typical direction in which people are moving. Flow matching trains a network to report that typical direction. Afterwards the people and their assignments are no longer needed: drop a new crowd on the field, tell everyone to follow the reported directions, and after one minute they are sitting in a ring.

How it works, step by step

  1. Draw a random noise point and a random real point. Join them with a straight line.
  2. Pick a random time between 0 and 1 and stand that far along the line. The correct velocity there is simply “data point minus noise point”.
  3. Ask the network for the velocity at that place and time, compare with the correct one, and backpropagate. Repeat for 2,500 batches.
  4. Measure: generate with 1, 2, 3 and up to 40 steps and count the points that land on the shape.
  5. Generate: start from pure noise at time 0. At each step ask the network for the velocity and move every point a short way along it.
  6. At time 1 the points have arrived.

What just happened

Animation

The sampler
The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Error at guessing the velocity
–
Times the network was called
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–
How straight the routes are (1 = ruler-straight)
–

Try this. Watch the top-right picture during training: every arrow there is known exactly, so the network has a clear target at every step. When generation starts, look at the routes on the left. They are not perfectly straight even though every training line was. Why not? (Hint: many lines cross at the same place, and the network can only give one answer there.) Now set the steps to 1: every point jumps in a single stride. Where do they land? Try 2, 4 and 8. Switch to Midpoint and compare 4 steps of Midpoint with 8 steps of Euler: both call the network eight times. Which lands more points on the shape?

The straight-line path

Take noise \(\mathbf x_0\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) and a real point \(\mathbf x_1\). For a time \(t\in[0,1]\) define the point on the line between them and its velocity:

$$\mathbf x_t=(1-t)\,\mathbf x_0+t\,\mathbf x_1,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf x_t}{dt}=\mathbf x_1-\mathbf x_0 .$$

The velocity does not depend on \(t\): each person walks at constant speed. This is the choice used by rectified flow (Liu, Gong and Liu, 2023) and by conditional flow matching (Lipman and others, 2023).

Training

The network \(\mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x,t)\) is trained by plain regression onto that velocity:

$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E_{\,t,\ \mathbf x_0,\ \mathbf x_1}\big\lVert \mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t)-(\mathbf x_1-\mathbf x_0)\big\rVert^2 .$$

As with diffusion, the target is known exactly because we built the path ourselves. There is no noise schedule to design and no \(\bar\alpha_t\).

What the network actually learns

Many different lines pass through the same place at the same time, each with its own velocity, and the network can give only one answer. The answer that minimises a squared error is the average:

$$\mathbf v^\star(\mathbf x,t)=\mathbb E\big[\mathbf x_1-\mathbf x_0\ \big|\ \mathbf x_t=\mathbf x\big].$$

So the error can never reach zero, for the same reason as in the diffusion tab. The remarkable fact is that following this averaged field still moves the whole noise distribution onto the whole data distribution. Individual routes bend where lines crossed, because the field cannot let two routes cross, but the crowd as a whole ends in the right place.

Generating

Solve the ordinary differential equation \(d\mathbf x/dt=\mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x,t)\) from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\). With \(N\) steps of Euler's method and \(h=1/N\):

$$\mathbf x_{t+h}=\mathbf x_t+h\,\mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t).$$

The midpoint method spends two network calls per step: it takes half a step, looks at the velocity there, and uses that velocity for the full step,

$$\mathbf x_{t+h}=\mathbf x_t+h\,\mathbf v_\theta\big(\mathbf x_t+\tfrac h2\mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x_t,t),\ t+\tfrac h2\big).$$

Nothing random is added along the way, so the same starting noise always gives the same result, as with DDIM.

Why straightness matters

Euler's method is exact on a straight route travelled at constant speed, whatever the step size. The straighter the learned routes, the fewer steps are needed. The readout compares the straight-line distance from start to finish with the length of the route actually taken. One further idea, called reflow, generates noise and data pairs with the trained model and retrains on those pairs. Their lines cross less, the routes become straighter, and good samples can then be made in one or two steps.

How it relates to diffusion

A diffusion model's \(\eta=0\) sampler also solves an ODE from noise to data. The difference is the path that training prescribes between the two ends: curved and tied to a noise schedule for diffusion, straight for flow matching. One can be rewritten as the other with a change of time and scale. The network's output is a velocity here and a noise estimate there, and each can be computed from the other.

What this page trains

A network with two hidden layers of 64 neurons, taking the two coordinates and eight numbers that encode the time, trained with Adam for 2,500 batches of 128. Training times are drawn a little more often from the data end of the line, where the field has the most detail. The quality number is the share of generated points within 0.1 of a real data point, measured on 200 fresh points for each setting in the chart.

Check yourself

With one Euler step, every point moves from its starting place by exactly the velocity the network gives at time 0. Why does that produce a blob near the middle of the data instead of the shape?

At time 0 a point is pure noise and carries no information about which data point it was paired with, because the pairing was random. The best single answer for its velocity is therefore the average over all data points: “head for the centre of the data”. One step with that velocity sends everything toward the centre. Only later, when a point has moved and its position starts to say something about where it is heading, does the field split toward the different parts of the shape. That needs more than one step.

entries.title: Normalizing flows: bend a bell curve into the data
entries.html:
Normalizing Flows: Bend a Bell Curve Into the Data

Start with the simplest cloud there is, a round Gaussian blob, printed on a rubber sheet. Stretch and turn the sheet, a little at a time, until the blob has the shape of the data. If every stretch can be undone, two things come for free: new samples, by pushing fresh blob points through the stretches, and the exact probability of any point, by pulling it back to the blob and keeping count of how much the sheet was stretched there.

Draw a round target on a sheet of rubber, densest at the bullseye. Now stretch the sheet. Where you stretch it, the ink thins out, and the density falls. Where you bunch it up, the ink concentrates, and the density rises. The total amount of ink never changes. A normalizing flow is a recipe for stretching, learned so that the ink ends up where the data is. Because you know exactly how much each spot was stretched, you know exactly how dense the ink is there. No other model in this module can tell you the exact probability of a point. This one can.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a batch of real points and pull them backwards through the six layers, toward the Gaussian.
  2. Score the result: the points should land where a round Gaussian is dense, and the layers get credit wherever they had to squeeze space to bring them there. This score is the exact log-probability of the data.
  3. Backpropagate to raise that log-probability. Repeat for 1,500 batches.
  4. Generate: draw points from a round Gaussian.
  5. Push them forwards through the layers, one at a time. Each layer slides and stretches points along one axis by an amount that depends on the other axis, then turns the picture by 60°.
  6. After the last layer the cloud has the shape of the data.

What just happened

Animation

Layer by layer
The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Loss: minus the average log-probability of the data
–
The same loss for a plain round Gaussian, with no layers
–
Layers applied in the left picture
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–

Try this. Watch the left picture during training: the round blob is pulled into the shape while the grid shows where the sheet is being stretched and squeezed. Where are the grid cells smallest, and what does the density picture show there? After training, drag the layer slider from 0 to 6 to see what each layer adds. Then type coordinates for your own point: one on the shape, one in the gap between the two moons. How do the two densities compare? Finally switch to A Ring. The model must cover the ring with a sheet that has no hole in it. Look closely at the density: where did it hide the seam?

Change of variables

Let \(f\) be an invertible map that carries a data point \(\mathbf x\) back to a point \(\mathbf z=f(\mathbf x)\) with a standard Gaussian density \(p_Z\). Then the density of the data is

$$\log p_X(\mathbf x)=\log p_Z\big(f(\mathbf x)\big)+\log\left|\det\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf x}\right| .$$

The first term asks whether \(\mathbf x\) is pulled back to a likely place under the bell. The second is the bookkeeping for stretched rubber: the determinant of the Jacobian says how much \(f\) expands or shrinks a small area around \(\mathbf x\). Training maximises the average of this quantity over the data, which is maximum likelihood with nothing approximated.

The difficulty, and the trick

For a general network, the inverse does not exist and the determinant costs far too much to compute. Coupling layers (Dinh and others, 2015 and 2017) are designed so that both are easy. Split the coordinates into two parts. Leave the first as it is, and move the second by an amount that depends only on the first:

$$y_1=x_1,\qquad y_2=x_2\,e^{\,s(x_1)}+t(x_1).$$

Here \(s\) and \(t\) are the two outputs of an ordinary small network. They can be as complicated as you like, and they are never inverted. To undo the layer, note that \(x_1=y_1\) is still available, so \(s\) and \(t\) can be recomputed, and then \(x_2=(y_2-t(y_1))\,e^{-s(y_1)}\). The Jacobian is triangular, so its determinant is the product of its diagonal:

$$\log\left|\det\frac{\partial\mathbf y}{\partial\mathbf x}\right|=s(x_1).$$

Stacking layers

One coupling layer leaves \(x_1\) untouched, so between layers the axes are changed. With many dimensions the two halves swap roles. In two dimensions this page turns the plane by 60° before each layer, which costs nothing because a turn does not change areas. For a chain \(f=f_K\circ\dots\circ f_1\) the log-determinants add:

$$\log p_X(\mathbf x)=\log p_Z(\mathbf z)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}s_k .$$

The loss shown is minus the average of this over a batch.

Sampling and density, both exact

To sample, draw \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) and apply the inverses in reverse order: this is the animation on the left. To evaluate the density at a point, apply the layers forwards and add up the \(s_k\): this is the top-right picture, and the readout for your own point. A density that can be evaluated exactly is useful for spotting unusual inputs, for compression, and for comparing models fairly.

What it cannot do

A smooth invertible map cannot tear the sheet or glue parts of it together. A blob has no hole, so its image has no hole. To cover a ring, or two separate groups, the model must stretch a thin film of density across the gap. You can see that film in the density picture, and some generated points land on it. More layers make the film thinner but never remove it. The second limit is cost: every layer must keep the same number of dimensions as the data, with no bottleneck.

Where flows went next

Glow applied coupling layers to images. Autoregressive flows make each coordinate depend on all the earlier ones. Continuous normalizing flows replace the stack of layers with an ODE, \(d\mathbf x/dt=\mathbf v_\theta(\mathbf x,t)\), and flow matching, which has its own tab, is the modern way of training those without ever computing a determinant.

What this page trains

Six coupling layers. Each has its own network with two hidden layers of 32 neurons, whose scale output is kept between −1.2 and 1.2. Training uses Adam on batches of 96 for 1,500 steps.

Check yourself

The model gives the exact density at any point. A student proposes using it as a spam filter for data: flag any input whose density is low. In the ring data set, which points would this wrongly accept?

Points on the thin film that the model had to stretch across the hole or the gap. A flow cannot tear the Gaussian apart, so some density always connects regions that the data keeps separate. A point on that bridge receives a moderate density even though no real data ever appears there. The exact density is exact for the model, not for the world: it is only as good as the fit.

entries.title: Energy-based models: carve valleys where the data lives
entries.html:
Energy-Based Models: Carve Valleys Where the Data Lives

Give every possible point a single number, its energy, and agree that low energy means “this looks like data”. The model is then a landscape: valleys under the data, high ground everywhere else. Nothing forces the numbers to add up to one, which makes the model very free and also makes it awkward to train. Watch the landscape being carved, then drop marbles on it and let them roll.

Lay a rubber sheet over a table and decide that marbles should collect where the data is. You are allowed two moves. Press the sheet down wherever a real data point sits. Then release a handful of marbles, see where they roll to, and pull the sheet up at those places. If the marbles rolled onto the data, the press and the pull cancel and nothing changes. If they rolled somewhere wrong, that wrong valley is filled in. Repeat until marbles only ever come to rest on data.

How it works, step by step

  1. Keep 96 points that belong to the model: its current idea of what data looks like. They start scattered at random.
  2. Let those points roll downhill on the energy landscape for five small steps, with a little jitter.
  3. Take 96 real points. Lower the landscape under the real points and raise it under the model’s points.
  4. Repeat. Where the model’s points already sit on the data the two pushes cancel, and the landscape stops changing there.
  5. Generate: scatter new points at random and let them roll downhill, with jitter, for 200 steps.
  6. Switch the jitter off for a few last steps so that each point settles in its valley.

What just happened

Animation

Looking at the landscape
The data
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Average energy at real points
–
Average energy at the model’s own points
–
Rolling steps while generating
–
Generated points that land on the shape
–

Try this. During training, watch the small dots: they are the model’s own guesses, and they chase the data. Every place they visit that holds no data gets pushed up, which is how the high ground is built. Move the dashed line so that it crosses the data and look at the slice: how many valleys does it show? After training, press Generate Again and watch the gold points roll. Do any get caught in a dip that is not on the data? Then type in your own point, once on the shape and once far away, and compare the two energies.

From energy to probability

An energy-based model is any function \(E_\theta(\mathbf x)\) that returns one number. It defines a density through

$$p_\theta(\mathbf x)=\frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf x)}}{Z_\theta},\qquad Z_\theta=\int e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf x)}\,d\mathbf x .$$

Lower energy means higher probability. The constant \(Z_\theta\) makes the total equal one. It is an integral over every possible input, which for images cannot be computed. Every difficulty with these models comes from \(Z_\theta\), and every training method is a way of avoiding it.

The gradient of the likelihood

Maximising the log-likelihood of the data gives a gradient with two parts:

$$\nabla_\theta\,\mathbb E_{\text{data}}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf x)\big]=-\,\mathbb E_{\text{data}}\big[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(\mathbf x)\big]+\mathbb E_{\mathbf x\sim p_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(\mathbf x)\big].$$

The first part lowers the energy at real data. The second, which comes from differentiating \(\log Z_\theta\), raises the energy at samples from the model itself. So the loss that is actually minimised is

$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E_{\text{data}}\big[E_\theta(\mathbf x)\big]-\mathbb E_{\text{model}}\big[E_\theta(\mathbf x)\big].$$

The bottom-right chart plots the negative of this, the gap between the two averages. When the model's samples cannot be told from data, the two averages are equal, the gap is zero and the gradient vanishes.

Where the model's samples come from

The second part needs samples from \(p_\theta\). These come from Langevin dynamics, which needs only the slope of the energy and never \(Z_\theta\):

$$\mathbf x\leftarrow\mathbf x-\frac{\alpha}{2}\,\nabla_{\mathbf x}E_\theta(\mathbf x)+\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mathbf z .$$

Roll downhill, jitter, repeat. The downhill direction \(-\nabla_{\mathbf x}E_\theta\) is the score from the Score Matching tab: an energy-based model is a score model whose arrows are guaranteed to be the slope of one surface. Running the chain until it forgets its start would take far too long, so this page uses persistent contrastive divergence (Tieleman, 2008): the 96 points are kept from one training step to the next and moved only five steps each time. One in twenty is thrown back to a random place so that distant regions keep being checked.

Keeping it stable

The loss only cares about differences in energy, so nothing stops both averages from drifting off to large values. A small penalty on the squared energies, \(0.1\,(\mathbb E_{\text{data}}[E^2]+\mathbb E_{\text{model}}[E^2])\), holds them near zero. That is why the energies shown stay small. The step size and jitter used here are chosen to look clear and train quickly. They are not matched as the formula above requires, so the points settle a little more tightly than the exact density would.

What the freedom buys

Any network can be an energy. There is no decoder, no invertibility requirement and no fixed order of variables. Energies combine by addition: the sum of two energies is low only where both are low, which gives a model of "satisfies both". The energy itself is a ready-made measure of how unusual an input is. The price is that both training and sampling need a slow inner loop of Langevin steps, and that the result is sensitive to the settings of that loop.

How it connects to the rest of the module

The critic of a GAN is close to an energy, with a generator network standing in for the Langevin sampler. A diffusion model learns the slope \(-\nabla E\) directly at many noise levels and never needs the inner loop during training, which is the main reason diffusion models displaced energy-based models for images. Boltzmann machines and Hopfield networks are energy-based models with particular forms for \(E\).

What this page trains

A network with two inputs, two hidden layers of 48 neurons and one output, trained with Adam for 800 steps. The landscape is drawn by evaluating that network on a grid.

Check yourself

Training lowers the energy at real data. Why is that alone not enough? What would the landscape look like if the second half of the update, raising the energy at the model’s own points, were left out?

Lowering the energy at data says nothing about anywhere else. The cheapest way to do it is to lower the energy everywhere: a flat landscape, or one that slopes away to minus infinity, gives low energy at the data and equally low energy at every other point, so it has learned nothing. A valley only exists relative to higher ground around it. The second half builds that higher ground, and it does so precisely where the model currently and wrongly believes data might be.

entries.title: Discrete diffusion: fill in the blanks, a few at a time
entries.html:
Discrete Diffusion: Fill in the Blanks, a Few at a Time

Gaussian noise suits pictures, where a pixel can be a little brighter or darker. A letter cannot be a little more “q”. For words, tokens and other things that come in separate kinds, the noise is different: tokens are hidden behind a blank. The model learns to guess what is under the blanks, and it generates by starting with everything hidden and revealing a few tokens at a time. Unlike a language model that writes left to right, it fills in the whole thing at once, in any order.

Think of a crossword with no clues, or the game where letters of a hidden phrase are turned over one at a time. With every square blank, all you can say is that E is common and Q is rare. Turn over one letter and the neighbours become easier. Turn over a few more and the rest is nearly forced. A discrete diffusion model is trained to play this game from any position: given some squares, state the odds for all the others. To write something new it starts from an empty board, lets its own odds decide a few squares, looks again, and carries on.

How it works, step by step

  1. Take a real example. Choose a random fraction between 0 and 1 and hide that fraction of its tokens behind a blank.
  2. Show the network the partly hidden example and ask, for every blank, how likely each token is. Score it only on the blanks and backpropagate. Repeat for 1,500 batches.
  3. Measure: generate with different numbers of reveal steps and count how many samples are real.
  4. Generate: start with everything hidden.
  5. Ask the network for its beliefs about every blank. Reveal a few blanks by drawing a token for each from those beliefs. The rest stay hidden.
  6. Ask again: the tokens just revealed change the beliefs about the rest. Repeat until nothing is hidden.

What just happened

Animation

Generating
Stage
–
Training steps
–
Error at guessing hidden tokens
–
Reveal steps
–
Tokens still hidden in each sample
–
Samples that came out real

Try this. Let it train, then watch a run with Letter Pictures. Early on the tint is the same in all eight samples: with nothing revealed the network can only report how often each square is black on average. After the first few reveals the samples go their separate ways. Now set the reveal steps to 1 and press Generate Again: every square is drawn at once. What comes out, and why? Raise the steps until the letters are clean. Compare Most Confident First with Random Order at a middle setting. Then switch to Five-Letter Words and try 1 step and 5 steps. With one step, are the letters at least plausible for their positions?

The forward process: hiding

Let \(\mathbf x=(x^1,\dots,x^L)\) be a sequence of tokens. At time \(t\in[0,1]\) each token is independently replaced by a special blank token \(\texttt{[M]}\) with probability \(t\) and otherwise left alone:

$$q(x_t^i\mid x^i)=\begin{cases}1-t & x_t^i=x^i\\[2pt] t & x_t^i=\texttt{[M]}\end{cases}$$

At \(t=0\) nothing is hidden and at \(t=1\) everything is. A blank never turns back into a token on its own, so this is called an absorbing process. It plays the part that adding Gaussian noise plays for pictures.

Training

The network sees the partly hidden sequence and outputs, for every position, a distribution over the vocabulary. It is scored with cross-entropy on the hidden positions only:

$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E_{\,t,\ \mathbf x,\ \mathbf x_t}\Big[\,w(t)\sum_{i:\ x_t^i=\texttt{[M]}}-\log p_\theta\big(x^i\mid\mathbf x_t\big)\Big].$$

With the weight \(w(t)=1/t\) this is a bound on the log-likelihood of the data (Sahoo and others, 2024; Shi and others, 2024). This page uses \(w(t)=1\) and averages over the hidden positions, which trains the same network a little less exactly. If you know BERT, this is its training task, with one change: the fraction hidden is not fixed at 15% but ranges over everything from none to all. That range is what turns a fill-in-the-blank model into a generator.

Generating: revealing

Start from \(\mathbf x_1=(\texttt{[M]},\dots,\texttt{[M]})\). Choose \(N\) steps. At each step run the network once, pick some of the positions that are still hidden, and for each draw a token from the network's distribution for that position. With a linear schedule, \(L/N\) positions are revealed per step. Which positions go first is a free choice. Random Order is what the forward process implies. Most Confident First, used by MaskGIT (Chang and others, 2022), reveals the positions where the network's top choice has the highest probability.

Why the number of steps matters

The network outputs one distribution per position. It does not output a joint distribution over several positions at once. Tokens revealed in the same step are therefore drawn independently: none of them knows what the others turned out to be.

$$p_\theta(x^i,x^j\mid\mathbf x_t)\ \text{is approximated by}\ p_\theta(x^i\mid\mathbf x_t)\,p_\theta(x^j\mid\mathbf x_t).$$

With one step, every position is drawn from its own average behaviour, and the result is a blend of all the training examples: letters that are each plausible for their place but do not form a word, or a picture with pieces of several letters. With \(N=L\) steps exactly one token is revealed at a time, each one sees all the earlier ones, and nothing is approximated. In between is the trade: fewer network calls against more tokens that had to be chosen blind. The chart measures it.

How it compares with writing left to right

An autoregressive model is the special case in which one token is revealed per step in a fixed left-to-right order. Discrete diffusion relaxes both parts: any order, and several tokens per step. That allows generation in far fewer network calls than there are tokens, and it makes filling a gap in the middle of a text as natural as continuing it. The cost is the independence error above, and the fact that a revealed token is never revisited in this simple form.

Other kinds of discrete noise

Hiding is not the only choice. D3PM (Austin and others, 2021) also studies replacing a token with a uniformly random one, or with a similar one. SEDD (Lou and others, 2024) learns ratios of probabilities, a discrete counterpart of the score. Hiding has become the common choice for text because it is simple and works well.

What this page trains

One network with two hidden layers of 96 neurons. Its input marks each position as one of the tokens or as hidden. For Letter Pictures the data is 150 slightly noisy pictures of the letters A, E, H, O, T and X on a 5 by 7 grid, and a sample counts as real if it is within two squares of one of those letters. For Five-Letter Words the data is 64 common words, and a sample counts as real if it is one of them. A list that short can only be memorised, so the words tab shows the process, not creativity.

Check yourself

With one reveal step the pictures come out as a blur of several letters, yet the network that produced them is exactly the one that draws clean letters in 35 steps. What does the one-step failure tell you about what the network outputs?

It outputs a separate probability for each hidden square, given what is visible. With nothing visible those probabilities are just how often each square is black across all six letters. Drawing all 35 squares from them at once treats the squares as independent, and independent squares cannot agree on which letter they are part of. The knowledge that squares go together is in the network, but it is only used when a revealed square is fed back in as input for the next step.

entries.title: Tokenization and BPE: how text becomes pieces
entries.html:
Tokenization and BPE: How Text Becomes Pieces

A language model never sees letters or words. It sees a list of numbered pieces called tokens. The pieces are chosen by a simple and slightly surprising procedure: start with single characters, find the pair that sits side by side most often, glue it into one new piece, and repeat. Common words end up as one token, rare words as several. Watch the vocabulary being built, then type your own sentence and see how it is cut.

Imagine taking notes by hand in a lecture. At first you write every letter. Soon you notice that you keep writing "t-h-e" and invent one squiggle for it. Then one for "ing", one for "tion", and later one for a whole word that the lecturer cannot stop saying. You never decided on a list of abbreviations in advance: each one appeared because writing it out again and again was wasteful. Words you meet once you still spell out in full, and you can still write any word at all. Byte pair encoding builds a shorthand in exactly this way, by counting.

How it works, step by step

  1. Split the text into words and every word into single characters. Those characters are the first vocabulary.
  2. Count every pair of neighbouring tokens inside the words.
  3. Take the pair that occurs most often and glue it into one new token. Add it to the vocabulary and write the rule down.
  4. Replace that pair everywhere in the text. The text now needs fewer tokens.
  5. Repeat from step 2 until no pair occurs more than once, or until the vocabulary is as large as you want.

What just happened

Animation

Try the tokenizer

The text it learns from

Merges learned
–
Different tokens in the vocabulary
–
Tokens needed for the training text
–
Characters per token, on average
–
Newest token
–
Longest token so far
–

Try this. Press One merge a few times and read the “what just happened” line: which pair wins first, and why that one? Keep going and watch whole endings such as “er”, “est” and “ing” become single tokens before most whole words do. Then press Run and let it finish. Now type sentences in the box. Try a word that is in the training text, a word that is not but is built from familiar parts (“slowest”, “talker”), and a word with nothing familiar in it (“zebra”). How many tokens does each cost? Use the stop box to halt after 20 merges and type the same sentences again. Finally paste a paragraph in another language into the training text and see what its first merges are.

Why not letters, and why not words?

A model could read one character at a time. The vocabulary would be tiny, but every sentence would become a very long list, and the model would have to rediscover spelling before it could learn anything else. It could instead read whole words. Sentences would be short, but the vocabulary would need every word in every language, every name, every typo, and any word not on the list could not be read at all. Subword tokens sit between the two: frequent words are one token, and any other string can still be spelled out of smaller pieces. Nothing is ever "out of vocabulary".

The algorithm

Let the text be split into words, and each word into a sequence of symbols, at first single characters. Let \(c(a,b)\) be the number of times symbol \(a\) is immediately followed by symbol \(b\). One step of byte pair encoding is

$$(a^\star,b^\star)=\arg\max_{(a,b)}\,c(a,b),\qquad\text{then replace every }a^\star b^\star\text{ by the new symbol }a^\star b^\star .$$

Each step adds exactly one token to the vocabulary and removes \(c(a^\star,b^\star)\) tokens from the text. After \(M\) merges the vocabulary holds the starting characters plus \(M\) new tokens. \(M\) is the only setting. Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2016) introduced this for machine translation, borrowing a data compression method from 1994.

Using the tokenizer on new text

The result of training is an ordered list of merge rules. To cut a new sentence, split it into characters and apply the rules in the order they were learned. A word that was common in training passes through many rules and comes out as one token. An unfamiliar word passes through only the early, general rules and comes out as several pieces: "slowest" might become "_slow" and "est" even if that exact word was never seen. Each final piece is then replaced by its number in the vocabulary, and those numbers are what the model receives.

Why the greedy choice works

Merging the most frequent pair is the single step that shortens the text the most, so the procedure is a greedy form of compression. Frequent pairs tend to be meaningful: word endings, prefixes, common short words. Nobody tells the algorithm about grammar. It finds "ing" for the same reason your shorthand did.

What real tokenizers add

Production tokenizers start from the 256 possible bytes, not from letters, so any text in any script, and even emoji, can be represented. They learn tens of thousands of merges, to reach vocabularies of roughly 30,000 to 200,000 tokens, from many gigabytes of text. The space is glued to the start of the following word, as the underscore shows here. WordPiece and unigram tokenizers, used by some models, choose their pieces by a likelihood score instead of a raw count, and the result looks much the same.

Consequences worth knowing

Prices and length limits of language models are counted in tokens, not words. For ordinary English a token is on average a little under one word, around four characters. Text in languages that were rarer in the tokenizer's training data, and unusual strings such as code or long numbers, are cut into more pieces and so cost more. And because the model sees "strawberry" as two or three opaque pieces and not as ten letters, questions about spelling or counting letters are harder for it than they look.

What this page does

It runs the algorithm exactly as described on the text in the box, lower-cased, with punctuation marks treated as words of their own. Ties are broken in favour of the pair that appears first. It stops by itself when no pair occurs more than once, since after that every further merge would only memorise a single word.

Check yourself

After training, the word “lowest” is a single token but “slowest” is cut into two. A classmate concludes that the tokenizer “knows” lowest and “does not know” slowest. What is a more accurate description?

The tokenizer knows nothing about meaning. It only records which neighbouring pieces were frequent enough to be glued together. “lowest” happened to occur often enough in the training text for its pieces to be merged all the way into one token. “slowest” did not, so it is represented by pieces that were merged for other reasons, such as “_slow” and “est”. Both words are represented exactly and without loss. The model that reads the tokens later can still learn what “slowest” means, and the shared piece “est” even helps it.

entries.title: Next-token sampling: temperature, top-k and top-p
entries.html:
Next-Token Sampling: Temperature, Top-K and Top-P

A language model does not write. It produces a list of probabilities for the next word, and a separate, very small piece of code picks one. That picking rule decides whether the text is dull and repetitive, lively, or nonsense, and it is the part you control with settings such as temperature and top-p. Here a small neural network learns from a few dozen sentences, and you choose how its next word is picked.

Think of a jazz player choosing the next note. At every moment some notes are obvious, some are interesting, and some are simply wrong. Always playing the most obvious note gives a tune that is correct and lifeless, and tends to loop. Choosing with no regard for what fits gives noise. Good playing stays among the notes that fit and does not always take the first one. A language model supplies the "how well does each note fit" numbers. The sampling rule is the player's taste.

How it works, step by step

  1. Train: the network reads the sentences and learns to give a probability to every word in its vocabulary, given the three words before.
  2. Write: feed in the last three words. The network returns a score for every word.
  3. Temperature: divide the scores by the temperature and turn them into probabilities. Low temperature sharpens them, high temperature flattens them.
  4. Top-k: keep only the k most likely words. Top-p: keep the most likely words until their probabilities add up to p. Everything else is cut.
  5. Rescale what is left so that it adds up to 1, and draw one word at random from it.
  6. Add the word to the text and go back to step 2.

What just happened

Animation

How the next word is picked
The start of the text

Stage
–
Words written
–
Probability of the word just picked
–
Words still allowed after the cuts
–
Effective number of choices before the cuts
–
Average surprise, bits per word
–
Three-word phrases that came up more than once
–

Try this. When training finishes, press Greedy and Run. The text is correct and soon starts going round in circles: count the repeated phrases. Press Plain Sampling and run again several times. More variety, and now and then an odd sentence. Raise the temperature to 2.5: what happens to the bars, and to the text? Bring it back to 1 and press Top-k = 5, then Top-p = 0.9. Step one word at a time and compare how many words each rule keeps at a step where the model is sure (after “on”) and at a step where it is not (after “the”). Which of the two rules adapts to the situation?

From scores to probabilities

For a given context the network outputs one score, or logit, \(z_i\) for every word \(i\) in the vocabulary. The softmax turns scores into probabilities. The temperature \(T\) rescales the scores first:

$$p_i=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}} .$$

With \(T=1\) these are the probabilities the model learned. As \(T\to0\) all the probability moves to the single highest score, which is greedy decoding. As \(T\) grows, the probabilities approach equal shares for every word, including the absurd ones. Temperature changes the gaps between words and never their order.

Top-k

Sort the words by probability and keep only the \(k\) most likely. Set the others to zero and rescale:

$$p_i'=\frac{p_i}{\sum_{j\in\text{top-}k}p_j}\ \text{ for } i\in\text{top-}k,\qquad p_i'=0\ \text{ otherwise}.$$

This removes the long tail of unlikely words, where most nonsense comes from. Its weakness is that \(k\) is fixed. When the model is sure, five words is too many and lets poor ones in. When many continuations are reasonable, five is too few.

Top-p, or nucleus sampling

Keep the smallest set of most likely words whose probabilities add up to at least \(p\) (Holtzman and others, 2020):

$$\text{keep the first } m \text{ words, where } m=\min\Big\{m:\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{(i)}\ge p\Big\}.$$

The number of words kept now adapts. If one word has probability 0.95, the set is that one word. If the model is unsure, the set is wide. This is why top-p is the usual default. The two cuts can be combined, and they are applied after the temperature.

Measuring what you see

The surprise of a chosen word is \(-\log_2 p\) bits, using the model's own probability \(p\) at \(T=1\). Greedy text has low surprise at every step. The effective number of choices is \(2^{H}\), where \(H=-\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i\) is the entropy of the distribution: it is 1 when the model is certain and equals the vocabulary size when every word is equally likely. Average surprise over a long text is the logarithm of the perplexity you met in the Autoregressive Models tab.

Why the most likely text is not the best text

It seems natural to want the most probable continuation. In practice the most probable long text is bland and repetitive: once a phrase has appeared, repeating it is likely, and that makes repeating it again more likely still. Human writing carries a steady, moderate amount of surprise. Sampling with a mild temperature and a top-p cut imitates that. For tasks with one right answer, such as arithmetic, extracting a date, or writing code that must compile, a low temperature is the better choice, because there the obvious note is the correct one.

Other rules you may meet

Beam search keeps several partial texts alive and extends the best ones. It suits translation, where the output is tightly determined, and gives dull open-ended text. A repetition penalty lowers the scores of words already used. Min-p keeps every word whose probability is at least a set fraction of the top word's.

What this page trains

A network in the style of Bengio and others (2003): each of the three previous words is looked up in a table of 12 learned numbers, the 36 numbers pass through one hidden layer of 48 neurons, and the output is one score for each word in the vocabulary. It is trained with Adam on about forty short sentences for 700 steps. It knows nothing else about the world, so its text never leaves cats, dogs and cheese. The sampling rules are exactly the ones used with large models.

Check yourself

A student sets the temperature to 0.1 and top-p to 0.9 and is surprised that changing top-p no longer does anything. Why not?

The temperature is applied first. At 0.1 the differences between scores are multiplied by ten before the softmax, so almost all of the probability lands on the single most likely word, often more than 0.99 of it. Top-p then keeps the smallest set of words that reaches 0.9, and that set is already just the one word. The cut has nothing left to remove. The two settings are not independent: a low temperature makes every cut irrelevant, and a very high temperature makes the cut do all the work.

entries.title: Retrieval-augmented generation: look it up, then answer
entries.html:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Look It Up, Then Answer

A language model only knows what was in its training text. It has never read your course handbook, last week’s report, or anything written after it was trained, and when asked about them it may invent an answer. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is the fix used almost everywhere: first search a collection of documents for the passages closest to the question, then hand those passages to the model together with the question. Here the search is real, and you can add your own passage and ask about it.

There are two kinds of exam. In a closed-book exam you answer from memory, and when memory fails you are tempted to write something that merely sounds right. In an open-book exam you first find the right page and then answer from what it says. A language model on its own always sits the closed-book exam. Retrieval turns it into an open-book one. The model does not become more knowledgeable. It is handed the right page at the moment it needs it. Everything then depends on finding the right page.

Or type your own question and press Enter

How it works, step by step

  1. Beforehand: cut the documents into passages and turn each passage into a list of numbers, its embedding. Store them.
  2. A question arrives. Turn it into an embedding in exactly the same way.
  3. Compare the question with every stored passage and score how close they are.
  4. Keep the k closest passages.
  5. Write a prompt: the retrieved passages, then the question, then an instruction to answer only from the passages.
  6. The language model answers from what is in front of it, and can say which passage it used.

What just happened

Animation
Retrieval
Add your own passage

Passages in the collection
–
Different words: the number of dimensions
–
Words of the question that carry weight
–
Best similarity found
–
Passages sent to the model
–
Length of the prompt, in words
–

Try this. Press One step repeatedly and follow the question through the pipeline. Then try the example questions. For “Who teaches machine learning?” set k to 1 and then to 2: which passage holds the answer, and was it ranked first? The search matched on “machine learning” and missed that “teaches” and “taught” are the same idea. Ask “What is the wifi password?”: nothing in the handbook covers it, and the system should say so. Switch to Without Retrieval and ask about the final project: what can a model do with only the question? Then write a passage of your own, add it, and ask a question about it. Finally ask the same thing using different words from the ones in your passage. Does the search still find it?

Embeddings: text as a point

To search by meaning, every passage \(d\) is turned into a vector \(\mathbf e(d)\). This page uses the classical choice, TF-IDF. There is one coordinate for every word \(w\) in the collection, and its value is

$$e_w(d)=\mathrm{tf}(w,d)\cdot\log\frac{N+1}{\mathrm{df}(w)+1},$$

where \(\mathrm{tf}\) counts how often the word occurs in the passage, \(N\) is the number of passages and \(\mathrm{df}(w)\) is the number of passages that contain the word. A word that appears everywhere, such as "student", gets a small weight. A word that appears in one passage, such as "parking", gets a large one. Very common words like "the" are dropped. The question is embedded in the same way.

Scoring

Closeness is measured by cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between two vectors:

$$\mathrm{sim}(q,d)=\frac{\mathbf e(q)\cdot\mathbf e(d)}{\lVert\mathbf e(q)\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf e(d)\rVert}.$$

It is 1 when the two texts use the same words in the same proportions and 0 when they share no weighted word. Dividing by the lengths means a long passage does not win merely by being long. The right-hand chart shows this number for every passage.

Retrieve, then generate

The \(k\) passages with the highest similarity are pasted into the prompt in front of the question. The model then computes its usual next-token probabilities, now conditioned on the retrieved text:

$$p(\text{answer}\mid\text{question})\ \longrightarrow\ p\big(\text{answer}\mid\text{passage}_1,\dots,\text{passage}_k,\ \text{question}\big).$$

Nothing about the model changes: no training, no new weights. That is the appeal. Updating what the system knows means editing the collection, which takes seconds.

Choosing k

With \(k\) too small the passage that holds the answer may be left out, and the model cannot answer however capable it is. With \(k\) too large the prompt fills with unrelated text, which costs more, runs slower, and gives the model more chances to be distracted by something irrelevant. Typical systems retrieve between 3 and 20 passages and often re-rank them with a second, more careful model.

Where it fails

Most failures of RAG are failures of the search, and you can produce each of them here. Vocabulary mismatch: the question says "teaches" and the passage says "taught", so a word-matching search sees no overlap. Nothing relevant exists: the search still returns its \(k\) best passages, however poor, so a good system checks the score and is told to say "I do not know". The answer is split across two passages and only one is retrieved. Bad chunking: a passage was cut in the middle of the fact.

Dense embeddings

Modern systems replace TF-IDF with a neural network that maps text to a vector of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, trained so that texts with the same meaning land close together even when they share no words. With such embeddings "who teaches" and "is taught by" are neighbours. The rest of the pipeline is exactly what you see here: embed, score with cosine similarity, take the top \(k\), build the prompt. Many systems combine the two kinds of search, because exact word matching is still the best way to find names, codes and numbers.

What this page does, and what stands in for the model

The embedding, the similarity scores, the ranking and the prompt are all computed for real in your browser. The map squeezes the embeddings into two dimensions with PCA, so nearness on the map is only a rough guide and the bar chart is the exact picture. There is no large language model inside this page. Its place is taken by a simple reader that picks, from the retrieved passages, the sentence that best matches the question and the kind of answer asked for (a name for “who”, a number for “how many”), and that refuses when the best similarity is below 0.12. A real model would phrase the answer in its own words and could combine several passages. It could not do better than the passages it was given.

Check yourself

A company adds retrieval to its chatbot, and the bot still answers a question about the refund policy wrongly. The refund policy is in the document collection. Name two different places the failure could be, and how you would tell them apart.

First look at what was retrieved. If the refund passage is not among the k passages in the prompt, the search failed: perhaps the customer’s wording shares no words with the passage, or the passage was cut badly, or k is too small. The fix is in the retrieval. If the passage is in the prompt and the answer is still wrong, the model failed to use it: perhaps it was buried among many irrelevant passages, or the instruction to answer only from the passages was weak. Reading the actual prompt, as this page lets you do, separates the two cases at once.

entries.title: LoRA and fine-tuning: teach an old network a new task cheaply
entries.html:
LoRA and Fine-Tuning: Teach an Old Network a New Task Cheaply

A model that was expensive to train can be taught something new by continuing its training on new examples. That is fine-tuning. Changing every weight works, but it produces a complete second copy of the model for every new task. LoRA freezes the original weights and learns a small correction beside them, built from two thin matrices. Here a network first learns one task, then is adapted to a second in three different ways, and you can see what each way changes and what it costs.

A concert pianist is asked to play one piece in a new style. One option is to retrain from the beginning, changing every habit: it works, it takes long, and the old style suffers. Another is to keep the technique exactly as it is and clip a short page of adjustments to the score: "here a little slower, there a little softer". The page is tiny compared with years of training. Remove it and the old playing is back, untouched. Keep a different page for every style and switch between them in a second. LoRA is that page of adjustments.

How it works, step by step

  1. Pretrain: the network learns the old task from scratch. All 1,218 weights are trained. Keep a copy of the result.
  2. Switch to the new task. Decide which numbers are allowed to change.
  3. Full fine-tuning: every weight may change. LoRA: the weights are frozen and each weight matrix W gets a correction A × B made of two thin matrices, and only those are trained. Last layer: only the final layer changes.
  4. Train on the new task until the accuracy stops improving.
  5. Compare: accuracy on the new task, what happened to the old task, and how many numbers had to be stored.

What just happened

Animation

LoRA
The new task
Stage
–
Adaptation steps
–
Numbers being trained
–
Accuracy on the new task
–
Accuracy on the old task, after adapting
–
Accuracy on the old task with the original weights put back
–
Share of the weight change in its two strongest directions
–

Try this. Let it pretrain, then watch Full Fine-Tuning learn the new task. Look at the third small picture: the change to the weight matrix could use 32 independent directions. How many does it really use? That observation is the whole idea behind LoRA. Now press LoRA with rank 2. How does its accuracy compare with full fine-tuning, and how many numbers did it train? Then press Last Layer Only: why is it so much worse on the spiral? Switch the new task to Diagonal Stripes and try LoRA at rank 1, 2, 4 and 8: on this task the rank matters more. Switch to A Blob Inside a Ring: here even the last layer alone copes. What does that tell you about the three tasks? Finally look at the old-task accuracy for each method. All of them forget. Which of them can get the old skill back exactly, and at what cost?

Full fine-tuning

Start from the pretrained weights \(\theta_0\) and continue gradient descent on the loss of the new task. Every weight moves: \(\theta=\theta_0+\Delta\theta\). The result is as large as the original model, so serving ten tasks means storing ten full models. And since nothing holds the weights near \(\theta_0\), the old task is usually damaged, which is called catastrophic forgetting.

The observation behind LoRA

Look at the change \(\Delta W=W-W_0\) that full fine-tuning makes to one weight matrix. A \(32\times32\) matrix can change in 32 independent directions. Its singular values say how much of the change lies along each. In practice a few are large and the rest are small: the change has low rank. The third small picture shows this for the network on this page. If the change is nearly rank 2, there is no need to train 1,024 numbers to describe it.

LoRA

Hu and others (2021) freeze \(W_0\) and write the change as a product of two thin matrices:

$$W=W_0+\Delta W,\qquad \Delta W=A\,B,\qquad A\in\mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}}\times r},\quad B\in\mathbb R^{r\times d_{\text{out}}} .$$

Only \(A\) and \(B\) are trained. \(B\) starts at zero, so at the first step \(\Delta W=0\) and the network is exactly the pretrained one. The product \(AB\) can never have rank above \(r\), which is the restriction, and it has

$$r\,(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})\quad\text{numbers in place of}\quad d_{\text{in}}\times d_{\text{out}} .$$
