For the \(32\times32\) matrix here and \(r=2\), that is 128 in place of 1,024. In a large language model \(d\) is in the thousands and \(r\) is typically 4 to 64, so the trained part is often well under one percent of the model.

What you gain

Size: an adapter is megabytes where the model is gigabytes. Swapping: one copy of the base model can serve many tasks, each with its own adapter. Reversibility: remove \(AB\) and the original model is back, bit for bit, which is why the old-task accuracy "with the original weights put back" is the same for every method on this page but only LoRA and Last Layer keep those weights around for free. No extra cost when running: \(W_0+AB\) can be added up once and used as an ordinary matrix.

What you give up

If the new task needs a change of higher rank than \(r\), LoRA cannot express it, and accuracy falls short of full fine-tuning. Raising \(r\) closes the gap and costs more. How much rank is needed depends on the task. On the spiral a rank of 1 is usually enough here. On the diagonal stripes rank 1 typically ends clearly below full fine-tuning, and rank 4 catches up. LoRA also still forgets the old task while the adapter is attached, as the readout shows. It does not prevent forgetting. It makes forgetting undoable.

Training only the last layer

The cheapest option keeps every layer but the last frozen. It works when the features computed by the earlier layers are already the right ones for the new task, which is the situation in the Transfer Learning tab. The spiral and the stripes need different features, so retraining only the final layer falls well short on them. The blob inside a ring is simple enough that the old features will do. LoRA is the middle road: every layer can adjust, each only a little.

What this page trains

A network with 2 inputs, two hidden layers of 32 neurons and 2 outputs, 1,218 weights in all. The old task is to tell two interleaved moons apart. There are three new tasks to choose from. With LoRA, each of the three weight matrices gets its own \(A\) and \(B\) and the biases stay frozen, for \(132\,r\) trained numbers. Adaptation stops when the accuracy on the new task has not improved for 200 steps, or after 1,200 steps.

Check yourself

With LoRA at rank 2 the adapted network scores well on the new task and poorly on the old one, exactly like full fine-tuning. So in what sense is LoRA “safer” for the old task?

While the adapter is attached, the network computes with W₀ + AB, and that sum has been pulled toward the new task just as fully fine-tuned weights would be, so the old task suffers. The difference is in what is stored. With LoRA the original W₀ was never altered: detach A and B and the old network is back exactly, with its old accuracy. With full fine-tuning the original weights have been overwritten, and the only way back is to have kept a complete second copy of the model. LoRA does not stop forgetting. It keeps the forgotten skill one subtraction away.

entries.title: Quantization: the same network in fewer bits
entries.html:
Quantization: The Same Network in Fewer Bits

A trained network is a long list of numbers, and each one is normally stored with 32 bits. A large language model has billions of them, which is why it needs a data centre. Quantization stores every weight with fewer bits by rounding it to the nearest value on a short list. The surprise is how far this can go: at 8 bits almost nothing is lost, at 4 bits very little, and then, quite suddenly, the network falls apart. Here a real letter-reading network is rounded while you watch.

Measure the height of everyone in a class to the nearest tenth of a millimetre and you have recorded far more than anyone needs. To the nearest centimetre is plenty: the list is much shorter to write down and nothing useful is lost. To the nearest half metre is too coarse: almost everyone becomes "1.5" and the list is useless. Somewhere between lies the coarsest ruler that still does the job. Quantization is the search for that ruler for the weights of a network. It works as well as it does because a network's answer comes from adding up thousands of weights, and small rounding errors in opposite directions largely cancel.

How it works, step by step

  1. Train the network as usual, with 32-bit weights, and measure its accuracy.
  2. Choose a number of bits b. That allows 2 to the power b different values, fewer one to keep them symmetric around zero.
  3. Find the range of the weights and spread the allowed values evenly across it.
  4. Round every weight to the nearest allowed value. Store only which one it was: a small whole number.
  5. Run the network with the rounded weights and measure the accuracy again.

What just happened

Animation
Rounding
Bits per weight
–
Different values a weight may take
–
Size of the 984 weights
–
Accuracy with rounded weights
–
Accuracy at full precision
–
Average rounding error, as a share of the weight range
–

Try this. Press Run: the bits fall from 32 to 1 and everything on the page follows. At how many bits does the accuracy first drop noticeably, and how much smaller is the model by then? Look at the 24 small pictures at 32 bits and at 2 bits: the neurons still look for roughly the same strokes. At 1 bit only the sign of each weight survives. Now compare the two range rules at 2 and 3 bits. Clipping throws away accuracy on the few largest weights to buy finer steps for all the others: does that trade pay here? Use the buttons under the test picture to find a letter that the rounded network gets wrong and the original gets right.

Uniform quantization

Take the weights of one layer and let \(m\) be the largest size among them. With \(b\) bits, use the whole numbers from \(-Q\) to \(Q\), where \(Q=2^{\,b-1}-1\), and a step

$$\Delta=\frac{m}{Q}.$$

Each weight \(w\) is replaced by a whole number \(q\), which is all that is stored, and is read back as \(\hat w\):

$$q=\operatorname{round}\!\Big(\frac{w}{\Delta}\Big),\qquad \hat w=q\,\Delta .$$

The line of calculations under the pictures does this for one weight. For 8 bits \(q\) runs from \(-127\) to \(127\). The layer also stores the single number \(\Delta\).

The error

Rounding moves a weight by at most half a step, \(|w-\hat w|\le\Delta/2\). If the errors are spread evenly inside that interval, their typical size is

$$\sqrt{\mathbb E\big[(w-\hat w)^2\big]}=\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{12}} .$$

Removing one bit doubles \(\Delta\) and so doubles the error, while the saving in size from that bit gets smaller each time: from 8 to 7 bits saves an eighth, from 2 to 1 saves a half. That is why the accuracy curve is flat for a long way and then falls off a cliff.

One bit

With a single bit there is no room for zero, so the rule changes: keep only the sign of each weight and give all of them the same size, the average size in the layer,

$$\hat w=\operatorname{sign}(w)\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_i|w_i| .$$

That a network still works at all like this says how much of what it knows is carried by the pattern of signs.

On this page 2 bits can score lower than 1 bit. With 2 bits and the full range the three allowed values are \(-m\), 0 and \(m\). Because \(m\) is set by the single largest weight, most weights are closer to 0 than to \(\pm m\) and are rounded to exactly zero, which switches them off. The 1-bit rule never produces a zero. Clipping the range, described next, repairs much of the 2-bit case.

The range matters

The allowed values are spread across the whole range \([-m,m]\). If one weight is far larger than the others, it stretches the range, the step \(\Delta\) grows, and all the ordinary weights are rounded more coarsely to accommodate one outlier. Clipping sets \(m\) to a percentile of the sizes, here the 99th, and squashes the few larger weights down to it. They are represented badly and everything else is represented better. Whether that pays depends on the layer, and choosing the range well is most of the craft in this simple form of quantization.

In large language models

A model with 7 billion weights takes 28 gigabytes at 32 bits, 14 at 16 bits, 7 at 8 bits and 3.5 at 4 bits. Four-bit versions of open models are what run on laptops and phones. Fewer bits also make the arithmetic itself faster and cheaper in energy. Rounding a finished model, as this page does, is called post-training quantization. When that loses too much, the model can be trained with the rounding already in place so that it learns weights that survive it, which is quantization-aware training. Practical schemes also use different steps for different groups of weights, and spend more bits on the layers that turn out to be most sensitive.

What this page trains

A network that reads 5 by 7 pictures of six letters, with 35 inputs, 24 hidden neurons and 6 outputs. Its 984 weights are quantized, one scale per layer. The 30 biases are left at full precision. The pictures have 12% of their squares flipped at random, which makes the task hard enough for errors to show. Accuracy is measured on 300 pictures the network did not train on.

Check yourself

Going from 32 bits to 8 bits makes the model four times smaller and costs almost no accuracy. Going from 2 bits to 1 bit makes it only twice smaller and destroys much of the accuracy. Why is the trade so different at the two ends?

Each bit removed doubles the size of the rounding step, and so doubles the error in every weight. At 32 bits the error is so far below what the network can notice that doubling it twenty times over still leaves it negligible: those bits were storing precision the network never used. At 2 bits the step is already about the size of a typical weight, so doubling it again erases the differences between weights that the network depends on. The saving, meanwhile, is measured against what is left, so the last bits removed save the fewest bytes in absolute terms and cost the most.

entries.title: Mixture of experts: many small specialists and a router
entries.html:
Mixture of Experts: Many Small Specialists and a Router

One big model that does everything must use all of itself for every input. A mixture of experts splits the work: several small models, each good at one kind of input, and a router that looks at each input and decides whose answer to use. Nobody assigns the specialities. The experts and the router are trained together and the division of labour appears by itself. Large language models use this idea to grow much bigger without becoming much slower. Here the experts are as simple as they can be, straight lines, so that you can watch each one find its job.

A hospital does not send every patient to every doctor. A receptionist looks at each patient and sends them to cardiology, orthopaedics or dermatology. Each department sees only its own kind of case and becomes good at it. Adding a department makes the hospital more capable without making any single visit slower, because a patient still sees one or two doctors, not all of them. The interesting part is that in a mixture of experts nobody draws up the departments. The receptionist and the doctors start out knowing nothing and sort it out between them from results alone.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with K experts, each a random straight line, and a router that splits every input almost evenly between them.
  2. For each data point the router gives every expert a share between 0 and 1. The mixture’s answer is the experts’ answers weighted by those shares.
  3. Measure the error of the mixture’s answer.
  4. Update the experts: each one is corrected in proportion to its share, so it learns mostly from the points it is responsible for.
  5. Update the router: it shifts more of each point to whichever expert was closer to the truth there.
  6. Repeat until the error stops falling. Each expert now owns a region.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data
Training steps
–
Error when all experts are blended
–
Error when only the top expert answers
–
Error of one straight line alone
–
Experts handling at least 5% of the data
–
Share of the expert weights used for one input, top expert only
–

Try this. Press Run with three experts on Three Straight Pieces and watch the bands in the top-right picture: they begin as an even blur and sharpen into three territories. Did anyone tell expert 2 to take the middle? Switch between Blend All Experts and Top Expert Only: how much accuracy is lost by letting a single expert answer each input, and how much computing is saved? Now set K to 1, then 2, then 6 on the same data. With six experts, how many are doing real work? Try the zigzag with 3 experts and with 6. Then choose the smooth wave and compare the two error readouts: blended, the fit is good, and with the top expert alone it is terrible. Look at the individual lines to see why. Finally type in your own x and read which expert answers it.

The model

There are \(K\) experts \(f_1,\dots,f_K\) and a router, also called a gate. For an input \(x\) the router produces one score per expert and turns the scores into shares with a softmax:

$$g_k(x)=\frac{e^{u_k(x)}}{\sum_j e^{u_j(x)}},\qquad \hat y(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_k(x)\,f_k(x).$$

On this page each expert is a line, \(f_k(x)=a_kx+b_k\), and each router score is a line too, \(u_k(x)=c_kx+d_k\). A single line cannot follow data with a bend in it. \(K\) lines, each used in its own region, can.

How the division of labour emerges

Train everything together on the squared error \(\tfrac12(\hat y-y)^2\). With \(\delta=\hat y-y\), the gradients are

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial f_k}=\delta\,g_k,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial u_k}=\delta\,g_k\,\big(f_k-\hat y\big).$$

The first says an expert is corrected in proportion to its share \(g_k\): it learns from the points it is trusted with and hardly at all from the others. The second says the router raises an expert's share where that expert's answer would pull the mixture toward the truth, and lowers it where it would pull away. The two feed each other. An expert that is slightly better in some region gets more of it, learns it better, and gets more still. That loop is what turns an even blur into sharp territories (Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton, 1991).

Blending against routing

Blending every expert's answer uses all \(K\) experts for every input, so nothing is saved. Once the territories are sharp, the shares are close to 0 or 1 and little is lost by asking only the expert with the largest share:

$$\hat y_{\text{top}}(x)=f_{k^\star}(x),\qquad k^\star=\arg\max_k g_k(x).$$

Now each input costs one expert, however many exist. The two error readouts show how much this costs. The cost is highest near the boundaries, where two experts are both partly right.

This only works if each expert can stand on its own. On the smooth wave the mixture on this page finds a different solution: no line fits a curve, so it produces the curve by blending several lines, none of which is close to the data by itself. Remove the blending and the answer collapses. Large models avoid this by routing each input to its top few experts during training as well, so that every expert is forced to give a usable answer alone.

In large language models

In a Transformer, most of the weights sit in the feed-forward part of each layer. A mixture-of-experts model replaces that part with several feed-forward networks, for instance 8, and a small router that sends each token to the best 2. The model holds the knowledge of all 8, and each token pays for 2. This is called a sparse mixture of experts (Shazeer and others, 2017), and it is how some open and commercial models reach very large sizes at a moderate running cost. The experts are not tidy human specialities such as "maths" or "French": what each one takes on is whatever division happened to lower the error.

What goes wrong

The reinforcing loop can run away. One expert gets ahead early, receives everything, and the others receive no data and never improve: these are dead experts. Watch the middle picture with a large \(K\). Large models add a load-balancing term to the loss that penalises uneven use, and often add noise to the router's scores during training. The opposite failure also occurs: the router never commits, every expert does a little of everything, and the model is an expensive average.

Not the same as an ensemble

An ensemble, as in the Ensembles module, runs every model on every input and averages. Its members are trained to solve the whole problem and it gains from their errors cancelling. A mixture of experts trains its members to solve different parts of the problem and gains from sending each input to the right one.

What this page trains

\(K\) lines and a router with \(2K\) numbers, trained together with Adam on all 160 points at every step. Training stops when the error has changed by less than one part in a thousand over 100 steps, or after 4,000 steps.

Check yourself

With six experts on the three-piece data, some experts end up handling almost none of the data. Is the model with idle experts worse than a model trained with three experts from the start?

Not in accuracy: the working experts fit the three pieces just as a three-expert model would, and the idle ones contribute almost nothing to the answer because their shares are near zero. What is lost is efficiency. The idle experts still take up memory and were paid for in training. In a large model that is a serious waste, which is why a load-balancing penalty is added to push the router into using every expert. On this data there are only three pieces to find, so there is nothing useful for the extra experts to do, and leaving them idle is the sensible outcome.

entries.title: Multi-armed bandits: try new things, or stick with what works?
entries.html:
Multi-Armed Bandits: Try New Things, or Stick with What Works?

Five food trucks park outside your office. Each has its own hidden chance of serving you a good lunch, and you have 1,500 lunches to spend. Every day at the best truck you have found so far is a day you learn nothing about the others. Every day spent testing another truck may be a wasted lunch. This is the simplest problem in reinforcement learning, and the same dilemma sits inside every harder one. Four strategies play it side by side here, and you can play against them.

You move to a new town with five restaurants on your street. On the first night you pick one at random and it is good. On the second night, do you go back? If you always return to the best place you know, you may eat for years at the third-best restaurant in town because of one lucky evening. If you keep trying everything for ever, you keep eating bad dinners you could have avoided. The sensible course is in between: try the others enough to be reasonably sure, and try them less and less as the evidence comes in. The strategies on this page are different precise versions of "enough".

How it works, step by step

  1. Each truck has a fixed chance of a good lunch. Nobody knows the five chances.
  2. Each day every player picks one truck by its own rule, using only its own past lunches.
  3. It gets a good lunch or a bad one, and updates its record for that truck: visits, and good lunches.
  4. Greedy always picks the truck with the best record so far. ε-greedy does the same but picks at random a share ε of the time.
  5. UCB adds a bonus to trucks it has rarely visited, and picks the highest total. Thompson sampling draws a plausible success rate for every truck from what it knows, and picks the highest draw.
  6. After 1,500 days, compare how many good lunches each player missed.

What just happened

Animation

Settings
Days so far
–
Watched player
–
Its good lunches
–
Its regret: good lunches missed
–
Share of its days at the best truck
–
Truck it currently rates highest
–

Try this. First choose Play Yourself and click on trucks for 40 or 50 days. Which truck do you think is best, and how sure are you? Press Reveal the True Chances to check. Now start over and press Run, several times. Greedy is a gamble: in most runs it happens to settle on the best truck early and looks unbeatable, and in the rest it locks on to a worse truck after one unlucky lunch and its regret climbs in a straight line for good. ε-greedy never locks on, and never stops wasting a fixed share of its days either. Watch UCB: which trucks get the large bonus, and what happens to the bonus as the days pass? Watch Thompson sampling: the bell shapes narrow for the trucks it visits. Which two strategies have a regret curve that bends over and flattens?

The problem

There are \(K\) options, called arms after the levers of slot machines. Arm \(k\) pays 1 with unknown probability \(\mu_k\) and 0 otherwise. On each of \(T\) days you choose one arm \(a_t\) and see only its result. The best arm has \(\mu^\star=\max_k\mu_k\). The regret after \(T\) days is the expected reward given up by not always choosing it:

$$\text{Regret}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(\mu^\star-\mu_{a_t}\big).$$

A strategy that keeps choosing a worse arm a fixed share of the time has regret that grows in a straight line. A good strategy has regret that grows more and more slowly, like \(\log T\), which is the best that can be achieved.

Greedy and ε-greedy

Keep the average result \(\hat\mu_k\) of each arm and its number of pulls \(n_k\). Greedy pulls \(\arg\max_k\hat\mu_k\). After trying each arm once it never explores again, so an unlucky first result on the best arm can banish it for good. ε-greedy pulls a uniformly random arm with probability \(\varepsilon\) and the greedy arm otherwise. It always finds the best arm in the end, and it always goes on spending the share \(\varepsilon\) on random pulls, most of them on arms it already knows are worse. Its regret is a straight line with a smaller slope.

UCB: optimism in the face of uncertainty

The upper confidence bound rule (Auer and others, 2002) gives each arm a score: its average plus a bonus that is large when the arm has been tried little,

$$\text{score}_k=\hat\mu_k+\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{2\,n_k}},$$

and pulls the highest score. An arm is chosen either because it looks good or because too little is known about it to rule it out. Each pull shrinks that arm's bonus. The \(\ln t\) makes every bonus creep up slowly, so no arm is abandoned for ever, and it is revisited more and more rarely. Exploration is directed at the arms where it can still change the decision. The original UCB1 rule uses the larger bonus \(\sqrt{2\ln t/n_k}\), which is safer in theory and explores noticeably more than is needed on a problem this small.

Thompson sampling: act on a plausible guess

Keep a full belief about each \(\mu_k\). Starting from "anything between 0 and 1 is equally likely", after \(w_k\) good and \(l_k\) bad results the belief is a Beta distribution,

$$\mu_k\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1+w_k,\ 1+l_k).$$

Each day, draw one value from every arm's belief and pull the arm whose draw is highest (Thompson, 1933). A rarely tried arm has a wide belief, so its draw is sometimes high and it gets tried. A well-known poor arm has a narrow belief around a low value and almost never wins the draw. The rule has no setting to tune, and it chooses each arm with exactly the probability that the arm is the best one given the evidence.

Why this matters beyond lunch

Websites choose which headline or advert to show with these rules, clinical trials use them to give fewer patients the worse treatment, and recommendation systems use them to try new items. In the rest of this module the same tension returns as the ε in Q-learning: a robot that only does what currently looks best never finds out that something else is better.

What this page runs

Five arms with success chances 0.20, 0.35, 0.50, 0.60 and 0.80, in a random order that is hidden until you ask. All four strategies face the same five trucks for 1,500 days, each with its own lunches. Regret is computed from the true chances, so it is exact and does not depend on the luck of individual lunches. One run is one sample, so press Start over a few times. Averaged over 300 runs of this exact setup, the regret after 1,500 days is about 99 for greedy (usually under 5, occasionally over 300), 68 for ε-greedy with ε = 0.1, 33 for UCB and 22 for Thompson sampling.

Check yourself

After 1,500 days ε-greedy with ε = 0.1 has found the best truck and rates it highest. Its regret is still rising steadily. Why, and what simple change would fix it?

It still chooses a random truck on one day in ten, and four times out of five that random truck is not the best one. Those days are wasted for ever, however certain it has become, so its regret rises by a fixed amount per day. The fix is to explore less as evidence accumulates, for example by shrinking ε over time. UCB and Thompson sampling do this automatically: their exploration fades exactly as fast as their uncertainty does.

entries.title: Value and policy iteration: planning when you know the rules
entries.html:
Value and Policy Iteration: Planning When You Know the Rules

Before learning by trial and error, take the easier case: the robot has a complete map. It knows every square, what each move does, and what each reward is. No experience is needed, only thinking. The thinking is one small calculation repeated over and over: the value of a square is the best you can get by making one move and then collecting the value of wherever you land. Watch values spread out from the goal like water, and the arrows fall into place behind them.

Suppose you want to know how many minutes each junction in a town is from the railway station, and you have a map. Write 0 on the station. Every junction next to it is "one street away": write that down. Every junction next to those is "one more street". Keep going and the numbers flood outward from the station until the map is covered. Once every junction has its number, finding the way from anywhere is trivial: at each junction, walk toward the neighbour with the smallest number. Value iteration is this flood, with rewards in place of minutes and with the complication that a move may not go where you intended.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with every value at zero.
  2. Value iteration: take a square. For each of the four moves, work out reward + γ × the value of where the move leads, averaged over where it might slip to.
  3. The new value of the square is the best of those four numbers, and the arrow points at the move that gave it.
  4. Do this for every square: that is one sweep. Repeat sweeps until no value changes by more than 0.001.
  5. Policy iteration instead fixes all the arrows, works out the values of following exactly those arrows, then redraws each arrow toward the best move, and repeats until no arrow changes.

What just happened

Animation

The world
Method
–
Sweeps so far
–
Largest change in the last sweep
–
Value of the start square
–
Route from the start, following the arrows
–
Arrows changed in the last sweep
–

Try this. Press One step repeatedly in the first sweep and read each calculation. Only squares next to the goal or the pit get interesting values at first. Why? Press Run and watch the values travel outward, one square per sweep. Notice the arrows settle long before the numbers do. Now set the reward for each step to 0 and the slippery slider to 0.3, and look at C4, the square under the pit: its arrow points down, into the wall. Then set the step reward to −3. With a very costly step, what does the robot next to the pit prefer? Finally switch to Policy Iteration: how many rounds does it need, compared with the number of sweeps value iteration took?

The setting: a Markov decision process

There is a set of states \(s\), a set of actions \(a\), transition probabilities \(P(s'\mid s,a)\) saying where each action leads, a reward \(r(s,a,s')\), and a discount \(\gamma\). A policy \(\pi\) says which action to take in each state. The value \(V^\pi(s)\) is the expected total discounted reward from \(s\) when following \(\pi\). The goal is the policy whose values are highest everywhere.

The Bellman optimality equation

The values of the best policy satisfy a consistency condition (Bellman, 1957). The value of a state is the best, over actions, of the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state:

$$V^\star(s)=\max_a\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)\,\big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma V^\star(s')\big].$$

This is one equation for every state, all tied together, and the \(\max\) makes them impossible to solve by ordinary algebra.

Value iteration

Turn the equation into an update. Start from \(V_0=0\) and compute, for every state,

$$V_{k+1}(s)=\max_a\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)\,\big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma V_k(s')\big].$$

The panel under the pictures writes this out for one square: four lines, one per move, then the best. Each sweep brings every value closer to \(V^\star\) by at least the factor \(\gamma\):

$$\max_s\big|V_{k+1}(s)-V^\star(s)\big|\le\gamma\,\max_s\big|V_k(s)-V^\star(s)\big|.$$

That is why the top-right curve falls steadily, and why a \(\gamma\) near 1 needs more sweeps. Information travels one square per sweep, so a goal ten squares away takes at least ten sweeps to be felt.

From values to behaviour

Given values, the best move in each state is the one that achieved the maximum:

$$\pi(s)=\arg\max_a\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)\,\big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma V(s')\big].$$

The arrows usually stop changing long before the values have converged, because the arrow only depends on which neighbour is better, not on by how much.

Policy iteration

Howard (1960) used that observation. Alternate two steps. Evaluate: with the arrows fixed, find the values of following them, by sweeping the simpler update without a \(\max\) until it settles,

$$V^\pi(s)=\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,\pi(s))\,\big[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\big].$$

Improve: redraw every arrow toward the best move under those values. Each round gives a policy at least as good as the last, and there are finitely many policies, so it stops, usually after very few rounds. Each round costs many sweeps, though, as the readout shows.

What the settings do

Slippery floor: with chance \(p\) a move slides to one side or the other. Next to the pit, when steps are cheap, the robot then prefers a move that cannot slide into it, even walking into a wall. Step reward: at 0 there is no hurry and the robot takes the safest route however long. At \(-3\) life is so costly that a risky short cut becomes worthwhile, and for squares far from the goal even the pit can be preferable to a long walk. \(\gamma\): small values make distant rewards nearly worthless.

Why this is not yet learning

Everything here needs \(P\) and \(r\) to be known: the robot is planning, not learning. In most real problems nobody hands you the rules. The next tabs keep the same Bellman idea and replace the known probabilities with experience: Monte Carlo and TD learning estimate values from sampled walks, and Q-learning does so while also choosing the moves.

Check yourself

In the room, set the reward for each step to 0 and the slippery floor to 0.3. The best move in C4, the square directly under the pit, is now “down”, straight into the wall, which gets the robot nowhere. Why is that the best move?

Because a move can slide sideways. The robot wants to go left, away from the pit. But a move to the left can slide up, and up from C4 is the pit. A move down pushes into the wall and keeps the robot where it is, and its two possible slides are left, to safety, and right, into another wall. So “down” can never enter the pit, and sooner or later it slides the robot to the left. When steps cost nothing, waiting for that lucky slide is better than taking a real chance of losing 10. Give each step a cost of 1 and the patience stops paying: click C4 to compare the four numbers.

entries.title: Monte Carlo and TD learning: wait for the end, or learn as you go?
entries.html:
Monte Carlo and TD Learning: Wait for the End, or Learn as You Go?

Now the map is gone. A walker wanders at random along a row of five squares until it falls off one end: nothing on the left, a reward of 1 on the right. How good is it to be on each square? Two ways of finding out from experience are compared. Monte Carlo waits until the walk is over and then tells every square it visited how things turned out. Temporal-difference learning does not wait: after every single step it corrects one square using its current guess about the next. That small change is the central idea of reinforcement learning.

You drive home from work every day and want to predict how long the trip takes. One method: note the time when you leave, and when you get home, compare the real total with what you had predicted at each point along the way. That is Monte Carlo. Nothing is learned until you are on your own doorstep. The other method: you leave expecting 30 minutes, reach the motorway, and find it jammed. At that moment you already know the trip will be nearer 45. Why wait until you are home to correct your prediction for "just left work"? Correct it now, using your new and better guess. That is temporal-difference learning: learning a guess from a later guess.

How it works, step by step

  1. Every square starts with the guess 0.5. The walker starts in the middle, C.
  2. It steps left or right with equal chance.
  3. TD, after each step: nudge the value of the square just left toward reward + value of the square just entered.
  4. Keep stepping until the walker falls off an end. The return of the walk is 1 if it left on the right and 0 if on the left.
  5. Monte Carlo, now that the walk is over: nudge the value of every square that was visited toward that return.
  6. Start a new walk from C. Repeat for 100 walks.

What just happened

Animation

Learning
Walks finished
–
TD: error now
–
Monte Carlo: error now
–
Last walk ended
–
Steps in the last walk
–
Average error over walks 1 to 100, across 100 runs: TD / MC
–

Try this. Step through the first walk. After each step TD changes one bar straight away, by a small amount, while Monte Carlo does nothing. When the walk ends, Monte Carlo moves every visited square at once, all in the same direction. Which of the two is jumpier? Press Run and compare the two error curves, then look at the average of 100 runs below. Now change α. At 0.02 both learn slowly and smoothly. At 0.3 both are quick and noisy. Is there an α at which Monte Carlo beats TD in the averaged chart? Why can neither error reach zero with a fixed α?

What is being estimated

For a fixed way of behaving, here walking at random, the value \(V(s)\) of a state is the expected total reward from that state onward. In this walk the only reward is 1 for leaving on the right, so \(V(s)\) is the probability of finishing on the right. The true values of the five squares A to E are \(\tfrac16,\tfrac26,\tfrac36,\tfrac46,\tfrac56\). Neither method is told this.

Monte Carlo

Run a whole episode. For each state \(s_t\) visited, the return \(G_t\) is the total reward actually collected from that point to the end. Move the estimate toward it:

$$V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\,\big[G_t-V(s_t)\big].$$

The target \(G_t\) is an honest sample of what the value is supposed to predict, so on average it is exactly right. It is also very noisy: here it is either 0 or 1, never the 0.5 that the middle square is really worth.

Temporal-difference learning, TD(0)

After a single step from \(s_t\) to \(s_{t+1}\) with reward \(r_{t+1}\), use the current estimate of the next state in place of the rest of the episode (Sutton, 1988):

$$V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\,\big[\underbrace{r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}}-V(s_t)\big].$$

The bracket is the TD error \(\delta_t\). The target leans on \(V(s_{t+1})\), which is itself only a guess, so it is biased while the guesses are poor. This use of an estimate to improve an estimate is called bootstrapping. In return the target varies much less than a full return, because it depends on one random step, not on a whole random walk.

The trade

Monte Carlo: no bias, high variance, must wait for the end, and cannot be used at all if episodes never end. TD: some bias early on, low variance, learns at every step. On problems like this one TD usually reaches a given accuracy sooner, as the averaged chart shows for most values of \(\alpha\). The two are the ends of a range: \(n\)-step methods and TD(\(\lambda\)) look a few steps ahead before bootstrapping.

Why the error does not reach zero

With a fixed \(\alpha\) every update moves the estimate by a fixed fraction toward a noisy target, so the estimates keep rattling around the true values for ever. A smaller \(\alpha\) rattles less and takes longer to arrive. Exact convergence needs \(\alpha\) to shrink over time.

What this page runs

The five-state random walk from Sutton and Barto's book. Both methods see exactly the same walks. The error shown is the root-mean-square difference between the five estimates and the five true values. The bottom chart repeats the whole experiment 100 times with fresh walks and averages the curves, because one run is too noisy to judge. There is no discounting, \(\gamma=1\).

Where this leads

Replace "value of a state" by "value of a move in a state" and let the learner choose its own moves, and TD learning becomes SARSA and Q-learning, the next two tabs.

Check yourself

The walker goes C → D → E → off the right edge, earning 1. Monte Carlo then raises the values of C, D and E. TD, during that same walk, may have lowered the value of C. How can that be, when the walk ended well?

TD updated C at the moment the walker stepped from C to D, long before the outcome was known. Its target was the reward for that step, 0, plus the current value of D. If D’s estimate happened to be lower than C’s at that moment, C was moved down. TD does not know how the walk ends. It only compares neighbouring guesses. The good news from the right edge reaches E at once, reaches D the next time a walk passes from D to E, and reaches C later still. Monte Carlo delivers the news to all three at once, along with all the luck in that one walk.

entries.title: Q-learning: fill in the table, one step at a time
entries.html:
Q-Learning: Fill in the Table, One Step at a Time

A robot is dropped into a room it has never seen. Nobody tells it where the goal is, where the pit is, or what its moves do. All it gets is a number after every step: −1 for an ordinary step, +10 for reaching the goal, −10 for falling into the pit. Q-learning turns that trickle of numbers into a table that says, for every square and every move, how good that move is. On this page you can watch every single entry of the table being computed, with the arithmetic written out.

Imagine learning your way round a new city with no map, by keeping a notebook. On each page is one street corner, and on that page four numbers: how good it has turned out to be to go north, east, south or west from there. At first every number is zero. You walk. Each time you take a step you look at the page for the corner you have just arrived at, find its best number, and use it to correct the number for the step you just took: "going east from the bakery got me to the fountain, and the fountain is a good place to be, so east from the bakery is good too". You never need to know the whole route. Good news spreads backwards through the notebook, one corner at a time, from the places where something actually happened.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start with a table of zeros: the robot knows nothing. Put it on the start square.
  2. Choose a move. Most of the time take the move with the highest value in the current row. With probability ε pick a random move instead, to explore.
  3. Make the move. See which square you land in and what reward you get.
  4. Look along the row of the new square and take its highest value: the best that can be expected from there.
  5. Target = reward + γ × that best value. Move the old table entry a fraction α of the way toward the target.
  6. If the episode has ended, go back to the start square. Repeat from step 2 until the table stops changing.

What just happened

Animation

Speed and episodes
Learning
The floor
Episodes finished
–
Steps in this episode
–
Reward of the last finished episode
–
Best route from the start, according to the table
–
Entries within 0.1 of their true value
–
Largest change in the table over the last 25 episodes
–

Try this. Start with The Hallway and press One step again and again, reading the worked update each time. The first time the robot reaches the goal, exactly one entry becomes positive. Which one? In the next episode, watch that value leak one square further back. That backward leak is the whole algorithm. Now choose The Room with a Pit and press Run. When it stops, click squares to ask the table for the best route. Then experiment: set ε to 0 and start over. Does the robot still find the best route, and why might it not? Set γ to 0: what can the robot no longer see? Set α to 1 on the slippery floor and watch the values refuse to settle.

What the table means

\(Q(s,a)\) is an estimate of the total reward the robot will collect from now on if it is in square \(s\), makes move \(a\), and behaves as well as possible afterwards. Rewards further in the future are counted a little less, by a factor \(\gamma\) for each step of delay:

$$Q^\star(s,a)=\mathbb E\big[r_1+\gamma r_2+\gamma^2r_3+\dots\ \big|\ s,a,\ \text{then act optimally}\big].$$

If the table were correct, behaving well would be easy: in every square, make the move with the highest value. Learning the table is the whole problem.

The update

The robot is in \(s\), makes move \(a\), receives reward \(r\) and lands in \(s'\). It then changes one entry of the table:

$$Q(s,a)\ \leftarrow\ Q(s,a)+\alpha\Big[\underbrace{r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')}_{\text{target}}-Q(s,a)\Big].$$

The target is a better guess of what \(Q(s,a)\) should be, made one step later: the reward that actually arrived plus the best value the table currently offers from the new square. The bracket is the temporal-difference error: how much better or worse things turned out than the table said. The learning rate \(\alpha\) decides how far to move: with \(\alpha=1\) the old value is thrown away, with \(\alpha=0.1\) it moves a tenth of the way. If \(s'\) ends the episode there is no future, and the target is \(r\) alone. The panel under the pictures writes these lines out with the numbers of the step just taken (Watkins, 1989).

A worked example

In the hallway with \(\alpha=0.5\) and \(\gamma=0.9\), suppose the robot stands on the square next to the goal, with the whole table at zero, and steps right. It reaches the goal and receives \(+10\). The goal ends the episode, so

$$Q(\text{A4},\rightarrow)\leftarrow0+0.5\,[\,10-0\,]=5 .$$

In a later episode it steps right from A3 into A4, with reward \(-1\). The best value now on offer in A4 is 5, so

$$Q(\text{A3},\rightarrow)\leftarrow0+0.5\,[\,-1+0.9\times5-0\,]=1.75 .$$

The reward at the goal has reached a square from which the goal cannot be seen. After enough visits the values settle at \(10\), \(8\), \(6.2\), \(4.58\) going back from the goal: each is \(-1+0.9\times\) the one in front of it.

Explore or exploit

Always taking the move that looks best is called exploiting. A robot that only exploits never tries the moves it wrongly believes are bad, so it can settle on a poor route for ever. With ε-greedy behaviour it makes a random move with probability \(\varepsilon\) and the best-looking move otherwise. Every entry of the table then keeps being tested.

Why it learns the best behaviour while behaving imperfectly

The target uses \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\), the value of the best next move, whatever move the robot actually makes next. So the table describes the best possible behaviour even while the robot is stumbling around at random one step in five. This is called off-policy learning, and it is the difference from SARSA in the next tab. Provided every square and move keeps being visited and \(\alpha\) is reduced gradually, the table is guaranteed to converge to \(Q^\star\).

The three settings

\(\alpha\): large values learn fast and are thrown about by luck when the floor is slippery. Small values are steady and slow. \(\gamma\): at 0 only the immediate reward counts, and since every ordinary step pays \(-1\), the robot cannot tell a step toward the goal from a step away. Near 1, distant rewards count almost fully. \(\varepsilon\): at 0 nothing is explored. At 1 the robot moves at random, which still fills in the table correctly but collects very little reward on the way.

How this page decides it has finished

The true values are known here, because the page also solves the world exactly with the method of the Value and Policy Iteration tab. They are used only to draw the right-hand chart. Learning stops when no entry has changed by more than 0.01 during 25 episodes in a row, or after 400 episodes. On the slippery floor with a fixed \(\alpha\) the entries never stop jiggling, so the limit is what ends the run.

Where the table stops being enough

A table needs one row for every situation. A 3 by 4 room has 11. Chess has more positions than there are atoms in the Earth. For such problems the table is replaced by a neural network that takes the situation as input and outputs the values of the moves, trained on the same target. That is the deep Q-network in the last tab of this module.

Check yourself

After the very first episode in The Room with a Pit, almost every entry the robot touched is negative, even on squares that lie on the best route. Why, and why does that not ruin the learning?

During the first episode nothing in the table knows about the goal yet, so every ordinary step is updated toward a target of −1 plus γ times zero. The squares along the route are therefore marked as slightly bad. Only the very last step, into the goal, gets a positive value. In later episodes that positive value is passed back one square per visit, and it soon outweighs the small negative numbers. The early negative values even help: they make squares the robot has already tried look slightly worse than squares it has not, which pushes it to try new moves.

entries.title: SARSA and Q-learning: two robots on a cliff edge
entries.html:
SARSA and Q-Learning: Two Robots on a Cliff Edge

Two robots learn the same walk: from the bottom-left corner to the bottom-right, with a cliff along the whole way between. Falling costs 100 and sends the robot back to the start. Both use a table and both explore by making an occasional random move. Their update rules differ in a single term. One learns the shortest path, right along the edge. The other learns to keep its distance. Which is the wiser depends on a question that matters far beyond this grid: are you being judged while you learn?

Two apprentices learn to carry trays through a crowded kitchen. Both are clumsy: one step in ten goes somewhere they did not intend. The first reasons, "the best route is the short one past the hot stove, and that is what I will learn", and gives no thought to its own clumsiness. The second reasons, "given how I actually walk, how do routes work out for me?", and finds that the route past the stove regularly ends in a burn. It learns to go the long way round. The first has learned the route that is best for a waiter who never stumbles. The second has learned the route that is best for the waiter it currently is.

How it works, step by step

  1. Both robots start with a table of zeros and behave the same way: the best-looking move most of the time, a random move with probability ε.
  2. Each makes a move, gets a reward and lands in a new square.
  3. Q-learning asks: what is the best move from the new square? Its target is reward + γ × the value of that best move.
  4. SARSA first chooses its next move, random slips included, and asks: what is the value of the move I am actually going to make? Its target is reward + γ × that value.
  5. Each moves its table entry a fraction α of the way toward its own target.
  6. Repeat for 500 episodes.

What just happened

Animation

Learning
Episodes finished
–
Q-learning: average reward, last 50 episodes
–
SARSA: average reward, last 50 episodes
–
Q-learning: recommended route
–
SARSA: recommended route
–
Falls so far: Q-learning / SARSA
–

Try this. Press Run and watch the gold routes. Which robot learns to hug the cliff, and which goes the long way round? Now compare the reward curves: the robot with the shorter route earns less. How can that be? (Count the falls.) Slide ε down to 0.02 and start over, then to 0: what happens to the difference between the two? Slide it up to 0.3. Finally step slowly and read the two updates side by side on a step where the robot explored: that is the only kind of step on which the two rules disagree.

The two updates

After the step \(s,a\to r,s'\), Q-learning uses the best next move in its target, and SARSA uses the next move \(a'\) that it has actually chosen:

$$\text{Q-learning:}\quad Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\alpha\big[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)\big]$$$$\text{SARSA:}\quad Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\alpha\big[r+\gamma\,Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)\big].$$

The name SARSA spells out what one update needs: \(s,a,r,s',a'\). When the next move is the best-looking one, the two targets are identical. They differ only when the next move is an exploratory one, which happens with probability \(\varepsilon\).

On-policy and off-policy

SARSA's table answers the question "how good is this move, given that I will go on behaving as I do now, random moves included?" It evaluates the policy it is following, so it is called on-policy. Q-learning's table answers "how good is this move, given that I behave perfectly from the next step on?" It learns about a policy it is not following, so it is off-policy.

Why the cliff separates them

On a square at the cliff edge, a random move has a one in four chance of stepping off, at a cost of 100. SARSA's targets include those accidents, so the values of edge squares are dragged down and the route moves away from the edge. Q-learning's targets ignore them, because the best move from an edge square is never to jump. Its table is right about the shortest path. But while it learns, it still explores, walks along the edge, and falls. That is why its reward during learning is lower although its route is better.

Which is right?

If learning happens in a simulator and only the final behaviour is used, with exploration switched off, Q-learning's route is the one you want. If mistakes during learning cost something real, as for a robot that can break or a system that serves customers while it learns, SARSA's caution is worth having. As \(\varepsilon\to0\) the accidents disappear and the two learn the same thing: try it.

What this page runs

The cliff walk of Sutton and Barto, here 4 squares high and 10 wide. Every step costs 1, the cliff costs 100 and returns the robot to the start, and the goal ends the episode. There is no discounting, \(\gamma=1\). Both robots run for 500 episodes. The reward curve shows the average of the last 20 episodes, since single episodes swing wildly whenever a robot falls.

Check yourself

With ε = 0.1, Q-learning’s recommended route is 11 steps and SARSA’s is longer. A classmate says SARSA has “learned the wrong answer”. In what sense is SARSA’s answer correct?

SARSA has learned the true values of moves for a robot that keeps making a random move one time in ten. For that robot, walking along the edge really is worse, because the expected cost of falls outweighs the steps saved. SARSA’s route is the best one available to the robot as it actually behaves. Q-learning’s route is the best one for a robot that will stop exploring. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions, and the right one to ask depends on whether the exploring will ever be switched off.

entries.title: Policy gradient: adjust the habits directly
entries.html:
Policy Gradient: Adjust the Habits Directly

Q-learning learns how good every move is and then picks the best. There is a more direct idea: skip the values, and learn the behaviour itself. Give every square four preferences, one per move, and choose moves at random in proportion to them. After each episode, strengthen the moves that were followed by a good outcome and weaken the ones followed by a bad one. Here the arrows in each square show the current probabilities, and you can watch a robot that starts by wandering aimlessly make up its mind.

Think of training a dog. You do not hand the dog a table of how valuable each action is in each situation. You wait until it does something, and if what follows is good, you reward it, and it becomes a little more inclined to do the same thing in the same situation. Policy gradient is exactly that, done with arithmetic: behave, see how it turned out, and make the things you did a little more or a little less likely.

How it works, step by step

  1. Every square has four preferences, all zero at first, so all four moves are equally likely.
  2. Play one whole episode, choosing each move at random according to the current probabilities.
  3. For every step of the episode, work out the return: the total discounted reward from that step to the end.
  4. Compare the return with what is usual for that square, the baseline. Better than usual counts as good, worse as bad.
  5. Raise the preference of the move that was made if the result was good, lower it if bad, by an amount proportional to how good or bad. The other three moves shift the opposite way.
  6. Repeat until the average reward stops improving.

What just happened

Animation

Learning
Episodes finished
–
Reward of the last episode
–
Average reward, last 30 episodes
–
Best possible reward
–
Chance of choosing a best move, averaged over the squares of the last episode
–
Steps in the last episode
–

Try this. Press One episode a few times. The first episodes are long and aimless, and they usually end badly: read the worked update to see a move being made less likely. Press Run and watch the arrows grow in one direction, square by square, starting near the goal. Click the start square and watch its four bars in the bottom-right picture. When learning stops, start over with Without a Baseline, two or three times. Most runs now settle into a poor habit and never reach the best reward. Then go back to the baseline and try a step size of 0.3: fast, and in a good share of runs it commits to a poor habit and cannot undo it. Why is that harder to recover from here than in Q-learning?

A policy with adjustable preferences

Each state \(s\) has one number \(\theta_{s,a}\) for each move, and the probability of a move comes from a softmax:

$$\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=\frac{e^{\theta_{s,a}}}{\sum_{b}e^{\theta_{s,b}}} .$$

With all preferences equal every move is equally likely. Raising one preference makes its move more likely and all the others less. The behaviour is random by construction, so exploration is built in and fades by itself as the preferences grow apart.

What is being maximised

The objective is the expected return of an episode played with the policy, \(J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[G_0]\). The aim is to climb its gradient. The policy gradient theorem says this gradient can be estimated from sampled episodes without knowing how the world works:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}\Big[\sum_t G_t\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\Big],\qquad G_t=\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^k r_{t+k+1}.$$

REINFORCE

Williams (1992) turned this into an algorithm: play an episode, then for every step move the preferences along \(G_t\nabla\log\pi\). For the softmax above the gradient is simple, and the update for the visited state \(s_t\) is

$$\theta_{s_t,a}\leftarrow\theta_{s_t,a}+\alpha\,\big(G_t-b(s_t)\big)\,\big(\mathbb 1[a=a_t]-\pi_\theta(a\mid s_t)\big)\quad\text{for each move }a.$$

For the move that was made, the last factor is \(1-\pi\), positive. For the others it is \(-\pi\), negative. So a good outcome pushes the chosen move up and the rest down. The push is larger when the chosen move was unlikely, because a surprising success is more informative.

The baseline

Without \(b\), every return is compared with zero. In a world where almost all returns are negative, every move ever made is pushed down, and only the differences between large pushes carry information. That works on average and is very noisy. Subtracting a baseline \(b(s)\), the usual return from that state, changes the question from "was the result good?" to "was it better than usual?". It does not change the expected gradient, because \(\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\,\nabla\log\pi(a\mid s)=0\), and it reduces the variance a great deal. Here the baseline is a running average of the returns seen from each square. On this page the difference is stark: in 40 test runs with a step size of 0.1, every run with the baseline reached the best reward, typically in about 75 episodes, and 27 of the 40 runs without it were still stuck after 1,500.

Compared with Q-learning

Policy gradient works unchanged when moves are continuous, such as a steering angle, and when the best behaviour is itself random. It has no \(\max\) over moves to compute. Its weaknesses are the ones visible here. It needs whole episodes before learning anything. Its updates are noisy. And it is on-policy: when the probabilities for some move have collapsed to nearly zero, that move is almost never tried again, so a bad habit formed early can be hard to unlearn. Q-learning with ε-greedy keeps testing every move for ever.

What this page runs

The room with a pit, with a firm floor and \(\gamma=0.95\). Each episode is cut off at 60 steps. Learning stops when the average reward of the last 30 episodes is within 1 of the best possible for 30 episodes in a row, or after 1,500 episodes. The next tab replaces the running-average baseline with a learned critic, which gives the actor-critic method.

Check yourself

An episode ends in the pit with a total reward of −14. With no baseline, the preference of every move made in that episode is lowered, including moves that were perfectly sensible. Why does learning still work?

Each single update is indeed a poor judge of each move. But the sensible moves also appear in the episodes that end well, where they are raised, and across many episodes they are followed by better returns on average than the foolish moves are. The updates are proportional to the returns, so on average the sensible moves come out ahead. The price of relying on averages is noise and slow learning. A baseline removes the part of every return that has nothing to do with the move, so each update points more nearly in the right direction.

entries.title: Actor-critic and DQN: when the table would never fit
entries.html:
Actor-Critic and DQN: When the Table Would Never Fit

A cart runs on a short track with a pole hinged on top, and the only controls are a push to the left and a push to the right. Keep the pole up for 200 steps. The situation is described by four continuous numbers, so there is no finite list of squares and no table can hold the answer. The table is replaced by a neural network. Two famous ways of training it are shown: a deep Q-network, which learns the value of each push, and an actor-critic, which learns the behaviour directly with a second network as its coach. Watch a controller go from dropping the pole in a tenth of a second to balancing it indefinitely.

Balance a broom upright on your palm. You could not write down a table of what to do for every possible lean and every possible speed: there are infinitely many. Yet you learn it in a minute, because nearby situations call for nearby responses, and your brain fills in the gaps. A neural network does the same for the robot. It is shown some situations and generalises to the ones in between. The two methods here differ in what the network is asked to output: a score for each push, or the push itself.

How it works, step by step

  1. The network sees four numbers: where the cart is, how fast it moves, how far the pole leans, how fast it is falling. Every step the pole stays up earns a reward.
  2. Act: choose a push using the network, with some randomness so that both pushes get tried.
  3. DQN stores every step in a memory. It then draws 32 old steps at random and, for each, moves its predicted value toward reward + γ × the best value of the next situation, as judged by a slowly updated copy of itself.
  4. Actor-critic waits for the episode to end. Its critic network predicts how long the pole will stay up from each situation. Pushes that led to a longer run than the critic predicted are made more likely, the others less.
  5. Repeat until the last 20 episodes average at least 180 of the 200 possible steps.
  6. Then watch the trained controller, and give the pole a shove.

What just happened

Animation

Test the controller

Stage
–
Episodes finished
–
Length of the last episode
–
Average length, last 20 episodes
–
Steps of experience so far
–
Randomness in its choices now
–

Try this. Press Run with DQN. For the first episodes the pole falls almost at once. Watch the bottom-right picture: it starts as noise and becomes two clean regions with a slanted border. What rule does that border express, in words? When training stops, press the two shove buttons and see how hard a push the controller can recover from. Now switch to Actor-Critic and compare: how many episodes and how many steps of experience does each method need? Run each two or three times with Start over. Which one is more consistent from run to run?

From a table to a function

The state is \(s=(x,\dot x,\theta,\dot\theta)\). In place of a table entry \(Q(s,a)\) there is a network \(Q_w(s,a)\) with weights \(w\), taking the four numbers in and giving one value per push out. Changing the weights to fix one situation also changes the answer for similar situations. That is the point, and also the source of all the trouble: the careful one-entry-at-a-time argument that made the table converge no longer applies.

Deep Q-network

DQN (Mnih and others, 2015) keeps the Q-learning target and trains the network to predict it, minimising the squared error

$$L(w)=\Big(r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_{w^-}(s',a')-Q_w(s,a)\Big)^2 .$$

Two additions make this stable. A replay memory stores past steps, and training uses random handfuls of them. Consecutive steps are almost identical, and training on them in order would make the network forget everything but the last few seconds. A target network \(Q_{w^-}\), a copy of the weights that is refreshed only now and then, computes the target. Without it the network would be chasing a target that moves every time it learns. When the pole falls the episode ends and the target is just the final reward, here \(-1\).

Actor-critic

The actor is a policy network \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\) giving the probability of each push, trained by the policy gradient of the previous tab. The critic is a value network \(V_\phi(s)\) that predicts the return from each situation and serves as the baseline:

$$\theta\leftarrow\theta+\alpha\,\big(G_t-V_\phi(s_t)\big)\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t),\qquad \phi\leftarrow\phi-\beta\,\nabla_\phi\big(G_t-V_\phi(s_t)\big)^2 .$$

The quantity \(G_t-V_\phi(s_t)\) is the advantage: how much better the run went than the critic expected. A push followed by a better-than-expected run is made more likely. The critic turns the vague signal "the pole stayed up 40 steps" into the sharp one "that was 15 more than usual from there".

How they compare

DQN is off-policy: it can reuse every old step many times, so it is sparing with experience, and it needs the replay memory and target network to stay stable. It only works for a small set of distinct actions, because of the \(\max\). Actor-critic is on-policy: it learns from each episode once and then discards it, but each update is cheap, it has no \(\max\), and it carries over directly to continuous actions such as a steering angle. Modern methods mix the two ideas.

Reading the policy picture

The bottom-right picture fixes the cart in the middle and at rest, and colours each combination of pole angle and falling speed by the push the network prefers. A good controller pushes toward the side the pole is falling to, which moves the cart back underneath it. The border is slanted because speed matters as well as position: a pole leaning slightly left and swinging quickly to the right needs a push to the right.

What this page trains

The standard cart-pole simulation, with episodes ending when the pole passes 12 degrees, the cart leaves the track, or 200 steps are reached. DQN: a network with two hidden layers of 32 neurons, a memory of 10,000 steps, a batch of 32 every second step, the target copy refreshed every 150 updates, and exploration falling from 100% to 5% over the first 2,500 steps. Actor-critic: an actor and a critic with one hidden layer of 32 neurons each, updated once after every episode. Training stops when the last 20 episodes average 180 steps, or after 400 episodes. Both methods are sensitive to luck, and an occasional run fails to reach the mark.

Check yourself

DQN trains on steps drawn at random from a memory of old experience, some of it collected thousands of steps ago by a much worse version of the network. Why is it legitimate to learn from such stale experience, when the actor-critic must throw each episode away?

A stored step records a fact about the world: in this situation, this push led to that situation and that reward. That fact is true whoever made the push and however badly they were behaving. The Q-learning target then asks only for the best value available from the next situation, using the current network, so nothing in the update depends on how the old agent would have continued. That is what off-policy means. The actor-critic update is an average over what the current policy does. Experience gathered by an older policy describes a different average, so using it without correction would point the update in the wrong direction.

entries.title: Bayesian updating: change your mind by the right amount
entries.html:
Bayesian Updating: Change Your Mind by the Right Amount

A café adds a new drink and wants to know what share of its customers like it. Before anyone has tried it, the owner has a hunch. Then customers answer one by one: yes or no. Bayesian updating is the rule for combining the hunch with the answers. It never gives a single number. It gives a whole curve of belief over every possible share, and the curve narrows as the evidence comes in. Watch three owners with very different hunches being pulled to the same conclusion.

A doctor sees a patient with a cough. Before any test, she thinks a common cold is far more likely than anything serious, because colds are common. A test comes back, and it shifts her opinion, a lot if the result would be very surprising under one of the explanations, a little otherwise. A second test shifts it again, starting from where the first left it. She never throws away what she knew before, and she never ignores the evidence. Bayes' rule is the exact arithmetic of that way of thinking: what you believe afterwards is what you believed before, reweighted by how well each possibility explains what you saw.

How it works, step by step

  1. Before any answers, write down a belief about the share: a curve over every value from 0 to 1. This is the prior.
  2. A customer answers yes or no.
  3. For every possible share, ask: how likely was that answer if this were the true share? Multiply the belief at that share by that likelihood.
  4. Rescale the curve so that its area is 1 again. This is the posterior.
  5. The posterior becomes the prior for the next customer. Repeat.
  6. Stop when the belief is narrow enough for the decision at hand: here, when 95% of it fits in a range 0.1 wide.

What just happened

Animation

Add answers yourself
The world and the prior
Customers asked
–
Said yes
–
Best estimate now (posterior mean)
–
95% of the belief lies between
–
Plain frequency: yes ÷ asked
–
Posterior
–

Try this. Press One customer a few times with No Opinion and read the worked update: each yes adds 1 to the first number of the curve, each no adds 1 to the second. That is the entire calculation. Press Run and watch the curve tighten around the true share. Now choose Stubborn and start over. How many customers does it take before the owner’s estimate is closer to the truth than to the original 80%? Look at the bottom-right chart: when do the three owners agree to within a few percent? Then use the two buttons to feed in a streak of ten yes answers by hand and see how each owner reacts.

Bayes' rule

Let \(\theta\) be the unknown share and \(D\) the data. The rule is

$$\underbrace{p(\theta\mid D)}_{\text{posterior}}=\frac{\overbrace{p(D\mid\theta)}^{\text{likelihood}}\ \overbrace{p(\theta)}^{\text{prior}}}{p(D)},\qquad p(D)=\int p(D\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\theta .$$

The prior is the belief before the data. The likelihood says how probable the data would be for each value of \(\theta\). The denominator is only there to make the posterior's area equal 1. Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior: that sentence is the whole method.

The café: a Beta prior and yes-or-no answers

If the true share is \(\theta\), a customer says yes with probability \(\theta\). After \(k\) yes answers among \(n\) customers the likelihood is \(\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\). For the prior, use the Beta family:

$$p(\theta)=\mathrm{Beta}(\theta;a,b)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}.$$

Multiplying the two gives another curve of the same shape,

$$p(\theta\mid D)\propto\theta^{a+k-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-k-1}=\mathrm{Beta}(\theta;\ a+k,\ b+n-k).$$

So updating is addition: every yes adds 1 to \(a\), every no adds 1 to \(b\). A prior that reproduces itself like this is called conjugate. The prior behaves exactly like \(a+b\) imagined earlier customers, \(a\) of whom said yes. "No opinion" is \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\), a flat line.

Reading the posterior

The mean of \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) is \(a/(a+b)\), so the best estimate after the data is

$$\mathbb E[\theta\mid D]=\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}=\underbrace{\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}}_{\text{weight on the prior}}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b}+\underbrace{\frac{n}{a+b+n}}_{\text{weight on the data}}\cdot\frac{k}{n}.$$

It is a weighted average of the prior guess and the plain frequency, and the weight on the data grows with every customer. That is why the stubborn owner is pulled to the truth slowly and the owner with no opinion almost at once, and why all three end in the same place. The 95% range, called a credible interval, is the middle 95% of the posterior's area. Its width shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\).

The same number is also a prediction

The probability that the next customer says yes, taking the uncertainty about \(\theta\) into account, is the posterior mean \((a+k)/(a+b+n)\). With no opinion and no data it is \(\tfrac12\). After one yes it is \(\tfrac23\), not 1: one happy customer does not prove that everyone will be happy. The plain frequency would have said 100%.

Why bother with a prior?

With a great deal of data the prior stops mattering, as the bottom chart shows. With little data it matters a lot, and that is when it is most useful: it keeps the estimate sensible after three answers, and it is the natural place to put real knowledge, such as "new drinks at this café are usually liked by 20 to 40 percent of people". The cost is that a confident wrong prior takes many observations to overturn. A prior should be as sure as you actually are, and no surer.

Beyond the café

The same recipe, prior times likelihood, underlies spam filters, medical diagnosis, A/B testing, the Thompson sampling of the Multi-Armed Bandits tab, and Gaussian process regression. For most models the product has no tidy formula like the Beta one. Then the posterior is explored by sampling, which is the subject of the next tab, MCMC.

What this page runs

Customers are drawn at random with the true share you set. The run stops when the 95% credible interval is narrower than 0.1, or after 1,000 customers. The interval is computed by adding up the area under the curve numerically.

Check yourself

With no opinion at the start, the first customer says yes. The plain frequency is now 1 out of 1, or 100%. The Bayesian estimate is 2/3. Which is the better forecast for the second customer, and why?

The Bayesian one. A frequency of 100% claims that every future customer will say yes, on the strength of one answer, and would be proved wrong by the first no. The posterior after one yes is Beta(2, 1): it has shifted toward high values and still gives real weight to everything from about 0.2 upward. Its mean, 2/3, says “probably more people like it than not, and I am far from sure”. That is what one answer actually tells you. As the answers accumulate the two estimates approach each other, and after a few hundred customers they agree to the second decimal place.

entries.title: MCMC: explore a landscape you can only feel underfoot
entries.html:
MCMC: Explore a Landscape You Can Only Feel Underfoot

Bayes’ rule often leaves you with a belief you can write down and cannot use: a formula for how plausible each answer is, but no way to draw examples from it or average over it. Markov chain Monte Carlo is the workaround. A walker wanders over the landscape of plausibility, and the places it visits, counted up, turn out to be exactly a sample from the belief. Five walkers live on this page, from the blind random stepper of 1953 to the No-U-Turn sampler that modern Bayesian software runs. They differ in one thing only: how the next place is proposed.

You are set down on a hilly island in thick fog and asked to draw a map showing how high the ground is everywhere. You cannot see anything. All you have is an altimeter that tells you the height where you stand. Here is a way to do it: wander about, and keep a diary of where you are once a minute. Whenever you consider a step, check the altimeter there. If it is higher, take the step. If it is lower, take it only sometimes, less often the bigger the drop. You will spend most of your time on the high ground and visit the low ground occasionally, and in the long run the number of diary entries in each place is proportional to its height. The diary is the map. Nobody ever needed the total volume of the island. The better walkers on this page add one more instrument: they can also feel which way the ground slopes, and use it to decide where to try next.

How it works, step by step

    What just happened

    Animation

    The walker
    Steps so far
    –
    Share of proposals accepted
    –
    Average position: walker / truth
    –
    Worth this many independent samples
    –
    Look-ups of height or slope used
    –
    Independent samples per 1,000 look-ups
    –
    Gap between the bars and the true line
    –
    Share of time on the right-hand side: walker / truth
    –

    Try this. Start with Random-Walk Metropolis. Press One step several times and read each decision. When is a downhill move accepted? Run it on the Slanted Bell, then set the stride to 0.05 and to 4 and watch the trace. Now switch to Langevin and press One step: the proposal leans uphill. Choose the Banana, switch off the correction and raise the step size to 0.6. Do the bars still match the line, however long you wait? Switch the correction back on. Choose Hamiltonian on the Banana and step once: the thick line is the path of a ball rolled across the landscape. Raise the leapfrog steps to 40 and watch some paths curl back to where they began. Then choose No-U-Turn and see where each path is cut. Compare the last two readouts across all five walkers on the Banana. Finally try every walker on Two Islands. Which one crosses, and why that one?

    The problem

    We want samples from a density \(\pi(\mathbf x)\) that we can only evaluate up to a constant: \(\pi(\mathbf x)=\tilde\pi(\mathbf x)/Z\) with \(Z\) unknown. This is the usual position after Bayes' rule, where \(\tilde\pi\) is prior times likelihood and \(Z\) is the awkward integral in the denominator. With samples \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_N\) any average can be estimated:

    $$\mathbb E_\pi[f(\mathbf x)]\approx\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\mathbf x_i).$$

    Random-walk Metropolis

    From the current point \(\mathbf x\), propose \(\mathbf x'=\mathbf x+\sigma\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) with \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\). Accept the proposal with probability

    $$A=\min\!\Big(1,\ \frac{\tilde\pi(\mathbf x')}{\tilde\pi(\mathbf x)}\Big).$$

    If it is accepted the walker moves to \(\mathbf x'\). If not, it stays at \(\mathbf x\), and \(\mathbf x\) is recorded again. The unknown \(Z\) cancels in the ratio, which is the entire trick (Metropolis and others, 1953).

    Metropolis-Hastings

    The random walk is fair: a step from \(\mathbf x\) to \(\mathbf x'\) is proposed exactly as often as the step back. Hastings (1970) removed that restriction. Let \(q(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)\) be any rule for proposing, and accept with probability

    $$A=\min\!\Big(1,\ \frac{\tilde\pi(\mathbf x')}{\tilde\pi(\mathbf x)}\cdot\frac{q(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf x')}{q(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)}\Big).$$

    The second fraction is the Hastings correction. It asks how much easier it is to propose the move than to propose its reverse, and cancels the unfairness. Every other sampler on this page is Metropolis-Hastings with a cleverer \(q\). The Metropolis-Hastings button here uses the simplest unfair proposal there is, an independence sampler: it ignores where the walker stands and proposes from one fixed wide bell centred on the picture, \(q(\mathbf x')=\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,s^2\mathbf I)\). The centre is proposed far more often than the edges, and the correction \(q(\mathbf x)/q(\mathbf x')\) pays that back. Switch the correction off and the bars pile up in the middle.

    Langevin dynamics

    A blind proposal wastes most of its tries. If the slope \(\nabla\log\tilde\pi\) is available, lean the proposal uphill:

    $$\mathbf x'=\mathbf x+\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\,\nabla\log\tilde\pi(\mathbf x)+\epsilon\,\boldsymbol\xi,\qquad\boldsymbol\xi\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I).$$

    This is one small time step of the Langevin diffusion \(d\mathbf x=\tfrac12\nabla\log\pi\,dt+d\mathbf W\), a random motion whose long-run distribution is exactly \(\pi\). Taken with a finite step and no check, it is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm: simple, and slightly wrong, with an error that grows with \(\epsilon\). Push \(\epsilon\) further and it becomes unstable: on a narrow ridge each drift overshoots the top by more than the last, and the walker is thrown to the edge of the picture. Adding the Metropolis-Hastings test, with \(q(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf x)=\mathcal N\big(\mathbf x+\tfrac{\epsilon^2}{2}\nabla\log\tilde\pi(\mathbf x),\,\epsilon^2\mathbf I\big)\), removes the error. That is the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm, MALA. The same uphill-plus-noise update, with a learned slope, is what generates pictures in the score-matching lesson.

    Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

    Langevin takes one slope-guided step and then re-randomizes, so it still diffuses. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo keeps going in the same direction. Think of the walker as a frictionless ball on the surface \(U(\mathbf x)=-\log\tilde\pi(\mathbf x)\), a bowl whose bottom is the most probable place. Give the ball a random kick \(\mathbf p\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) and let it roll. Its total energy

    $$H(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)=U(\mathbf x)+\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf p\rVert^2$$
