    stays constant along the true path. The path is computed with the leapfrog rule, repeated \(L\) times:

    $$\mathbf p\leftarrow\mathbf p-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(\mathbf x),\qquad\mathbf x\leftarrow\mathbf x+\epsilon\,\mathbf p,\qquad\mathbf p\leftarrow\mathbf p-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(\mathbf x).$$

    Leapfrog is reversible and preserves volume, so the Hastings correction reduces to the change in energy. The end of the path is accepted with probability

    $$A=\min\!\big(1,\ \exp(H_{\text{start}}-H_{\text{end}})\big).$$

    Because leapfrog nearly conserves energy, \(A\) is close to 1 even for a path that crosses the whole distribution. That is the point: far-away proposals that are almost always accepted (Duane and others, 1987; Neal, 2011).

    The No-U-Turn sampler

    Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has an awkward setting: the number of leapfrog steps. Too few and it behaves like Langevin. Too many and the ball swings round and comes back, having paid for a long path to end where it started. The No-U-Turn sampler (Hoffman and Gelman, 2014) chooses the length afresh at every move. It grows the path forwards and backwards in time, doubling its length each round, and stops as soon as the two ends begin to approach each other:

    $$(\mathbf x^{+}-\mathbf x^{-})\cdot\mathbf p^{-}<0\quad\text{or}\quad(\mathbf x^{+}-\mathbf x^{-})\cdot\mathbf p^{+}<0.$$

    The new place is then drawn from the points on the path, each allowed with probability set by its energy, in a way that keeps detailed balance. Growing in both directions is what makes the move reversible. There is no accept or reject at the end and no path length to tune.

    Why they all work

    Each rule satisfies detailed balance: for any two points, the long-run flow of the walker from \(\mathbf x\) to \(\mathbf x'\) equals the flow back,

    $$\pi(\mathbf x)\,P(\mathbf x\to\mathbf x')=\pi(\mathbf x')\,P(\mathbf x'\to\mathbf x).$$

    If the walker is already distributed like \(\pi\), one more step leaves it distributed like \(\pi\). As long as it can eventually reach every region, it converges to that distribution from any start. Recording the repeats when a proposal is rejected is essential: leave them out and the high ground is under-counted.

    How many samples do you really have?

    The samples are not independent. The effective sample size says how many independent samples would give the same accuracy as the \(N\) correlated ones:

    $$\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k},$$

    where \(\rho_k\) is the correlation between samples \(k\) steps apart. Steps are not equally expensive, though. A random-walk step looks up the height once. A Hamiltonian move with 15 leapfrog steps looks up the slope 15 times. The honest comparison is effective samples per look-up, which is the last-but-two readout. Run the five walkers on the Banana and compare. In the two dimensions of this page the result is humbling: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo beats the random walk by a factor of two or three, the No-U-Turn sampler roughly ties with it, and the independence proposal beats everything, because the whole picture fits under one wide bell. None of that survives in higher dimension. In hundreds of dimensions no fixed bell covers the target, a random walk must shrink its stride towards nothing, and Hamiltonian paths still travel far. That is where the gradient methods earn their cost. Note also what the effective sample size does not measure: whether the walker is sampling the right landscape. With the correction switched off a walker can move briskly and be wrong.

    Separate islands

    If the target has two regions separated by low ground, a local walker stays on the island where it started for a very long time. Its samples look perfectly healthy and describe half of the answer. Slopes do not help: they point back up the hill the walker is already on, and a rolling ball needs a kick with enough energy to clear the gap, which is rare. On this page only the independence proposal crosses freely, because it does not care where the walker stands, and it works only because the picture is small enough for one wide bell to cover. Defences in real problems include running several chains from different starts and checking that they agree.

    What this page runs

    All five samplers in two dimensions, with slopes computed by finite differences. The true left-to-right distribution is known here, because in two dimensions it can be added up on a grid, and it is used for the comparison line. A run stops when the bars are within 0.08 of that line in total area, or after 8,000 steps. The No-U-Turn sampler is the slice-sampling version from the original paper, with at most six doublings (64 leapfrog steps) and a fixed step size; production software also tunes the step size during warm-up.

    Check yourself

    On the Banana, raising the Hamiltonian walker from 15 to 40 leapfrog steps makes every move nearly three times as expensive, and the samples per 1,000 look-ups go down, not up. Where does the extra work go? And what does the No-U-Turn walker do about it?

    A path of 15 steps already carries the ball most of the way across the Banana, so its end is nearly independent of its start. The extra 25 steps cannot make the sample any more independent than that. Often they do harm: the ball runs up the far side of the valley, turns round and rolls back, and a long, costly path ends near its own beginning. The right length also differs from place to place and from kick to kick, so no single setting is right everywhere. The No-U-Turn walker watches the two ends of its path as it grows and stops when they begin to approach each other, which is the moment more steps stop adding distance. It never has to be told a length. On this small picture you can see what that convenience costs: it builds the path in both directions and uses one point from it, so per look-up it does no better here than a well-chosen fixed length. Its value is that in a real problem nobody knows the well-chosen length in advance.

entries.title: Variational Bayes: replace a hard belief with the closest easy one
entries.html:
Variational Bayes: Replace a Hard Belief with the Closest Easy One

MCMC answers "what does this awkward belief look like?" by wandering over it for a long time. Variational Bayes takes a shortcut. Pick a simple family of distributions, here a bell curve, and slide and stretch it until it sits as close to the true belief as that family allows. Sampling becomes optimization, and it is fast. What you pay is that the answer is an approximation with a characteristic bias, which you can watch on this page.

You need to describe the shape of a country to someone over the phone, and all you are allowed to say is "an oval, this wide, this tall, centred here". For a country shaped like an oval the description is perfect. For a long thin country lying on a diagonal, an upright oval must choose: cover the whole length and include a great deal of sea, or stay on land and leave most of the country out. Variational Bayes always makes the second choice. It hates to put weight where the truth has none, so it fits inside, and reports a country smaller than the real one. That bias is the price of the speed.

How it works, step by step

  1. Choose a simple family for the approximation q. Mean-field means one independent bell curve per coordinate.
  2. Start q somewhere.
  3. Score it with the ELBO: how much of the true belief q covers, plus a reward for staying spread out.
  4. Improve one piece of q while holding the others fixed (or take a gradient step on all of them).
  5. Each update can only raise the ELBO. Repeat.
  6. Stop when the ELBO stops rising. The gap left to the dashed line is the error of the approximation.

What just happened

Animation

Animation speed
Steps so far
–
ELBO
–
True log evidence (the ceiling)
–
Gap: KL divergence from q to the truth
–
Spread of q ÷ true spread: left-right, up-down
–
Share on the right-hand side: q / truth
–

Try this. On A Slanted Bell with Mean-Field, press One step and read the panel: each step moves one coordinate of the centre to its best value given the other, and the centre zig-zags home. When it stops, compare the top-right chart. The centre is exactly right. What about the width? Switch to A Full Bell: the gap drops to almost nothing. Why? Go back to Mean-Field and choose Two Islands. Click near the left island and run, then near the right one. Now choose Moment Matching on the same target. Which answer would you rather use to say where the probability is, and which to quote a mean and a variance?

The problem

After Bayes' rule the posterior is known up to a constant, \(p(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x)=\tilde p(\mathbf z)/Z\), where \(Z=p(\mathbf x)\) is the evidence. Choose a family \(\mathcal Q\) of tractable distributions and look for the member closest to the posterior:

$$q^*=\arg\min_{q\in\mathcal Q}\ \mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\Vert\,p(\cdot\mid\mathbf x)\big),\qquad\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p)=\mathbb E_q\Big[\log\frac{q(\mathbf z)}{p(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x)}\Big].$$

The evidence lower bound

The KL divergence contains the unknown \(Z\). Rearranging removes it:

$$\log Z=\underbrace{\mathbb E_q[\log\tilde p(\mathbf z)]+\mathbb H[q]}_{\text{ELBO}(q)}+\mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\Vert\,p(\cdot\mid\mathbf x)\big).$$

The left side does not depend on \(q\) and the KL term is never negative. So the ELBO is a lower bound on \(\log Z\), and raising it is the same as lowering the KL. The first term rewards putting \(q\) where the belief is high. The entropy \(\mathbb H[q]\) rewards keeping \(q\) wide. On this page \(\log Z\) can be computed on a grid, so you can see the gap directly. In a real problem you see only the ELBO.

Mean-field

The mean-field family assumes the coordinates are independent: \(q(\mathbf z)=\prod_j q_j(z_j)\). Holding all factors but one fixed, the best choice for that factor has a closed form:

$$\log q_j^*(z_j)=\mathbb E_{q_{-j}}\big[\log\tilde p(\mathbf z)\big]+\text{const}.$$

Cycling through the factors is coordinate-ascent variational inference. For a Gaussian target with mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and precision matrix \(\boldsymbol\Lambda=\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\), the update for the first coordinate is itself a Gaussian with

$$m_1\leftarrow\mu_1-\frac{\Lambda_{12}}{\Lambda_{11}}(m_2-\mu_2),\qquad s_1^2=\frac{1}{\Lambda_{11}},$$

and the same with the indices swapped. The Slanted Bell with Mean-Field runs exactly these updates.

The characteristic bias

The means converge to the true means. The variance does not: \(1/\Lambda_{11}\) is the variance of \(z_1\) given \(z_2\), which is smaller than its overall variance \(\Sigma_{11}\) whenever the two are correlated. For correlation \(\rho\),

$$\frac{s_1^2}{\Sigma_{11}}=1-\rho^2.$$

With \(\rho=0.85\) the approximation reports a standard deviation of about half the truth. Mean-field variational Bayes is overconfident, and more so the stronger the dependence it has been forced to ignore.

Why it hugs one mode

\(\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p)\) averages over \(q\). Any region where \(q\) has weight and \(p\) has almost none costs a great deal, while regions where \(p\) has weight and \(q\) has none cost nothing. So \(q\) avoids the empty gap between two islands by sitting on one of them, and which one depends on where it started. The gap it leaves on Two Islands is close to \(\ln 2\approx0.69\), which is exactly the cost of describing one of two equal halves perfectly and missing the other. The opposite divergence, \(\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q)\), averages over \(p\) and punishes missing any of the truth. For a Gaussian \(q\) its minimizer simply matches the mean and covariance of \(p\), and it covers both islands with one wide bell that peaks in the empty middle. That is the criterion behind expectation propagation. It needs expectations under \(p\), which is the thing we could not compute, so here it is found from the grid in a single step.

Richer families and gradients

The Full Bell adds a covariance term. It can tilt, so it fits the Slanted Bell exactly (the small gap that remains on the page comes from estimating the ELBO with a finite number of draws), but it is still one bell and cannot bend round the Banana or cover two islands. When no closed-form update exists, the ELBO is climbed by gradient ascent using the reparameterization \(\mathbf z=\mathbf m+\mathbf L\boldsymbol\epsilon\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\), which is how the Banana and Islands are fitted here (with 128 fixed draws of \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\)) and how a variational autoencoder is trained. The run stops when the ELBO gains less than \(10^{-5}\) for ten steps in a row.

Against MCMC

MCMC is asymptotically exact and slow, with no simple test for when it has finished. Variational Bayes is fast, scales to very large models, and gives a number, the ELBO, to monitor and to compare models with. Its error does not go away with more computing, and its uncertainties are usually too small.

Check yourself

On the Slanted Bell, mean-field gets the centre exactly right and reports a spread about half the true one. More steps do not help. Where does the missing spread go?

The true belief is wide along its diagonal because the two coordinates move together. A product of independent bell curves cannot represent "together": its ellipse must stand upright. If it were made as wide as the true left-to-right spread, its corners would stick out into regions where the truth has almost no probability, and the KL divergence from q to p punishes that severely. The best upright ellipse is therefore the one that fits inside the slanted one, whose width is the spread of one coordinate when the other is held fixed. The spread that came from the coordinates varying together has nowhere to go in this family, so it is simply lost. Allowing the bell to tilt recovers it.

entries.title: Hidden Markov models: guess what you cannot see from what you can
entries.html:
Hidden Markov Models: Guess What You Cannot See from What You Can

A friend who lives far away tells you every evening what she did that day: went for a walk, went shopping, or stayed in and cleaned. She never mentions the weather. Can you work out, day by day, whether it was sunny or rainy there? You know two things: weather tends to last, and she walks more in the sun. A hidden Markov model turns those two facts into a calculation. The same calculation recognises speech from sound, finds genes in DNA and follows a phone’s position between GPS fixes.

You are in a room with no windows, and every so often a colleague walks in. Sometimes they carry a wet umbrella. One wet umbrella makes rain likely. A dry colleague five minutes later does not make you think the rain has stopped, because rain rarely stops that quickly and not everyone carries an umbrella. You are combining two kinds of knowledge without noticing: how the hidden thing behaves over time, and how it shows itself. A hidden Markov model writes both down as tables and does the combining exactly.

How it works, step by step

  1. Day 1: start from even odds for sun and rain, and weigh each by how likely today’s activity is in that weather.
  2. Each later day, first predict: push yesterday’s belief through the “weather tends to last” table. This is the belief before hearing from her.
  3. Then update: multiply the belief in each weather by how likely her activity is in that weather, and rescale so the two add up to 1.
  4. Repeat to the last day. These are the day-by-day beliefs.
  5. Viterbi instead keeps, for each weather on each day, the single most probable story that ends there, and remembers which weather it came from.
  6. At the last day, pick the better ending and trace the remembered links backwards. That is the single best story.

What just happened

Animation
The model
The data
Day
–
Belief today: sunny / rainy
–
Days guessed right, judging each day as it comes
–
Days guessed right, judging afterwards with all the evidence
–
Days guessed right by the single best story
–
Probability of the whole fortnight of activities under the model
–

Try this. Press One day and read the calculation: predict, then update. Find a day where she went shopping, which she does equally often in any weather. What does the belief do on such a day? Press Run to the end, then press Show the True Weather. Compare the two lines on the right: on which days does hindsight change the answer, and why can a later walk change your mind about an earlier day? Click days in the top row to make her clean on a single day in the middle of a sunny spell: is one day enough to convince the model it rained? Lower the first slider to 0.5 and try again. Switch to The Single Best Story and compare its answer with the day-by-day one.

The model

There is a hidden state \(z_t\) for each day, here sunny or rainy, and an observation \(x_t\), here walk, shop or clean. Two assumptions make the model tractable. The state depends only on yesterday's state, through a transition table \(A_{ij}=P(z_t=j\mid z_{t-1}=i)\). The observation depends only on today's state, through an emission table \(B_j(x)=P(x_t=x\mid z_t=j)\). With a starting distribution \(\pi\), the probability of a whole hidden story together with the observations is

$$P(z_{1:T},x_{1:T})=\pi_{z_1}B_{z_1}(x_1)\prod_{t=2}^{T}A_{z_{t-1}z_t}\,B_{z_t}(x_t).$$

The forward algorithm: belief day by day

Let \(\alpha_t(j)=P(z_t=j\mid x_{1:t})\) be the belief on day \(t\) given everything heard so far. It is computed from yesterday's belief in two moves:

$$\text{predict:}\quad \bar\alpha_t(j)=\sum_i\alpha_{t-1}(i)\,A_{ij},\qquad\text{update:}\quad \alpha_t(j)=\frac{\bar\alpha_t(j)\,B_j(x_t)}{\sum_k\bar\alpha_t(k)\,B_k(x_t)}.$$

Predict blurs the belief a little, because the weather might have changed overnight. Update sharpens it with today's evidence. This is Bayes' rule applied once per day, with yesterday's posterior serving as today's prior. The cost is proportional to the number of days, although the number of possible stories doubles with every day. The normalising sums, multiplied together, give \(P(x_{1:T})\), the probability of all the observations, shown in the last readout.

Hindsight: smoothing

Once the fortnight is over, earlier days can be judged again using what came after. A second pass runs backwards, \(\beta_t(i)=\sum_jA_{ij}B_j(x_{t+1})\beta_{t+1}(j)\), and the two are combined:

$$P(z_t=j\mid x_{1:T})\propto\alpha_t(j)\,\beta_t(j).$$

This is the forward-backward algorithm, and it is the second line in the top-right chart. It is never less informed than the day-by-day belief, and it is usually right more often.

Viterbi: the single best story

The most probable whole sequence is a different question, and choosing the most probable state on each day separately does not answer it: the separate choices might string together into a story the model considers nearly impossible. Viterbi (1967) keeps, for each state on each day, the probability of the best story ending there,

$$\delta_t(j)=\max_i\ \delta_{t-1}(i)\,A_{ij}\,B_j(x_t),$$

and remembers which \(i\) achieved the maximum. At the end it takes the larger \(\delta_T\) and follows the remembered links back to day 1. It is the forward algorithm with a maximum in place of a sum.

What the two sliders do

When the weather is very persistent, one odd activity is explained away as an off day, and the belief hardly moves. When persistence is 0.5 the weather has no memory, and each day is judged by its own activity alone. When the second slider is at 0 her activities say nothing about the weather, and the belief stays at even odds whatever she does. The model is only as informative as its two tables.

Where the tables come from

Here they are given. In practice they are learned from sequences of observations alone with the Baum-Welch algorithm, a form of the expectation-maximisation method from the Gaussian Mixtures tab: guess the tables, use forward-backward to estimate the hidden states, re-estimate the tables from those, and repeat.

What this page runs

Fourteen days. The true weather is drawn from the model itself, then her activities from the weather. In sunny weather she walks 60% of the time, shops 30% and cleans 10%, and in rain the reverse, when the second slider is at 1. All probabilities are computed exactly.

Check yourself

On day 6 the day-by-day belief said 70% sunny. After the fortnight is over, the hindsight line says day 6 was 75% rainy. Nothing about day 6 itself has changed. Where did the new information come from?

From days 7 onward. Weather tends to last, so what happened after day 6 is evidence about day 6 itself. If she cleaned on days 7, 8 and 9, those days were very probably rainy, and a rainy spell probably did not begin exactly on day 7: it is quite likely to have started a day earlier, with day 6 being a rainy day on which she happened to shop or walk. The forward pass could not know this on day 6. The backward pass carries the later evidence back through the “weather tends to last” table.

entries.title: The Kalman filter: trust the forecast and the sensor, each as much as it deserves
entries.html:
The Kalman Filter: Trust the Forecast and the Sensor, Each as Much as It Deserves

A delivery drone flies along a street. Its GPS reports a position every second, and every report is off by a few metres. Plotting the raw reports gives a jagged, jumping line. But the drone cannot jump: it has a speed, and where it will be in a second is predictable. The Kalman filter blends the two sources, the prediction from physics and the noisy reading, weighting each by how much it can be trusted at that moment. It is the reason your phone’s blue dot moves smoothly, and it flew to the Moon.

You are a passenger on a train at night, trying to guess where you are. You know the train's speed, so you can keep a running estimate: "ten minutes at this speed, so about twelve kilometres from the last station". Your estimate drifts, because the speed varies a little. Now and then a station sign flashes past, half-read. If your running estimate is fresh and the sign was a blur, you mostly trust the estimate. If you have been guessing for an hour and the sign was clear, you mostly trust the sign. Either way you end up more certain than either source alone would make you. The Kalman filter is this weighing done optimally, every second.

How it works, step by step

  1. Keep two things: a best estimate of position and speed, and a measure of how unsure you are about each.
  2. Predict: move the position forward by one second of travel at the estimated speed. Become a little less sure, because the speed may have changed.
  3. A GPS reading arrives. Compare it with the prediction: the difference is the surprise.
  4. Work out the gain: the share of the surprise to believe. It is large when the prediction is shaky and the sensor is good, and small the other way round.
  5. Update: shift the estimate by gain × surprise, and become more sure.
  6. Repeat every second. With no reading, only predict, and watch the uncertainty grow.

What just happened

Animation
How much to trust each source
Make trouble
Second
–
Gain: share of the surprise believed
–
Uncertainty in position, ± metres
–
Estimated speed / true speed, m/s
–
Typical error of the raw GPS
–
Typical error of the filter, on the seconds with a reading
–

Try this. Press One second a few times and read the calculation: predict, compare, weigh, update. Notice the gain: it starts near 1, when the filter knows nothing, and settles to a steady value. Press Run and compare the two error readouts. Then press Lose the Signal: the estimate coasts on at the last known speed and the band widens. What happens to the gain on the first reading after the signal returns? Press One Wild Reading and see how far the estimate is pulled. Now raise the GPS error slider to 12 and start over: the filter leans on its prediction. Set the second slider to its maximum: the filter believes the drone may change speed wildly, and follows every reading.

The model

The hidden state is position and speed, \(\mathbf x_t=(p_t,v_t)\). It moves by simple physics plus a random disturbance, and the sensor reports the position plus noise:

$$\mathbf x_t=F\,\mathbf x_{t-1}+\mathbf w_t,\quad \mathbf w_t\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,Q),\qquad y_t=H\,\mathbf x_t+e_t,\quad e_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R),$$$$F=\begin{pmatrix}1&\Delta t\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

This has the same shape as a hidden Markov model: a hidden state that evolves, and observations that depend on it. The difference is that the state is continuous and everything is Gaussian. Because Gaussians stay Gaussian under these operations, the belief is fully described by a mean \(\hat{\mathbf x}\) and a covariance \(P\).

Predict

$$\hat{\mathbf x}^-_t=F\,\hat{\mathbf x}_{t-1},\qquad P^-_t=F\,P_{t-1}F^{\top}+Q .$$

The estimate moves forward by one step of physics. The uncertainty grows: \(Q\) is how much the world may have changed that we could not foresee.

Update

The reading \(y_t\) differs from what was predicted by the innovation, or surprise, \(y_t-H\hat{\mathbf x}^-_t\). The Kalman gain decides how much of it to believe:

$$K_t=P^-_tH^{\top}\big(HP^-_tH^{\top}+R\big)^{-1},\qquad \hat{\mathbf x}_t=\hat{\mathbf x}^-_t+K_t\,\big(y_t-H\hat{\mathbf x}^-_t\big),\qquad P_t=(I-K_tH)\,P^-_t .$$

For the position alone the gain is a single number,

$$K=\frac{\sigma^2_{\text{prediction}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{prediction}}+\sigma^2_{\text{sensor}}},$$

the share of the total uncertainty that belongs to the prediction. If the prediction is poor, \(K\) is near 1 and the estimate jumps to the reading. If the sensor is poor, \(K\) is near 0 and the reading is nearly ignored. The top-right picture shows the same thing as curves: multiplying the prediction bell by the reading bell gives a narrower bell between them, nearer to the narrower of the two. This is Bayes' rule with a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood (Kalman, 1960).

How it learns the speed without measuring it

The GPS reports position only. Yet \(P\) records that errors in position and in speed go together: if the drone is further along than predicted, it was probably flying faster than estimated. The gain has a second component that corrects the speed in proportion to the position surprise. After a few seconds the filter knows the speed quite well.

When the signal drops

With no reading there is nothing to update, so only the predict step runs. The estimate coasts in a straight line and \(P\) grows every second, which the widening band shows. When readings return, the prediction is very uncertain, so the gain is high and the estimate snaps back.

The two settings are beliefs, not facts

\(R\) and \(Q\) say how much the filter trusts the sensor and the physics. Set \(R\) too low and it chases every jitter. Set \(Q\) too low and it is over-confident in its straight line and lags behind real turns. A single wild reading pulls the estimate by \(K\) times the error, because a Gaussian model has no notion of an outlier: practical systems reject readings whose surprise is implausibly large.

Beyond straight lines

When the physics or the sensor is not linear, the extended and unscented Kalman filters apply the same two steps to a local approximation. When the belief is not bell-shaped at all, particle filters carry a cloud of samples in place of a mean and covariance.

What this page runs

An 80-second flight with a speed that wanders slowly. The GPS error slider sets both the real noise in the readings and the filter's \(R\). The second slider sets the filter's \(Q\) only. The two "typical error" readouts are root-mean-square distances from the true position, over the seconds on which a reading arrived.

Check yourself

After the signal has been lost for 12 seconds, the first reading that arrives moves the estimate almost all the way to the reading. Ten seconds later, a reading that is just as far from the estimate moves it only a little. The sensor has not changed. What has?

The filter’s confidence in its own prediction. During the outage only the predict step ran, and every second added uncertainty, so by the time the signal returned the prediction was far less trustworthy than the sensor. The gain is the prediction’s share of the total uncertainty, so it was close to 1 and the reading was believed almost entirely. Each reading after that shrank the uncertainty again, the gain fell back to its steady value, and a surprise of the same size was mostly attributed to sensor noise.

entries.title: Recommender systems: fill in the ratings nobody gave
entries.html:
Recommender Systems: Fill in the Ratings Nobody Gave

Ten people have rated some of ten films, each from 1 to 5. Most of the table is empty, because nobody has seen everything. A recommender has to guess the empty cells: would Ben like a film he has never seen? The idea that won a famous million-dollar prize is to describe every person and every film by a few hidden numbers, such as “how much action” and “how much romance”, learned only from the ratings that exist. Add your own ratings in the bottom row and get recommendations.

You ask a well-read friend for a book. She does not look up statistics. She has a rough picture of your taste, "likes slow novels, dislikes violence", and a rough picture of each book along the same lines, and she looks for a match. Nobody ever filled in a questionnaire to produce those pictures. She formed them from the handful of books she knows you loved or hated. Matrix factorisation gives a computer the same two sets of pictures, as short lists of numbers, and learns both at once from the ratings alone.

How it works, step by step

  1. Give every person and every film K hidden numbers, small and random at first. Set a few real ratings aside to test on later.
  2. Predict a rating: the overall average, plus how generous this person is, plus how well liked this film is, plus the match between the person’s numbers and the film’s.
  3. Take one real rating. Compare it with the prediction: the difference is the error.
  4. Nudge the person’s numbers toward the film’s, and the film’s toward the person’s, in proportion to the error. Shrink everything slightly so that nothing grows without need.
  5. Do this for every real rating: one pass. Repeat passes until the error on the hidden ratings stops falling.
  6. Fill every empty cell with its prediction, and recommend each person their highest unseen films.

What just happened

Animation

The model
The data

Passes so far
–
Error on the ratings it trains on
–
Error on the hidden ratings
–
Error of always guessing the film’s average
–
Real ratings: used for training / hidden for testing
–
Numbers the model learns
–

Try this. Press Run and watch the faint numbers settle. In the top-right map, the films separate into groups without anyone telling the model their genres. Which films are close together? Which people sit near which films? Now rate four or five films in the bottom row, giving the action films 5 and the romances 1, or the other way round, and press Run again. Where do you land on the map, and what does it recommend? Then set K to 4 and λ to 0 and start over. Watch the two error curves: the error on the training ratings falls almost to zero. Does the error on the hidden ratings follow it down? With a table this small the answer varies from table to table, so press New Ratings Table a few times before you decide which settings are best.

The table and the model

Let \(r_{ui}\) be the rating person \(u\) gave film \(i\), known only for some pairs. Each person gets a vector \(\mathbf p_u\in\mathbb R^K\) and each film a vector \(\mathbf q_i\in\mathbb R^K\). The predicted rating is

$$\hat r_{ui}=\mu+b_u+b_i+\mathbf p_u^{\top}\mathbf q_i .$$

\(\mu\) is the average of all ratings, \(b_u\) says whether this person rates high or low in general, \(b_i\) whether the film is generally liked, and the dot product is large when the person's tastes and the film's qualities point the same way. Stacking the vectors gives two thin matrices whose product approximates the whole table, which is where the name comes from.

What is minimised

Only the known ratings enter the loss, with a penalty that keeps the numbers small:

$$\min_{b,\mathbf p,\mathbf q}\ \sum_{(u,i)\ \text{known}}\big(r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui}\big)^2+\lambda\big(\lVert\mathbf p_u\rVert^2+\lVert\mathbf q_i\rVert^2+b_u^2+b_i^2\big).$$

The empty cells are not treated as zeros. They are simply left out, and that is what distinguishes this from ordinary matrix decompositions such as PCA.

One update

Stochastic gradient descent visits the known ratings one at a time. With error \(e_{ui}=r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui}\) and step size \(\eta\),

$$\mathbf p_u\leftarrow\mathbf p_u+\eta\,(e_{ui}\,\mathbf q_i-\lambda\,\mathbf p_u),\qquad \mathbf q_i\leftarrow\mathbf q_i+\eta\,(e_{ui}\,\mathbf p_u-\lambda\,\mathbf q_i),$$

and similarly for the two biases. If the person liked the film more than predicted, their vector moves toward the film's and the film's toward theirs, so the next prediction is higher. This is the approach Simon Funk published during the Netflix Prize, later refined by Koren, Bell and Volinsky (2009).

Why it can guess a cell it has never seen

Ana and Ben have both rated several films, and where they overlap they agree. Their vectors therefore end up close together. Ana has also rated a film that Ben has not. The film's vector was shaped by Ana's rating, and since Ben's vector resembles Ana's, the dot product gives Ben a similar prediction. Information flows from person to person through the films they share, and from film to film through the people who rated both. This is called collaborative filtering: nothing about the content of the films is used.

Choosing K and λ

More hidden numbers can describe taste more finely, and can also memorise the training ratings, noise included. The honest test is the error on ratings the model never saw. With a table this small, a large \(K\) with no shrinkage drives the training error toward zero while the hidden-rating error stays far above it: the model has memorised its training ratings, which is overfitting, exactly as in the Foundations module. \(\lambda\) pulls the vectors toward zero and guards against it. In repeated tests on this page a larger \(\lambda\) gave the lower hidden-rating error more often than not, and with only about twenty hidden ratings any single table can go either way.

What it cannot do

A new person or a new film with no ratings has no vector worth the name: the cold start problem. Real systems fall back on content, such as genre or description, or on popularity, until ratings arrive. Most real feedback is also not a rating at all but a click, a purchase or a watch, where "no data" may mean "did not like" or "never saw". And a recommender that only reinforces what people already chose narrows what they see.

What this page runs

Ten people, ten invented films of three kinds, and a table with roughly 75% of the ratings present, generated from hidden tastes plus noise. About one rating in four is set aside for testing. Training runs for at least 80 passes and stops when the error on those has not improved for 40 passes, or after 400. Your own ratings are visited four times in every pass, so that a handful of them is enough to place you on the map. The error shown is the root-mean-square difference in rating points.

Check yourself

A new film is added to the table with no ratings at all. What rating does the model predict for it, for every person, and why is that the best it can do?

It predicts each person’s usual level: the overall average plus that person’s own bias. The film’s bias and its hidden numbers have never been updated, because updates happen only when a rating for that film is visited, and with shrinkage they stay at or near zero. Nothing in the ratings table says anything about this film, so nothing better is available from ratings alone. To do better the system needs information from outside the table, such as the film’s genre, cast or description.

entries.title: Time series: forecast tomorrow from the shape of yesterday
entries.html:
Time Series: Forecast Tomorrow from the Shape of Yesterday

An ice-cream shop has eight years of monthly sales. Sales climb a little every year and swing up every summer. Next month’s stock has to be ordered now. Forecasting from a series like this differs from everything else in this course in one way: the order of the data is the information. Four forecasters, from the laziest possible to a proper statistical model, are tested the only honest way, by walking through history and predicting each month before it is revealed.

A sailor forecasts the tide without any physics. Today's tide will be much like the one twelve and a half hours ago, a little like yesterday's at the same hour, and shaped by where we are in the month. A good forecast leans on the regular patterns in the past: the slow drift, the repeating cycle, and the fact that things do not usually jump. What is left over after those is noise, and no method can forecast noise. The skill is in telling which is which.

How it works, step by step

  1. Hide everything after the first stretch of history.
  2. Each forecaster predicts the next value, using only what has been revealed.
  3. Reveal the true value. Record how far off each forecast was.
  4. Let each forecaster learn from the new value, then move one step forward.
  5. Repeat to the end of the data. The forecaster with the smallest average miss has earned the most trust.
  6. Now forecast the real future, as far ahead as needed. The further ahead, the wider the range of what could happen.

What just happened

Animation
The forecasters
The data

Points revealed
–
Forecast for the next point
–
Average miss: Last Value
–
Average miss: Same Season Last Cycle
–
Average miss: Holt-Winters
–
Average miss: Autoregression
–

Try this. Press Run on the ice-cream data and watch the four error lines. Which forecaster is worst, and why is Last Value so bad on data with seasons? Look at the top-right bars: at which gap do values most resemble each other? Switch the watched forecaster between the four during the walk. Now choose the share price and run again. Which forecaster wins? What does that tell you about predicting share prices from their own past? Choose the website visits and set the cycle length to 12, the wrong value: see what the seasonal methods do. Set it to 7. Finally type a number of steps ahead in the box and read the forecast and its range.

What a series is made of

A useful way to think of a series \(y_t\) is as a sum of three parts:

$$y_t=\underbrace{T_t}_{\text{trend}}+\underbrace{S_t}_{\text{season}}+\underbrace{\varepsilon_t}_{\text{noise}},$$

where the season repeats with period \(m\): \(S_t=S_{t-m}\). The autocorrelation at lag \(k\) measures how alike \(y_t\) and \(y_{t-k}\) are, on a scale from \(-1\) to \(1\). The bars at the top right show it for every lag. A peak at lag 12 says the series repeats every 12 steps. Bars that fade slowly from lag 1 say the series drifts.

Two benchmarks

Last value: \(\hat y_{t+1}=y_t\). Seasonal naive: \(\hat y_{t+1}=y_{t+1-m}\), the value one cycle ago. Neither has anything to learn. Any serious method must beat both, and surprisingly often it does not. For a random walk, where each value is the last one plus pure noise, the last value is the best possible forecast.

Holt-Winters exponential smoothing

Keep three running estimates: a level \(\ell\), a slope \(b\) and one seasonal offset \(s\) for each position in the cycle. Each new value updates them by a weighted average of "what the new value says" and "what I thought before":

$$\ell_t=\alpha\,(y_t-s_{t-m})+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}),\quad b_t=\beta\,(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta)\,b_{t-1},\quad s_t=\gamma\,(y_t-\ell_t)+(1-\gamma)\,s_{t-m},$$$$\hat y_{t+h}=\ell_t+h\,b_t+s_{t+h-m}.$$

With \(\alpha\) near 1 the level chases every wobble. Near 0 it barely moves. Old data is never thrown away, only given exponentially less weight, which is where the name comes from (Holt, 1957; Winters, 1960).

Autoregression

An AR(\(p\)) model predicts the next value as a weighted sum of the last \(p\):

$$\hat y_{t+1}=c+\phi_1y_t+\phi_2y_{t-1}+\dots+\phi_py_{t-p+1}.$$

The weights are found by least squares, exactly as in the Regression module, with the past values as the features. If \(p\) reaches back a whole cycle, the model can learn the seasonal pattern by itself, as a large weight near lag \(m\). ARIMA models extend this by first differencing the series to remove trend and by adding terms for past forecast errors.

Testing honestly: walking forward

Shuffling the data into random training and test sets, as elsewhere in this course, would let the model see the future. The honest test respects time: at each step fit on the past only, forecast one step, then reveal it. The average absolute miss over the walk,

$$\mathrm{MAE}=\frac1n\sum_t\big|y_t-\hat y_t\big|,$$

is what the bottom chart tracks.

Forecasting further ahead

For \(h\) steps ahead, Holt-Winters extends its line and repeats its seasonal offsets, and the autoregression feeds its own forecasts back in as if they were data. Errors accumulate, so the range of plausible outcomes widens with \(h\). The range drawn on this page is a rough one: plus or minus twice the method's typical one-step miss, multiplied by \(\sqrt h\). It is right for a random walk and a cautious overestimate for strongly seasonal data.

What this page runs

The walk starts after the first 40% of the series, or after three full cycles if that is longer. Holt-Winters uses your \(\alpha\) with \(\beta=0.05\) and \(\gamma=0.25\). The autoregression is refitted at every step on everything revealed so far. An uploaded file should have one number per line, or its first numeric column is used.

Check yourself

On the share-price series, the sophisticated autoregression does no better than simply repeating the last value. Does that mean the autoregression is badly built?

No. It means there is nothing in the past of that series for any method to exploit. In a random walk each change is independent of everything before it, so the best forecast of the next value is the current one, and every extra weight the autoregression estimates is fitting noise. It ends up with a weight close to 1 on the last value and weights near 0 on the rest, which is the Last Value forecaster with some added jitter. A benchmark that cannot be beaten is informative: it tells you the series has no usable memory beyond its last value.

entries.title: Explainability: ask a model why
entries.html:
Explainability: Ask a Model Why

A neural network has learned to estimate house prices from five facts about a house. It prices one particular house at well over 400 thousand. Why? “Because of 600 weights” is true and useless. A useful answer splits the estimate into parts: so much because it is large, so much off because it is old, so much because it is close to the centre. Shapley values are the one fair way to make that split. Describe a house with the sliders and watch its price being explained.

Four friends share a taxi home, each living further along the same road, and the fare comes to 40. How should they split it? Charging each the fare to their own door adds up to far more than 40. Splitting evenly is unfair to the one who gets out first. One fair scheme imagines the friends joining the ride one at a time in some order, charges each the extra cost they add, and then averages over every possible order of joining. A model's estimate is the fare, the features are the passengers, and the Shapley value is each feature's fair share.

How it works, step by step

  1. Start from the model’s estimate for an average house: nothing about this house is known yet.
  2. Pick a random order for the five features. Reveal the first one: replace the average house’s value with this house’s, and see how the estimate moves.
  3. Reveal the next feature, and the next, noting each move. After the fifth, the estimate is the one for this house.
  4. That was one order. A feature’s effect depends on which others were already revealed, so try another order.
  5. Average each feature’s moves over all the orders tried. That average is its Shapley value.
  6. Stop when the averages have settled. They add up exactly to the difference between this house and the average house.

What just happened

Animation

Describe the house
The curve at the bottom right
The model’s estimate for this house
–
Its estimate for the average house
–
Orders tried
–
Feature that adds the most
–
Feature that takes away the most
–
Largest gap between the running averages and the exact values
–

Try this. Press One order several times. Floor area appears in a different position each time: is its contribution the same every time? That variation is why one order is not an explanation. Press Run and watch the bars settle onto the dark ticks. Check the arithmetic: the average house’s estimate plus the five bars equals this house’s estimate. Now move the garden slider to 0 and back. Then set the distance to 25 km and compare the garden’s share with before. In this model a garden is worth more close to the centre. Can a single “importance of the garden” number be right for every house? Look at the top-right chart for the answer the model gives on average.

What is being explained

Take a trained model \(f\) and one input \(\mathbf x\), here a house with five features. The base value is the average prediction over typical houses, \(\phi_0=\mathbb E[f(\mathbf X)]\). An explanation is a set of numbers \(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_d\), one per feature, that account for the difference:

$$f(\mathbf x)=\phi_0+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\phi_j .$$

The value of knowing some features

For a subset \(S\) of features, let \(v(S)\) be the model's average prediction when the features in \(S\) are fixed to this house's values and the others are drawn from typical houses:

$$v(S)=\mathbb E\big[f(\mathbf x_S,\mathbf X_{\bar S})\big].$$

So \(v(\varnothing)=\phi_0\) and \(v(\text{all})=f(\mathbf x)\). Revealing feature \(j\) after the set \(S\) changes the prediction by \(v(S\cup\{j\})-v(S)\).

The Shapley value

That change depends on \(S\). The Shapley value (Shapley, 1953) averages it over every order in which the features could be revealed:

$$\phi_j=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1..d\}\setminus\{j\}}\frac{|S|!\,(d-|S|-1)!}{d!}\,\big[v(S\cup\{j\})-v(S)\big].$$

The weight is the share of orderings in which exactly the features in \(S\) come before \(j\). With 5 features there are 32 subsets and the sum can be computed exactly, which gives the dark ticks. With hundreds of features it cannot, and the practical method is the one animated here: sample random orders and average. Lundberg and Lee (2017) made this the basis of the SHAP library.

Why this split and no other

It is the only attribution that satisfies four reasonable demands at once. Efficiency: the shares add up to the difference from the base value. Symmetry: two features that always contribute equally get equal shares. Dummy: a feature that never changes the prediction gets zero. Additivity: the explanation of a sum of models is the sum of their explanations.

Interactions

If the model were a plain weighted sum of the features, every order would give the same moves, and one order would be enough. The moves differ between orders because features interact: in this model a garden adds more to a large house near the centre than to a small one far out. The Shapley value shares each interaction equally among the features involved. That is fair, and it also means the garden's number is specific to this house.

Local and global

A Shapley explanation is local: it is about one house. Averaging the sizes \(|\phi_j|\) over many houses gives a global ranking of features, the top-right chart. The curve at the bottom right is a different tool. The line for "this house" changes one feature and holds the others at this house's values. The line for "on average" does the same for many houses and averages, which is called a partial dependence plot.

What an explanation is not

These numbers explain the model, not the world. If the model has learned that houses with gardens cost more, the garden gets a positive share, whether or not building a garden would raise a price. They are not causes. When features are strongly related, such as floor area and bedrooms, replacing one while keeping the other creates houses that do not exist, and the credit between the two is divided somewhat arbitrarily. And a faithful explanation of a wrong model is still an explanation of something wrong.

What this page runs

A network with two hidden layers of 24 neurons, trained when the page opens on 700 invented houses whose prices follow a formula with interactions and some noise. "Typical houses" are a fixed sample of 60 of them. The run stops when no running average has moved by more than 0.3 thousand over 60 orders, or after 1,500 orders.

Check yourself

In one order, floor area is revealed first and moves the estimate by +70. In another it is revealed last and moves it by +95. Which number is the true effect of floor area for this house?

Neither, and both. Each is the correct answer to a slightly different question: “how much does knowing the area change the estimate when nothing else is known?” and “how much does it change when everything else is already known?”. They differ because area interacts with the other features. A large house close to the centre gains more from its size than a house whose location is still treated as average. There is no single order that is the right one, which is why the Shapley value averages over all of them. The average is a fair summary, and the spread between orders is itself a sign of how strongly the feature interacts.

entries.title: Acknowledgements
entries.html:
About Manifold

Acknowledgements

Manifold did not come out of nowhere.

The idea for this site came to me while discussing teaching strategies in machine learning with Professor Ethan Prihar at Worcester Polytechnic Institute. We kept returning to the same observation: students follow a derivation on the board, and still cannot say what the algorithm will do when the data change. What they need is a way to take hold of a method, change one thing and watch what happens. That conversation is where the whole project started, and I am grateful to him for it and for his thinking about how people actually learn.

I thank Professor Raha Moraffah, also at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, for many discussions and for her feedback, which shaped both what is covered here and how it is explained.

I thank Professor Dachun Sun, also at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, for constant discussion. Many of the choices here, from which methods to include to how to show them, were settled in those conversations.

I also thank my students. Their questions decided which sliders exist, which examples were kept, and which explanations were rewritten until they were clear.

The mathematics is typeset with MathJax, and the text is set in freely licensed typefaces served by Google Fonts. Everything else runs in your browser, with nothing sent anywhere.

Bahman Moraffah2026
